Autonomous weapons, the Geneva week: states decide whether machines that choose whom to strike will have rules

From 16 to 20 November the Review Conference of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons decides whether to open negotiations on a treaty for autonomous weapons. What is on the table, who is pushing, who is holding back, and what happens if consensus does not come.

In brief From 16 to 20 November the 128 states of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) meet in Geneva for the Review Conference, held every five years. The most awaited question: whether or not to open negotiations on a treaty for autonomous weapons. In September government experts adopted by consensus a list of "elements" for a future instrument, without deciding whether it will be binding. According to the Washington Post, in the final hours the United States and Russia had the requirement of human verification before an attack removed from the text. 76 states, the UN Secretary-General and the International Committee of the Red Cross are calling for negotiations on a binding treaty. The European Union is asking for an "ambitious negotiating mandate". The United States and Russia argue that existing law is enough. The Conference decides by consensus. If consensus is lacking, the Convention provides another route: if at least 65 states request it, a negotiating conference open to all is convened. An autonomous weapon is a system that, once activated, selects and strikes a target without a person approving that individual attack. This is not science fiction: systems with autonomous functions are already in use in Ukraine ( Stop Killer Robots, August 2026 ), and artificial intelligence systems suggest targets to armies, as we reconstructed in the case of the Minab school . The question states are asking in Geneva is simple to state and hard to solve: how much of the decision to kill can be left to a machine, and who answers for it when it gets it wrong. The facts The Conference. The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons is the UN treaty that bans or restricts weapons considered too cruel or indiscriminate: fragments undetectable by X-rays, incendiary weapons, blinding lasers. It does so through additional protocols, one for each type of weapon. From 16 to 20 November the states parties meet in Geneva for the seventh Review Conference ( Italian mission to the Conference on Disarmament ). There they can decide to negotiate a new protocol on autonomous weapons. The September text. Since 2023 a group of governmental experts had a precise task: to draft, by consensus, the "elements of an instrument, without prejudging its nature". In other words, what a future rule should contain, without saying whether it will be a binding treaty or a set of recommendations. On 4 September the group adopted its final report ( UNODA, CCW/GGE.1/2026/3 ). The text reaffirms that international humanitarian law applies to these weapons, and asks states to review the legality of every new system before adopting it and to assess its risks. On responsibility it is weaker than earlier drafts: where there was talk of obligations, states now "should promote" human responsibility and "are encouraged" to investigate incidents ( Opinio Juris ). What was removed. According to the Washington Post, in roughly fifteen hours on the last day American and Russian diplomats had three things removed: the requirement that a person verify the target indicated by a system before the attack, the requirement that systems function predictably and reliably, and the reference to ethical considerations. The newspaper cites three people present at the negotiations, who asked for anonymity, and says it saw the documents ( Washington Post, reported by IBTimes ). The two governments have not commented publicly. Who is asking for the treaty. On 25 August the UN Secretary-General and the President of the International Committee of the Red Cross pointed to the November Conference as the clearest path to decide on negotiations for a binding instrument ( UN Geneva ). At the end of the September session 76 states had said they were ready to negotiate (Washington Post, same source). On 12 October the Council of the European Union asked the Conference for an "ambitious negotiating mandate" and reaffirmed the two-tier approach: ban autonomous weapons that cannot be used in compliance with humanitarian law, regulate the others ( EU Council, paragraphs 11 and 13 ). The EU conclusions, however, do not say the instrument must be binding. Civil society. The main voice calling for a treaty is the international campaign Stop Killer Robots, which brings together 270 organisations in more than 70 countries. In Italy it includes the Istituto di ricerche internazionali Archivio Disarmo, which together with the Rete Italiana Pace e Disarmo brought the issue to the Senate in January ( Archivio Disarmo, press release of 15/1/2026 ). Its president, the sociologist Fabrizio Battistelli, explained in July the question the campaign considers decisive: an algorithm completes the task it has been given even where a human being would stop, and with artificial intelligence responsibility slides from the operators to the system. That is why, Battistelli argues, taking up the position of the International Committee of the Red Cross, "meaningful human control" is indispensable over every use of force assisted by artificial intelligence ( interview with Il Sole 24 Ore, 12/7/2026, published by Archivio Disarmo ). Archivio Disarmo is part of the campaign: it is a committed voice, and we cite it as such. Who is holding back. According to Amnesty International, the United States, Russia, China and India prefer national guidelines or existing international law to a new treaty ( Reuters, via Dawn, 2025 ). Washington has also repeatedly pointed to the possible advantages of these systems, starting with precision ( Reuters, 2021 ). Beijing says it supports a treaty only "when conditions are ripe", and a ban only for the most extreme systems ( Lieber Institute ). Meanwhile the Pentagon is rewriting its own directive on autonomous weapons, as required by a presidential memorandum in June; at the end of September the new text was not public (IBTimes, same source). Italy. In 2025 the Italian mission in Geneva described the core of Italy's position as full respect for humanitarian law and the development of norms "towards an additional protocol" ( Italian mission ). On 7 September, in the preparatory committee, it welcomed the September text and said it wanted to agree on "further steps" at the Conference, without saying which ( Italian statement ). What Archivio Disarmo asks of Italy. Asked by us, Battistelli sets out three conditions for Italy to carry more weight in regulating military artificial intelligence (note sent to iwillnotlookaway.org on 11/11/2026). The first is a more explicit mandate from Parliament, through bills, questions and motions, backed by the moral pressure of institutions such as the Presidency of the Republic and the Church. The second is government initiatives, including at European level, on the model of those taken by other countries: the REAIM summit on the responsible use of artificial intelligence in the military domain, launched on the proposal of the Netherlands and South Korea, and NURIST, a platform that simulates how new technologies can distort information flows and compress the time available for nuclear decisions, developed by the European Leadership Network with the support of the German Foreign Ministry ( ELN ). National initiatives, Battistelli observes, that could involve the whole Union, "the only political entity that to date has carried out a regulation of AI" with the AI Act ( EU Regulation 2024/1689 ), while recalling that it excludes military applications from its scope (Article 2, paragraph 3). The third is for civil society and public opinion to speak up. How we got here The states of the Convention have been discussing autonomous weapons since 2014. In 2019 they adopted by consensus eleven guiding principles, including one that matters more than the others: human responsibility for decisions on the use of weapons cannot be transferred to machines. They were non-binding principles. We wrote about them, together with the other instruments under discussion for artificial intelligence, in "How to govern a machine" . Since 2023 the UN General Assembly has voted every year on a resolution calling for the problem to be addressed urgently ( Stop Killer Robots ). In the meantime the weapons have arrived before the rules. The other route. The Convention decides by consensus: one country is enough to block. But its Article 8 also allows a group of states to propose a new protocol in writing. The UN Secretary-General, depositary of the treaty, then consults everyone: if the majority, that is at least 65 states, agrees, he convenes a negotiating conference, open also to those who are not party to the Convention ( Stop Killer Robots, August 2026 ). It would not be the first time states chose to get around a deadlock. In 1996 the Convention failed to ban anti-personnel mines; the following year a group of countries negotiated the Ottawa Treaty outside it. The same happened in 2008 with cluster munitions. Legal commentary The rules that already apply. No one argues that autonomous weapons are outside the law. International humanitarian law, starting with the Geneva Conventions and their protocols, requires those who attack to distinguish between combatants and civilians, not to cause civilians harm that is disproportionate to the military advantage, and to take every feasible precaution. Article 36 of the first Additional Protocol obliges the states that have joined it to verify, before adopting a new weapon, that its use is lawful. These rules apply to an autonomous drone as much as to a rifle. Where the law is not enough. The problem is who applies these rules. Distinguishing, assessing proportionality, calling off an attack when the situation changes are judgements. The law asks people to make them, and punishes people when they violate them. If a machine chooses the target, the possible responsibilities are split between the commander who activated it, those who programmed it, and those who supplied the data. When each of them can say the choice was not theirs, no one answers. That is why the 2019 principle says responsibility is not transferred to the machine, and why the human verification removed from the September text was not a detail. What a treaty would change. A binding protocol would turn what is now interpretation into precise obligations: which systems are banned, what human control is required, how incidents are investigated. It would, however, bind only those who ratify it. The Ottawa Treaty has never been signed by the United States, Russia and China, yet for almost thirty years it made anti-personnel mines a weapon that almost nobody admitted to using. It also shows the limit: since 2025 several countries bordering Russia have announced that they will withdraw from it. Symmetry test Who is holding back. Many are developing autonomous weapons. Besides the United States and Russia, Human Rights Watch names China, India, Iran, Israel and Turkey among those investing the most ( HRW ). The front holding back the treaty does not coincide with a political bloc: it unites Washington and Moscow, which are adversaries on almost everything else. The same yardstick must be applied to all: whoever produces these weapons has an interest in not tying their own hands, whoever they are. Who is pushing. The European Union is asking for an ambitious mandate, but does not write that the instrument must be binding. Italy, which Archivio Disarmo would like to see among the promoters, did not say publicly in September which mandate it will support. Supporting rules costs little when you do not say which ones. The opposing argument. Those who oppose a treaty do not argue that killing without rules is lawful. They argue that current law is enough and that a well-designed machine can make fewer mistakes than a tired or frightened soldier. It is a serious argument, but it assumes what has to be proven: that the system is predictable and that someone can control it. Those are exactly the two requirements removed from the text. Our judgment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. The September text is the most that ten years of consensus have produced, and to get there, according to the Washington Post, the most important sentence was removed: that before striking someone, a human being should look. If in Geneva the consensus rule also blocks the negotiation, the states calling for a treaty have a tool provided by the Convention itself to move forward. Using it would not be forcing the issue: faced with similar deadlocks, for mines and for cluster munitions, states have already found other routes. Waiting for everyone to agree, while these weapons are already on the battlefield, means letting the facts write the rules. What to watch The final document of the Conference, on 20 November: whether it contains a negotiating mandate and whether the word "binding" is there. What Italy declares and how it moves in the debate. Whether, in the absence of consensus, a group of states submits a written proposal under Article 8. The Pentagon's new directive on autonomous weapons, expected since September. We will update this piece with the outcome of the Conference. Cuba in the dark: the embargo, the oil cut-off and the vote the UN has repeated for thirty years

Since 1962 the United States has not traded with Cuba. The reasons have changed three times; the embargo has not. In 2026 it also became an oil blockade, and the island lives with a few hours of electricity a day. What international law says, and what Washington and Havana are each responsible for.

In brief The US embargo on Cuba was born in 1960-1962, after the revolution's nationalisations and Havana's alliance with the USSR. After the Cold War it stayed, with other reasons: first democracy, today, openly, changing the government. In 2026 Washington added an oil blockade. After Maduro's capture, Venezuelan supplies stopped, and those who sold oil to the island were threatened with tariffs. Since January a single tanker, a Russian one, has arrived. In Cuba the power comes on for a few hours a day. Washington says food and medicine are exempt and that the crisis is the Cuban government's fault. The Cuban government holds more than 1,200 political prisoners, according to an NGO, and food production had already collapsed before the blockade. Tested against international law, the three stated reasons do not hold up equally: human rights are not defended by hitting a whole population, alliances are every state's free choice, and coercion to change a government is prohibited. Since 1992 the General Assembly has called every year for an end to the embargo: in 2025, 165 voted in favour and 7 against. The vote is not binding, and no judge can compel Washington. On 28 October 2026 the resolution passed again, but by the narrowest margin in its history: 130 in favour, 17 against, 25 abstentions. The background Why there is an embargo. The reasons have changed three times. The first is the revolution. Fidel Castro took power in 1959. In the summer of 1960 Cuba seized the American refineries, which had refused to process Soviet oil; Washington cut its purchases of Cuban sugar, and Havana responded by nationalising all American property on the island, without compensation. In October 1960 the United States banned exports to Cuba, except food and medicine. In January 1961 it broke off diplomatic relations, in April it backed the failed landing of exiles at the Bay of Pigs, and on 7 February 1962 Kennedy imposed a near-total embargo. In October, with Soviet missiles on the island, Cuba became the most dangerous front of the Cold War. There were two reasons: the confiscated property, for which the US government has certified more than 5,900 compensation claims, and the alliance with Moscow ( Congressional Research Service ). The second is democracy. With the Soviet Union gone, the military threat disappeared, but the embargo was not lifted: it became law and grew harsher. A 1992 law extended it to the foreign subsidiaries of American companies. In February 1996 Cuban fighter jets shot down two small planes belonging to an exile group, killing four people; less than three weeks later Clinton signed the Helms-Burton Act. The law states that the embargo can end only when Cuba has a democratically elected government, and since then no president can lift it alone: Congress is needed. A 2000 law allows food and medicine to be sold to Cuba, but only for cash in advance and without credit ( Congressional Research Service ). In 2014-2016 Obama reopened the embassies, but the embargo stayed. The third is changing the government. Today Washington speaks of repression, of political prisoners, of Havana's ties with Russia, China and Iran, and keeps it on the list of state sponsors of terrorism. But in 2026 President Trump said openly that the goal is to bring down the government. The UN vote. Every year since 1992 the General Assembly has voted on a resolution calling for an end to the embargo. Its resolutions are not binding. In 2025 only the United States, Israel, Argentina, Paraguay, Hungary, North Macedonia and Ukraine voted against ( PassBlue ). The facts From trade to oil. On 3 January 2026 the United States attacked Venezuela and captured President Nicolás Maduro ( we wrote about it here ). Venezuelan oil supplies to Cuba stopped, and Mexico suspended its own: together they covered about three quarters of the island's oil imports ( House of Commons Library ). On 29 January an executive order by Trump declared a national emergency over Cuba and provided for tariffs on countries selling it oil. On 20 February the Supreme Court ruled that the law used does not allow the president to impose tariffs, but the emergency remains in force and supplies have not resumed. According to legal scholars Michael Schmitt and Rob McLaughlin, Washington has seized tankers under its sanctions on Venezuela and Iran, and US patrols and drones watch the routes to the island ( Just Security ). Since January a single tanker, a Russian one, has reached Cuba. On 7 October US authorities seized 90 shipments of biodiesel bound for Cuban private businesses ( Al Jazeera ). Trump's words. On 5 March Trump said a change of government in Cuba is "just a question of time" ( Al Jazeera ). On 27 March, speaking about military successes in Venezuela and Iran, he added: "And Cuba is next, by the way. But pretend I didn't say that" ( Malay Mail ). Secretary of State Marco Rubio explained that the campaign is "engineered to make the government feel like there are no escape valves" ( CBS News ). What is happening on the island. The power grid, old and dependent on oil, is close to collapse: in most of the country, Havana included, electricity comes on for a few hours a day. At a children's hospital, doctors say they can no longer obtain life-saving drugs ( CBS News ). In May the UN humanitarian office and the World Health Organization counted more than 100,000 patients waiting for a postponed operation, including 11,000 children ( House of Commons Library ). Meanwhile the sanctions have widened: in July to energy companies, in August to mining and construction companies ( Al Jazeera ), in October to a state bank accused of ties to Iran ( CBS News ). Washington's version. US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz denies that the crisis is caused by the embargo or by an oil blockade, and blames it on the failure of the communist economy and on corruption. In June he announced 100 million dollars in aid to be distributed through the Catholic Church, and pointed out that fuel supplies to private businesses are allowed ( House of Commons Library ). The United States is also one of the island's food suppliers: in 2025 it sold Cuba nearly half a billion dollars of farm products, mostly chicken ( US Department of Agriculture ). According to Cuba's energy minister, however, private fuel covers less than 3% of the country's needs ( Al Jazeera ). Havana's responsibilities. According to the NGO Prisoners Defenders, in April there were 1,260 political prisoners in Cuba, including some minors arrested after the protests over the blackouts. That same month the government pardoned 2,010 inmates, but according to the NGO none of them was a political prisoner ( RTP ). Between 2021 and 2025, before the oil blockade, the island's food production had more than halved. In June parliament approved reforms opening the door to private banks and to businesses with more than a hundred employees, with no timetable for applying them. According to Human Rights Watch, the government uses the embargo as a pretext for repression ( House of Commons Library ). At the UN. On 6 August a group of independent UN experts called on the United States to revoke its measures, describing them as contrary to international law: "Food must never be used as an instrument of political pressure" ( DevelopmentAid ). In July, during a special debate in the General Assembly, the European Union acknowledged the embargo's humanitarian impact but said that the plight of Cubans is not due to the embargo alone, and criticised Havana's positions on the war in Ukraine ( UN ). On 19 October, ahead of the vote, Waltz organised a meeting with Cuban dissidents at UN headquarters and asked diplomats to vote against the resolution; the Cuban ambassador accused him of lying ( PassBlue ). Legal commentary Refusing to trade is not unlawful. International law does not oblige one state to trade with another: an embargo, in itself, is a political choice. But the three reasons used to justify it today need to be tested one by one. Human rights. Sanctioning those who violate human rights is permitted: freezing the assets of those responsible or banning them from travel is a widespread and accepted practice. The problem arises when a whole population is hit to punish its government. The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights wrote as much in 1997: those who impose sanctions must take account of their effect on the population. A state may respond to a wrongful act with countermeasures, but these may not affect fundamental human rights. Michael Schmitt, professor emeritus at the US Naval War College, and Rob McLaughlin, who teaches at Australia's military academy after twenty years in the navy, note that the US measures respond to no wrongful act committed by Cuba against the United States, and that the collapse of the power grid and of medical care falls squarely within that limit ( Just Security ). The exemption for food and medicine is not enough when there is no fuel for ambulances and no power for operating theatres. Alliances. Choosing one's allies is one of the decisions international law leaves to each state. The International Court of Justice said so in its 1986 Nicaragua judgment, against the United States itself: a state may not use coercion on matters that another state is entitled to decide freely, such as its political system and its foreign policy. A foreign military base near one's borders can be a legitimate security concern. But it is a reason to negotiate, not to coerce. Changing the government. This is the clearest reason, and the one the law most clearly forbids. The Helms-Burton Act ties the end of the embargo to a change of government, and Trump has said openly that this is the goal. For Schmitt and McLaughlin, cutting off a country's oil to force it to change its government violates the prohibition on intervening in another state's internal affairs. They also conclude that Trump's threats ("Cuba is next") may violate the prohibition on the threat of force in the UN Charter (art. 2, para. 4). For now, however, it is not a naval blockade in the legal sense, because there is no war between the two countries. Rules imposed on others. Part of the embargo hits third countries: the foreign subsidiaries of American companies, those who use confiscated property, and now those who sell oil to Cuba. The European Union considers these rules contrary to international law and since 1996 has had a regulation forbidding European companies to comply with them ( Regulation (EC) No 2271/96 ). The missing judge. Even when a rule is broken, no court can enforce it against Washington. In 1985, while it was losing the Nicaragua case itself, the Reagan administration withdrew its acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice ( Christian Science Monitor ). General Assembly resolutions are not binding, and in the Security Council the United States has a veto. That is why the vote has been repeated, unchanged, for thirty years without changing anything. Symmetry test Washington has not achieved the embargo's stated goal in 64 years. In 2026 it chose measures that hit the whole population, and its leaders say openly that the aim is to bring down the government. Havana represses dissent and holds more than a thousand political prisoners, and its economy was already in deep crisis before the oil blockade. Blaming everything on the embargo is an excuse, as Human Rights Watch and the European Union note. Bases near borders. If a Russian or Chinese military presence 150 kilometres from Florida is a legitimate concern for Washington, so is the presence of NATO troops in the Baltic states, along the Russian border, for Moscow. There is only one yardstick: Cuba has the right to choose its allies just as Estonia, Poland or Finland chose NATO, and in neither case does a neighbour's fear justify coercion or war. Understanding Moscow's reasons, as we wrote in our seven proposals for Europe , does not mean putting the aggressor against Ukraine and its victim on the same level. The 1962 precedent. The missile crisis did not end with a harsher embargo, but with a trade: the Soviet missiles left Cuba, the United States pledged not to invade the island and secretly withdrew its own missiles from Turkey ( National Security Archive ). Two powers acknowledged the same fear in each other. Europe votes against the embargo and forbids its companies to comply with it. Yet it applies sanctions of its own, against Russia, and since 2023 has also targeted companies from third countries, Chinese, Emirati and Uzbek, accused of helping Moscow get around them ( Euronews ). The stated difference is the purpose: stopping a war of aggression, not changing a government. But those who challenge American extraterritoriality must accept that the same yardstick applies to them. Russia and Venezuela supported Cuba when it suited them. Today Venezuela no longer sends oil, and a single tanker has arrived from Russia. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Taken one by one, the reasons for the embargo contradict each other. Cubans' human rights are defended by hitting all Cubans. Havana is punished for its alliances, which the law leaves to its free choice. And the last reason, the one stated openly, bringing down the government, is the most clearly prohibited. But a distinction must be made. A country has the right not to trade with a government it dislikes, and the trade embargo, however useless after 64 years, is a political choice. It does not have the right to leave a whole population in the dark to force it to change its government. That is the line the United States crossed in 2026. It is not only Cuba and the UN who say so: so do two legal scholars who teach law to the American and Australian military. When the Secretary of State explains that the aim is to leave no "escape valves", the target is no longer a government, but those who live under it. This does not absolve Havana. The Cuban government jails those who protest over the power cuts, has wrecked the economy partly on its own and uses the embargo to avoid answering for anything. But a government's faults do not transfer the punishment to those who suffer under it. It is the same rule we ask for in sanctions against Russia: hit those who decide, not the hospitals. In 1962 Washington and Moscow, on the brink of nuclear war, managed to acknowledge the same fears in each other and make a trade. Sixty years later, with an island without electricity, it seems harder. On 27 and 28 October the General Assembly will vote again, and the resolution will in all likelihood pass by a large majority. Nothing will change, as every year. What would matter more than the vote is for European governments, which have voted against the embargo for thirty years, to apply their own law, and for fuel to reach Cuban hospitals. Update, 28 October 2026. The resolution against the embargo passed for the thirty-fourth time, but with the lowest result in its history: 130 votes in favour, 17 against and 25 abstentions, compared with 165 in favour and 7 against in 2025. Germany and Italy abstained for the first time in many years ( Reuters ). Lithuania and Slovenia, which had always supported it, voted against. US ambassador Mike Waltz led a campaign to persuade governments to change their vote; Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez accused Washington of threatening tariffs, visa denials and aid cuts, without presenting evidence ( Responsible Statecraft ). The 1996 European regulation forbidding European companies to comply with the embargo remains in force. What to watch Whether the countries that changed their vote on 28 October, Germany and Italy among them, keep their new position. New sanctions or seizures of cargo bound for Cuba. The implementation of the economic reforms approved in June. Political prisoners and arrests after the protests over the blackouts. The warning from their own generals: settler violence threatens Israel's security
Over 550 former Israeli security officials warn Trump: settler impunity threatens Israel itself. The OCHA and Yesh Din data behind the alarm.

“The consequences could prove even more catastrophic than the October 7 Hamas atrocities.” — Commanders for Israel's Security, letter to Trump, July 27, 2026 The facts On July 27, 2026, on the eve of the meeting between Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu in Washington, more than 550 former senior Israeli security officials — retired IDF generals and colonels, together with former heads of Mossad, Shin Bet, the police, the National Security Council and the diplomatic corps — made public a letter addressed to the US president. The document, promoted by the group Commanders for Israel's Security and signed on the group's behalf by former deputy chief of staff Matan Vilnai, comes after a weekend of particularly violent clashes between settlers and Palestinians. The signatories ask Trump to deliver an explicit message to Netanyahu during the meeting, warning that the escalation, if not stopped, risks jeopardizing the US plan for Gaza and the expansion of the Abraham Accords, as well as Israel's own security. Yair Golan, a former deputy chief of staff and former leader of The Democrats party, added that the current government is creating a dangerous reality for soldiers, police officers and Israeli citizens. The picture the appeal describes The available data place the alarm within an already-measured trend, not an isolated episode. According to OCHA, since the start of 2026 about 850 Palestinians have been injured in attacks attributed to settlers — 55% of all Palestinians injured in the West Bank this year — with the rate rising from one injury every three days in 2020 to more than three a day in early 2026. In March alone, the ACLED series recorded at least eight Palestinians killed in incidents involving settlers, the highest monthly figure of the decade of data collection. Between January 2023 and July 2026, 122 Palestinian communities suffered total or partial displacement, 47 of them completely abandoned. On the economic side, the Association for Cooperation and Solidarity estimates more than 120,000 olive trees destroyed or damaged since October 7, 2023, nearly 92,000 in the last year alone. Legal reading Two distinct obligations are at stake, not one. The first: Article 43 of the Hague Regulations (1907), read together with Article 27 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, requires the occupying power to ensure public order and protect the occupied civilian population from any act of violence, regardless of who commits it. The second, distinct obligation: Articles 46 and 53 of the same Regulations protect private property in occupied territory, prohibiting its destruction except where rendered absolutely necessary by military operations — relevant to the systematic destruction of olive groves and water infrastructure. The International Court of Justice's advisory opinion of July 2024 further found the confiscation of land and the transfer of population in the West Bank to be illegal, citing UN Security Council Resolution 2334. Add to this a verifiable institutional fact, not an inference: the same state apparatus that tries Israeli citizens residing in the occupied territories in civilian courts tries the Palestinian population of the same area in military courts. Twenty years of monitoring (2005-2025) by the Israeli NGO Yesh Din, covering more than 1,700 case files, shows that 93.6% of investigations into offenses committed by settlers against Palestinians closed without indictment; only 3% led to full or partial convictions. This is not violence tolerated "because" Israel is a democracy, or "despite" being one: it is a system that applies democratic guarantees to one part of the population under its control and military law to the other, in the same territory. Symmetry test The obligation to prevent and prosecute violence against a protected population does not change according to who occupies the territory, nor according to the occupier's political system. Applying it more leniently to a democracy — or more severely because of the label "democracy" — would be the same asymmetry, reversed. What matters for this site is not the identity of the state, but the verifiable fact of a dual legal regime operating in the same space. Counterweight (Phase 4b), declared In this cycle we searched for a comparator with equally rigorous documentation — another state that legally tolerates, with a comparable apparatus for measuring impunity, violence by civilian settlers against a protected population. None of the four cases checked (Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories, Western Sahara, West Papua, Northern Cyprus) presents the same combination of a codified dual judicial system and impunity data measured with two decades of continuity. This should be stated honestly: it is probably a fact about one civil society's capacity to monitor itself over time, not proof that the phenomenon is rarer elsewhere. Why international pressure remains muted There have been sanctions, but partial ones. On May 11, 2026 the EU Foreign Affairs Council sanctioned individual settlers responsible for violence, rejecting the trade measures proposed by Spain; on June 9 six Western capitals banned entry to 25 settlers and 25 other people linked to the movement; on July 23 a new summit of EU ambassadors ended without agreement on a ban on imports from the settlements, for lack of the numbers for a qualified majority. Suspending the EU-Israel Association Agreement — the measure with the most real weight — requires unanimity among the 27 and has been blocked by Italy and Germany: Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said he preferred individual sanctions on violent settlers to a measure targeting the trade agreement. These votes do not happen in a vacuum. EU-Israel trade reached €43.3 billion in 2025 — the EU is Israel's largest trading partner, while Israel is only the EU's 27th-largest partner, a real asymmetry of dependence. France and Germany remain the leading European exporters of weapons to Israel; the share of German military exports going to Israel rose from 6% to 33% in recent years. Italy renewed, in April 2026, through an automatic mechanism, its military cooperation memorandum with Israel through 2031. On the technology side, Europe is the main market for Israel's arms industry (about 54% of Israeli arms exports), with imports up 155% between 2020 and 2024; when Spain suspended arms trade with Israel in 2025, it found it genuinely difficult to quickly replace Israeli suppliers. In Italy, public incentives (November 2025) reward companies that buy cybersecurity from the more than 500 Israeli firms in the sector — against the backdrop of the Paragon case, the Israeli company accused of spying on Italian journalists and activists with the Graphite spyware. A specialized industry source has raised the risk of potential backdoors in national critical systems linked to these technologies — a concern to be attributed to that source, not established fact here. These figures show a documented correlation between commercial, military and technological dependence and the vote against the most incisive measures: we do not prove, and do not claim, a direct causal link — it is for the reader to draw their own conclusions from verifiable facts. Editorial note (declared judgment) It is worth noting that the signatories' alarm is argued primarily in terms of Israeli security, US interests and the survival of the Abraham Accords — a security register, not a human-rights one. This is a notable absence in the text, not proof of what the signatories think of the Palestinian population: Commanders for Israel's Security has historically been a group that has spoken in favor of a two-state solution and strengthening the governance of the Palestinian Authority. It remains a fact that, in this specific letter, the risk to Palestinians does not appear as an independent argument. One question remains open, and it is legitimate to leave it to the reader rather than close it with a definitive answer: how is it possible that facts of this magnitude — 850 injured, 122 displaced communities, 120,000 olive trees destroyed, a judicial system that closes 93.6% of investigations without indictment — remain on the margins of international attention, treated more as material for electoral statements than as a matter of law? Interests first, order second. And no nuclear power is pushing back

Rubio at the UN: the United States will never put the international order above its own interests. Venezuela, Greenland, Argentina and Hormuz show what that means; China, Russia, India and Pakistan do not really contest it.

“We'll never put the international order above the interests of the United States.” — Marco Rubio, Secretary of State, United Nations, September 23, 2026 The facts On September 23, 2026, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio summed up his administration's doctrine for reporters in a single sentence: the United States will never put the international order above its own interests. He added that this is not an attack on the international system but an acknowledgment of reality: states act in their national interest, and the system, in his view, is failing because it has grown beyond its mandate. The sentence is not new in substance. At his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Rubio had already called the postwar global order obsolete and now used against America. What is new is the context in which he repeats it: in the same weeks, Washington closed two agreements that, placed side by side, show what it means in practice. The first concerns Venezuela. Since U.S. forces captured Nicolás Maduro in early January, the country has been led by acting president Delcy Rodríguez, in office by order of the Supreme Court and without any election. On September 2 her government signed energy agreements giving U.S. companies majority control over some 65 billion barrels, roughly one fifth of Venezuela's reserves, under concessions lasting one hundred years. Italy's Eni is among the participants. In parallel, talks are under way to move about 31 tonnes of Venezuelan gold, worth around $4 billion, from the Bank of England to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; the Bank of England has said it will move nothing without a new ruling from a British court. The second concerns Greenland. After a year and a half of pressure, which this site covered when Trump revived it at the NATO summit in Ankara, on September 22 the United States, Denmark and Greenland's government signed an agreement in New York that amends and supplements their 1951 defense agreement. Besides the Pituffik base, the United States will gain two new ones, at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, with freedom of movement on land, in the air, in territorial waters and in undersea approaches. Non-NATO countries are excluded from military facilities and strategic resources, and foreign investment in those sectors must be agreed with Washington: in practice, Russia and China are shut out of Greenland's rare earths. The Danish government stresses that the agreement respects the Kingdom's sovereignty and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination. Yet the text also provides that it remains in force if Greenland becomes independent, with an obligation to join NATO. It still needs ratification by the Danish parliament. Other interests at stake The method had already been on display a year earlier, in Buenos Aires. In October 2025, on the eve of Argentina's midterm elections, the U.S. Treasury opened a $20 billion swap line with the country's central bank. On October 14, hosting Javier Milei at the White House, Trump said openly that the support depended on his ally winning: if he lost, the United States would not be generous with Argentina. Milei won on October 26. This is neither a coup nor a military operation: it is financial aid, legitimate in itself, made conditional on another people's vote, and declared as such in public. The Gulf completes the picture. On September 2, 2026, as fighting with Iran concentrated around the Strait of Hormuz, Trump wrote on Truth Social that, now that the strait was under U.S. control, perhaps it should be renamed the "Trump Strait": an idea he had already floated in March and later described himself as just thrown out there. The name does not matter: straits are not renamed by decree, and no formal step followed. The premise does. Hormuz is made up of the territorial waters of Iran and Oman, and the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees everyone transit passage, not control to whoever has the largest fleet. Claiming control of it is the logic of Greenland applied to the sea. This site wrote about it when Trump threatened Iran's water and power facilities . In the same days, according to three sources cited by Reuters and ABC News on September 16, the administration informally notified congressional committees of a $2.8 billion sale to Israel: 20,000 MK-84 and 20,000 BLU-117 bombs, each weighing one ton. The package had been neither finalized nor formally notified at the time of publication, and the State Department replied that its commitment to Israel remains ironclad. Online, the shipment has been compared to Hiroshima. The comparison only partly holds. One ton is the weight of the bomb, not of the explosive, which makes up just under half of it: 429 kilograms each. Calculated on explosive content, the total comes to around 20 kilotons of TNT equivalent, against the roughly 15 estimated for Hiroshima. The claim "more than Hiroshima" is therefore numerically plausible, while the "40 kilotons" figure in circulation also counts the steel casings. Above all, an atomic bomb releases its energy in an instant and in one place; forty thousand conventional bombs are dropped one at a time, on targets chosen one by one, and every choice is bound by humanitarian law. The thread linking Buenos Aires, Caracas and Nuuk is the same one this site has already followed in eastern Congo, where minerals are traded for security and the price is not set by whoever owns the resource. In Venezuela the oil comes under an unelected government born of an outside military operation. In Greenland the rare earths are closed to competitors with the formal consent of Copenhagen and Nuuk, after months in which Trump had not ruled out force. That leaves the question missing from most commentary: who is the counterweight? The other nuclear powers protested. But what did they do? China condemned the Venezuela operation as a reckless use of force, and its foreign minister Wang Yi rejected the idea that any country can act as the world's policeman. The sources consulted, however, record no concrete Chinese countermeasures in Latin America. Beijing's real lever is economic: the rare earth export controls announced on October 9, 2025, suspended until November 10, 2026. At the Washington summit of September 23-25, Xi Jinping and Trump extended their tariff truce by two months, with no progress on either Taiwan or rare earths. China uses its leverage to negotiate its own position, not to defend the principle it invokes. Russia called the Venezuela operation an armed aggression and raised it at the Security Council on January 5. On Greenland, the Kremlin dismissed the agreement as a matter only for the countries involved. This is not indifference: the sphere-of-influence logic Moscow claims in Ukraine is the same one Washington applies in the Western Hemisphere. Protesting too loudly against the latter would weaken the defense of the former. India did not condemn the Venezuela operation: it called for calm and advised its citizens against travel to the country. Its form of resistance is a different, quieter one. In August, Russian crude accounted for more than 40% of its imports, despite February's trade deal with Washington and despite the law Trump signed on September 18 authorizing tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian energy. The BRICS New Delhi declaration , too, adopted under India's chairmanship, defended international law without ever naming the United States. Pakistan , a non-permanent member of the Security Council, warned in January, together with other countries, that the selective application of international law puts the whole collective security system at risk. In the same period it became one of Trump's favorite interlocutors: a mediator between Washington and Tehran, signatory of a $500 million mining agreement with American counterparts and, since August 7, party with Saudi Arabia and Turkey to a mutual defense pact signed in Mecca, under which an attack on one is considered an attack on all. It is the only nuclear power to have built a new alliance, but inside the American orbit, not against it. Legal commentary Three principles are at stake, and they must be kept apart. The first is the prohibition on the use of force, set out in Article 2(4) of the UN Charter . The capture of a sitting head of state on his own territory, without Security Council authorization, was described as aggression by Russia and China and criticized also by Brazil, Colombia and several U.S. allies. The official U.S. justification, the fight against drug trafficking, falls under neither of the two exceptions the Charter allows: self-defense or Council authorization. The second is permanent sovereignty over natural resources, affirmed by General Assembly Resolution 1803 of 1962: peoples' rights over their resources must be exercised in the interest of their national development. An unelected interim government, installed after a foreign military intervention, granting one fifth of the reserves for a hundred years to companies from that same country raises a serious question under this principle. It is a question, not a verdict: the resolution is not binding like a treaty, and no court has ruled. The third is self-determination. On Greenland, formally, the principle is respected: the agreement was signed by Greenland's government and will go before the Danish parliament. The clause binding a future independent Greenland to NATO membership, however, settles today a choice that would belong to a state that does not yet exist. Implications — the symmetry test The first friction is Rubio's sentence itself. No state has ever truly placed the international order above its own interests: the difference is that the others deny it. Russia invokes international law for Caracas while violating it in Ukraine. China invokes it for Caracas while rejecting the 2016 arbitral award on the South China Sea. Pakistan invokes it at the Security Council while sending back to Afghanistan people the UN says cannot safely return . Rubio has simply dropped the pretense. The symmetry test does not absolve Washington: it says the problem is not a single "rogue state" but a system in which no great power accepts being bound. The second friction concerns the missing counterweight. Anyone imagining an alternative bloc, the BRICS or a Moscow-Beijing axis, finds in practice a sum of bilateral negotiations: China trades rare earths, India trades oil, Pakistan trades minerals and mediation, Russia trades recognition of its own sphere. No one defends the principle when defending it costs something. The third friction is close to home for Europe. An Italian company takes part in the Venezuelan oil agreements. Europe, which is indignant at Russian spheres of influence, has watched a member state, Denmark, negotiate under pressure the future of its own territory with its main ally. If the law only applies when convenient, that holds for us too.
