Israel after the vote: a majority that cannot govern, the Arab vote under attack, the Palestinian elections postponed

On 27 October Israelis took Netanyahu's majority away, but gave it to no one else. Eisenkot holds the mandate and 67 lawmakers back him, but 19 of them are Arab and some of his allies reject their support. What happened, and what the law says about the vote of Arab citizens, the International Criminal Court warrants and the postponed Palestinian elections.

In brief In the 27 October election Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc stopped at 53 seats out of 120. The opposition led by former chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot has 48, the Arab parties 19, the best result in their history. Turnout, 77.9%, was the highest since 1999. Counted in votes rather than percentages, the numbers read differently: Netanyahu's bloc won 92,000 more votes than in 2022, Likud alone 52,000 more. It lost its majority because almost 930,000 more people voted, and they mostly chose others: the Arab parties went from 511,000 to 838,000 votes. In the consultations 67 lawmakers recommended Eisenkot and 46 Netanyahu. On 8 November President Herzog gave Eisenkot the mandate; he has 28 days, plus another 14 if needed, to form a government. Until then Netanyahu remains prime minister. The 67 include the 19 Arab lawmakers. Eisenkot does not want them in the government but is willing to accept their outside support; Avigdor Lieberman, his ally, rejects it and proposes replacing them with the ultra-Orthodox parties. On election day Arab citizens were the target of the campaign: Netanyahu wrote that they were "stealing the elections", Likud sent activists to their polling stations, civil rights groups reported delays and missing ballots. After the vote the Elections Committee reviewed 9,069 polling stations and found no irregularities capable of changing the result. A security service investigation into alleged foreign funding is still open. The hypothesis of bought votes does not, for now, explain the jump: seven people have been arrested, and Arab turnout rose by more than twenty points in every region, not only in the Negev where the arrests took place. International law guarantees every citizen an equal vote, without discrimination. The International Criminal Court's arrest warrants do not depend on who governs. The Palestinian elections, scheduled for 28 November, have been postponed to 11 September 2027. On Tuesday 27 October, at four in the afternoon, 55.7% of Israelis had already voted: never so many at that hour since the Elections Committee began keeping count. In Arab towns the queues were longer than elsewhere. From his account, Netanyahu posted photos of those queues and urged his voters to go to the polls because it was "a matter of life and death". Two weeks later, those voters are the reason Netanyahu no longer has a majority, and also the reason his opponent is struggling to find one. The facts The vote. The Central Elections Committee published the final results on 30 October and delivered them to President Isaac Herzog on 4 November. Likud remains the largest party with 27 seats. Next come Yashar, Eisenkot's party, with 21; B'Yachad ("Together") of former prime minister Naftali Bennett with 12; the Arab Joint List with 11; Yair Golan's Democrats and Ra'am, Mansour Abbas's Islamist party, with 8 each; Lieberman's Yisrael Beytenu, Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) with 7; Shas and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism with 6. Netanyahu's bloc, which held 68 seats in the outgoing Knesset, falls to 53 ( Times of Israel ; Agenzia Nova ). Neither bloc reaches the 61 seats needed to govern without the Arab parties. Votes, not just percentages. When the number of voters changes, percentages can mislead. In 2022 there were 4,764,742 valid votes ( Central Bureau of Statistics ); this year there were 5,691,426 ( Central Elections Committee, data compiled by the US think tank Middle East Forum ): almost 927,000 more, 19% more. The number of eligible voters grew by 543,000, but the number of people who stayed home fell from almost two million to 1.6 million. Counted in votes, the results tell a different story. 2022 2026 Difference Netanyahu bloc (Likud, Otzma Yehudit, Religious Zionism, Shas, UTJ) 2,304,964 (48.4%) 2,397,098 (42.1%) +92,134 of which Likud 1,115,336 (23.4%) 1,167,591 (20.5%) +52,255 Jewish opposition 1,820,292 (38.2%) 2,149,375 (37.8%) +329,083 Arab parties 511,399 (10.7%) 838,475 (14.7%) +327,076 Sources: for 2022, Central Bureau of Statistics and Elections Committee; for 2026, results approved by the Committee on 4 November. In 2022 the Jewish opposition includes Yesh Atid, National Unity, Yisrael Beytenu, Labor and Meretz; the Arab parties Ra'am, Hadash-Ta'al and Balad. Netanyahu's bloc did not lose voters: it gained 92,000. Likud has 52,000 more votes than in 2022, yet its share fell by almost three points and its seats from 32 to 27: with more voters, each seat costs more, about 45,000 votes against 36,000. Had Likud won exactly the same votes as four years ago, it would have 19.6% today. Within the bloc, votes moved: Shas lost 93,000, while Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, which ran together in 2022, gained 101,000. Of the 927,000 additional valid votes, about a third went to the Jewish opposition, a third to the Arab parties and one in ten to the right; the rest, about 180,000, went to lists outside the three groups, almost all of which fell below the threshold, such as Yoaz Hendel's Reservists with 155,000 votes. Two caveats. First, the blocs are not identical to those of 2022. Back then Benny Gantz's party also included Eisenkot and Gideon Sa'ar, who later joined Netanyahu, and Bennett did not run. Second, these are net balances, not flows. They do not tell us how many voters switched sides, because a move in one direction can offset a move in the other. But they do say one thing with certainty: Netanyahu did not lose his majority because his voters abandoned him, but because hundreds of thousands of people who had not voted in 2022, or could not yet vote, went to the polls and chose others. The consultations. On 4 and 5 November Herzog met all the parties. Yashar, B'Yachad, the Democrats, Yisrael Beytenu, Ra'am and the Joint List recommended Eisenkot: 67 lawmakers, the broadest backing for any candidate since 2015. Likud, Otzma Yehudit, Shas and Religious Zionism, which ran together with Zehut, recommended Netanyahu: 46. UTJ, Netanyahu's long-standing ally, recommended no one: it will back whoever guarantees military service exemptions for religious seminary students ( JNS ; Ynet ; Al Jazeera ). The mandate. On Sunday 8 November Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming the government. Eisenkot spoke of a "national emergency government" and invited Likud too to join it under his leadership ( ANSA, via l'Adige ; Alhurra ). The next day Netanyahu replied by proposing the opposite: a unity government led by him, open to any "Zionist" party ( Open ). The new Knesset is sworn in on 10 November. The knot. Eisenkot's 67 lawmakers are 48 from the Jewish opposition and 19 from the two Arab parties. During the campaign Eisenkot, like almost the entire Jewish opposition, had ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties, and had denied promising Ra'am a place in it ( The Jerusalem Post ). After the vote he began studying a minority government: four parties in government and, outside it, the support or abstention of Ra'am, the Joint List and UTJ ( Ynet ; Ynet ). Lieberman sees this as a gift to Netanyahu, who in his view would return to power within six months ( Ynet ). On 9 November the two met. Lieberman asked him to give up Arab support in exchange for his commitment to bring the ultra-Orthodox into the majority ( Ynet ); according to Channel 13 they agreed to try with them first and to return to the minority-government option only if those talks fail ( Channel 13, via JFeed ). The official statement says only that both have "full confidence" they can form a stable government ( ANI ). Until a new government is sworn in, Netanyahu remains prime minister with full formal powers and, according to the Israel Democracy Institute, a "duty of restraint" ( Reuters, via The Nightly ). If Eisenkot fails, Herzog can give the mandate to someone else; if that person fails too, Israel goes back to the polls. The vote of Arab citizens Arab citizens of Israel are about a fifth of the population. They are descendants of the Palestinians who stayed in 1948; they have always voted, and have always voted less than Jews: in 2022, 53.2% went to the polls. This time, in Arab and Druze localities, about 77% voted, according to the Israel Democracy Institute's analysis of polling-station data; the first estimates on election night spoke of 80% ( IDI ; Al Jazeera ). The IDI count excludes mixed cities such as Haifa or Lod, so it is not yet the full figure. The certain figure is another one: the two Arab parties won 838,000 votes, against 511,000 for the three Arab lists in 2022, 64% more. In 2022 Balad fell below the threshold and its 138,000 votes elected no one; this time Arab votes went almost entirely to lists that entered parliament, and the seats rose from 10 to 19. Not all votes for Arab parties come from Arab citizens, and not all Arab citizens vote for Arab parties: the count is an indication, not an exact measure. Before the vote. In September the Elections Committee, made up almost entirely of party representatives, had barred both Ra'am and the Joint List from the elections, at the request of Likud, Otzma Yehudit and other right-wing groups. The attorney general had opposed barring either list: the evidence, she wrote, was not enough ( Al Jazeera ). On 2 October the Supreme Court, with nine judges ruling unanimously, overturned the bans: the evidence presented, it wrote, did not meet the standard set by case law ( Times of Israel ; Al Jazeera ). This has happened at almost every election, and almost every time the Court has ruled the same way. For Balad's leader, Sami Abu Shehadeh, the attorney general had instead asked for the ban to be upheld over an article he wrote the day after 7 October; the Court let him understand it would uphold it, and he withdrew ( Al Jazeera ). The campaign. In the final days Netanyahu campaigned on precisely that turnout. On X he wrote that Muslim Brotherhood supporters were storming the polling stations to "steal the elections" and warned that the alternative was a government "of Mansour Abbas and Ahmed Tibi" ( Al Jazeera ; Reuters, via GV Wire ). Likud and Smotrich's party had announced about two thousand activists at Arab polling stations, with no official role, to prevent fraud for which they had no evidence ( Times of Israel ). According to Haaretz, Likud had also prepared teams to film Arab voters outside polling stations ( Haaretz, via Middle East Monitor ). The polling stations. The Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) reported delays in opening polling stations in sixteen Arab localities, from Rahat to Tamra. In Segev Shalom, in the Negev, police and Border Police kept about two hundred people outside for "overcrowding" ( ACRI, via The Jerusalem Post ). Adalah, the Arab minority's legal centre, reported a shortage of Arabic ballots at polling stations in Haifa, Nazareth, Shefa-'Amr and other towns ( The New Arab ). ACRI wrote that the Arab vote "may have been deliberately obstructed". That is a documented suspicion, not a proven intention. The police have not explained what happened in Segev Shalom. After the vote. On 27 October, before the polls opened, police arrested three Ra'am activists in the Negev with envelopes of cash, on suspicion of vote-buying; two days later they arrested four more. According to N12, the information that led to the first arrests had been passed to the police by Netanyahu's chief of staff ( The Jerusalem Post ). On 1 November a judge released one of the three and granted the police less than they asked for on the other two ( AP, via News4Jax ). Meanwhile, the chairman of the Elections Committee, Supreme Court justice Noam Sohlberg, had asked the Shin Bet, the domestic security service, to check information about foreign funding, attributed to Qatar and Turkey, to boost Arab turnout ( Israel Hayom ). Qatar denies it. Likud spoke of a "political 7 October". The Shin Bet stated that its investigation is "focused and limited", does not concern the Arab community as a whole, and that no one should attribute to it conclusions it has not drawn ( Arutz Sheva ). On 3 November Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected the Shin Bet chief's request to question four Arab leaders, including Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi: without sufficient evidence, her office wrote, no one can be questioned ( Ynet ; Outlook India ). On 4 November the Elections Committee announced that it had reviewed the protocols of 9,069 polling stations and found no irregularities that compromised the vote or changed the result (same source). The Shin Bet investigation remains open. Can bribes explain the jump? The hypothesis deserves to be taken seriously. Buying votes is a crime, and the arrests of 27 October suggest someone may have tried. Ad Kan, an Israeli right-wing association known for its undercover investigations, claims that up to 200,000 votes were "tainted", with payments of 400 or 500 shekels, but has not explained how it reached that figure ( JNS ). We put the hypothesis to the test of the numbers. The scale. The Arab parties won 327,000 more votes than in 2022. Buying them all at that price would cost between 130 and 165 million shekels and would require hundreds of thousands of cash deliveries, each with a potential witness. So far seven people have been arrested, and a judge has already released one. The geography. According to the Israel Democracy Institute, which analysed polling-station data in Arab and Druze localities, turnout rose everywhere: from 54% to 76% in the Galilee and the north, from 52% to 78% in the Triangle, from about 51% to almost 80% among the Bedouin of the Negev, from 38% to 74% in the unrecognised Bedouin villages ( IDI ). The arrests concern the Negev, where the increase is somewhat stronger and where Ra'am is most deeply rooted, and Ra'am is the party that grew most: from 194,000 to 338,000 votes. There, a role for money cannot be ruled out. But it does not explain the Galilee and the Triangle, where Arab and Druze eligible voters number more than 800,000 and where no one has been arrested. The stated motives. The mobilisation was visible before the vote. In an IDI survey, 87% of young Arab first-time voters said they intended to vote. After the vote, in a survey by the Arabic-language newspaper Kul al-Arab, almost 92% named fear of Smotrich and Ben-Gvir as their main reason ( The Jerusalem Post ). There is no shortage of reasons. In 2022 there were 116 homicides in Arab communities; in 2023, Ben-Gvir's first full year at the National Security Ministry, there were 244; in 2025 there were 252, the record ( Abraham Initiatives, via Times of Israel ). In September the two Arab parties had been barred from the elections, and reinstated only by the Court. And the increase is not limited to Arabs: the Jewish opposition also won 329,000 more votes, and no one claims they were bought. The figure that does not add up. There is, however, one number that sceptics can rightly use. In the last polls the Arab parties reached at most 15 seats, already a record ( Arutz Sheva ); the exit polls gave them 17 or 18 ( JNS ); they won 19. The gap is real and needs explaining. It may stem from the difficulty of measuring such unusual turnout, but it is also the point a serious investigation must examine, polling station by polling station. The legal threshold. Changing one seat takes about 45,000 votes. Any vote-buying, even on a small scale, is serious if proven and must be punished. To change the result, however, it would have to involve tens of thousands of people. Likud has announced an appeal to the Jerusalem District Court, to be filed by 17 November: it will focus mainly on the use of apps to track turnout, banned by the Supreme Court shortly before the vote ( Times of Israel ). The election law requires showing that the irregularities could have changed the result. No Israeli court has ever annulled a national election. Until proven otherwise, the explanation the data support is the simplest one: a community that felt threatened went to vote. If the investigations show otherwise, we will report it. The report the day before. On 26 October, the eve of the vote, the UN Independent Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory published a report accusing Israel of crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, and of continuing genocide in Gaza despite the ceasefire; the same report criticises the Palestinian Authority for failing to investigate killings by its own forces ( Al Jazeera ; AFP, via Korea Times ). Israel called it a disinformation campaign. We checked whether the report weighed on the vote: no candidate used it in the last hours of the campaign, and no winner mentioned it afterwards. We have no grounds to attribute any effect to it. We wrote about the Commission in "A UN commission of inquiry finds the deliberate targeting of Palestinian children" . The vote that is not happening In Ramallah, twenty kilometres from Jerusalem, Palestinians were due to vote on 28 November for the first time in twenty years. On 10 October the president of the Palestinian Authority, Mahmoud Abbas, signed a decree cancelling the legislative elections and merging them with the presidential ones, set for 11 September 2027 ( Wafa, via Al Jazeera ). Three days earlier, in Cairo, Fatah and Hamas had agreed to recommend the postponement ( Reuters, via The Jerusalem Post ). The official reason is the obstacles imposed by Israel: the Palestinian election commission and observers were denied access to East Jerusalem and Gaza, and raids, settlement building and settler violence continue in the West Bank ( Khaleej Times ). Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar replied that it was "yet another lie" to evade responsibility. Many Palestinians do not believe it either: Mustafa Barghouti, secretary general of the Palestinian National Initiative, spoke of deep disappointment ( Al Jazeera ). The last Palestinian legislative elections were held in 2006. The Legislative Council has not met since 2007 and was dissolved in 2018. Abbas was elected in 2005 for four years and has governed by decree ever since. This is the second postponement in five years: in 2021 the reason was East Jerusalem. According to a Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research poll last August, 79% of Palestinians want Abbas to resign ( The National ). On 27 October there was voting in the West Bank anyway, but only on one side. At polling stations set up inside the settlements, such as the school in Kiryat Arba on the edge of Hebron, the Israeli citizens who live there voted: more than half a million settlers, in a territory home to more than three million Palestinians ( AFP, via Ahram Online ). Those Palestinians do not vote for the Knesset. In all, across the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, about three million adult Palestinians have no say in choosing the government that controls their borders, their movement and their papers; in East Jerusalem almost all of them are residents, not citizens, and can vote only for the city council ( Al Jazeera ). On the same land, whoever lives in a settlement chooses the government; whoever lives in the village next door chooses neither that one nor their own. Western reactions were regretful. EU High Representative Kaja Kallas tied European support to reforms; Australia, Canada, France and the United Kingdom said they were "deeply disappointed" ( The Jerusalem Post ). No one announced consequences. Yet several of those countries had tied their recognition of the State of Palestine, in September 2025, partly to the promise of elections within a year; and some, such as Canada, had called for elections without Hamas ( The Jerusalem Post ). Legal commentary The equal vote. Israel is a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Article 25 guarantees every citizen the right to vote in periodic elections by universal and equal suffrage; Article 26 prohibits all discrimination, including on grounds of national origin or religion. An Arab citizen's vote counts as much as a Jewish citizen's, and weighs the same. The Covenant does not prevent a party from saying it will not govern with another: that is a political choice. What it prohibits is the State making it harder for part of its citizens to vote, or to stand for election: that is why barring an entire list must rest on serious evidence, and why the Supreme Court reinstated Ra'am and the Joint List. The details matter too, then: polling stations opening late, missing ballots, officers keeping people outside. Today we do not know whether these were the result of design or disorganisation. We do know that those who should answer, the police, have given no explanation. Suspicion and proof. An investigation into foreign funding of an election campaign is legitimate: almost every legal system forbids a foreign government from paying to influence a vote. But an investigation into some individuals does not authorise treating a million voters as suspects. Israel's institutions have so far kept the two things apart: the Elections Committee checked the protocols, the attorney general asked for evidence before questioning lawmakers, a judge scaled back the arrests. That is the ordinary functioning of the rule of law. It is precisely for this reason that Likud accuses the attorney general of trying to "cover up" the investigation. The Covenant, in Article 14, requires the presumption of innocence; the Basic Law: The Knesset requires elections that are "general, national, direct, equal, secret and proportional". The government that stays on. An outgoing government in Israel keeps its formal powers, but the Supreme Court has long asked it to show restraint in decisions that bind the future, such as senior appointments. The point matters more than usual, because with the new Knesset the March 2025 law comes into force, changing the judicial selection committee and increasing the weight of politicians in the choice ( Times of Israel, via Forward ). The opposition had promised to repeal it if it came to power ( Axios ). The Supreme Court has heard the petitions against the law with its full bench, but no ruling has yet been issued ( The Jerusalem Post ). The Criminal Court warrants. The arrest warrants against Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant, issued by the International Criminal Court in November 2024, do not depend on the outcome of an election. They apply to the individuals, not to the office: if Netanyahu leaves government, they remain in force. A new Israeli government could ask the Court to leave the case to national judges, under the principle of complementarity (Article 17 of the Rome Statute). But to do so it would have to genuinely investigate the same people for the same conduct: the use of starvation as a method of warfare and attacks against civilians. In December 2025 the Appeals Chamber rejected, by three judges to two, Israel's appeal on this point, and the warrants remained valid ( Ynet ). Israel also contests the Court's jurisdiction, because it has not joined the Statute; the judges have reaffirmed that the warrants remain valid until they rule on that point ( JNS ). Eisenkot has promised to set up a state commission of inquiry within two weeks of taking office ( Israel Hayom ). That commission would investigate the failures of 7 October, not the conduct of the war in Gaza: it is a different thing, and on its own it would not affect the warrants. We wrote about those warrants, never executed, in "Two warrants, zero arrests" . The West Bank. In July 2024 the International Court of Justice found, in an advisory opinion, that the occupation of the Palestinian territories is unlawful, that the settlements violate the Fourth Geneva Convention and that Israel must end it as rapidly as possible. On this, the two candidates differ less than one might think. Netanyahu and Eisenkot both oppose a Palestinian state ( Reuters, via Khaleej Times ). The difference lies elsewhere: Eisenkot opposes annexing the entire West Bank and the E1 project, which would cut Palestinian territory in two, and promises to enforce the law against violent settlers ( Reuters, via WHTC ; The Jerusalem Post ); but he supports the settlements the Israeli government has authorised, the ones he calls "legal", and opposes only the outposts that not even Israeli law recognises ( Reuters, via Al-Monitor ). Netanyahu governs with two parties, Ben-Gvir's and Smotrich's, that call for annexation. Under international law that distinction does not exist: "legal" means legal for Israel, not for international law. The Fourth Geneva Convention prohibits an occupying power from transferring its own population into the occupied territory (Article 49), and in its 2024 opinion the Court specified that Israel must immediately cease all new settlement activity and evacuate all settlers, without distinguishing between authorised settlements and outposts. It is an advisory opinion, not a judgment: it cannot be enforced by force, but it sets out obligations that, in the Court's view, already bind Israel. We wrote about settler violence in "The warning from their own generals" . The Palestinian vote. Palestine also acceded to the Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, in 2014: Article 25 applies to Palestinians too. A postponement can be justified if voting is truly impossible, and in East Jerusalem and Gaza today it is, at least in part. It cannot become a way of governing: a president whose mandate expired seventeen years ago and a parliament that has not met for nineteen are not an emergency, they are a system. The Palestinian Basic Law itself sets a four-year term for both the president and the Legislative Council. Symmetry test The fraud claims. Let us apply the same yardstick to both accusations. Against the Arab vote: three arrests with envelopes of cash, then four more, and a security service investigation into foreign money that no one has yet proven. Against those who obstructed the Arab vote: the reports by ACRI and Adalah, the party activists sent to polling stations, the announced filming. Even on the accusation on which Likud is building its appeal, the banned apps for tracking who has voted, the count by a group of volunteer observers, the Civilian Election Guard, points the other way: of 374 cases reported, 32% involved Likud activists, 2% Ra'am and 1% the Joint List ( Times of Israel ). In neither case is there, for now, proof of a scheme capable of changing the result. But only one of the two accusations has been used to claim the elections were "stolen". Foreign money. If Qatar paid to boost Arab turnout, that is serious interference and must be punished. It is the same Qatar whose funds for Gaza, from 2018 to 2023, flowed with the permission of the Netanyahu government, as we reconstructed in "Qatar's money and Hamas" . Those who today call it an enemy of Israeli democracy yesterday considered it a useful channel. The excluded. Almost all Jewish parties, on the right as in the centre, promised not to govern with the Arab parties. No Arab party promised not to govern with Jewish parties: Ra'am is asking to join the government, the Joint List offers outside support. Excluding a fifth of the lawmakers is not illegal. But a democracy in which the votes of one citizen in five serve to count the others, and not to govern, has a problem no law can solve. The postponed elections. The Israeli obstacles to the Palestinian vote are real and documented. But the postponement also suits those who govern in Ramallah and in Gaza, who have not faced a count in twenty years. And it suits Western governments, which demanded both swift elections and the exclusion of Hamas, and now limit themselves to saying they are disappointed. The UN report. We had a hypothesis: that the report published on the eve of the vote had pushed voters to the right by making them feel accused. We checked it, and it does not hold: the data do not confirm it and no one used it in the campaign. We say so because the same yardstick applies to the hypotheses we find convincing. Our judgment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. The result of 27 October says two things. The first is that the government in office on 7 October lost its majority without losing its voters: its votes even grew. It was defeated by those who stayed home in 2022 and this time went to vote, in numbers not seen for a generation. The second is that this majority exists only by counting Arab citizens, and part of those who formed it do not want to count them. The campaign tried to keep them at home, and they voted more than ever. Now they risk discovering that their vote is good for removing a government but not for forming one. The institutions held: the Elections Committee, the attorney general and the judge who scaled back the arrests asked for evidence before accusing. It is the least reported news of these elections, and the most important for anyone who believes the rules apply to everyone. A change of government would not change everything. Netanyahu and Eisenkot both oppose a Palestinian state, and the Criminal Court's warrants stay where they are. But it would change something that is not small: who decides in the West Bank, whether violent settlers are stopped, whether 7 October is investigated by an independent commission. And twenty kilometres from Jerusalem, Palestinians are still waiting to be able to vote. Twenty years is too long, whoever is to blame. What to watch Whether Eisenkot forms a government within the 28 days, or the 14-day extension, and with whom: the ultra-Orthodox, outside Arab support, or neither. The first decisions of any new government: the state commission of inquiry into 7 October, the E1 project, the judicial selection law. The outcome of the Shin Bet investigation into foreign funding, which is due to be delivered to the chairman of the Elections Committee. Whether the police explain what happened at the Segev Shalom polling stations and respond to the reports by ACRI and Adalah. The Palestinian calendar: the factions' "national dialogue" and the date of 11 September 2027. The rules they wrote: how the United States built the 1945 order, and the first exceptions
The UN Charter, Nuremberg, Bretton Woods: much of the post-war rulebook bears Washington's signature. Even then, the first exceptions appeared. Opening episode of the series "What example do we set".

In brief After the Second World War the United States led the building of the new order's rules: the UN Charter, the Nuremberg trial, the economic institutions of Bretton Woods. From the start it kept a way out: the veto in the Security Council, and a reservation that left Washington to decide which cases the International Court could hear. During the Cold War the exceptions came: the coup in Iran, then Grenada, Nicaragua and Panama. The UN condemned them in words almost identical to those it used for the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. There are also cases in which Washington applied the rules to its allies (Suez, 1956) or sought a legal basis before acting (Cuba, 1962; Kuwait, 1990). Today the difference is another one: the exception is no longer hidden, it is declared as doctrine. In September 2026 the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, told the UN that the United States will never put the international order above its own interests. We wrote about it in "Interests first, order second" . The sentence weighs more than it seems, because that order was not imposed on the United States by others: they designed it. This series starts here. What do other countries learn when the most powerful democracy breaks the rules it wrote, and what do we Europeans do about it? Before today's cases, we need to know how those rules were born and when the exceptions began. The rules they wrote The UN Charter. The idea of a world organisation to prevent new wars came from Franklin D. Roosevelt. In the spring of 1945 fifty countries drafted the Charter in San Francisco, and the US Senate approved it almost unanimously ( Office of the Historian, US State Department ). The heart of the text is Article 2, paragraph 4: no state may use or threaten force against another, except in self-defence or with the authorisation of the Security Council (we explain it in the entry Use of force and self-defence ). The same Charter, however, gives the five permanent members of the Council, the United States included, the power of veto: no binding decision can pass against any of them ( entry on the Security Council ). Nuremberg. To try the Nazi leaders, the four victorious powers set up an international tribunal, the first to put rulers on trial for starting a war of aggression. The chief US prosecutor, Supreme Court Justice Robert H. Jackson, opened the trial with a sentence that already contains the question of this series: passing the defendants a poisoned chalice "is to put it to our own lips as well" ( opening address, Avalon Project, Yale ). If the rules apply to the defeated, they also apply to those who judge them. The economy. At Bretton Woods, in 1944, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were born; in 1947 in Geneva the GATT was signed, the trade agreement from which the World Trade Organization would come ( Office of the Historian ). We will come back to it in the episode on tariffs. The Court, with a clause. In 1946 the United States accepted the compulsory jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice : any state that had done the same could take it to court. But the Senate added a reservation: excluded are matters within the domestic jurisdiction of the United States "as determined by the United States" ( Senate resolution, 2 August 1946 ). It was called the Connally reservation, after the senator who proposed it, and the American Bar Association opposed it from the first day ( American Journal of International Law ). Whoever decides alone whether a case concerns them accepts the judge only as long as it suits them. The first exceptions Iran, 1953. Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadeq had nationalised Iranian oil, until then in the hands of a British company. In August 1953 he was overthrown in a coup. For decades Washington denied it. In 2013 an internal CIA document put it in writing: the coup was carried out "under CIA direction as an act of U.S. foreign policy" ( National Security Archive ). A year later, in Guatemala, the CIA organised the fall of the elected president Jacobo Árbenz ( Office of the Historian ). Suez, 1956: the rule applied to allies. When Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal, the United Kingdom, France and Israel attacked it under a plan agreed in secret. President Dwight Eisenhower, who had not been told, opposed it and pressed the International Monetary Fund to deny aid to London. The invaders withdrew ( Imperial War Museum ). This is the case in which the rules of 1945 worked as promised: against two allies of the United States, by the will of the United States. Cuba, 1962: the rule taken seriously. After the failed Bay of Pigs landing, which we reconstructed in the piece on the embargo , the Soviets installed nuclear missiles on the island. The Kennedy administration set aside the argument of pre-emptive defence and asked the Organization of American States to authorise a naval blockade, called a "quarantine". According to the State Department's legal adviser at the time, Abram Chayes, it did so largely because it believed it had a legal obligation to do so ( Just Security ). Many lawyers consider that basis fragile all the same. But Washington felt it had to justify the use of force before the law. Grenada, 1983. After Prime Minister Maurice Bishop was murdered by a military faction, the United States invaded the island. The UN General Assembly condemned the intervention as a "flagrant violation of international law" ( resolution 38/7 ), after a similar text had been blocked by the US veto in the Security Council. Nicaragua, 1984-1986: when the judge says you are wrong. Sandinista Nicaragua took the United States to the International Court over its support for the Contra rebels and the mines in its ports. Washington argued that the Court had no jurisdiction; when the Court decided otherwise, it stopped taking part in the case and withdrew its acceptance of compulsory jurisdiction. In 1986 the Court found the United States guilty of the unlawful use of force. The United States rejected the judgment and vetoed the Council resolution calling for compliance ( Britannica ). Panama, 1989. The United States invaded Panama to capture General Manuel Noriega, who had annulled the elections and was indicted in the United States for drug trafficking. The General Assembly again spoke of a "flagrant violation of international law" ( resolution 44/240 ). Thirty-seven years later, a similar pattern repeated itself with Venezuela: we will discuss it in episode 1. Kuwait, 1990: the system that works. When Iraq invaded Kuwait, Washington did not act alone. It built a majority in the Security Council, which authorised the use of "all necessary means" to free the country ( resolution 678 ). It was the moment when the order of 1945, with the United States in the lead, seemed to do what it had been written for. Legal commentary What the rules prohibit. The ban on the use of force applies to everyone, even to those with good reasons or a hateful enemy. In the Nicaragua judgment the Court added that a state may not intervene in the internal affairs of another, by arming rebels or trying to change its government. A coup organised from outside falls under the ban even if no soldier crosses a border. The weak point. To enforce the rules you have to go through the Security Council, where each permanent member can block any decision concerning it. When the violator is one of them, only the General Assembly remains, and it can condemn but not compel. Grenada, Panama, Nicaragua: three condemnations, no consequences. The same was true for the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. It is not a flaw discovered later: the veto was a choice made by those who wrote the Charter, the United States included. Hiding or declaring. Were the legal justifications of the Cold War sincere or just for show? For the law it matters less than it seems. A state that denies, hides or looks for a legal argument recognises that the rule exists. A state that declares it puts its own interests above the rule treats it as if it no longer existed. Washington's version The central argument must be set out in full. The rules of 1945 assumed that the great powers would cooperate, and the Soviet Union did not. Without American power, on this reading, there would have been no order to defend, and leaving room to Moscow would have meant handing it entire countries. The CIA document on 1953 says so itself, speaking of the risk of leaving Iran open to Soviet aggression. For each intervention, Washington also offered a legal basis. In Grenada: the request of the neighbouring states of the Eastern Caribbean, an appeal from the island's governor-general and the protection of about a thousand American citizens, mostly students ( Christian Science Monitor, 1983 ). In Nicaragua: the collective defence of El Salvador, which accused the Sandinistas of arming the guerrillas. In Panama: self-defence, the protection of American citizens and the return of democracy; the US delegate accused the Assembly of turning a blind eye to Noriega's repression ( Deseret News, 1989 ). Some American lawyers considered these arguments valid. Most states, at the UN, rejected them. Symmetry test The same words. In January 1980 the General Assembly "deplored" the Soviet armed intervention in Afghanistan, by a large majority that included the United States ( International Legal Materials ). Moscow said it had been invited by the Afghan government. Three years later the same Assembly used almost the same formula for Grenada, where Washington said it had been invited by the governor-general. Already then some American experts noted that Grenada had cost the United States the advantage it had gained over Afghanistan (Christian Science Monitor, same source). If an invitation was not enough for Moscow, it could not be enough for Washington. In the same autumn. In November 1956, while Eisenhower was forcing London and Paris to withdraw from Suez, the Soviet Union was crushing the Hungarian revolution. In those days Washington applied the rules to its allies better than Moscow applied them to itself. The test works in both directions: the Cold War is not a story of American hypocrisy alone. What remains. The comparison absolves no one, but it says something about credibility: whoever asks others to respect a rule must be able to say they respect it. It is the same question raised today when Moscow cites Kosovo or Iraq to justify Ukraine. What about Europe? Europe does not come out of this story any better. At Suez the violators were the United Kingdom and France, and it was Washington that stopped them. On Grenada, a former British colony, Margaret Thatcher opposed the invasion before it began; then the United Kingdom abstained on the condemnation ( Declassified UK ). On Panama, the United Kingdom and France cast their vetoes together with the United States in the Security Council and voted against the condemnation in the Assembly ( United Nations University ; Deseret News, same source). On Afghanistan, by contrast, Western Europe voted as one to condemn Moscow. The same act, judged differently depending on who committed it. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. The rules of 1945 are not an invention against America: they are largely American. That is what makes what is happening today serious. Jackson knew that one day they would also be applied to those who had written them, and he said so before the world. From the start Washington kept a way out, the veto and the Connally reservation, and during the Cold War the exceptions were many and serious. But for the most part they were hidden, denied or covered by a legal argument, and at some decisive moments, at Suez and in Kuwait, the United States defended the rules even when it was costly. Vice still paid tribute to virtue. Today that tribute is over. When the Secretary of State says that interests come before order, he is not looking for an excuse for an exception: he is saying that the exception is the rule. From Moscow, from Beijing or from any other capital the lesson reads clearly, and it is the reason for this series. The same yardstick must be used for everyone, Europe included, which at Suez and in Panama chose not to see. The next episodes Tariffs as sanctions : the trade rules written in 1947 and their use as a weapon. Venezuela : capturing a president, from Panama to Caracas. Greenland : threatening an ally. The piece on Cuba, already online, is part of the series: Cuba in the dark . Europe has committed to raising military spending to 5% of GDP by 2035. This manifesto does not dispute the right to self-defence: it disputes a number set before the needs, under the threat of tariffs, with rules changed for weapons and not for public services. And it makes six concrete demands.

A manifesto against disproportionate rearmament, decided under pressure and paid for with public services · 2026 Manifesto — Needs first, then the number This manifesto is not against defence. Ukraine was attacked, it has the right to defend itself, and helping it do so is lawful. Russia spends 7.5% of its GDP on its armed forces. Nobody writing these lines pretends the threat does not exist. It is against something else: the way Europe decided how much to spend, and who will pay. (How this war came about, with the wrongs of all sides, we reconstructed in "From 1990 to 2022" .) A number born in a negotiation At the summit in The Hague, in June 2025, NATO allies committed to spending 5% of GDP on defence and security by 2035. The number was requested by Washington. The only government that held back, Spain's, argued that 2.1% was enough to meet the capabilities required by the Alliance without cutting social spending; the American president responded by threatening to double tariffs. A month later, the trade deal between the United States and the European Union put 15% tariffs and the purchase of large quantities of American weapons in the same package. Not everything was imposed: many European governments feared Russia, and feared that the United States would no longer defend them. But the number and the timetable were set this way. NATO's capability targets, to which the number is linked, are classified. No citizen, and almost no parliament, can check whether 5% matches what is needed. Rules changed in one direction only For weapons, Europe found fast tools. A hundred and fifty billion in loans approved in ten weeks, through an emergency procedure that left out the European Parliament, so much so that Parliament took the matter to the Court of Justice. An exemption from the Stability Pact that lets states run larger deficits, but only if they spend the money on defence (and, since June 2026, on part of their energy spending). A proposal for the common budget that increases funds for defence and space fivefold. For schools, healthcare, justice and the upkeep of civilian infrastructure, no exemption. For diplomacy, none either: the share of the European budget devoted to conflict prevention has fallen, and the Union has been discussing for more than a year and a half whether to appoint an envoy for negotiations on Ukraine, without having done so. When needs are equal, the spending with the most convenient rules always wins. Who has already paid The bill has started to arrive. The United Kingdom funded higher defence spending by cutting development aid and, in 2026, road and energy projects. Belgium cut its aid by a quarter. Denmark abolished a public holiday. In Italy the Parliamentary Budget Office warns that once the exemption ends the accounts will get harder, because staff and multi-year programmes do not stop. The government says healthcare and schools will not be touched. But today the money is borrowed, and someone will pay the debt back. And while the percentage is being debated, some try to reach it by changing the labels: calling a bridge or a dam already decided "defence", or hiding military spending among infrastructure. Either way, those who pay no longer know what they are paying for. Why we call it disproportionate, and dangerous Disproportionate not because the threat is invented, but because the number comes before the needs. A spending target can be met by buying the wrong things. It can be missed while having what is needed. Dangerous for two reasons. The first is economic: rearmament paid for with debt and taken from public services weakens the very societies it claims to protect. The second is political: when every alarm has only one ready answer, more weapons, and diplomacy is left without tools, war stops being an exception and becomes a horizon. We have written it on this site before: before any choice of force, it should be possible to show that the negotiating path was exhausted, not abandoned halfway ( "We Will Not Look Away While War Is Chosen" ). The objections, and our answers "Without security there is no welfare either." True, and serious economists argue it: a defenceless Europe would attract less investment and grow less. But the argument holds for useful spending, based on needs. It does not say who pays while the growth, if it comes, has not yet arrived. "Those who criticise rearmament play Moscow's game." No. Asking that spending be justified, that Parliament decide and that diplomacy have its means does not weaken Europe: it makes it more credible. It is spending without a plan, and without consent, that an adversary can exploit. "Russia spends more than we do." It depends on how you measure it. In dollars Europe spends almost three times as much; at purchasing power parity the gap shrinks a great deal, and some estimates reverse it. That is exactly why a public assessment of needs is required, not a race of percentages. What we ask A social clause. No increase in defence spending funded by cuts to healthcare, education, justice and civilian infrastructure. If larger deficits are allowed for weapons, the same rule should protect essential services. Needs first, then the number. Every government should present to Parliament a public version of the capabilities that are missing and what they cost, and justify spending on that basis, not with a percentage of GDP. Honest labels. Separate, verifiable accounts for defence and for civil security. No civilian works counted as defence, no military spending hidden in infrastructure. Parliament decides. No emergency procedures that shut out elected representatives for programmes lasting decades. Equal standing for diplomacy. Conflict prevention should not be cut more than the rest of the budget, and the Union should appoint an envoy with a mandate for negotiations on Ukraine. What that envoy could bring to the table we proposed in "What Europe could do: seven proposals" . We decide. Defence spending should be set on European needs, not under the threat of tariffs, and should not be tied to trade deals. Purchases should be chosen for what they are for, not for the flag of whoever makes them. The limit of this manifesto We do not say how much Europe should spend: we do not have the information to say it, and no citizen does. That is precisely the point. We ask that the number come after the needs, that the needs be explained, that parliaments decide, and that the bill not be paid, in silence, by the school, the hospital and the courthouse down the road. The facts and sources behind this manifesto are in the Analysis "The bill for rearmament: who pays, and under what rules" . If you agree, you can sign the petition on change.org. Freezers at 50 degrees: who attacked Europe's supermarkets, and what we really know

On 2 November the refrigeration systems of hundreds of supermarkets in at least eleven European countries were tampered with remotely. Two pro-Russian groups claimed responsibility, without verified evidence. What is established, what is not, and what the law says when an attack comes from a keyboard.

In brief On the night of 1 to 2 November cyberattacks tampered with the refrigeration systems of supermarkets in at least eleven European countries, Italy included. In many cases freezers were pushed to 50 degrees. Tonnes of food were thrown away. It repeated an attack carried out in France on 12 October. In both cases the target was remote-control software, partly outdated and exposed online without adequate protection. On 4 November two pro-Russian groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest, claimed the attacks on Telegram. The messages were later deleted and nobody has verified them independently. In 2025 the United States and Denmark had already pointed to links between these groups and the Russian state; according to the American indictment, Z-Pentest is another name for a group directed by Russian military intelligence. For the attacks on the fridges, however, no authority has published evidence of state direction. The Kremlin denies it. Under international law the difference is decisive: a state is responsible for what its organs do, or those acting under its control, not for what sympathisers do. But it also has a duty not to let its territory be used to harm others. A supermarket fridge is an ordinary object. It becomes less ordinary when you discover that, to make it go haywire, you do not need to enter the shop: you only need to find online the panel that controls it. On the night of 2 November someone did this in hundreds of stores, from Dublin to Bucharest. Who did it is the question on which, within a few days, an entire political reading was built. This piece tries to separate what we know from what is being said. The facts France, 12 October. The first attack in this series hit several hundred French supermarkets. Police counted about 700 refrigeration units tampered with, in chains such as Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, with damage above 130,000 euros ( GreenMe ). The attackers had exploited old versions of Danfoss software for remote monitoring of the systems ( Informat.ro ). According to an expert quoted by CNN, more than 1,700 installations of that software were visible online before the attack ( QN ). Europe, 2 November. Three weeks later the same technique was repeated on a continental scale. The attackers switched the evaporators of fridges and freezers into defrost mode, pushing temperatures up to 50 degrees ( Teleborsa ; Cybernews ). At least eleven countries were hit ( Euronews ); other sources count twelve, including Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Estonia, Ireland, Germany, Romania and Portugal ( RetailDetail ). In Ireland the SuperValu chain pulled products from 13 stores; in Belgium Carrefour spoke of about 15 outlets out of 700 ( Cybernews ; TweakTown ). Italy. Attacks were recorded in Sicily, at least three stores in Catania and one in Palermo, as well as in Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna, where the National Cybersecurity Agency identified one against a frozen-food company ( Open ). On 3 November the government convened the Agency and the heads of the intelligence services at Palazzo Chigi; the final statement spoke of a limited impact on the distribution chain ( ItaliaOggi ). The investigations. In Belgium prosecutors opened a criminal investigation ( Al Jazeera ). The European Commission convened agencies and national authorities, but did not attribute the attacks to any state or group ( Informat.ro ). Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen called them a deliberate attempt to hit the food supply chain ( Informat.ro ). Who did it: three levels not to confuse 1. The claim. On 4 November NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest jointly claimed the attacks, with a video and some Telegram messages that were later deleted. NoName057(16) also reportedly published a sample of more than 2,500 lines with usernames and passwords of Danfoss employees and customers. Nobody has verified it. A researcher quoted by Cybernews doubts that the groups actually breached the systems, rather than taking credit after the media had named them as suspects ( Cybernews ). According to Agenda Digitale, the statement contains no exclusive technical data that only the perpetrators could know ( Agenda Digitale ). 2. The groups' links to Moscow. Here there is evidence, but it concerns the past. On 9 December 2025 the US Department of Justice brought charges describing the Russian government's support for NoName057(16) and for another group, Cyber Army of Russia Reborn, which according to the indictment also uses the name Z-Pentest and was founded, funded and directed by Russian military intelligence, the GRU ( Kyiv Independent ). A few days later Denmark attributed to Z-Pentest a 2024 attack on a water treatment plant. According to the security firm Forescout, since the start of 2026 Russia-based groups have claimed at least 20 attacks on refrigeration systems ( Pillitteri, summarising the DOJ, the Danish government and Forescout ). The suspicion, then, does not come from nowhere. 3. Direction by the Russian state. This is the unproven part. For the attacks on the fridges no authority has published evidence of state direction (same source). The Kremlin called the accusations "absurd" ( AFP, via Macau Business ). A Belgian expert said he was "95% sure" it was Russian sabotage ( RetailDetail ): that is a professional assessment, not proof. The jump from the first level to the third is the one public debate made fastest. In Italy, for example, the government spoke of a Russian lead on 3 November, before any claim of responsibility ( Pillitteri ). The weak spot Whoever the perpetrator, the door was open. According to security experts, about 13,000 refrigeration systems in Europe still run on outdated software with known vulnerabilities ( dev.ua ). Until this wave, nobody had thought these systems needed high-level cyber defences ( QN ). The countermeasures set out by the French agency CERT-FR are simple: take the systems off direct internet access, change default passwords, update the firmware, and reopen access only through a VPN ( Pillitteri ). On 4 November in France an attack of the same kind against the cold rooms of three blood storage centres was foiled ( Liga.net ). Legal commentary When an attack belongs to a state. Under international law a state is responsible for the actions of its organs and of persons or groups acting on its instructions, or under its direction or control (articles 4 and 8 of the International Law Commission's Articles on State Responsibility, 2001). In Nicaragua v. United States (1986) the International Court of Justice required "effective control" over the specific operations ( ICJ ). General support, or political sympathy, is not enough. The duty of vigilance. There is, however, a second obligation. As early as 1949, in the Corfu Channel case, the Court held that no state may knowingly allow its territory to be used for acts contrary to the rights of other states ( ICJ ). If groups known to a country's authorities repeatedly hit another country's infrastructure, the state from which they operate has a duty to stop them, even if it does not direct them. What kind of violation. Remotely damaging another country's civilian installations, with economic losses but without deaths or destruction comparable to military action, hardly reaches the threshold of an "armed attack" that allows self-defence (Article 51 of the UN Charter). It is closer to a violation of sovereignty or of the prohibition of intervention. The permitted responses are therefore of another kind: investigations, diplomatic measures, sanctions. Since 2019 the EU has had a specific sanctions regime for cyberattacks. Symmetry test The same yardstick for evidence. If we demand public proof before attributing an attack to Moscow, the same demand applies to cyberattacks the press attributes to Western states, such as the Stuxnet virus against Iranian centrifuges, which the United States and Israel have never officially acknowledged. The same night. In the same hours as the attacks on the fridges, the air-raid alert apps of Ukraine and Russia showed false nuclear alerts. Kyiv blamed Moscow; the Russian app had been hit too, and nobody claimed it ( TweakTown ). Cyber warfare does not have a single author. The same yardstick for prevention. Those who ask Moscow to stop the groups operating from its territory must ask European operators to close the doors they leave open. The two responsibilities do not exclude each other. Our judgment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. The suspicion towards pro-Russian groups is well founded: they have a record, they boasted, and two Western governments have documented their links with the Russian state. But a well-founded suspicion is not proof, and the difference matters precisely because the political consequences are large. Authorities that speak of "hybrid war" should publish what they know, as Denmark did for the water plant. In the meantime there is something that can be done without waiting for any attribution: update the software and take exposed panels off the network. It costs little, and it is the defence that would have prevented freezers at 50 degrees. What to watch The investigations by Belgian prosecutors and national authorities: whether anyone publishes technical evidence about the perpetrator. Whether the Commission or the Council formally attributes the attacks, and whether they use the cyber sanctions regime. Verification of the sample of Danfoss credentials published by NoName057(16). New attacks against the cold rooms of hospitals, transfusion centres and food warehouses. The numbers: how many of the exposed systems are secured. Was Nord Stream a military objective?

In Hamburg, the defence of the Ukrainian accused of the sabotage argues that the pipeline was a legitimate target. We tested the claim against the law of war, with the same yardstick used for Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.

In brief On 26 September 2022 a series of explosions ripped open three of the four Nord Stream lines, in the economic waters of Denmark and Sweden. Since 14 October 2026 a former Ukrainian officer, Serhii Kuznietsov, has been on trial in Hamburg. He denies any involvement. The defence also argues something else: the pipeline was a legitimate military objective, "a weapon in the hands of the Russians". In 2025 a Polish judge said something similar, speaking of a "just war". American and Russian theories have also circulated: no investigation has confirmed them. According to Der Spiegel and the Wall Street Journal, the CIA knew of the Ukrainian plan and in June 2022 asked for it to be stopped. Under the law of war, an object is a military objective only if it makes an "effective contribution to military action" and destroying it offers a definite military advantage. When it was hit, Nord Stream was carrying no gas, was partly owned by European companies and lay in the waters of neutral countries. Germany's Federal Court of Justice has already written, in a ruling on pre-trial detention, that it was civilian infrastructure. The same criteria led the International Criminal Court to seek the arrest of Russia's top military commanders for the strikes on Ukraine's power grid. Our assessment: by the same yardstick, the military-objective argument does not hold. The justice of a war does not make every blow lawful. It is for the court, however, to establish who acted and on whose orders. The question We wrote about Nord Stream in the first piece of this series , on energy, to explain how Europe's dependence changed. Here we ask two questions. Who destroyed it, on the evidence available? And if it really was Ukraine, as the prosecution in Hamburg argues, was it a lawful act of war? The question matters beyond this trial. It concerns all energy infrastructure: pipelines, cables, refineries, power plants. And it concerns the yardstick Europe uses to judge attacks, depending on who carries them out. The charges against Kuznietsov have yet to be proven: we reason on the prosecution's hypothesis, not on established guilt. The facts The explosions. On 26 September 2022 a series of explosions damaged three of the four lines of Nord Stream 1 and 2, at a depth of about 80 metres near the Danish island of Bornholm ( Intellinews ). The explosions took place outside territorial waters, but within the exclusive economic zones of Denmark and Sweden. Neither country was at war. The state of the pipelines. Nord Stream 1 was no longer carrying gas: Moscow had cut off supplies at the end of August 2022. Nord Stream 2 had never entered service, because in February 2022 Germany had suspended its certification ( AP via ClickOnDetroit, 26/2/2024 ). Both, however, contained gas, which escaped into the sea. The owners. Nord Stream 1 was 51% owned by Russia's Gazprom. The rest belonged to four European companies: Germany's Wintershall Dea and E.ON (15.5% each), the Dutch Gasunie and France's Engie (9% each) ( Euronews, 27/9/2022 ). The damage to the environment. According to a study published in Nature, the lines released up to 485,000 tonnes of methane: four to five times the Aliso Canyon leak in California in 2015 ( Queen Mary University of London ). The investigations. Sweden and Denmark closed their investigations in February 2024 without charging anyone. Germany went ahead. Kuznietsov, arrested in Italy in August 2025, was handed over to Germany in November after Italy's Court of Cassation gave the green light ( Maritime Executive, 28/11/2025 ). The trial opened on 14 October 2026 before the Higher Regional Court in Hamburg. According to the prosecution, Kuznietsov and other Ukrainian military personnel acted "by order of Ukrainian state agencies" to permanently disrupt gas supplies. The defendant denies it and did not speak in court ( Courthouse News, 14/10/2026 ). There are four charges: a war crime (attacking protected civilian objects) and three ordinary offences, namely causing an explosion, destroying structures and disrupting public services ( Diplomacy and Law, 13/10/2026 ). Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office says it found no evidence of state involvement. A second suspect. Ukrainian diver Volodymyr Zhuravlyov was arrested in Poland in 2025. On 17 October 2025 a Warsaw court refused to hand him over to Germany and released him ( Notes from Poland, 17/10/2025 ). Arrested again in Croatia in August 2026, in September a Croatian court authorised his extradition; his lawyers have announced an appeal ( Euromaidan Press, 24/9/2026 ). Who was behind it: the theories Over these four years three different accounts have circulated, alongside the German prosecution's. We compared them with the same questions: who put them forward, what they rest on, who denies them, what investigations have made of them. United States Russia Ukraine, with the CIA informed Ukraine (German prosecution) Who put it forward Journalist Seymour Hersh, February 2023 German news site t-online, March 2023 Wall Street Journal (August 2024) and Der Spiegel (February 2026) German Federal Prosecutor What it rests on A single anonymous source Russian military ships in the area a few days before, with position signals switched off Anonymous sources, including one person who says he took part Judicial investigation: the rented yacht, false identity documents Who denies it White House and CIA Moscow blames the West CIA ("completely false"); Zaluzhny ("a provocation") Kyiv; the defendant What investigations have made of it None has confirmed it None has confirmed it Partly matches the German investigation Trial under way in Hamburg Sources for the table: Hersh and the denials ( Snopes, 10/2/2023 ); the Russian ships ( t-online, 25/3/2023 ); the Wall Street Journal ( Ukrainska Pravda, 15/8/2024 ); Der Spiegel ( taz, 19/2/2026 ); the charges and the false documents, from the German Federal Court of Justice ruling cited below. A few more details, because each theory has a strong point and a weak one. United States. Hersh wrote that US Navy divers, with Norway's help, planted the charges in June 2022 during a NATO exercise. In its favour, people cite a remark by Joe Biden on 7 February 2022: if Russia invades, "there will no longer be a Nord Stream 2. We will bring an end to it." But the whole account rests on one person nobody can verify. In March 2023 Russia asked the UN Security Council for an international inquiry: only Russia, China and Brazil voted in favour, while the other twelve members abstained ( Arab News, 28/3/2023 ). Russia. The theory of self-sabotage rests on movements of Russian ships reconstructed from satellite images and anonymous sources. The article itself uses the conditional: no ship was identified with certainty and no investigator has confirmed the lead. Ukraine, with the CIA informed. This is the most detailed account. According to Der Spiegel, in spring 2022 the Ukrainian group presented the plan to CIA contacts, who at first did not object. In June Dutch intelligence reportedly warned the CIA and German intelligence; at that point Washington reportedly asked Kyiv to stop, without success. The operation, costing about $300,000, was reportedly paid for by a private businessman. The two investigations, however, disagree on one point: for the Wall Street Journal, Zelensky had approved the plan and then asked for it to be stopped; for Der Spiegel he had not been informed, and the final word came from then commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhny. One thing is certain: the theories about the United States and Russia have, to date, found no confirmation in a court of law. The Ukrainian trail is the only one to have reached trial. What the law of war says The central rule is Article 52 of the First Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions. Attacks must be limited to military objectives. An object is a military objective only if two conditions are met together : by its nature, location, purpose or use it makes "an effective contribution to military action"; and its destruction offers, in the circumstances ruling at the time, "a definite military advantage". In case of doubt, an object normally used for civilian purposes is presumed civilian ( First Protocol, official text, Swiss Confederation ). The same Protocol lays down a principle that matters a great deal here: the rules apply to everyone, "without any adverse distinction based on the nature or origin of the armed conflict or on the causes espoused" by the parties. The law of war does not ask who is right in the war. It asks how the war is fought. It applies to the aggressor and to the victim of aggression alike. Experts are divided on one point: whether objects that finance a war, such as oil and gas exports, can become military objectives. The United States takes the broadest reading, but even for Washington an object that generates revenue is not, in itself, a military objective: a concrete link with operations is needed ( Lieber Institute, West Point, 7/7/2026 ). According to a number of scholars, most states take a narrower view. The two arguments The defence. In court, lawyer Nicola Canestrini called the pipelines "a weapon in the hands of the Russians" and asked for the charges to be dismissed ( Courthouse News ). The argument is that Moscow used gas to blackmail Europe and to finance the war. The Polish judge. In refusing Zhuravlyov's extradition, judge Dariusz Łubowski said Ukraine's defence is a "just war", and that blowing up the enemy's infrastructure in such a war "is not sabotage, but military action": "justified, rational and just". Prime Minister Donald Tusk commented: "The case is closed" ( Notes from Poland ). The German Federal Court of Justice. On 10 December 2025, ruling on Kuznietsov's pre-trial detention, the Federal Court of Justice wrote that the pipelines were civilian infrastructure and therefore not a legitimate target. It also ruled out combatant privilege: it does not cover military personnel who act covertly, without distinguishing themselves from civilians. And it found "strong grounds" to believe that the operation was decided and directed by the Ukrainian state. It was a provisional assessment, not a verdict ( LTO, 16/1/2026 ). The scholars. As early as 2023, legal scholar Alexander Lott of the Norwegian Centre for the Law of the Sea had reached the same conclusion: a doubtful military objective, because the pipelines also served Germany, which was not at war, and they carried no gas when they were hit. He added that the attack failed to take account of the marine environment ( University of Tromsø, 21/11/2023 ). The same yardstick To see whether the judgment changes depending on who strikes, we compared three campaigns against energy, with the same questions. Ukraine's power grid Russian refineries Nord Stream Who strikes Russia Ukraine Ukraine, according to the German prosecution (Kyiv denies it) Where In Ukraine, a country at war In Russia, a country at war In Danish and Swedish waters, countries not at war Did it serve the armed forces when it was hit? In part: a grid with civilian and military use In part: some supply the army, others export No: no gas flowing, one line never in service What courts or experts have said The International Criminal Court sought the arrest of four senior Russian officers for attacks on civilian objects and excessive harm to civilians Lawful for those that supply the army; for export facilities the call is "too close" German Federal Court of Justice (provisionally): civilian infrastructure Sources for the table: for the power grid, the International Criminal Court warrants against Kobylash and Sokolov (March 2024) and against Shoigu and Gerasimov (June 2024), for strikes between October 2022 and March 2023 ( JusticeInfo, 25/6/2024 ); for the refineries, the Lieber Institute analysis; for Nord Stream, the German Federal Court of Justice ruling cited above. The comparison says something simple: the same criteria that make Russia's strikes on Ukraine's power grid unlawful also weigh on Nord Stream, and weigh more heavily. Nord Stream is the case furthest from a military objective: it was not in use, it was not in a country at war and it was partly owned by companies from Ukraine's allies. What worked European judicial cooperation worked, at least in part. Italy handed Kuznietsov over under the European arrest warrant, and a Croatian court authorised the surrender of the second suspect. Germany is trying in public a citizen of a country it supports with weapons and money, on a charge that implicates the Ukrainian state. The trial will allow the evidence to be tested in court, with the defence present. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. By the same yardstick we apply to Russia, the military-objective argument does not hold. An idle pipeline, in the waters of countries not at war, partly European-owned, was making no effective contribution to Russian military action. Depriving Moscow of future revenue is not enough: if it were, every income-producing asset would become a target, in every war. And the damage to the environment, hundreds of thousands of tonnes of methane, fell on everyone. The Warsaw judge's "just war" conflates two questions that the law deliberately keeps apart: why a war is fought and how it is fought. Ukraine has the right to defend itself. That does not make every blow lawful, just as the defence claimed by Moscow does not make it lawful to bomb Ukraine's power stations in winter. Whoever accepts the argument for Nord Stream must accept it when the other side uses it too. Then there is a European point. If the accounts by Der Spiegel and the Wall Street Journal are true, Dutch, German and American intelligence knew of the plan three months in advance: it is legitimate to ask what they did to stop it, and why they failed. An infrastructure in which German, Dutch and French companies had invested was destroyed; the head of an EU government welcomed the release of one suspect, while Germany is trying another. If the prosecution's case is confirmed, Europe will have to say clearly what it has so far avoided saying: that even a country under attack, and supported by Europe, is bound by the rules Europe asks others to respect. But Kuznietsov's responsibility, and that of the Ukrainian state, will be established by the court, not by us. What to watch The next hearings in Hamburg, scheduled until December, and the testimony of the military commanders called by the defence. Whether the trial brings out what American, Dutch and German intelligence knew, and when. Whether the court finds the war crime proven, or only the ordinary offences. Zhuravlyov's appeal in Croatia and his possible surrender to Germany. Attacks on energy in the ongoing war, by both sides, with winter approaching.
