The bill for rearmament: who pays, and under what rules

Europe has decided to raise defence spending to 5% of GDP by 2035. For weapons, budget rules can be suspended and procedures shortened; for healthcare, schools and diplomacy, they cannot. What the numbers say, who has already paid, and what remains to be decided.

In brief At the NATO summit in The Hague (June 2025) the allies committed to spending 5% of GDP by 2035: at least 3.5% on defence proper, up to 1.5% on critical infrastructure, networks and civil protection. The figure was requested by Washington, which then threatened tariffs against the only government that held back, Spain's. The EU-US trade deal of July 2025 puts 15% tariffs and purchases of American weapons in the same package; according to the US ambassador to NATO, about half of the allies' new commitments concern weapons made in the United States. The European Union has created fast tools for defence: 150 billion in loans (SAFE), approved in about ten weeks through an emergency procedure that excludes the European Parliament; a derogation from the Stability Pact that allows a larger deficit, but only for defence (and, since June 2026, for part of energy spending); a 2028-2034 budget proposal that multiplies funds for defence and space by five. The same derogations do not exist for healthcare, education, justice or diplomacy. The share of the EU budget for conflict prevention has fallen, and a proposal under discussion would cut the instrument that funds it twice as much as the rest. Who has already paid: development aid in the United Kingdom and Belgium, civilian infrastructure in the United Kingdom, a public holiday in Denmark. In Italy the Parliamentary Budget Office warns that once the derogation ends, from 2029 the accounts get more complicated; the government says welfare will not be touched. Whether spending is "too much" depends on a comparison the numbers do not settle: measured in dollars, Europe spends almost three times as much as Russia; measured in purchasing power, the gap narrows sharply. The NATO declaration ties the 3.5% to the Alliance's capability targets, which are classified: no citizen can check whether the figure matches the needs. The number that will decide European military spending over the next ten years was born in a negotiation. 5% of GDP is the figure demanded by the Trump administration and accepted by the allies in The Hague, split into two items to make it bearable. NATO says the first item serves to meet its capability targets; those targets, however, are not public. So, in the debate, European governments do not explain what is needed: they explain how they will reach the percentage. This Analysis follows the money: where it comes from, which rules were changed to find it, and who risks losing it. The facts The commitment. On 25 June 2025 the 32 allies signed a declaration committing them to spend by 2035 at least 3.5% of GDP on "core defence requirements" and up to 1.5% on protecting critical infrastructure, defending networks, and ensuring civil preparedness and resilience ( LaPresse ). The second item is less defined than the first, and we will come back to this. The European tools. In March 2025 the Commission presented the ReArm Europe plan, later renamed Readiness 2030, aiming to mobilise more than 800 billion ( European Commission ). The first pillar, SAFE, offers up to 150 billion in loans for joint arms purchases ( EU Council ). The second is a derogation from budget rules, discussed below. In its proposal for the 2028-2034 budget the Commission foresees 131 billion for defence and space, five times more than today ( Commission, via FastForward ). Actual spending. According to the Swedish institute SIPRI, in 2025 the 29 European members of NATO spent 559 billion dollars, and 22 of them exceeded 2% of GDP. Russia spent 190 billion, 7.5% of its GDP; Ukraine 84 billion, 40% of its own ( SIPRI ). Where the 5% comes from The pressure. The figure was requested by Washington, and accompanied by trade threats. In The Hague the only government that rejected the target was Spain's, which signed the declaration but committed to 2.1%, arguing that this was enough to meet the capabilities required by the Alliance without compromising social spending ( La Notizia ). The US president replied at a press conference that he would make Spain pay "twice as much" in the tariff deal ( Sky TG24 ); in October he suggested expelling it from NATO ( Open ); at the Ankara summit, in July 2026, he said he no longer wanted to do business with Spain and asked his Treasury Secretary to "cut" ( AFP, via Kuwait Times ). On the eve of the same summit the administration did not rule out sanctions for allies lagging behind, tariffs included ( Washington Examiner ). Weapons and trade in the same package. A month after The Hague, on 27 July 2025, the trade deal between the United States and the EU set 15% tariffs on most European goods and placed, next to energy purchases, the European intention to buy large quantities of American weapons ( Al Jazeera ). According to the US ambassador to NATO, of the roughly 139 billion dollars in new commitments made by the allies after The Hague, about half concerns equipment, weapons and ammunition produced in the United States ( Washington Examiner ). Not only Washington. It would be wrong, however, to tell the story of European rearmament as an order carried out. The ReArm Europe plan was presented in March 2025, three months before The Hague, partly out of fear that the United States would no longer defend Europe. Poland and the Baltic states had been calling for more spending for years, and the Estonian prime minister said that everyone, Spain included, should reach 5% ( Euronews ). American pressure set the figure and the timetable; fear of Russia, and of the United States, did the rest. A rule for weapons, none for services The derogation. The Stability Pact limits the growth of public spending in EU countries. On 19 March 2025 the Commission established that Russia's invasion of Ukraine is an "exceptional circumstance" that allows the national escape clause to be activated, and invited states to use it in a coordinated way ( Osservatorio CPI ). In practice a state can spend up to 1.5% of GDP more, for four years, without breaching the Pact, provided the money goes to defence ( Italpress ). By February 2026 seventeen states had been authorised ( Eunews ). On 8 October the Commission gave the green light to Italy too, for defence and, since this year, for part of its energy spending ( Il Post ). What is missing. A similar derogation for healthcare, education, justice or the maintenance of civilian infrastructure does not exist. A government wanting to hire doctors or rebuild schools with the same deficit granted for weapons would break the rules. This is not an accusation: it is the text of the rules. The consequence, however, is that for the same need, military spending is the easiest to finance. The procedure. The timing differs too. SAFE was proposed on 19 March 2025 and adopted on 27 May. To move fast the Commission chose Article 122 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, an emergency clause that leaves the European Parliament out of the decision. Parliament asked the Court of Justice to annul the regulation, challenging not its content but its method ( La Notizia ); the case is pending. Who has already paid Development aid. In February 2025 the United Kingdom decided to bring defence to 2.5% of GDP by 2027, financing the increase by cutting development aid from 0.5% to 0.3% of GDP; the responsible minister resigned ( LaPresse ). Belgium cut its aid budget by 25% ( Brussels Times ). Civilian infrastructure. In the plan presented on 30 June 2026, the British government also financed the defence increase by cutting civilian infrastructure projects, from roads to energy ( laRegione ). Work. In 2023 Denmark abolished a religious holiday, Store Bededag, to raise about 400 million euros a year for defence; three Danes in four were against it ( Il Post ; Italian Chamber of Commerce in Denmark ). Conflict prevention. In the EU budget the share devoted to peacebuilding and conflict prevention has fallen since 2021 from 3.7% to 2.6% ( FIIA ). For 2028-2034 a proposal by the Irish presidency would cut the instrument that also funds peacebuilding, Global Europe, by almost 16%, twice the average cut ( IRC ). The Italian case. Here there are no cuts yet, and the debate is open. In mid-October the prime minister said that defence funds "are not money taken from healthcare or schools". On 12 October, at a hearing, the Parliamentary Budget Office had explained that the derogation increases the deficit but does not create permanent spending room, and that from 2029, once the clause closes, the picture gets more complicated: a large part of the allocations concerns personnel and multi-year programmes that do not stop with the derogation. The Office asked the government to state already in the budget law how defence and energy will be financed after 2028 ( Teleborsa ; Il Fatto Quotidiano ). In other words: today we pay with debt, tomorrow someone will have to pay the debt. The labelling trick The 1.5% item is broad: infrastructure protection, networks, civil preparedness, innovation, industrial base. This is where some governments try to fit in spending already decided. In July 2025 the Italian government considered counting the bridge over the Strait of Messina, about 13.5 billion, and the new breakwater of the port of Genoa as infrastructure of military value ( Il Post ; Il Fatto Quotidiano ). The US ambassador to NATO replied that the bridge has no military value; the transport ministry responded that the project is financed with state funds and not with defence funds ( Il Post ; Open ). The label can be used in two directions. You can call a civilian project "defence" to reach the percentage without spending more; or you can pass off as "civil security" spending that is in fact military. Either way the citizen no longer knows what he is paying for. L'Espresso wrote as much about Italy: for years defence spending has been judged by accounting targets, not strategic ones ( L'Espresso ). Too much, or enough? This is the hardest question, and the numbers do not settle it. Measured in dollars at market exchange rates, spending by NATO's European members is almost triple Russia's. Measured at purchasing power parity, that is, taking into account that in Russia a soldier or a shell costs much less, the gap shrinks almost to nothing, and some argue that Russia spends more than all of Europe combined ( Money.it ; IISS, via Startmag ). The two measures answer different questions, and whoever quotes only one has already chosen the conclusion. What is missing, in any case, is the intermediate step in public form. NATO's capability targets, to which the Hague declaration ties the 3.5%, are classified ( LaPresse ). Secrecy about exactly what is lacking has understandable military reasons; but without at least a public version, no Parliament can judge whether the figure is right. The 5% is a spending target, not a result target. You can reach it by buying the wrong things, or miss it and have what you need. Legal commentary The EU budget and weapons. The Treaty on European Union prohibits financing from the common budget operations with military or defence implications (Article 41(2)). This is why the common European part of military aid to Ukraine goes through the European Peace Facility, which sits off-budget and is paid by the states, and why SAFE takes the form of loans. These are legitimate solutions, but they reduce the control of the European Parliament, which has co-decision powers over the ordinary budget. Article 122. The clause is designed for severe difficulties in the supply of certain products or for exceptional circumstances. It was used for the pandemic and for the energy crisis. Using it for a long-term loan programme is the choice Parliament is challenging before the Court. If the Court upholds it, Article 122 will become the ordinary route for urgent decisions, and the definition of "urgent" will be given by the government of the day. The derogation from the Pact. The national escape clause (Article 26 of EU Regulation 2024/1263) requires exceptional circumstances outside the state's control and spending that does not endanger debt sustainability in the medium term. The war in Ukraine can be an exceptional circumstance. A spending commitment running to 2035, with personnel and programmes lasting decades, is harder to fit into the word "temporary". Symmetry test The opposing argument. Some argue that defence and welfare are not alternatives but complements: without security Europe attracts less investment, grows less and in the end cannot pay for the welfare state. Lorenzo Bini Smaghi is among those who make this case, noting that the Nordic countries, with the strongest welfare states, are also those that have increased military spending most ( IEP Bocconi ). It is a serious argument. But it holds only if growth really comes, and it does not say who pays in the meantime. The threat is real. Russia has attacked a European country, spends 7.5% of GDP on defence, and Danish intelligence believes it could be ready for a large-scale war against Europe within five years (same IISS source). Those who criticise rearmament must say what they propose instead: it is not enough to say it costs too much. The same yardstick for the accounts. If we denounce "creative accounting" when a government calls a bridge defence, we must also denounce it when a government calls weapons spending infrastructure, or when critics of rearmament set side by side figures that measure different things. Our judgment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. The problem is not that Europe defends itself. It is that the rules have been changed in one direction only. For weapons, the deficit is allowed, the procedure is shortened, Parliament is bypassed, the labels are widened. For schools, healthcare, justice and diplomacy the old rules apply, and in some cases deeper cuts. For the same need, the spending with the most convenient rules always wins. Rearmament decided this way is disproportionate not because the threat is invented, but because the figure comes before the needs, and the costs are pushed forward, onto budgets that will have to repay the debt once the derogation is over. And it is dangerous because every euro spent without a plan is a euro that buys no security, and every year spent rearming without a diplomatic channel makes more likely the very war it claims to want to avoid. What can be done The proposals that follow are also the basis of a manifesto and a petition on this site. A social clause. No increase in defence spending financed by cuts to healthcare, education, justice and civilian infrastructure. If a larger deficit is allowed for weapons, the same rule must protect essential services. Needs first, then the number. Every government should present to Parliament a public version of the missing capabilities and their costs, and justify spending on that basis, not on a percentage of GDP. Honest labels. Separate, verifiable accounts for defence proper and for civil security. No civilian project counted as defence, no military spending hidden among infrastructure. Parliament decides. No emergency procedures such as Article 122 for long-term programmes. Parity for diplomacy. Conflict prevention is not cut more than the rest of the budget, and the EU equips itself with an envoy with a mandate for negotiations on Ukraine. We decide. Defence spending is set on European needs, not under the threat of tariffs, and is not tied to trade deals. Purchases are chosen for what they are needed for, not for the flag of whoever makes them: neither to please Washington nor to favour European industry. Those who want to act have some real levers: the national Parliament, which votes on the budget and gives direction to the government in the Council; petitions to the European Parliament (Article 227 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU); the vote. What to watch The Court of Justice ruling on the European Parliament's challenge to SAFE. Negotiations on the 2028-2034 EU budget: funds for defence and for Global Europe. National budget laws for 2027: where the funding for defence is found. The Council's decision on the escape clause for Italy, expected by November. The national plans the allies must submit to NATO every year, and what they count in them. How far self-defence goes: Ukraine's attacks inside Russia, one by one

Ukraine strikes air bases, refineries, tankers and generals on Russian territory. Is it lawful to defend yourself by attacking? It depends on the target and the means. A map by category, with the same yardstick we use for Russia.

— Russia – Ukraine – Black Sea In brief The UN Charter recognises the right of a state under attack to defend itself (Article 51). This right does not stop at the border: against an ongoing armed attack, Ukraine may strike military objectives in Russia too, provided it does so in a necessary and proportionate way. Each individual attack, however, must also respect humanitarian law: military objectives only, no disproportionate harm to civilians, all feasible precautions. Lawful without serious doubt: attacks on air bases and bombers (operation "Spiderweb", June 2025), the incursion into the Kursk region (2024), the killing of officers on active duty, with a limit on the means. Contested : attacks on refineries and pipelines, and on tankers of the "shadow fleet", especially far from the front and under the flags of third countries. Unlawful : the killing of targeted civilians, such as Darya Dugina and the blogger Vladlen Tatarsky; indiscriminate attacks on border towns, if confirmed; the sabotage of Nord Stream, according to the German court that is trying a former Ukrainian officer. The same yardstick applies to Russia, which has caused the great majority of civilian casualties in this war: according to the UN, 96% of civilian casualties in the first half of 2026 were on Ukrainian territory. In June 2025 more than a hundred drones, hidden in the trailers of trucks that had entered Russia, took off near four air bases, as far as the Arctic. In July 2026 Ukrainian naval drones hit 28 vessels in one night in the Sea of Azov. In less than two years, in and around Moscow, at least three Russian generals have been killed by bombs. Ukraine is taking the war inside Russia, and part of the European public wonders whether this is still defence. International law has an answer, but it is not a yes or a no: it is a list of conditions, to be applied case by case. How the war came about we reconstructed in "From 1990 to 2022" , with the wrongs of all sides; the conclusion of that piece is also the starting point of this one: no Western mistake makes an invasion lawful, and therefore Ukraine has the right to defend itself. The question here is how far. The rule Two levels. International law looks at war on two planes. The first concerns why force is used: the UN Charter prohibits it (Article 2(4); see use of force ) with one exception, self-defence against an armed attack (Article 51). The International Court of Justice has made clear that defence must be necessary and proportionate (Nicaragua, 1986; Oil Platforms, 2003). Proportionality is measured against the aim, stopping the aggression, and not blow by blow. Against an ongoing invasion that occupies about a fifth of Ukrainian territory, striking the bases from which missiles and bombers take off is hard to regard as disproportionate. The second plane concerns how : humanitarian law, which applies to the aggressor and the victim alike. Only military objectives may be attacked, that is, objects which by their nature, location, purpose or use make an effective contribution to military action and whose destruction offers a definite military advantage (Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, Article 52). Even a military objective may not be attacked if the expected harm to civilians is excessive in relation to the advantage (Article 51). And all feasible precautions must be taken (Article 57). Russia and Ukraine are parties to these treaties, and the rules are customary law in any case. Being attacked, then, does not give the right to do anything at all. But nor does it take the right away. Lawful Air bases and bombers. On 1 June 2025 Ukraine's security service (SBU) launched operation "Spiderweb". According to Al Jazeera, 117 drones smuggled into Russia were launched together near the airfields where strategic bombers were parked, including the Olenya base in the Arctic, about 2,000 kilometres from Ukraine ( Al Jazeera ). The SBU spoke of 41 aircraft hit; satellite images analysed by independent sources confirmed at least thirteen in the first days ( The Insider ). The bombers from which missiles are launched at Ukrainian cities are military objectives by nature. This is the clearest case. The Kursk incursion. In August 2024 the Ukrainian army entered Russia's Kursk region and occupied part of it for some months, before Russian troops, helped by North Korean soldiers, took it back. Taking the war onto the aggressor's territory falls within self-defence. But whoever occupies territory, even briefly, has the obligations of an occupying power towards the civilians who live there (Fourth Geneva Convention). The judgment on those months depends on how they were treated. Officers on duty. In December 2024 General Igor Kirillov, head of Russia's chemical defence troops, was killed in Moscow by a bomb hidden in a scooter; the SBU openly claimed it. There followed General Yaroslav Moskalik, in April 2025, and General Fanil Sarvarov, in December 2025, both by car bombs, and in June 2026 Damir Davydov, who ran the army's supply of missiles and artillery ammunition; Ukraine has not commented ( Euromaidan Press ; The Washington Times ). A soldier on active duty is a legitimate target, even far from the front and outside working hours. The limit is the means. A bomb in a courtyard or a car park in a residential neighbourhood must avoid disproportionate harm to passers-by, and the law prohibits killing by feigning protected status, that is, by perfidy (Article 37 of Protocol I). A hidden bomb is not in itself perfidy. Trump's envoy for Ukraine, Keith Kellogg, said however that the killing of Kirillov violated the rules of war ( Strat News Global ). Contested Refineries and pipelines. This is the broadest campaign. According to the International Energy Agency, at the end of August 2026 only five large Russian refineries had not yet been hit by Ukrainian drones ( IEA ). The legal question is whether a refinery is a military objective. According to the prevailing view, oil infrastructure is not one by nature: it can become one through use or purpose ( Lieber Institute, West Point ). A refinery that supplies the army becomes one: an analysis by Global Witness found that some of the refineries hit had supplied fuel to the Russian armed forces ( Global Witness ). In April 2024 the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe declared Russian refineries legitimate targets (same source). More doubtful is the case of a plant hit only because it earns money for Russia: American doctrine accepts striking objects that "sustain the war" by financing it; the International Committee of the Red Cross does not. The judgment must be made plant by plant. The Druzhba pipeline adds a problem: it carries Russian oil to Hungary and Slovakia, the last EU countries still receiving it by this route. In July the two governments protested over three interruptions in less than two weeks caused by Ukrainian attacks ( The Moscow Times ). But the longest stoppage, from January, had been caused by a Russian attack on a station in western Ukraine ( Reuters, via Devdiscourse ). Hitting a plant in Russia that also serves allies does not make it unlawful, but the harm to third parties enters the proportionality calculation. The tankers of the "shadow fleet". Since late 2025 Ukraine has been hitting with naval drones the tankers that carry Russian oil while evading sanctions: in the Black Sea, including off the Turkish coast, and in December 2025, for the first time, in the Mediterranean, where an SBU source called the ship "an absolutely legitimate target" ( Kyiv Post ). Putin spoke of piracy ( Dawn ). Here the law is stricter than on land. An enemy merchant ship may be attacked only if it has become a military objective; a ship flying the flag of a neutral country may, as a rule, be stopped and captured, not sunk (San Remo Manual on International Law Applicable to Armed Conflicts at Sea, 1994, paragraphs 59-60 and 67). Many ships of the shadow fleet fly the flags of third countries. Hitting them only because they bring money to Moscow is the same controversial thesis of objects that "sustain the war", with an added risk for neutral countries and their crews. The position is stronger for the ships in the Sea of Azov carrying fuel to occupied Crimea, where Russian troops use it: on 11 July 2026 Ukraine hit 28 of them in one night ( Ground News, summarising several sources ). Unlawful Targeted civilians. In August 2022 Darya Dugina, a nationalist commentator and daughter of the ideologue Alexander Dugin, was killed by a car bomb near Moscow. American officials said they believed the attack had been authorised by elements of the Ukrainian government ( The Washington Times ); Kyiv denied it. In April 2023 the military blogger Vladlen Tatarsky (Maxim Fomin) was killed by an explosive statuette in a café in St Petersburg ( Kyiv Post ). Someone who makes war propaganda is not a combatant. Killing a civilian for supporting the enemy is murder, and in war it is a crime. Attacks on border towns. Russia's Belgorod region has been hit for years. On 20 July 2026 a Ukrainian drone hit a bus in Shebekino, killing five people, including a child ( AFP, via BSS ); in December 2023 Moscow reported at least 20 dead in central Belgorod, accusing Ukraine of using cluster munitions ( SBS ). Russian authorities speak of 250 civilians killed in Russia in the first half of 2026, but the UN is unable to verify this ( Arab News ). Not all these attacks are necessarily unlawful: a border town may host military objectives. But if an attack hits a bus or a square without a precise military objective, or with weapons that do not discriminate, it is a war crime. Judging requires independent investigations, which are not possible in Russia today. Nord Stream. On 30 June 2026 the German federal prosecutor indicted a former Ukrainian officer, Serhii Kuznietsov, as head of the group that blew up the Baltic pipelines in September 2022. According to the indictment, he and the others were soldiers acting on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities, and the charge includes complicity in a war crime: the attack on civilian infrastructure ( Eurointegration ). The trial opened in Hamburg on 14 October ( Euronews ). Germany's Federal Court of Justice, in a decision on pre-trial detention, wrote that the pipeline was civilian infrastructure in neutral waters and could not be a military objective ( Babel ); the defence argues the opposite. Kyiv denies organising the sabotage. If the charge is proven, Nord Stream will be the clearest example of the limit of defence: a civilian asset, in the waters of third countries, owned in part by European companies. We analysed the question in detail in "Was Nord Stream a military objective?" , in the series "Europe's choices" . Is the arms supplier complicit? In general, no. Helping a state exercising self-defence is not a wrongful act, because the defence is lawful. The supplier is responsible in two cases. The first: if it supplies weapons knowing they will be used to commit war crimes (Article 16 of the Articles on State Responsibility; Arms Trade Treaty, Articles 6 and 7, for states parties; EU Common Position 2008/944). The second: if it takes direct part in operations, for example by choosing targets. The restrictions some allies placed on the use of their long-range weapons against Russian territory were political choices, not legal obligations. According to Kyiv, most of the attacks described here, refineries included, are carried out with drones built in Ukraine. And the price of energy? The attacks on refineries have reduced Russian fuel production and pushed Moscow to restrict diesel exports. According to Axios, the drone campaign is helping to push up world energy prices, already high because of the war with Iran ( Axios ). The effect concerns diesel above all. The cost of energy for European industry depends mainly on gas and electricity, and the EU has not imported Russian refined products since 2023. A cost to third parties does not make an attack on a military objective unlawful; it can, however, enter into the allies' political choices. Symmetry test The same rule for Moscow. If a refinery that supplies the army is a legitimate target, so is a Ukrainian fuel depot. If a power station that serves homes is a civilian object, it is one on both sides. In 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants against four senior Russian commanders, including former defence minister Shoigu and chief of the general staff Gerasimov, for attacks on the Ukrainian power grid, considered directed against civilian objects or in any case disproportionate ( see our page on ICC fugitives ). The proportions. The yardstick is the same, the numbers are not. According to the UN, in the first half of 2026, 96% of civilian casualties were recorded on Ukrainian territory, caused largely by Russian long-range missiles and drones; the same source reports Russian figures on casualties in Russia, without being able to verify them ( Gwara Media ). Saying that Ukraine commits wrongful acts does not reduce Russia's responsibility; saying that Russia commits many more does not erase Ukraine's. The same Court for everyone. Ukraine rightly asks the International Criminal Court to judge Russian crimes. It has been a party to the Rome Statute since 1 January 2025. But at ratification it used a transitional provision, Article 124, to exclude for seven years the Court's jurisdiction over war crimes allegedly committed by its nationals: it is the first time a state has used it in this way ( Coalition for the ICC ). Amnesty International has asked for the declaration to be withdrawn ( Amnesty ). It is a clause provided by the Statute, but it is also the point where the yardstick risks not being the same for everyone. The sources. On many of these episodes the sources are partisan: the Russian authorities for casualties in Russia, the SBU for the results of its operations. We have flagged them as such, and where independent verification exists we have preferred it. Our judgment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. The question "can you defend yourself by attacking?" has a clear answer: yes. A country that has been invaded is not obliged to wait for missiles on its own territory, and striking the bases from which they are launched is defence in the strictest sense. Those who ask Ukraine not to touch Russian territory are asking it, in practice, to fight with one hand tied. But the law that protects Ukraine from aggression is the same law that sets it limits. A bomb for a blogger, a drone on a bus, a civilian pipeline in neutral waters are not defence: they are the same logic Ukraine rightly denounces when Moscow applies it. Supporting Ukraine's defence and demanding that it respect humanitarian law are not two positions in conflict. They are the same position. What to watch The Hamburg trial on Nord Stream and the possible extradition of the other suspects. Independent investigations, if they ever become possible, into the attacks in the Belgorod region. The position of flag states and of Turkey on attacks on tankers in or near their waters. Allies' statements on the use of the weapons they supply against Russian territory. Whether Ukraine withdraws its Article 124 declaration (see the symmetry test), and whether the International Criminal Court opens investigations into Ukrainian conduct. The blindfold: Europe trading cars for weapons
An editorial by N3R1-70: Europe's car industry crisis is being used to justify converting car plants into weapons plants — without a European peace initiative to match Europe's rearmament.

«Europe's car industry isn't dying. It's being killed.» — N3R1-70 For decades, the car industry was a pillar of the continent's economy: millions of jobs, know-how built up over generations, a symbol of the Old Continent's manufacturing capacity itself. Today that pillar is buckling. And the wreckage is not an accident along the way, but the result of political mistakes, strategic short-sightedness, and a chronic inability to read one's own times. A crisis foretold, and badly handled The shift to electric vehicles was necessary. But it was imposed on unrealistic deadlines, without the European industrial supply chain — batteries, raw materials, charging infrastructure — being remotely ready. On the same transition, the Chinese had invested years ahead of time, with consistent state backing. Europe chased an ideology without building the material conditions to achieve it. The slow decision-making of our democracies did the rest. Twenty-seven national interests to mediate. Biblical implementation timelines. Rules that change mid-course. The result is there for everyone to see: factories closing, the supply chain crumbling, hundreds of thousands of workers at risk of losing their jobs. People watched, discussed, produced papers. But nobody saw the avalanche coming. Or perhaps nobody wanted to. From jobs crisis to the wartime shortcut Faced with this scenario, the response taking shape in several European capitals is not an industrial strategy for recovery, but a conversion: turning car plants into weapons production sites. Europe's rearmament, fueled by the war in Ukraine, now offers a perfect cover for anyone looking for a quick fix to the jobs problem. It is presented as a pragmatic choice: save jobs, retrain skills, give new momentum to a struggling sector. But it is a patch stitched over a much deeper wound. «Dependence on a market in crisis is being swapped for dependence on a war economy — inherently unstable, tied to conflict cycles that no one should wish to feed for industrial reasons.» The paradox: no diplomatic initiative of its own What makes this choice even more serious is the contrast with Europe's political inaction on the diplomatic front. The European Union has mobilized huge resources to support Ukraine militarily and financially — but that is wartime support, not a European diplomatic initiative for a negotiated solution. This past year's peace-plan attempts have come almost entirely from Washington: the 28-point Witkoff-Dmitriev plan is the initiative that opened the most concrete phase of negotiations. Europe responded with its own counter-proposal — also 28 points, with substantial changes to the terms least favorable to Kyiv — but that was a reaction to the American text, not a negotiating initiative born in Brussels. On the Middle East front, the picture is no different: no European diplomatic initiative of weight comparable to the American, Egyptian, or Qatari ones. If the stated goal were truly the continent's security and stability, one would expect Europe to build its own peace initiative, not just its own arsenal. Instead: on the peace front, a marginal role or one of playing catch-up. On the arms front, an unrestrained race. Keeping tension high, cultivating a permanent state of alarm, has a precise effect on public opinion: it makes it more pliable, more willing to accept as necessary a choice that, under normal conditions, would meet with far more resistance. Fear becomes the tool for building consent around a long-term industrial decision. It is a strategy as old as the world: manufacture the enemy to legitimize rearmament. The wrong ally There is a further layer to this story that needs to be brought to light: the nature of the alliance on which Europe is betting its rearmament. The United States, the continent's historic partner, is going through a phase of structural economic fragility, with public debt having reached record levels. This is not a marginal detail: a long-term security strategy is being built on the reliability of an ally whose own economic solidity is a matter of growing uncertainty. And yet Europe keeps following it, not out of an updated calculation of strategic advantage, but out of historical habit — the inertia of an Atlantic bond built after the Second World War and never truly rethought. An ally that shares many values, but that in recent years has repeatedly shown itself moving in directions distant from, if not opposite to, the principles Europe claims to defend. There is also an equally delicate technical issue: most of the weapons systems and security infrastructure on which Europe has built its defense depend on technologies, software, and command systems that remain under US control. «It is like buying a house whose seller keeps a set of the keys: how autonomous is European security, if the keys to those systems are not in European hands?» A change of administration in Washington, a shift in priorities, and the balance on which Europe has built its defense could prove extremely fragile. And there is a demographic fact that is systematically ignored: the West, with Europe at the front, has for years registered a birth-rate decline that undermines, at the root, the sustainability of its own social and economic model. A far more decisive problem, over the coming decades, than any contingent military balance. But it is discussed in hushed tones, almost as a taboo — it's easier to deal with tanks, which at least give the illusion of doing something. In this scenario, the prospect of closer relations with Russia, with Middle Eastern countries, and along the routes of the new Silk Road — anchored to respect for European values, not accepted uncritically — would have offered a more lasting horizon than one built on an Atlantic alliance increasingly marked by its own contradictions. It is a reflection that requires an effort of political imagination that, in Brussels, for now, no one seems willing to make. A missed opportunity The question Europe should be asking itself is not how to convert car factories into weapons factories, but how to stabilize its own economy, revive innovation, invest in research and training, and build structural growth that does not depend on scenarios of conflict. That would mean tackling the unresolved knots of the energy transition, supporting research into new technologies, creating the industrial conditions — not just the regulatory ones — for Europe to become competitive again. It would mean looking forward instead of backward. Those who support wartime conversion make non-trivial arguments: deterrence is a recognized element of international relations, and the geopolitical context has pushed other countries too to strengthen their defense capabilities. But these objections do not erase the fact that Europe is handling the car crisis with the same short-sightedness that generated it: without a vision, without a project, without the courage to look beyond the immediate emergency. Choosing the arms route to stem the jobs hemorrhage is understandable in the urgency of the short term. But it is a blindfold with respect to the future: it solves a problem today by creating a structurally more serious one tomorrow, and it diverts attention — and resources — from what would truly be needed to guarantee a stable, innovative, and prosperous Europe. The real indictment Europe keeps producing weapons to defend a present it failed to build, while the future — made of innovation, intelligent ecological transition, diplomacy — waits in vain for someone to look up beyond its own backyard. Gripped by fear and inertia, Europe's leadership prefers to keep its eyes down and its hands busy: better a rifle than a strategy. This, in the end, is the real indictment. Not the car crisis, not Chinese competition, not the badly managed electric transition. It is the inability to think about tomorrow because too busy surviving today. And while everyone's mouth is full of 'security' and 'deterrence,' Europe is missing the chance to build something that lasts: a solid economy, a cohesive society, a future written with research and knowledge, not with steel. «The blindfold will have to fall, sooner or later. The question is whether, when it falls, we will still find a horizon ahead of us, or only a wall.» Related pieces: The bill for rearmament: who pays, and under what rules European Union Russia–Ukraine Rearmament Automotive industry
Rearmament is a dish best served cold

To arm itself, the European Union found an emergency procedure in ten weeks. To talk to those who threaten it, after more than a year and a half, it has still not found a name. An Opinion on the asymmetry between defence and diplomacy.

On the night of 2 November the freezers of hundreds of supermarkets, in at least eleven European countries, rose to 50 degrees. Nobody forced a door: someone got into control software left exposed online, often old, sometimes with the factory password ( the facts here ). Two pro-Russian groups claimed responsibility, without verified evidence. Within a few days the episode was absorbed into a bigger story, the one about hybrid war and a Europe that must rearm. The countermeasures experts pointed to, however, were of another order: take the panels off the network, change the passwords, update the software. For the freezers, that was enough. Let me start with what must be conceded, because it is true. The threat exists. The groups that claimed the attacks have a record, and two Western governments have documented their links with the Russian state. Ukraine has the right to defend itself, and helping it do so is lawful. Those who say that appointing a European envoy today to negotiate with Moscow would be a gift to the Kremlin have a serious argument: in May Russia threatened foreign diplomats in Kyiv, and Kaja Kallas maintains that Europe cannot be a neutral mediator, because it stands with the victim of aggression ( Euronews ). Perhaps she is right. Perhaps an envoy today would only get a refusal. I do not know. But I do know something else: the question is not whether Europe should defend itself, but how fast its two hands move, the one that arms and the one that negotiates. And here is the point. The SAFE regulation, 150 billion in loans for defence, was proposed on 19 March 2025 and adopted on 27 May: about ten weeks ( EU Council ). To move fast, Article 122 of the Treaties was used, the emergency clause that leaves the European Parliament out, so much so that Parliament took the Council to the Court of Justice ( La Notizia ). The idea of an envoy for the negotiations had been under discussion since March 2025 ( Politico, via Torre ); in May 2026 ministers decided to postpone it until the demands to be made of Moscow are defined ( Table.Media ). For weapons, the emergency. For peace, the preconditions. The same imbalance shows in the budget: the proposal for 2028-2034 multiplies funds for defence and space by five ( Commission, via FastForward ), while the instrument that also funds conflict prevention faces a cut twice as deep as the rest ( IRC ). Emergency procedures, joint loans, budgets multiplied by five, a Parliament left out. And for diplomacy, a postponement. Not all of Europe thinks the same way, and it is right to say so. France, Italy, Austria and Belgium have openly asked to open a channel with Moscow; Germany, Poland, the Baltic and Nordic countries prefer to increase the pressure ( Euronews ). In June the President of the European Council, António Costa, had his cabinet open a contact with the Kremlin: several governments protested because they had not been consulted, and those contacts served only to open a line, without going into substance ( Euronews ). The problem is not that someone wants war. It is that rearmament has fast tools, ready to use, and diplomacy does not: appointing an envoy takes the unanimity of twenty-seven governments, and a single no is enough to stop everything. So, with every new alarm, the easiest response to approve is always the same. There is no need to imagine a conspiracy. It is enough to look at which door opens with the least effort. On this site we wrote, in a manifesto, that before any choice of force it should be possible to show that the path of negotiation had truly been exhausted, not abandoned halfway ( "We Will Not Look Away While War Is Chosen" ). Today that proof does not exist: a line opened without a mandate is not a negotiation attempted. So far, others have done the negotiating. For the freezers, a new password was enough. For peace, a name and a mandate would be enough. After more than a year and a half, we are still looking for them. Bitcoin, who freezes and who flees: Russia's reserves, sanctions and the Hormuz toll

Central banks choose gold, those under sanctions use stablecoins, states seize the keys. Who really uses the property that makes Bitcoin impossible to freeze. Second piece in the series "Bitcoin, a refuge from whom?".

— Moscow / Brussels / Strait of Hormuz In brief In 2022 the West froze about 300 billion dollars of Russian reserves. The gold held in Moscow stayed untouched, and since then central banks have been buying gold as they had not for decades. Those under sanctions use cryptocurrencies, but almost never Bitcoin: 84% of illicit volume goes through stablecoins pegged to the dollar. Illicit traffic remains below 1% of the total. At Hormuz, Iran charges a toll payable in Bitcoin too, but large-scale payments cannot be seen. A toll on mere passage is prohibited by the law of the sea, whoever imposes it and whatever it asks in return. Those who impose sanctions freeze stablecoins, which have an issuer. With Bitcoin they cannot: so they seize the keys. The means is not the culprit: cartels have laundered hundreds of millions through large banks too. On 28 February 2022, four days after the invasion of Ukraine, the European Union banned all transactions involving the reserves of the Russian central bank. The United States, the United Kingdom and the other allies did the same. Within days Moscow lost access to about 300 billion dollars , almost half its reserves: dollars, euros and government bonds held abroad. One part, however, stayed intact. The Bank of Russia's gold was in vaults in Moscow, and no one could touch it. Every central bank in the world saw the scene. And each asked itself the same question: what if it happened to us? In the first part we saw that Bitcoin has a property that neither gold in a foreign vault nor a bank account has: on the network no one can freeze it. Here we look at who really uses this property, who fights it, and how. A premise: the means is not the culprit Before talking about sanctions, weapons and tolls, one thing must be said clearly. Lawbreakers use whatever moves easily and is hard to seize, and they have always done so with everyone's money. Between 2006 and 2010 Mexican and Colombian cartels laundered at least 881 million dollars through HSBC's American branch, which in 2012 paid 1.9 billion to settle the case. In 2024 TD Bank pleaded guilty to money laundering for letting more than 670 million dollars from criminal networks pass through its accounts, and paid over 3 billion. No one concluded that the dollar was to blame. States do, however, act on the tools that make crime easier. In 2019 the European Central Bank stopped issuing the 500-euro note because, it explained , it could "facilitate illicit activities": a million euros in those notes weighed little more than two kilos. The note remains legal tender, but no more are printed. The same reasoning is applied to cryptocurrencies today: the means is not put on trial; the aim is to make it less convenient for lawbreakers. What follows, then, is not an indictment of Bitcoin. It is a map of who uses this property, who fights it and how. 1. States choose gold, not Bitcoin Since 2022 central banks have been buying gold as they had not for decades. According to the European Central Bank , by the end of 2025 gold had become the largest item in world reserves, ahead of US Treasury bonds: this had not happened since the mid-1990s. Partly it is down to the price, which has risen enormously; partly to purchases, above a thousand tonnes a year for three years in a row. Central banks have said why themselves. In a 2023 survey of 85 sovereign funds and central banks, the majority answered that the freezing of Russia's reserves had made gold more attractive. And more and more central banks are bringing it home: India, for example, repatriated more than a hundred tonnes from the Bank of England in 2024. Bitcoin barely features in this race. Central banks buy an asset they have known for centuries, that can be touched and kept in a national vault. The lesson of Moscow, for them, is not "use something no one controls" but "keep your reserves where you control them". There is a legal detail. Russia's reserves in Europe, today about 210 billion euros, almost all held by the Belgian company Euroclear, are immobilised , not confiscated: they still belong to Russia, but Moscow cannot use them. In December 2025 the Union decided to keep them frozen indefinitely, but it failed to use them to finance Ukraine, mainly because of Belgium's opposition, and borrowed 90 billion on the markets instead. The Russian central bank has sued the Union before the General Court in Luxembourg, and a Moscow court has ordered Euroclear to pay it compensation. How far one may go with a foreign central bank's assets is one of the most open questions in international law today. 2. Those under sanctions choose cryptocurrencies, but not Bitcoin If states that fear sanctions choose gold, states already subject to them have chosen cryptocurrencies. According to the analytics firm Chainalysis , in 2025 cryptocurrency flows to sanctioned entities grew almost eightfold compared with the year before, driven above all by Russia, Iran and North Korea. It must be said straight away, though, that all illicit traffic remains below 1% of cryptocurrency transactions. But the surprise is which cryptocurrencies. Not Bitcoin: 84% of illicit volume, Chainalysis writes, is in stablecoins, the digital coins pegged to the dollar. Bitcoin has fallen to about 7% ; in 2020 it was the other way round. In short, those who want to escape the dollar system use digital dollars. Russia tried to go further. In January 2025 a Russian company launched A7A5, a stablecoin pegged to the rouble and designed specifically to get around sanctions. In less than a year it moved more than 100 billion dollars, according to the analytics firm Elliptic . But it served mainly as a bridge to Tether, that is, back to the dollar. And after sanctions by the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union its volume collapsed : the platforms that traded it were hit one by one. North Korea takes another route: it steals. According to Chainalysis, in 2025 North Korean hackers stole more than 2 billion dollars in cryptocurrencies; the October 2026 theft from Binance, attributed by the FBI to North Korea, is worth three times as much on its own. According to Western governments, that money funds the missile and nuclear programmes. Pyongyang rejects the accusations. 3. Hormuz: the toll in cryptocurrencies The newest case is that of the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world's oil passes. From mid-March 2026, with the war under way, the Revolutionary Guards began charging a toll on ships in transit: up to 2 million dollars per ship, payable in Chinese yuan, in Bitcoin or in stablecoins. On 30 and 31 March the Iranian parliament turned it into law, with the "Strait of Hormuz Management Plan". In May came a maritime "insurance" too, Hormuz Safe , with premiums in Bitcoin. Headlines spoke of a "Bitcoin toll". The reality is more modest. The analytics firm TRM Labs wrote that it had found no evidence on the blockchain of large-scale payments, and according to several accounts Iran prefers stablecoins. Bitcoin, here, is above all a symbol: the promise of a payment system Washington cannot switch off. In legal terms, the point is not what the toll is paid with, but whether it can be charged at all. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees all ships "transit passage" through international straits, prohibits hampering or suspending it and provides for no toll on mere passage; even in territorial waters a coastal state may charge only for specific services rendered to a ship. Iran has signed the Convention but not ratified it, and argues that the right applies only to those who have ratified it. On this site we have already run the symmetry test: in July 2026 the United States too, which has not ratified the Convention but recognises its rules on transit, announced a 20% toll on the cargo of third-country ships ( the news ; the opinion ). A toll on mere passage is contrary to the law of the sea whoever imposes it, and whatever it asks in return: yuan, Bitcoin, dollars, or eggs, chickens and timber. The means of payment does not make the toll more or less unlawful. 4. Who freezes: the new weapon is the stablecoin If those fleeing sanctions use stablecoins, those imposing them have learned to use them in turn. Every stablecoin has an issuer, and the issuer can freeze the tokens in any wallet in the world. Tether, the most widely used, does so regularly at the request of the US authorities: in January 2026 it blocked in a single day about 182 million dollars in wallets linked to the Revolutionary Guards. After the Binance theft, Tether and Circle froze part of the stolen funds within hours. In the United States a July 2025 law, the GENIUS Act, requires stablecoin issuers to be able to freeze funds and to comply with sanctions. The result is a paradox. Cryptocurrencies were supposed to free money from states; stablecoins have brought the dollar, and the power to freeze it, inside the blockchain. 5. And bitcoins? They take the keys With Bitcoin, as we have seen, there is no one to order to freeze anything. But a state can do something else: take the keys. In October 2025 the US Department of Justice launched the forfeiture of 127,271 bitcoins, the largest cryptocurrency seizure in its history. According to the prosecution they belonged to Chen Zhi, chairman of the Cambodian Prince group, accused of running online scams in compounds where trafficked workers were held by force. Chen Zhi and the group reject the accusations. In January 2026 Cambodia arrested him and handed him over to China, where he was formally arrested in July; in the United States the indictment is still pending, and the forfeiture case is still open in Brooklyn, where his lawyers have asked for it to be dismissed. Those bitcoins are already in government custody. If the forfeiture is upheld, they should not be sold: they would go into the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve created by Donald Trump in March 2025, which is fed exclusively with seized bitcoins and has so far bought none. Counting these too, the US government holds about 328,000 bitcoins : it is the largest public holder in the world. So the asset that "no one can freeze" ends up, it too, in a state's safe. Not because the network allows it, but because people have keys, computers, homes and bank accounts, and states know where to look for them. The mirror What it chooses Why Central banks gold, kept at home since 2022 they fear their reserves abroad could be frozen States under sanctions stablecoins, more than Bitcoin they need dollars, digital ones too, to trade Those who impose sanctions freezing stablecoins and seizing keys on the Bitcoin network they cannot intervene People at war or under a regime Bitcoin too it is the only asset that can be carried in memory and that no one freezes on the network Our judgement: a refuge from whom? The answer is twofold. Bitcoin protects from the power to freeze, and that power is neither good nor bad in itself. It is used by a European Union that blocks the reserves of a country that invaded its neighbour, and it is used by an authoritarian government that blocks the accounts of its opponents. The same property serves a family in flight and those who break the rules, exactly like cash, gold and an account at an accommodating bank. The blame, when there is any, lies with those who break the rules, not with the means they use. On this, the law offers only one yardstick: whoever freezes, seizes or charges must do so under a law, before a judge, with the same criterion for everyone. It is the yardstick we use for Russia's reserves, for Chen Zhi's bitcoins, for the Hormuz tolls, whoever imposes them. In the third part we look at how states control and tax those who buy and sell cryptocurrencies. What we think about the fear Bitcoin inspires in banks and institutions we say in a separate Opinion , signed. Bitcoin, who controls and who taxes: the new rules in Europe and the world

Licences for platforms, names on every transfer, data for the tax authorities and different taxes in every country: how states control those who buy and sell cryptocurrencies, set against gold and money. Third piece in the series "Bitcoin, a refuge from whom?".

— European Union / United States In brief Since 1 July 2026 in the European Union only licensed firms may sell or hold cryptocurrencies for others, like a bank. Every transfer between platforms carries the name of the sender and the recipient. From 10 July 2027 platforms may no longer offer anonymous accounts or handle coins built to hide transactions. Keeping bitcoins in a personal wallet remains legal: the rules target intermediaries, not individuals. Since 2026 platforms collect customers' data for the tax authorities, which will exchange it with those of dozens of other countries. Taxes on gains, by contrast, vary from country to country: from zero to a third of the profit. In the United States the stablecoin law is in force; the one on the rest of the market has stalled in the Senate. For its first ten years Bitcoin lived in a grey zone. The platforms where it was bought and sold opened and closed without a licence, many users did not know whether or how much tax they owed, and tax authorities across half the world had no way of knowing who owned what. In Europe, that grey zone closed in 2026. In the first part we saw that on the Bitcoin network no one can freeze a payment, and that states therefore act "at the entrances and exits", that is, on the platforms. This third part explains how they do it: who may sell cryptocurrencies, who must know who you are, what the tax authorities know and how much you pay. As in the other parts, we set it against gold and everyday money. We focus on the rules of the European Union and international ones, because they apply in many countries at once; on taxes, each country goes its own way. 1. Who may sell and hold them Bitcoin. Since 30 December 2024 the European Union has applied MiCA , the regulation on markets in crypto-assets: anyone who buys, sells, exchanges or holds cryptocurrencies on behalf of others must be authorised, like a bank or an investment firm. Platforms already operating under national rules had a transition period, which ended for all on 1 July 2026. Since that day those without a licence can no longer serve European customers. The European markets authority, ESMA, asked unauthorised platforms to wind down in an orderly way, and savers to move their funds to an authorised platform or to a wallet of their own. Gold. Buying and selling investment gold has long been a regulated activity: dealers are subject to anti-money-laundering rules and, in many countries, must be listed in special registers. Money. Taking deposits requires a banking licence, and banks have been supervised by central banks for more than a century. MiCA, in essence, brings cryptocurrency platforms inside the same fence. 2. Who must know who you are Bitcoin. Since 30 December 2024 the so-called travel rule has applied to cryptocurrencies too: every transfer between two platforms must carry with it the name of the sender and of the recipient, for any amount. If the transfer goes to or comes from a personal wallet, the platform must check, above 1,000 euros, that the wallet really belongs to the customer. From 10 July 2027, under the new European anti-money-laundering regulation , platforms may no longer offer anonymous accounts or handle so-called privacy coins , cryptocurrencies built to hide transactions, such as Monero and Zcash. Privacy advocates argue that this violates the right to privacy protected by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. The ban, however, does not concern cryptocurrencies alone: the same regulation also bans anonymous accounts at banks. One clarification is needed, because many false rumours circulate online: keeping your own bitcoins in a personal wallet remains legal. The rules target platforms, not individuals who hold their own keys, and direct transfers between two personal wallets remain outside the travel rule . Gold. A bar bought in a shop, above a certain threshold, requires ID. Then, locked away at home, it leaves no trace. Money. A bank transfer always carries the name of the payer and the payee: the travel rule was born there, for banks, and has been extended to cryptocurrencies. Cash remains anonymous, but from 10 July 2027, throughout the Union, it will not be possible to pay a business more than 10,000 euros in cash. 3. What the tax authorities know Bitcoin. Since 1 January 2026 platforms serving European customers must collect their users' tax data and record purchases, sales and transfers. This is required by the European DAC8 directive . In 2027 they will send the 2026 data to the tax authority of their own country, which will pass it on to that of the country where the customer lives. Those who do not provide their data may, after two reminders, have their transactions blocked. DAC8 applies in Europe an OECD standard, the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework , which by June 2026 76 countries had joined : 46 will start exchanging data in 2027, others in 2028, the United States in 2029. In the United States, meanwhile, platforms already report customers' sales to the tax authority: the first form, the 1099-DA , covers transactions from 2025. Gold. For gold kept at home or in a safe-deposit box there is no automatic exchange of information between states. A gold account at a bank, however, depending on how it is set up, may fall within the reporting on financial accounts. Money. For bank accounts an automatic exchange has existed since 2017: it is called the Common Reporting Standard , the OECD created it after the 2008 crisis to fight capital hidden abroad, and today more than a hundred countries apply it. The cryptocurrency standard is, in effect, its copy. 4. How much you pay Bitcoin. Here the European Union has no common rules: each country decides for itself, and the differences are huge. In Germany those who hold bitcoins for more than a year and then sell them pay nothing ; in Portugal a similar rule applies, while sales within the year pay 28% ; in France the gain pays 31.4% (it was 30% until 2025); in Italy, since 2026, 33% . The same sale, with the same gain, can cost from nothing to a third of the profit depending on where you live. Then there is a detail that surprises many. In many countries paying for something in bitcoin , a coffee or a car, counts as selling bitcoin: if the price has risen since you bought it, that payment produces a gain to be declared. It is one of the reasons few people use Bitcoin for their shopping. On VAT, by contrast, a common rule does exist. In 2015 the Court of Justice of the European Union , in the case of a Swede who wanted to open an exchange service, ruled that exchanging euros for bitcoin and vice versa is exempt from VAT, like exchanging currencies. Gold. Investment gold is also exempt from VAT throughout the Union, under a European rule . The gain on a sale, as with Bitcoin, is taxed in different ways from country to country. Money. Interest on an account or a government bond is taxed everywhere, but no one pays tax for spending a euro. For the tax authorities, Bitcoin looks more like an investment than like money. 5. And the United States? The United States has moved in another direction. In July 2025 it passed the GENIUS Act, the first federal law on stablecoins, which requires issuers to hold reserves and to be able to freeze funds on the authorities' orders. The broader law, the CLARITY Act, which is meant to establish who supervises the rest of the market, passed the House in July 2025 but stalled in the Senate: on 15 September 2026 it failed to get the 60 votes needed to be debated on the floor, and it is unlikely to return before 2027. Meanwhile Washington has created the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve. In short, the country in whose currency almost all stablecoins are denominated regulated those first. 6. Where the rules do not reach All these rules have one thing in common: they target intermediaries. Platforms, banks, dealers. Those who keep bitcoins in their own wallet and exchange them directly with another person remain outside automatic controls, like those who keep gold under the mattress or pay each other in cash. Outside the controls, however, does not mean outside the law. The gain must be declared anyway, and sooner or later, to convert bitcoins into euros and pay the rent, almost everyone goes through a platform, that is, through a door that now records who comes in and who goes out. The freedom Bitcoin promises remains intact on the network. At the entrances and exits, by now, it gets the same treatment as money. The mirror Bitcoin Gold Money Who may sell or hold it only authorised platforms (EU, since 1 July 2026) regulated dealers only licensed banks Name of payer and payee mandatory between platforms; check above €1,000 with a personal wallet ID above a threshold, then no trace mandatory in transfers; cash limited from 2027 Does the tax office know? since 2026, through the platforms (EU and dozens of other countries) it depends: a gold account may be covered, gold at home is not yes, since 2017, for accounts abroad VAT exempt (EU Court of Justice, 2015) exempt (investment gold) does not apply Tax on gains different in every country: from zero to a third different in every country interest is taxed, not spending Outside the controls personal wallet and private exchanges gold kept at home cash between individuals What changes For seventeen years Bitcoin was presented as the money that escapes states. In Europe, since 2026, anyone using a platform is treated more or less like anyone using a bank: licence, ID, data for the tax authorities. Only those who give up intermediaries and take on themselves the burden, and the risk, of keeping their own keys remain free. Is it a step towards normality or an attempt to tame a system born to do without it? Institutions say they want to stop money laundering and tax evasion, with the same rules that already apply to money. Bitcoin supporters reply that every new control makes the original promise less true. On this question the site takes a position in a separate Opinion , signed. This article describes the rules; it is not tax or investment advice: rules change from country to country and over time.
