Bitcoin in the mirror: how it works, compared with gold and with money
What Bitcoin is, who creates it, who really owns it and who can stop it: one feature at a time, set against gold and the euro. First piece in the series "Bitcoin, a refuge from whom?".

In brief Bitcoin is a public ledger of payments, copied on thousands of computers. No one issues it, and there will never be more than 21 million. Whoever holds the keys owns the bitcoins. Those who leave them on a platform own a promise, like someone with gold in a vault or money in a bank. On the network no one can stop a payment or freeze an account. Intervention is possible only at the entrances and exits, on the platforms. In wartime none of the three is a perfect refuge: Bitcoin is the hardest to seize, gold the easiest to exchange, the money of a stable country the easiest to spend. "Crypto" is not one thing. More than half the tokens created since 2021 are already dead; Bitcoin alone is worth about 59% of the market. On 31 October 2008 the financial world was still buried under the rubble of Lehman Brothers, which had collapsed six weeks earlier. That day, on a mailing list for cryptography enthusiasts, someone signing as Satoshi Nakamoto published a nine-page paper : it described a "peer-to-peer electronic cash system" that needed no bank at all. On 3 January 2009 the network went live. In the first block of data Nakamoto left a message: that day's headline from the British newspaper The Times , "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks". It was a signature and a manifesto. Who Nakamoto is, even today, no one knows. Seventeen years later Bitcoin is called "digital gold", and some regard it as a safe haven. To find out whether it is one, we hold it up against the two benchmarks we all use: gold, the oldest refuge, and everyday money, the euro or the dollar. Economists call it fiat money, from the Latin for "let it be done": it has value because a state declares it legal tender, not because it is tied to anything physical. One feature at a time, without jargon. Before we start: Bitcoin is not "crypto" People often say "crypto" as if it were one thing. It is not. Since 2021 more than 20 million digital tokens have been created, and more than half have already stopped trading: in 2025 alone, according to the data platform CoinGecko , 11.6 million of them died. They were mostly memecoins , coins created as a joke or to speculate, often in a few minutes and with no project behind them: on Pump.fun, the site most used to launch them, about 98% never reach a real market. Value, by contrast, is concentrated in very few names. On 7 November 2026 Bitcoin alone accounted for about 59% of the whole market for cryptocurrencies; Ethereum, the largest platform for automated contracts, about 11%; stablecoins pegged to the dollar another 11%. The entire memecoin sector is worth just over 1% , and more than a third of it is a single coin, Dogecoin, created in 2013 as a joke. This series is about Bitcoin, and when it talks about something else, such as stablecoins, it says so. What holds for Bitcoin, the 21 million cap or a network no one controls, does not automatically hold for the others: every cryptocurrency has its own rules, and many have an issuer or a group of founders who can change them. 1. Who keeps the ledger Bitcoin. The ledger of payments, called the blockchain , is public, and identical copies of it exist on thousands of computers around the world. Roughly every ten minutes a new "block" of payments is added, linked to the previous one so that no one can alter the past without everyone noticing. Anyone can read every transaction from 2009 to today. Gold. A bar in a safe needs no ledger: it belongs to whoever holds it. But most investment gold sits in the vaults of banks and custodians, and there ownership is written in their own ledgers, which only they can see. Money. Our account exists in the bank's ledgers, and accounts between banks in those of the central bank. They are private ledgers: the bank, the central bank and, when needed, the authorities can see them. 2. Who creates it Bitcoin. No one. The rules, including the one on how many bitcoins can exist, are written into the software. Changing them would require the agreement of the great majority of those who run the network, and that is what makes them hard to touch. Gold. Nature. Mines extract it, and no one decides how much will reach the market: it depends on how much is found and how much it costs to get out. Money. The central bank creates it and, for the largest part, so do commercial banks every time they make a loan: the Bank of England itself explained this in 2014. It is a political and economic choice, and someone makes it. 3. How much of it exists Bitcoin. Never more than 21 million. They are created as a reward for those who keep the network running, and roughly every four years that reward is halved: this is the so-called halving , and the latest was in April 2024. In March 2026 the twenty-millionth bitcoin was created: more than 95% of all those that will ever exist are already in circulation, and the last will arrive around 2140. Some are lost forever because their owners lost the keys: estimates range from two to four million. Gold. It is scarce, but its total is not fixed. Throughout history about 220,000 tonnes have been mined, almost all still in existence, because gold does not get used up. Each year mines add less than 2% . If the price rises, it pays to dig more. Money. There is no cap. The European Central Bank targets inflation of 2% a year: by design, money loses a little value every year. Sometimes much more: in October 2022 inflation in the euro area reached 10.6% , the highest level since the euro has existed. 4. How much energy Bitcoin. Those who add blocks to the ledger are called miners . To do so they must solve a calculation that takes a lot of electricity, and whoever succeeds first receives the new bitcoins. The consumption is the price of security: to forge the ledger you would have to spend more energy than everyone else combined. According to the University of Cambridge , the network uses about half a percentage point of the world's electricity, as much as a medium-sized country. Gold. Gold is "mined" too, literally: digging, crushing and refining rock uses a lot of energy. Estimates, however, vary widely. According to a 2021 analysis by Galaxy Digital , a firm that invests in Bitcoin, built on World Gold Council data, the gold industry then used about twice as much energy as Bitcoin; other estimates give figures close to the network's. On top of that comes the impact of mines on the land. Money. Banks, branches, data centres and payment networks use energy too. A reliable, comparable estimate, however, does not exist: it is the least known term of the comparison. 5. Who really owns it Bitcoin. A bitcoin is an entry in the public ledger, and only the holder of the corresponding "private key" can move it. Whoever has the key has the bitcoins; whoever loses it loses them. Many people, for convenience, leave their bitcoins on a trading platform, an exchange : in that case they own a promise from the exchange. Users have long repeated a motto that says it in five words: "Not your keys, not your coins" . If the keys are not yours, neither are the bitcoins. On 29 October 2026 about 6.3 billion dollars in cryptocurrencies vanished from the wallets of Binance, the largest of these platforms, the biggest theft ever recorded; the FBI attributes it to North Korea . Binance set aside its own funds to cover customers' losses. This time it could: the guarantee, though, was the soundness of a private company. Gold. The same rule applies. A bar at home is yours; gold in an account or a fund is a promise from whoever holds it. Venezuela knows this: about 31 tonnes of its reserves sit in the vaults of the Bank of England, and for years Caracas has been unable to get them back. London did not recognise Nicolás Maduro as the legitimate president, and a long court case followed over who could dispose of it. After Maduro's capture by the United States in January 2026, the British government said the gold would remain frozen; in October Venezuela's government and opposition formed a joint commission to ask for its return. Money. A bank account is a promise too: the money is a claim on the bank. In the European Union that promise is guaranteed by law up to 100,000 euros per person per bank. Where the guarantee fails, the promise breaks: in Lebanon, since 2019, savers have been unable to withdraw their deposits, the pound has lost more than 90% of its value and the World Bank counts the crisis among the worst in the world since the mid-nineteenth century. 6. With or without a name Bitcoin. Addresses do not carry the owner's name, but every transaction remains written in the public ledger forever. Bitcoin is pseudonymous , not anonymous: specialised firms follow the money from one address to another, and that is how within hours the funds stolen from Binance were linked to North Korean hackers. The name appears when the money passes through an exchange that asks for ID. Gold. A bar has no name. But in many European countries, to buy gold above a certain threshold, the dealer must ask for ID. Money. Cash is anonymous, a bank account is not. And cash will have a limit: from 10 July 2027, throughout the European Union, it will be forbidden to pay in cash more than 10,000 euros to a business. 7. Who can stop it Bitcoin. On the network, no one. A confirmed payment cannot be reversed or stopped, not even if it is a theft, and it knows no borders or opening hours. For someone living under a regime that controls bank accounts, that is freedom; for someone who has to enforce a sanction, it is a problem. Intervention is possible only at the entrances and exits, that is, at the exchanges, which can freeze customers' accounts. Gold. Physical gold can be seized: at home, in a safe, at the border. Gold deposited abroad can be blocked by whoever holds it, as the Venezuelan case shows. Money. A transfer can be stopped, an account can be frozen, by a judge's order or a government sanction. It is the fastest tool states have. A halfway house: stablecoins. There are digital coins that travel on a blockchain like Bitcoin but are pegged to a currency, almost always the dollar: one is worth one dollar. They are called stablecoins , and they are fiat money in digital dress. Like money, they have an issuer, a private company such as Tether or Circle, which can freeze them: after the Binance theft both did so within hours with part of the stolen funds. With bitcoins this is not possible. They come back in the second part. 8. In wartime Imagine a family forced to leave its city under the bombs. Money. Money in the bank may stay blocked, as in Lebanon; cash runs out, and in a country at war it can lose value fast. Gold. It is valuable everywhere and depends on no bank. But it is heavy, it shows, and at the border or a checkpoint it can be seized. Bitcoin. That family's bitcoins are not at home, nor in a computer, nor in a bank: they are written in the public ledger, which has copies in dozens of countries. If the city loses power, if the government shuts down the internet, if the phone is destroyed, the ledger keeps working elsewhere and loses nothing. It does not need restarting: it depends on no single country, and as long as part of the network stays on somewhere in the world, it keeps running. And the key can be carried in memory: the most widely used wallets turn it into twelve or twenty-four ordinary words, with which access can be rebuilt from any device. Wealth can cross a border inside a person's head, with no suitcases and no declarations. In March 2022, in the first days of the Russian invasion, the specialist press told the story of a Ukrainian refugee who reached Poland with about 2,000 dollars in bitcoin, almost half his savings, on a USB stick: he said he could also have written his words on a piece of paper and taken them with him. But in wartime there are three risks, and they apply to all three. What changes is the degree. Theft. Whoever has the safe's combination takes the gold; whoever has the account's credentials takes the euros; whoever has the twelve words takes the bitcoins. A threat is enough, at a checkpoint or at home. The difference lies in what happens next. With gold and with Bitcoin the theft is final: there is no one to ask to reverse it. With a bank account, at least in Europe, an unauthorised payment can be disputed, and the bank must refund it by the end of the following business day , unless it has reasonable grounds to suspect fraud by the customer: the EU Court of Justice confirmed this in October 2026. Meanwhile, physical attacks to force people to hand over their Bitcoin keys are rising sharply: in 2025 the security firm CertiK verified 72 of them worldwide, the highest number ever recorded. Collapse in value. It applies to all three, at different speeds. Bitcoin can lose a lot in little time: on 28 February 2026, when the bombing of Iran began, it fell within minutes , while gold rose. Gold fluctuates less, but in 2026 it fell too. And money depends on which one: the euro has lost at most about a tenth of its purchasing power in a year; the Lebanese pound has lost more than 90%. For someone fleeing a country whose currency is collapsing, Bitcoin may be the lesser risk. Who accepts it. Here too the problem is shared. A farmer does not want grains of gold in exchange for eggs, and abroad a shop may refuse euros. Bitcoins can be spent directly, without exchanging them: online, in some shops, between individuals, and with systems such as Lightning the payment arrives in a few seconds. But the difference lies in how easy they are to exchange. Euros and dollars can be exchanged at any bank in the world, gold at any jeweller; for bitcoins you need a connection and someone willing to take them. In 2021 El Salvador made them legal tender and required shops to accept them; in October 2024, according to a survey by Francisco Gavidia University , more than nine Salvadorans in ten said they did not use them to pay, and in January 2025, to obtain a loan from the International Monetary Fund, the country dropped the requirement . In wartime, then, none of the three is a perfect refuge. Bitcoin is the hardest to seize and the easiest to take away; gold is the easiest to exchange anywhere; the money of a stable country is the easiest to spend and the only one that offers some protection against theft, while that of a country in crisis can be the worst of the three. 9. What it is worth, and why Bitcoin. On its own it pays no interest or dividends and produces nothing: it is worth what someone is willing to pay for it. That is why its price moves so much: since its record of 126,000 dollars in October 2025 it has lost about 40%, and today it trades at around 76,000. Those who own it, however, can lend it to whomever they choose, as people do privately with gold or money. And services are emerging around Bitcoin that put it to work. With automated contracts on the blockchain, smart contracts , it can be pledged as collateral for a loan without selling it: since 2025, for example, a large American platform has allowed its customers to do this, requiring collateral at least a third larger than the amount lent. Almost always, though, to use these services the bitcoins must be handed to a custodian that turns them into a token usable on another network: the keys go back to an intermediary. Gold. Gold pays no interest either. But it has real uses, in jewellery and industry, and buyers who do not sell in a panic: central banks, which in recent years have bought it at record rates . It moves less than Bitcoin, but it is not motionless: at the end of October 2026 both Bitcoin and gold were down about 7% since the start of the year, the last two in a ranking of 21 major asset classes. Money. In the short run it is the most stable of the three: a euro today is worth a euro tomorrow. In the long run it loses purchasing power, a little each year by design and a lot when inflation runs high. The mirror at a glance Bitcoin Gold Money (euro, dollar) Who creates it no one, the software nature, the mines central bank and banks Quantity fixed, 21 million scarce, grows slowly no limit Who owns it whoever has the key whoever holds it the bank, on your behalf Who can stop it no one on the network; exchanges can whoever seizes or holds it banks, judges, governments Crossing a border in your memory heavy and visible cash limited, account can be blocked If it is stolen lost forever lost forever often refunded Value very unstable stable in the long run stable in the short run, declines in the long run; collapses in countries in crisis Easy to exchange needs a network and a counterparty anywhere, at a jeweller anywhere, if it is a strong currency Bitcoin shares with gold its scarcity and the absence of an issuer. But gold can be touched, has existed for millennia and works without electricity; Bitcoin lives only as long as the internet and the power grid run, has seventeen years of history and is kept with a key that, if lost, cannot be recovered. With money it shares almost nothing: and that is precisely why some people choose it. The question we started from remains. A safe haven protects from something. In 2026 Bitcoin did not protect from market crashes. But it has a property that neither gold in a foreign vault nor a bank account has: no one can freeze it. In the second part we look at who really uses this property, and against whom. Trump threatens Iran's water and power plants. It wouldn't be the first time — and it would be a war crime.
The Iran-US truce over the Strait of Hormuz collapses. Trump threatens desalination plants and a naval blockade; Iran had struck Qatari and Saudi ships to enforce a unilateral route.

«They have desalination plants — we'll take them out if we have to.» — Donald Trump, July 8, 2026 The facts On July 8, 2026, the ceasefire reached between the United States and Iran on June 17 collapses — a memorandum of understanding that guaranteed free, toll-free passage through the Strait of Hormuz for 60 days, leaving it to Iran and Oman to jointly define the 'future administration of maritime services' beyond that period, a clause that leaves the possibility of future tolls open and contested. Within that free-passage window, on July 6-7 the IRGC struck three commercial vessels in Omani waters — the Qatari LNG tanker Al Rekayyat, the Saudi tanker Wedyan, and the Cyprus Prosperity — for failing to follow a route Iran claims the right to unilaterally approve. Lawmaker Alaeddin Boroujerdi announced legislation to formalize Iranian management of the strait, declaring that any arrangement without Tehran's coordination is 'doomed to fail': a declared strategy, not an isolated act. The attacks took place on the fifth day of funeral processions for Supreme Leader Khamenei — marked by crowds explicitly calling for revenge against Trump, and by turnout perceived domestically as disappointing; showing resolve over the strait also serves an internal cohesion function for a weakened leadership. A US official called it a 'gross violation' of the memorandum; Riyadh called it 'an assault on the security of international navigation.' The US responded with strikes on over 80 targets, including an attack on Kharg Island; Iran struck US installations in Bahrain and Kuwait. In Ankara, Trump confirmed the strike on Kharg ('Maybe we'll take over the island'), threatened desalination plants ('we'll take them out if we have to') and a naval blockade, called the Iranian leadership 'scum,' and on the truce: 'For me, I think it's over.' Legal commentary Deliberately striking desalination plants and civilian power grids means striking objects indispensable to the survival of the population, protected under Art. 54 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions : the laws of war allow striking dual-use infrastructure only when the military advantage clearly outweighs civilian harm — a very high bar. This is not the first time Trump has made this exact threat: in late March 2026 he spoke of 'completely obliterating' Iranian power plants, oil wells, and desalination plants, only to back off when negotiations seemed to progress. Asked then about the risk of a war crime, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt replied that the administration would 'always act within the confines of the law,' while confirming Trump would proceed 'unabated' — without explaining how striking desalination plants would serve that goal. Implications — the symmetry test The principle at stake here — civilian infrastructure indispensable to the population's survival is not to be struck, regardless of who threatens to do so — is the same one this site applies to any other wartime actor targeting civilian water or power grids. It does not change because it is spoken by the president of the power leading the Atlantic Alliance. But the symmetry must be completed: the Iranian attack on the ships was not random, but punishment for failing to follow a 'safe route' Iran claims the right to impose unilaterally, within the free, toll-free passage window the June agreement guaranteed for 60 days. Striking third-country merchant ships (Qatar, Saudi Arabia) to enforce it is not an application of the current agreement: it is a violation of it. Neither side comes out of this clean, and neither deserves to be presented as the one resisting the other's abuse: Iran here is pursuing its own strategic interest — control of a strait through which a fifth of the world's oil passes — by means that strike third-country civilians, not a principle of resistance. Escalation, July 13, 2026 Five days after the threat to desalination plants, the crisis reaches a new formal threshold. On July 13, 2026, Trump announced on Truth Social the reinstatement of the naval blockade — "THE IRANIAN BLOCKADE," stressing it would only stop Iranian ships and customers — effective 20:00 GMT Tuesday the 14th, confirmed by CENTCOM. In the same post, the United States declared itself "GUARDIAN OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT" and announced a 20% toll on the cargo value of any third-country vessel in transit, justified as reimbursement for security costs. The announcement follows a new exchange of attacks over the weekend of July 11-12, further eroding the June 17 truce — the same one that explicitly banned tolls on passage through the strait. According to analytics firm Kpler, actual transits have fallen by more than half compared to the previous week; Brent crude has risen above $82 a barrel. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) stated it has always been consistent in opposing fees for passage through straits used for international navigation, saying there is no legal basis for mandatory tolls on mere transit — a principle codified by the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) , Part III on transit passage, and by GATT Article V on freedom of transit. Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi responded by claiming that "Iran has always been the GUARDIAN of the Strait and will remain so FOREVER" — disputing not the principle of a toll, but the percentage ("20% is of course too much"). A month earlier, US Secretary of State Rubio had stated that no country may charge tolls on an international waterway, calling it settled international law. Symmetry test — update The condemnation holds for both actors. The June truce explicitly barred Tehran from the same conduct Araghchi now claims in words; Washington denied it in words through Rubio and enacted it in fact five weeks later. Neither side can be presented as the one defending a principle: both assert it when convenient and abandon it when more convenient still. It's Not the Strait. It's the Example.
An editorial by N3R1-70: the 20% toll and naval blockade at Hormuz are not an isolated incident, but public proof of a double standard — and a dangerous pedagogical lesson for the next generation.

«The U.S.A. will be, from this point forward, known as 'THE GUARDIAN OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT.'» — Donald Trump, July 13, 2026 Related news, with dated facts and sources: Bitcoin, who freezes and who flees: Russia's reserves, sanctions and the Hormuz toll · Washington declares itself "guardian" of the Strait of Hormuz and imposes a 20% toll . There is a temptation to treat this story as a piece of maritime news. A toll, a naval blockade, a bombastic declaration on Truth Social: it looks like the kind of episode that vanishes from the headlines within a week, replaced by the next one. It won't be. Not because the Strait of Hormuz will stop mattering — it will always matter, as long as a fifth of the world's oil passes through it — but because what is being played out here is not strait geopolitics. It is yet another public lesson, delivered by whoever holds the planet's largest megaphone, on what "rules-based international order" really means once the rule touches the one writing it. The rule that vanishes when it matters A month before the announcement, the American Secretary of State had said something simply true: no country may tax an international waterway, that is settled law. Five weeks later, the same government does exactly that. Not through a secret act, not through a technical loophole — through a public post, claimed openly, almost proud of its own inconsistency. There is no diplomatic fiction covering the gap: there is the confidence of someone who knows that no one with real power will make him pay for it. And here the symmetry test — which this site applies as method, not aesthetics — produces its most uncomfortable result: Iran, for its part, does not dispute the principle. It disputes the percentage. "20% is of course too much, we will be fair," Tehran replied, claiming to be itself "the guardian of the strait forever." Neither power, faced with an opening to exert force over an international commons, resisted the temptation. The difference between the two is not in principle. It is that one of them already has the means to do it — and is doing it as we write. This absolves no one. It simply sharpens the diagnosis: the problem is not the hypocrisy of a single government. It is that, when tested, the current international system has no real barriers against either of them — only rhetorical ones, which collapse at the first push whenever convenient. The real cost isn't oil The rise in Brent crude, the collapse in transits, the economic damage to countries that import much of their crude through the strait: all real, all measurable, all already documented in the related news piece. But it is the lesser cost. The greater cost — the one that shows up on no stock index — is the one deposited every time a power publicly demonstrates that international law is a costume worn for others and shed whenever convenient. This is not the first time we have documented this on these pages, and it will not be the last: we wrote it for Iraq, for Libya, for Serbia, for Venezuela. Every time the same structure: law is preached when applied to the rival, suspended when it touches oneself, betting that collective memory is shorter than the next crisis. What makes the Hormuz case instructive is not its exceptionalism. It is its ordinariness, declared with an almost didactic bluntness: there isn't even an effort here to simulate an elaborate legal justification. There is a social media post, and the certainty that it will suffice. «It is no gratuitous cynicism to call this a school. It is an accurate description of what it means to grow up watching, edition after edition, that the gap between what is proclaimed and what is practiced is not a temporary flaw, but the system's normal operation.» The unintentional school And this is where this piece wants to reach beyond the single episode's chronicle. Those who are eighteen, twenty, twenty-five today are not witnessing an isolated incident. They are receiving, repeated with enough consistency to become structure rather than exception, an implicit lesson in how power really works: the law is for those who lack the strength to ignore it. Multilateral institutions — the IMO declaring the toll illegitimate, and being simply ignored in the very statement that declares it — serve to certify the violation, not to prevent it. Words spoken a month earlier by a minister do not bind the actions of the following month, even when they come from the same government. A generation taught — not in words, but through the repetition of facts — that ideals are a surface language and that immediate profit is the only variable that truly counts, is not a disillusioned generation by accident. It is a generation trained, methodically, by those whose job was the opposite. Why we write this anyway We do not write this piece to point to an easy culprit or to offer a solution — we have none, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. We write it because the first step toward not becoming numb to cynicism is to name it precisely, every time, with no discount for either side involved. It is a minimal, almost artisanal act relative to the scale of the problem. But it is the only one this site can perform: not looking away, even when looking away would be more comfortable, more neutral, easier to defend in polite conversation. «It isn't the Strait, in the end. It's the example it leaves behind for whoever is watching.» Iran United States Trump International law
Institutions are not afraid of Bitcoin: they buy it. They are afraid of people who hold their own keys. An Opinion on the series "Bitcoin, a refuge from whom?".

The first block of the Bitcoin ledger, on 3 January 2009, contains a newspaper headline : "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks". Whoever wrote it in there knew it could never be erased. It has stayed. Seventeen years later it is still the clearest thing ever said about what Bitcoin is: not an investment, but an answer to a question. What happens to your money when those who keep it get it wrong, and someone else pays? Let me say it straight away, because readers have the right to know: I own some cryptocurrencies. I do not put them all on the same level: many, like memecoins, are to me nothing but speculation. I am not writing to say whether to buy them. I am writing because in the three parts of this series ( how it works , who freezes and who flees , who controls and who taxes ) a thesis has emerged that is not in the data but runs through all of it, and it has to be said in the first person. The thesis is this: the real fear Bitcoin arouses is not that of savers. It is that of institutions. A currency no one can print allows no accounting tricks, cannot be rescued by decree, needs no bank to keep it. If everyone used it, many of the giants of our age, from payment networks to the systems that link banks together, would have fewer reasons to exist. Before defending it, I have to prove it wrong where it is wrong. Institutions have not rejected Bitcoin: they have bought it. BlackRock's fund , run by the world's largest asset manager, held more bitcoins in 2026 than any government, and its chief executive, who in 2017 called it "an index of money laundering", now calls it "digital gold". The accounting tricks have not gone away: they have moved to the intermediaries, and FTX made eight billion dollars of its customers' money disappear, which cost its founder twenty-five years in prison. And banks do not only make payments: they lend. People who own bitcoins can lend them too, to whomever they choose and on whatever terms they choose, as people do privately with gold or money, and with smart contracts services are emerging that make it easier. Bitcoin is not a bank, and it should not become one. But this is exactly where the difference that matters lies. Whoever lends a bitcoin gives it up, and the total stays the same. A bank that grants a mortgage, by contrast, creates money that did not exist before . For some this is Bitcoin's virtue: no one can inflate its quantity. For others it is its limit: in 2008 the bailouts that headline denounced also saved the deposits of people who were to blame for nothing, and with a currency no one can expand that lifebelt does not exist. And when someone tried to make customers' bitcoins earn money like a bank, lending them and investing them in risky operations, it ended badly: in 2022 Celsius and BlockFi went bankrupt . And here is the point. If institutions buy Bitcoin, what are they afraid of, then? Perhaps nothing: perhaps regulating is simply their job. Perhaps they fear money laundering, tax evasion, North Korea, and they are right to fear them. Perhaps they fear losing sanctions, the fastest weapon a state has. I do not know for certain, and I do not want to pretend I know. I know what they do. Licences for those who sell, names on every transfer, data for the tax office, anonymous accounts banned, keys seized from those who slip up. All at the doors. On the network, nothing. The answer, then, is more precise than my starting thesis. Institutions are not afraid of Bitcoin. They are afraid of people who hold their own keys. A bitcoin inside a fund is a financial product like any other: the keys are held by an authorised custodian, answerable to a supervisor and, if need be, to a judge. A bitcoin in a person's wallet, by contrast, is the only asset that can be carried in memory and that no one can freeze. Bitcoin users have repeated a motto for years: not your keys, not your coins , if the keys are not yours, neither are the bitcoins. Finance took it literally. It took the keys, and sold us the rest. I do not think this is a conspiracy. I think it is a choice, and that it should be judged by the yardstick this site uses for everything. A state has the right to know who is making money, and to tax it; it has the duty to stop those who finance a war with stolen cryptocurrencies. But the same rule must apply to those who freeze the reserves of an aggressor country and to those who freeze the accounts of an opponent, to an Iranian toll and to an American one, to a launderer with a digital wallet and to a bank that lets cartel money through. And every person must keep the possibility of holding something of their own outside the door: not to hide, but because sometimes the door is shut by the very people who should be guarding it. Lebanese families have known this since 2019. That newspaper headline is still there, in the first block. No one can erase it, no one can seize it, no regulation can reach it. Of this whole story, it is the only thing no one has managed to freeze. Houthis (Ansar Allah): who they are, where they come from, what they want
The armed movement that controls Sanaa and north-western Yemen: Zaydi origins, ideology, relationship with Iran, documented violations and designations. An updatable entry.

When an article on this site talks about "the Houthis", it assumes the reader knows who they are. Often that is not the case: in the news they appear as "pro-Iranian rebels" or as "terrorists", two labels that say little about their history or about what they are asking for. This entry gathers the essential facts. It can be updated: every change is recorded at the bottom, with date and source. Who they are The Houthis are a political, religious and armed movement from northern Yemen. The official name is Ansar Allah, "the supporters of God". "Houthi" comes from the family that founded it and leads it. Since 2014 they have controlled the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north-west, including the port of Hodeidah on the Red Sea, and they govern there as a de facto authority. The UN-recognised government is based in Aden, in the south. Where they come from The Houthis emerged from within Zaydism, a branch of Shia Islam present in Yemen since the ninth century and different from the Shiism practised in Iran. States led by Zaydi imams ruled northern Yemen, in various forms, until 1962, when the republican revolution overthrew the last imam ( Sana'a Center ). In the early 1990s, in Saada province, a group of clerics launched a Zaydi revival movement made up of lectures, summer camps and recorded sermons. Its leading figure was Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi. The movement presented itself as the voice of an oppressed minority and as a response to two developments: the decline of Zaydism's role after the revolution and the spread in the north of Wahhabi Salafism coming from Saudi Arabia ( Sana'a Center ). In 2004 the government of President Ali Abdullah Saleh tried to arrest Hussein al-Houthi; this started the first of six wars in Saada province, which lasted until 2010. Hussein was killed in the first months of fighting, in 2004. Since then the movement has been led by his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi. In 2011 the Houthis took part in the uprising against Saleh under the name Ansar Allah. On 21 September 2014, allied with Saleh himself, they entered Sanaa. On 26 March 2015 a coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened against them ( Sana'a Center ). In December 2017 they killed Saleh, who was switching sides. What they believe Their motto, the sarkha ("the scream"), was according to the Houthis first uttered by Hussein al-Houthi in 2002: "God is great, death to America, death to Israel, a curse on the Jews, victory to Islam". It echoes the mottos of the Iranian revolution and of Hezbollah ( Sana'a Center ). It must be quoted in full because it contains an invective explicitly aimed at Jews, not only at the United States and Israel. At the heart of their political doctrine is wilayah : the divine right to lead the community in politics and religion, reserved for the descendants of the al-Houthi family. In the areas they control, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi is the supreme authority over the economic, judicial and security apparatus. According to the Sana'a Center, only a minority of Yemenis accept this conception of power ( Sana'a Center ). The relationship with Iran The Houthis are part of the "axis of resistance", the network of Tehran's allies that includes Hezbollah. As early as 2021 a UN panel of experts reported growing evidence of shipments of weapons and components to the Houthis by individuals or entities in Iran, in violation of Security Council resolutions ( Fox News, quoting the report ). The report speaks of actors in Iran, not directly of the Iranian government. Alliance, however, does not mean dependence. The Houthis have their own social base, history and doctrine, born in Yemen decades before Iranian support. In 2026 they presented the resumption of the war with Saudi Arabia as a continuation of the Yemeni war, not as a front of the Iran war ( AP, via Al-Ahram ). What they demand Their demands have changed over time. During the 2022 truce and the talks with Riyadh they asked above all for the payment of public-sector salaries in the areas they control, the opening of the ports and of Sanaa airport, and oil and gas revenues ( AFP, via Naharnet ). Much of this went into the commitments announced by the UN envoy at the end of 2023 for a peace "roadmap", which then stalled ( UN News ). According to the International Crisis Group, in 2026 the discourse shifted to Yemen's sovereignty over airspace, ports and territorial waters ( AP, via Al-Ahram ). On 19 August 2026 they told Saudi Arabia that the only way out was to lift the blockade, implement the measures already agreed, pay salaries, withdraw foreign forces and leave natural resources to Yemenis ( Shafaq News ). Documented violations The Houthis are a party to a conflict in which all actors have violated international law, and this site documents it for all of them. As far as the Houthis are concerned, the documented violations include: the arbitrary detention of dozens of United Nations staff since 2024 ( we covered it here ); the recruitment of children as fighters ( here ); the siege of the city of Taiz, which began in 2016 ( AFP, via Naharnet ); since 2023, attacks on commercial ships in the Red Sea, which the Houthis present as solidarity with Gaza; in 2026, missile and drone attacks on Saudi civilian airports. In the same conflict the Houthis and the population of the areas they control are also targets of violations by others, from the Saudi coalition's air strikes to the American ones of 2025. We cover them in the dedicated pieces. What they are called No label is neutral. "Rebels" stresses that they rose up against a recognised government; "de facto authority" describes the real control they exercise over millions of people; "terrorists" echoes the designations of some governments. This site normally uses "Houthis" and, when speaking of their administration, "Houthi de facto authorities". US designations have changed with administrations. In January 2021 the first Trump administration designated them a foreign terrorist organisation; a month later the Biden administration revoked the designation, fearing it would hinder humanitarian aid. In February 2024 the same Biden administration designated them again, but in a narrower category, after the attacks in the Red Sea ( Baker McKenzie ). On 4 March 2025 the State Department designated them a foreign terrorist organisation again ( State Department, via GlobalSecurity ). For the UN Security Council, resolution 2216 of 2015 demands that the Houthis withdraw from the areas they seized and imposes an arms embargo on them ( UN ). Yemen: its peoples, its history, who is fighting and why

Country profile on Yemen: the ancient kingdom of Saba, a thousand years of Zaydi imams, North and South divided until 1990, Saleh, the 2011 uprising, the Houthis in Sanaa, the Saudi intervention, the 2022 truce and the war that returned in 2026, who gains and what international law says. An entry we keep updated.

The news from Yemen talks about missiles fired at Saudi airports, ships hit in the Red Sea, a besieged city, but it rarely explains why the poorest country in the Arab world has been at war for more than ten years, who the parties are and why so many foreign states have got involved. This profile tries to give the background. It is kept up to date: every change is recorded at the bottom, with date and source. In brief Yemen has about 33.7 million inhabitants, almost all Arab and Muslim. The difference that matters most is religious and geographical: a Sunni majority of the Shafi'i school, mainly in the centre and south, and a large Zaydi minority, a branch of Shia Islam, in the northern mountains. For a thousand years, until 1962, the north was ruled on and off by Zaydi imams. The south was a British colony around Aden for more than a century, then a Marxist state. The two Yemens united only in 1990, and by 1994 they had already fought a war. Since 2014 the Houthis, an armed Zaydi movement allied with Iran, have controlled the capital Sanaa and the north-west, where most Yemenis live. Since 2015 a coalition led by Saudi Arabia has fought for the recognised government, now based in Aden. The 2022 truce stopped the war without ending it. In 2026 the war returned on every front. No international court is investigating the crimes committed. The peoples Yemen occupies the south-western corner of the Arabian Peninsula. To the west it faces the Red Sea, to the south the Gulf of Aden; the Bab el-Mandeb strait, between Yemen and Djibouti, is one of the busiest waterways in the world. The country is made up of high, fertile mountains in the west, a hot coastal plain on the Red Sea (the Tihama) and deserts and plateaus in the east, up to Hadramawt and the border with Oman. Offshore, in the Indian Ocean, lies the island of Socotra. Yemen is divided into 21 governorates plus the capital. Yemen al-Jawf Lahij Saudi Arabia Oman Eritrea Djibouti Somalia Red Sea Gulf of Aden Bab el-Mandeb Socotra Sanaa Aden Taiz Mokha Hodeidah Saada Marib Mukalla Heaviest fighting, October-November 2026 In dark red, the provinces where, according to our analysis of 4 November 2026, the fighting is heaviest: al-Jawf, Taiz (with the Mokha coast, taken by the Houthis in September) and Lahij. We do not draw front lines or the areas held by each side, which change from week to week. The square marks the capital, Sanaa, held by the Houthis since 2014; the recognised government sits in Aden. Boundaries: Natural Earth (21 governorates and the capital). The population. Freedom House estimates about 33.7 million inhabitants ( Freedom House ). The last census dates from 2004, when there were 19.7 million Yemenis ( GlobalSecurity, on census data ): since then every figure is an estimate. A warning about the numbers. There are no official statistics on the religion or origin of Yemenis, and the estimates in circulation differ widely. We give them side by side, with the source, and say when they diverge. Arabs, Sunnis of the Shafi'i school — the majority: 65% according to the US government ( US State Department, 2023, via ecoi.net ), 55% of Muslims according to ACLED (same source). They live mainly in the cities of Taiz, Ibb and Aden, in the Tihama and in Hadramawt. The Shafi'i school is one of the four schools of Sunni Islamic law. Arabs, Zaydis — 35% according to the US government, 45% of Muslims according to ACLED (same source). Zaydism is a branch of Shia Islam present in Yemen since the 9th century, different from Iranian Shiism; Zaydis live mainly in the mountains north of Dhamar ( Minority Rights Group ). The Houthis present themselves as defenders of the Zaydis, but not all Zaydis are Houthis. Ismailis — about 15,000 people, concentrated in the Haraz area near Sanaa (same source). They are another Shia branch. Muhamasheen ("the marginalised") — from 500,000 to 3.5 million people, according to estimates cited by the UN and other studies ( Sana'a Center ); the highest figure would be about 10% of the population ( Minority Rights Group ). They are Black Yemenis, scornfully called akhdam , "servants". They belong to none of the big tribes and live on the margins, facing caste-like discrimination (same source). Mahri, Soqotri and other South Arabian peoples — they speak ancient languages distinct from Arabic, such as Mehri, Soqotri and Bathari ( Minority Rights Group ). They live in the far east, in al-Mahra province, and on the island of Socotra. We have not found a reliable estimate of their number. Jews, Baha'is, Christians and Hindus — together less than 1% (US State Department, 2022, via ecoi.net). The Jewish community, present for millennia, has almost disappeared: most emigrated to Israel after 1948, and in 2019 about fifty remained ( US State Department, 2019, via ecoi.net ). The economy. The International Monetary Fund considers Yemen the poorest country in the world ( Grundberg to the Security Council, DPPA ). Its little oil and gas is almost all in the east, between Marib and Shabwa ( AP, via Korea Times ), far from where most of the population lives. Whoever controls those fields, the ports and the roads controls the state's revenue. A short history Arabia Felix. In antiquity Yemen was the "Arabia Felix", happy Arabia, of Greek and Roman geographers: kingdoms grown rich on frankincense and myrrh and on irrigated farming. The best known is the kingdom of Saba, with its capital at Marib and its great dam; its remains, from the 1st millennium BC to the arrival of Islam around 630, have been a World Heritage site in danger since 2023, because they lie on a front line ( UNESCO ; Arab News ). A thousand years of imams (897-1962). In 897 a descendant of the Prophet, al-Hadi ila al-Haqq Yahya, arrived in Saada, in the north, and founded the Zaydi imamate: a state in which the imam is both religious and political leader ( Encyclopedia.com ). With many changes of fortune and long interruptions, the imams ruled the northern mountains for more than a thousand years. The Ottomans occupied the towns several times; in 1918, at the end of the Ottoman Empire, the north became independent under Imam Yahya ( US Marine Corps, country profile ). British Aden (1839-1967). In 1839 the British occupied the port of Aden, a useful stop on the route to India; in 1904 a boundary line separated the Ottoman north from the south under British influence ( Carnegie ). This is where two Yemens were born. Revolution and war in the north (1962-1970). On 26 September 1962 a group of officers overthrew the new imam, Muhammad al-Badr, and proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic. The imam fled and rallied the tribes: a civil war began in which Nasser's Egypt sent troops for the republic and Saudi Arabia backed the royalists. In 1967 Egypt withdrew most of its soldiers for the Six-Day War; in 1970 the two sides were reconciled ( Encyclopedia.com ; MIT, CASCON project ). The independent, Marxist South (1967-1990). From 1963 a guerrilla war was fought against the British; on 30 November 1967 the South became independent. In 1969 the Marxists took power, founded the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen, the only Marxist state in the Arab world, and nationalised property ( Carnegie ; Orient XXI ; PBS ). In 1972 and 1979 North and South fought two short border wars, both ended by agreements that promised a unification that never came ( UCDP ). Unification and the 1994 war. With the end of the Soviet Union the South lost its backer, and on 22 May 1990 the two states merged into the Republic of Yemen, with the North's leader, Ali Abdullah Saleh, as president ( WorldAtlas ). Many Southern leaders soon felt sidelined. In 1994 the South declared secession; on 7 July Saleh's troops took Aden and the war ended ( US Marine Corps ). Since then part of the South has experienced unity as an annexation. Saleh and the Saada wars (1994-2011). Saleh ruled through a system of alliances between tribes, the army and parties, including the Islamist party Islah. From 2004 to 2010 he fought six wars in the north against the Houthi movement, born in the 1990s from a Zaydi religious revival ( our Glossary ). Uprising and transition (2011-2014). In 2011, during the Arab Spring, millions of Yemenis took to the streets against Saleh. On 23 November 2011 Saleh signed a deal brokered by the Gulf states and handed power to his deputy, Abd Rabbu Mansour Hadi ( Minority Rights Group, via Refworld ). A national dialogue conference followed, meant to rewrite the state, possibly as a federation. The Houthis in Sanaa and the Saudi coalition (2014-2022). On 21 September 2014 the Houthis, allied with none other than Saleh, entered Sanaa. On 26 March 2015 a coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened for Hadi; in April Security Council resolution 2216 demanded that the Houthis withdraw and imposed an arms embargo on them ( our Glossary ; our analysis ). In December 2017 the Houthis killed Saleh, who was switching sides. By the end of 2021 the war had caused, according to the UN Development Programme, 377,000 deaths, 60% of them from hunger and disease ( our analysis ). The truce and the Presidential Council (2022). In April 2022 the UN brokered a truce. On 7 April Hadi handed his powers to an eight-member Presidential Leadership Council led by Rashad al-Alimi, formed in Riyadh, which brings together the various anti-Houthi forces, Southern separatists included ( Sana'a Center ). The truce expired in October but has largely held. The Red Sea (2023-2025). From November 2023 the Houthis attacked ships in the Red Sea over the Gaza war; in 2025 came US and Israeli strikes ( our analysis ). The South splits (December 2025 – January 2026). In December 2025 the Southern Transitional Council, the separatist movement backed by the Emirates, occupied Hadramawt and al-Mahra, on the Saudi border. Saudi Arabia responded with air strikes and with forces loyal to it, which retook the two provinces and Aden. Separatist leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi fled to the Emirates; on 9 January a Council delegation announced its dissolution from Riyadh, which its supporters call extorted under pressure ( AP, via WTOP ; Dawn ). The war returns in full (2026). After the war between the United States, Israel and Iran that began in February 2026, in July the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia and the two sides struck each other's airports. In September the Houthis took Mokha and the coast on the Bab el-Mandeb; in October they closed off Taiz and the government launched an offensive to retake the whole country ( our analysis ). Who governs, and how On paper Yemen is a republic with an elected president and a parliament. In practice there has been no parliamentary vote since 2003 and no presidential vote since 2012, when Hadi was the only candidate ( Abaad Studies ; Al Jazeera, 2012 ). Today there are two authorities that each claim to be the state: The recognised government , led by the Presidential Council based in Aden. It is recognised by the UN and depends on Saudi Arabia for money and protection; after January 2026 the members close to the Emirates were replaced by pro-Saudi figures ( TRT World ). The Houthi authorities in Sanaa, who govern the north-west in practice. At the top is Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, who claims a religious right to lead the community reserved for his lineage ( our Glossary ). Freedom House, in its 2026 report, rates Yemen "not free", with 10 points out of 100: 1 out of 40 for political rights and 9 out of 60 for civil liberties; elections are years overdue and many institutions no longer function ( Freedom House ). What separates an autocracy from a democracy is explained in our entry on Autocracy . Who's who Who Led by Position Houthis (Ansar Allah) Abdul-Malik al-Houthi Have held Sanaa and the north-west since 2014; since September 2026 also the coast on the Bab el-Mandeb. Allies of Iran ( Glossary ) Presidential Council Rashad al-Alimi Recognised government, in Aden. Since 4 October 2026 leading the offensive to retake the whole country ( our analysis ) National Resistance Tareq Saleh, nephew of the former president West-coast forces, on the Presidential Council ( Sana'a Center ) Marib forces Sultan al-Arada, governor Defend the oil and gas province; on the Presidential Council (same source) Giants Brigades and National Shield — Southern forces and pro-Saudi forces fighting alongside the government; the National Shield retook Hadramawt from the separatists in January 2026 ( AP, via WTOP ) Southern separatists Aidarous al-Zubaidi, in the Emirates Their Council was dissolved in January 2026, but supporters reject the dissolution and still demonstrate for independence ( Dawn ) Islah — The Sunni Islamist party, close to the Muslim Brotherhood; present on the Presidential Council ( Arab Center Washington ) Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) — Jihadist group present mainly in the south-east; also threatens non-Sunni Muslims ( US State Department, 2023, via ecoi.net ) Where the conflict comes from We use the four levels from our piece "Are the world's wars 'Muslim'?" . The ground: two countries badly stitched together. North and South had different histories, states and even opposing ideologies until 1990. Unity came out of necessity and was imposed by force in 1994. In the north, the end of the imamate in 1962 took power away from the families descended from the Prophet, and Salafism from Saudi Arabia spread into Zaydi lands: two wounds on which the Houthis built their movement ( our Glossary ). The spark: the vacuum after Saleh. In 2011 Saleh's system collapsed, but no new system took its place. The Houthis exploited a weak transition and, paradoxically, their alliance with Saleh himself to take the capital in 2014. The flag: religion and independence. The Houthis speak the language of resistance against America, Israel and Saudi Arabia, and of Zaydi rights; the South speaks the language of independence. But the war is also fought among Sunnis, as in the South in January 2026, and religion alone does not explain who sides with whom. The outside multiplier. Saudi Arabia does not want an ally of Iran on its border; for Iran the Houthis are the most distant and most autonomous ally in its network; the Emirates backed the Southern separatists and the ports for years; the United States and Israel strike the Houthis when the Houthis strike ships or Israel. Since 2026, with Hormuz almost closed, whoever controls the Bab el-Mandeb controls part of the world's oil. Who gains We document stated or verifiable interests, not motives. If an actor denies something, we say so. The Houthis. The war has turned them from a rebel group in one province into the de facto government of millions of people, with regional weight. They demand public salaries, an end to the blockade, the withdrawal of foreign forces and oil revenue ( our Glossary ). Saudi Arabia. It wants a friendly government in Sanaa and secure borders, and now also safe routes for its oil in the Red Sea. It pays part of the salaries and expenses of the Aden government: 346.6 million dollars in February 2026 alone; in all, Riyadh says, more than 12.6 billion dollars between 2012 and 2026 ( Arab News ; Gulf Business, on Saudi sources ). The Emirates. They backed the Southern separatists and the west-coast forces; after January 2026 they were pushed out of the country ( TRT World ). Iran. Through the Houthis it holds leverage over the Red Sea and Saudi Arabia. UN experts have reported arms shipments from entities in Iran; Tehran denies it ( our Glossary ). How far the Houthis really depend on Iran, and where they decide on their own, is explained in our analysis : they depend on it for their most advanced weapons, not for the choices that touch their survival. Arms sellers. For years the United States and other allies authorised arms sales to coalition members; Amnesty International called for them to stop because of strikes on civilians ( Amnesty International, via Dawn ). Who intervenes from outside Saudi Arabia. Has led the coalition since 2015; aircraft, money for salaries, allied forces on the ground. United Arab Emirates. Coalition member; backed the Southern separatists until January 2026. Iran. Ally of the Houthis; weapons and components according to the UN. United States. Strikes against the Houthis in 2024 and 2025; in 2026 it is calling on Iran to stop supporting them ( Al Jazeera ). Israel. Strikes on Sanaa and Hodeidah in response to Houthi missiles; in a single day of strikes on Sanaa, according to the Houthi health ministry, 46 people were killed, journalists among them ( AP, via Arab News ). Oman. Mediator: in July 2026 it let the Iranian flight turned away from Sanaa land in Hodeidah ( our analysis ). UN. A special envoy, Hans Grundberg since 2021; a sanctions regime with its panel of experts (resolution 2140 of 2014) and the arms embargo on the Houthis (resolution 2216 of 2015) ( UN, resolution 2140 ). The human cost. The UN Development Programme estimated 377,000 deaths by the end of 2021, including hunger and disease. ACLED counts more than 160,000 deaths directly caused by the war since 2015 ( ACLED, via dpa ). In 2026 the UN estimated 22.3 million people in need of aid, including 5.2 million internally displaced ( our analysis ). Documented violence. Some examples, attributed to different parties: Saudi coalition, 2015-2019 : about two thirds of the civilians killed in direct attacks on civilians, according to ACLED, died in coalition air strikes ( ACLED, June 2019 ). On 9 August 2018 a strike hit a school bus in the Dahyan market, in Saada province: according to the UN at least 21 children died; the Secretary-General called for an independent and prompt investigation ( UN, UNifeed ). Houthis, Taiz, since 2015 : the siege of the city, which Human Rights Watch considers a possible war crime of starvation as a method of warfare ( HRW ); recruitment of child soldiers ( our analysis ). United States, April 2025 : a strike on a migrant detention centre in Saada killed at least 68 people; Amnesty called for an investigation into a possible war crime ( via News.az ). Houthis, October 2026 : missiles on a training camp in Shabwa, 73 recruits killed ( AP ). International law The treaties. Yemen: is party to the Geneva Conventions (the North since 1970, the South since 1977) and to both Additional Protocols since 1990: so the second Protocol, on civil wars, also applies, which prohibits starving civilians as a method of combat ( ICRC, International Review of the Red Cross ; Cambridge ); signed the Rome Statute in 2000 but never ratified it; nor have Saudi Arabia, the Emirates and Iran. The International Criminal Court could act only on a referral from the Security Council ( PGA ; ReliefWeb ). The Saudi intervention. The coalition says it intervened at the invitation of the legitimate government; with resolution 2216 the Security Council recognised that government and demanded the Houthis withdraw. The invitation can make the intervention lawful, but it does not make individual strikes lawful: each remains subject to humanitarian law. We discuss this in the entry Use of force and self-defence . An armed group is bound. The Houthis are not a state, but humanitarian law binds them like any party to a civil war: attacking civilians or civilian airports, starving a city and recruiting children are violations for them too. The missing justice. The UN group of experts that from 2017 investigated crimes by all parties was shut down in 2021 by a vote of the Human Rights Council ( International Commission of Jurists ). Since then no international body has been investigating. 72 UN staff remain detained by the Houthis ( Grundberg, DPPA ). Ethiopia: the peace signed in South Africa that no one defended
Since 23 September 2026 fighting has resumed in northern Ethiopia: the peace agreement signed in Pretoria in 2022 has collapsed. The UN documents violations on both sides.

— Ethiopia (Tigray, Amhara, Afar) “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” — Amanuel Assefa, TPLF vice-president, to Al Jazeera, 24 September 2026 On 2 November 2022, in Pretoria, South Africa, the Ethiopian government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) signed, under African Union mediation, an agreement for a permanent cessation of hostilities, known ever since as the “Pretoria agreement”. It ended one of the bloodiest wars of the century: two years of fighting in the north of the country, whose toll remains disputed. The African Union mediator, former Nigerian president Olusegun Obasanjo, spoke in January 2023 of about 600,000 dead; a Ghent University study estimated up to 500,000, while some Ethiopian officials put the figure below 100,000. In recent days that agreement has collapsed, and the people paying the price are once again the same. Facts On 21 September 2026 seven armed groups, including the TPLF and forces active in Amhara and Afar, announced an alliance against the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. From 23 September an offensive was launched on several fronts; Tigrayan forces took control of three local airports, including Lalibela's. The federal army says it killed at least 272 TPLF fighters in Amhara: this is a partisan figure that no independent source has so far verified. On 25 September the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, described a rising civilian toll. According to his office, on 22 September federal army airstrikes, some carried out with drones, hit five schools in Tigray, causing deaths and injuries; a mortar strike attributed to the army killed civilians in the town of Kobo, in Amhara (on 23 September according to the High Commissioner, on 24 September according to UN News: the sources differ on the date). The same office denounces the forced mass recruitment of civilians, children included, by the TPLF across Tigray, with reprisals against those who refuse and their families, and reports cases of arbitrary conscription by government forces as well. The Secretary-General's spokesperson added that a drone hit a truck carrying food for displaced people in north-western Tigray, that phone and internet services are cut in the region, and that armed groups in Amhara have seized humanitarian vehicles. All this is happening where the IOM already counts some 750,000 internally displaced people left homeless by the previous war. Why the agreement collapsed The November 2022 agreement rested on a few precise commitments: the disarmament of Tigrayan fighters, the restoration of humanitarian aid, the return of the displaced and, later, a solution for the territories disputed between Tigray and Amhara. According to the analysis published by the International Crisis Group on 25 September, none of these knots was ever truly untied: disarmament was not completed, the contested lands remained under Amhara control, preventing many Tigrayans from returning, and outside diplomatic pressure to reach a compromise was insufficient. Meanwhile the Tigrayan camp split. Between April and May 2026 the TPLF ousted the interim administration created by the agreement and reinstated Debretsion Gebremichael at the head of the region; his predecessor, Getachew Reda, now an adviser to Abiy, accuses the TPLF of starting the hostilities. Then there is Eritrea. In the 2020-22 war its troops fought alongside the Ethiopian army and were accused of some of the worst atrocities of that conflict. Asmara never signed the Pretoria agreement. Today the Ethiopian government accuses it of financing the new alliance, and Eritrea denies it; according to Crisis Group's assessment, it has quietly moved closer to its former enemy. These are a partisan accusation and an analysis, not established facts, and we report them as such. Legal reading The frame of reference is international humanitarian law governing non-international armed conflicts. Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol II, which Ethiopia has ratified, bind the federal army and every armed group in the same way: they prohibit attacks on civilians and on civilian objects such as schools, and require the passage of humanitarian aid to be allowed. The same Protocol prohibits recruiting children under fifteen; the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child, also ratified by Ethiopia, raises to eighteen the limit for recruitment by armed groups. The limit already pointed out on this site for the war in Amhara remains: Ethiopia has not ratified the Rome Statute, and the International Criminal Court can act only on a referral by the Security Council. Finally, the Pretoria agreement is not a treaty with a judge: it is a political commitment mediated by the African Union, whose survival depended on the will of the parties and on pressure from those who had promoted it. Implications — symmetry test The symmetry test takes no effort here, because the source itself applies it: the UN High Commissioner's office attributes violations to the federal army (the strikes on schools, the mortar on Kobo, arbitrary conscription) and to the TPLF (the forced recruitment of children). Neither side can present itself as the only victim, and neither of the political causes at stake, the unity of the state or the autonomy of Tigray, makes it lawful to strike a school or enlist a child. This site's judgment is that the collapse of Pretoria shows the same problem we see elsewhere: an agreement without guarantors and a rule without anyone to enforce it hold only as long as they suit everyone. When Ethiopia slipped out of international attention, no one watched over disarmament, returns and the contested borders. The price of that distraction is being paid again today by the civilians of the north, the same ones as four years ago. Israel allowed and encouraged Qatari funding of Hamas for years — a month before October 7 it asked for more

From 2018 to October 7, 2023, Israel approved and encouraged the transfer of hundreds of millions of dollars from Qatar to Hamas, with the aim, according to a 2019 account that Netanyahu denies, of preventing Palestinian national unity. A month before the attack, Israel asked for more.

«Whoever is against a Palestinian state should be in favor» of transferring funds to Gaza. — words attributed to Benjamin Netanyahu by a source present at a Likud meeting, 11 March 2019 (The Jerusalem Post). Netanyahu denies saying them. The mechanism: how it worked, materially From 2018 until October 7, 2023, Qatar transferred cash to Gaza — physically, in suitcases, through the Israeli Erez crossing — peaking at around $30-35 million a month. The first shipment, $15 million, arrived in November 2018. According to Israeli sources, Qatar itself asked Netanyahu to put his funding requests in writing, anticipating he might later deny authorizing them. He did not: the Israeli security cabinet meeting that approved the mechanism, in August 2018, is documented, as is the cross-agency support maintained over the years by the IDF, military intelligence, Shin Bet, Mossad and the National Security Council. The strategic logic: why, not just how Netanyahu publicly justified the operation as humanitarian necessity — "preventing a disaster in Gaza." But according to a source present at a Likud meeting on 11 March 2019, quoted by The Jerusalem Post, Netanyahu explained a different calculation to his party: keeping Gaza under Hamas and the West Bank under the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority would prevent any unified Palestinian national movement — and therefore any real possibility of a Palestinian state. In 2024, interviewed by TIME, Netanyahu denied ever saying it; documents published by TIME in October 2026, however, show that Israel encouraged the payments and steered their distribution more than he had acknowledged. Retired Israeli general Shlomo Brom summarized the logic: "One effective way to prevent a two-state solution is to divide the Gaza Strip from the West Bank." The choice had a precise origin: after the 2014 Gaza war, Netanyahu rejected a Saudi offer to rebuild the Strip by removing Hamas and replacing it with the Palestinian Authority — a deal that would have normalized relations with Riyadh — opting instead for the Qatari funding channel, despite repeated Mossad warnings. How the money reached the weapons: the fungibility mechanism Between 2012 and 2018 Qatar funneled roughly $1.1 billion into Gaza, officially earmarked for state salaries, fuel, and humanitarian aid. No one claims those funds went directly to Hamas's military wing — but, as a retired senior CIA analyst explained to the New York Times, "money is fungible: anything Hamas didn't have to pay out of its own budget freed up its own funds for other things." It's the same principle by which funding an organization's civilian expenses lets it divert its own resources to whatever that external funding doesn't cover — in this case, according to a Shin Bet investigation published in March, the tunnel network and arsenal used on October 7, 2023. The attempt to bury accountability In June 2022, Mossad chief Yossi Cohen publicly called the Qatari channel "a blessing." A month before October 7, in September 2023, Israeli officials met with Qatar's envoy to Gaza, Mohammed al-Emadi, to ask not for a reduction but for an increase in transfers. After the attack, Netanyahu blocked the formation of a state commission of inquiry into the political-security failures that made it possible, and removed Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar, who had requested that commission — a removal Israel's Supreme Court ruled "unfair and unlawful." Legal commentary This episode does not constitute a single isolated violation of a specific treaty, but falls within the general obligation of states to prevent the financing of terrorist organizations, enshrined in UN Security Council Resolution 1373 (2001). Here the obligation was not violated through negligence, but knowingly suspended for political calculation — this is the reading that emerges from the account of the 2019 Likud meeting, which Netanyahu denies, and from the documents published by TIME in 2026. Implications — symmetry test This site has already condemned, without exception, the financing of non-state armed actors when that financing turned against the sponsors themselves or against third-party civilians. In Yemen: 73 UN staff still arbitrarily detained by the Houthis, as Hodeidah bleeds again , we documented how Iran, through the Houthis, supports a proxy that now acts according to its own autonomous agenda — attacks on commercial shipping, missiles against Israel — well beyond Tehran's original mandate. In Mali: army and Russian Africa Corps mercenaries arrange a corpse into a swastika after killing four civilians , we showed how Russia uses a paramilitary actor — the former Wagner Group — that commits systematic violations without Moscow answering for it directly. The same standard applies here. The fact that October 7's ultimate victims were Israeli citizens does not exempt Israel from having chosen, knowingly and for declared political calculation, to financially fuel the organization that then carried out the massacre — nor from having subsequently tried to obstruct the accounting of its own political responsibility for it. A note of methodological honesty: the history of US sponsorship of proxies that later turned against their own sponsors (from the Afghan mujahideen onward) would deserve the same treatment — a piece of its own, with facts verified one by one, not yet published on this site. Correction, 5 November 2026. The first version of this piece presented the March 2019 remark as a certain statement by Netanyahu and as his “own admission”. In fact it was reported by The Jerusalem Post , quoting a source present at the Likud meeting, and in 2024 Netanyahu denied having said it ( TIME ). We have corrected the text and added his denial.
