Sudan and Ethiopia, the war of the consulates: drones launched from Assosa and the risk of a war between states

Sudan accuses Ethiopia of letting RSF drones take off from its territory: 187 in eight months, according to Khartoum. Addis Ababa denies it and accuses Sudan of arming the Tigray rebels. Now the two countries are closing each other's consulates. What is proven, what is not, and what the law says.

— Assosa, Ethiopia – Gedaref, Sudan In brief On Sunday 1 November Sudan filed complaints against Ethiopia with the UN Security Council and the African Union's Peace and Security Council. According to Khartoum, since February the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have launched 187 attack drones from Ethiopian territory, in 70 attacks, with 484 civilian victims. These are Sudanese government figures that no one has verified. Between 2 and 4 November Ethiopia closed the Sudanese consulate in Assosa, near the border, and Sudan closed the Ethiopian consulate in Gedaref. Neither foreign ministry has officially explained why. Ethiopia denies the charge and accuses the Sudanese army of arming the Tigrayan fighters who resumed their war against Addis Ababa in September. Sudan denies that in turn. Both accusations have a basis documented by independent sources: a Reuters investigation into an RSF camp in Ethiopia, and reports of thousands of Tigrayan fighters fighting alongside the Sudanese army. Neither, however, is proven in its most serious part: drones launched with Ethiopia's consent, weapons supplied by Sudan to attack Ethiopia. International law forbids a state both to arm a neighbour's rebels and to let its own territory be used against that neighbour. The rule applies in both directions. Assosa is a small town in western Ethiopia, a few dozen kilometres from the Sudanese border. Until a week ago it hosted a small Sudanese consulate. According to the Sudanese government, it also hosts something else: the runway from which, since February, drones have taken off to strike Sudanese power stations, fuel depots and cities. This week the consulate is gone. The accusations remain, and with them the risk that Sudan's civil war and Ethiopia's become a war between the two states. The facts The power stations go dark (26–27 October). On 26 October drones attributed to the RSF hit six power stations in the states of Al-Jazira, White Nile, Sennar and Gedaref, leaving millions of people without electricity. The next day it was the turn of the Al-Markhiyat transformer station on the outskirts of Omdurman, which supplies much of the capital ( AFP, via Ahram Online ). According to a UN count reported by the same agency, in the first three weeks of October drones killed more than 300 people in Sudan. That figure covers all drones, from all parties and wherever they take off. The report and the complaint (1 November). On Sunday the Sovereignty Council, the army-led body that governs Sudan, published a report entitled "Launched from Ethiopia". It lists 70 attacks between 15 February and 27 October, with 187 "kamikaze" drones, the kind that crash into their target, and 82 munitions dropped by larger drones. It names three launch sites: Assosa airport, the Kurmuk and Geissan border area, and the Bahir Dar air base in Ethiopia's Amhara region. In October alone there would have been 28 attacks, with 97 drones ( Arab News ). As its main evidence, the report presents the onboard memory of a drone shot down on 20 September near Damazin, in Blue Nile state: the programmed route started from a point which, according to the Sudanese analysis, lies 1.7 kilometres inside Ethiopia. It also cites wreckage of Turkish-made Bayraktar Akinci drones said to have taken off from Bahir Dar ( Middle East Monitor ). There would be 484 civilian victims; the sources reporting on the document disagree on one point: whether they are all dead, or dead and wounded together ( Euronews Arabic ). The report also counts 176 soldiers killed. Among the incidents it cites, on 9 October in Wad al-Mahi, Blue Nile state, an attack on displaced families allegedly killed 30 civilians, 26 women and 4 children. Sudan asks Ethiopia to stop the attacks, to close the facilities used by the RSF and to pay compensation for the damage (same source). The same day the foreign ministry filed the complaint with the UN and the African Union. The use of Ethiopian territory by the RSF, it writes, "is a hostile act" that places Ethiopia in violation of international law ( AFP, via Kuwait Times ). The report has not been published in full, and the flight data have not been examined by independent experts. The consulates (2–4 November). According to a Sudanese official quoted by AFP, on 2 November Ethiopia declared the six staff of the Sudanese consulate in Assosa "persona non grata" and gave them 48 hours to leave ( AFP, via Kahawatungu ). A senior Ethiopian official confirmed the closure to Reuters without explaining the reason ( Reuters, via TimesLIVE ). On Wednesday 4 November Sudan responded with the same measure against the Ethiopian consulate in Gedaref. The two foreign ministries have not issued statements on the expulsions ( Sudan Tribune ). Amjad Farid, political adviser to the Sovereignty Council, said Sudan remains determined to defend its territory but "is making every possible effort to avoid an open war with Ethiopia" ( Reuters, via Arab News ). Ethiopia's version. Addis Ababa denies supporting the RSF. Its last detailed official response dates from May, when Sudan made similar accusations. The Ethiopian foreign ministry called them "baseless" and turned the argument around: it is Sudan, it wrote, that violates Ethiopia's territorial integrity by hosting "mercenaries" of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), and Sudan has become a base for forces hostile to Ethiopia ( Addis Media Network, Ethiopian state media ). The Sudanese army, it added, gives those fighters "arms and financial support" ( Al-Monitor ). Since September, when the Tigrayan fighters resumed their offensive against the federal army, Ethiopia has also accused Egypt and Eritrea of supporting them ( Al Jazeera, 28/9/2026 ). All three deny it. How we got here The quarrel did not start this week. On 2 March Sudan reported for the first time drones entering from Ethiopian territory, without saying who was flying them ( SUNA, via allAfrica ). In May, after a drone attack on Khartoum airport, it recalled its ambassador from Addis Ababa, accusing Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates ( Fides ). The RSF camp. On 10 February Reuters published an investigation, based on fifteen sources and on satellite imagery, into a training camp for the RSF in Ethiopia's Benishangul-Gumuz region, the same region as Assosa. The images showed hundreds of tents; a note by the Ethiopian security services, seen by the agency, spoke of 4,300 fighters in training in early January, with supplies provided by the Emirates. At Assosa airport the images showed works begun in August 2025: a hangar, new aprons and a ground control station for drones ( Reuters, via TimesLIVE ; The EastAfrican ). Reuters said it could not independently verify the role of the Emirates or the purpose of the works at the airport; the Emirates denied it ( The National ). A few days later Ethiopia refused to renew the accreditation of three Reuters journalists ( CPJ ). The Tigrayan fighters. Ethiopia's accusation also has a documented basis. During the Tigray war, between 2020 and 2022, thousands of Tigrayan fighters took refuge in Sudan's Gedaref state; some were trained soldiers, former UN peacekeepers ( The New Humanitarian ). According to Sudanese and Ethiopian sources interviewed by the independent Egyptian outlet Mada Masr, they formed a group called "Army 70", with thousands of men, which fights alongside the Sudanese army against the RSF; in August one of its units reportedly crossed the border into Ethiopia near Humera before being pushed back ( Mada Masr ). These are anonymous sources, and one of the two is an Ethiopian military officer, that is, a party to the dispute. The region. On 1 October Ethiopia expelled ten Eritrean diplomats and Eritrea broke off relations ( Sudan Tribune ). The same day Ethiopia expelled an Egyptian diplomat without giving a reason, and Egypt responded in kind ( Ahram Online ). Meanwhile Sudan's civil war, which began in April 2023, has forced more than 14 million people to flee, according to the UN ( Reuters, via The National ). For the Norwegian Refugee Council, Sudan's is the most neglected displacement crisis in the world ( NRC, June 2026 ). We wrote about the supply network that feeds this war in "Sudan, the war at a distance" ; about the war in Ethiopia, in the "Ethiopia" series. Legal commentary What the law forbids. The UN Charter forbids every state to use force against another state (Article 2, paragraph 4; see use of force ). A state does not need to send its own army to violate it. In 1986, in Nicaragua v. United States, the International Court of Justice ruled that arming and training another country's rebels is an unlawful use of force and a prohibited intervention ( ICJ ). The Friendly Relations Declaration, adopted by the General Assembly in 1970 and regarded as an authoritative interpretation of the Charter, adds a second prohibition: a state must not even tolerate armed activities organised on its territory against a neighbour ( resolution 2625 ). As early as 1949, in the Corfu Channel case, the Court said that no state may knowingly allow its territory to be used against the rights of another ( ICJ ). What would need to be proven. If the drones really take off from Assosa, the legal question is what Ethiopia knew and what it did. Letting drones take off from one's own airport, with infrastructure built for the purpose, can hardly be an activity the state knows nothing about. But it is an "if": today it is asserted by a party to the war, with evidence no third party has examined, and made plausible by a press investigation, not an international inquiry. The rule also applies the other way. If the Sudanese army hosts, pays and arms Tigrayan fighters who cross the border to fight in Ethiopia, it violates exactly the same rules. Using them against the RSF inside Sudan is another matter; letting them leave for Ethiopia is not. Self-defence. Sudan says it reserves the right to defend itself. The Charter allows this against an "armed attack" (Article 51), but here the attack comes from an armed group, not from the Ethiopian army. In 2005, in the case between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, the Court rejected the self-defence claimed by Uganda against rebels operating from Congolese territory, because their attacks were not attributable to Congo ( ICJ ). Striking Ethiopia on its own territory, without proof of a direct Ethiopian role, would put Sudan in the wrong and open a war between states. Power stations and civilians. A power station that serves a city is a civilian object, unless it is used for military purposes; even then, an attack must not cause disproportionate harm to civilians. Leaving millions of people in the dark is harm that has to be weighed before striking. Whoever launches the drones bears first responsibility. Whoever supplies or hosts them knowing how they are used cannot claim to be uninvolved. Who judges. Almost no one. The UN arms embargo covers only Darfur. On 8 October the Security Council extended it until 11 December, but Russia and China blocked the US proposal to extend it to the whole of Sudan ( Al Jazeera, 9/10/2026 ): drones striking Blue Nile, Kordofan or Omdurman fall outside it. In 2025 Sudan took the Emirates to the International Court of Justice, but the case was struck off because the Emirates, when joining the Genocide Convention, had excluded the Court's jurisdiction ( ICJ, 5/5/2025 ). The African Union's Peace and Security Council sits in Addis Ababa, the capital of the accused country, and Sudan has been suspended from the Union since the 2021 coup ( Sudan Tribune ). Symmetry test The evidence. We apply the same yardstick to both accusations. Against Ethiopia: the Sudanese government's figures, from a party to the war that has not had them verified, and the Reuters investigation, with satellite imagery and internal documents but also anonymous sources. Against Sudan: the statements of the Ethiopian government, also a party to the war, and reports by The New Humanitarian and Mada Masr on Tigrayan fighters alongside the Sudanese army, with largely anonymous sources. On one point the two accusations are alike: the least proven part is the most serious. No one has shown that Ethiopia authorises the drone launches, nor that Sudan arms the Tigrayans to attack Ethiopia. The embargo. Sudan asks the UN to stop the weapons reaching the RSF from abroad. But in October its ambassador to the UN opposed extending the embargo to the whole country, arguing that it would violate the right to self-defence (same Al Jazeera source). An embargo for everyone would also have hit the army's weapons. The drones. Sudan denounces RSF drones over its power stations. But the Sudanese army also uses drones, and its drones also kill civilians, as we documented in "Sudan, the war at a distance" . Whoever asks the UN to stop other people's drones is implicitly asking it to look at their own as well. The press. A government that disputes an investigation answers with evidence, not by withdrawing the accreditation of those who wrote it. Our judgement This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Closing a consulate costs little and kills no one. But in this region it is the gesture that usually comes before the ones that cost and kill. Sudan and Ethiopia are each fighting a civil war, and each helps, or is accused of helping, the other's enemies. If the two accusations are true even in part, the road leads to a war between states, right where there is already the largest and most neglected displacement crisis in the world. Sudan did the right thing: instead of responding on its own, it turned to the UN and the African Union. Now it is up to them. An independent commission to examine the flight data, the wreckage and Assosa airport, and with the same mandate the camps of Tigrayan fighters in eastern Sudan, would cost little. Not setting one up would mean leaving the truth to those who use it as a weapon. What to watch Whether the Security Council or the AU Peace and Security Council discusses Sudan's complaint, and whether Ethiopia responds formally. The expiry of the Darfur embargo on 11 December: whether it is renewed, and whether extending it to all of Sudan comes back on the table. Whether the UN panel of experts on Sudan, in office until 11 January 2027, examines the flight data and the wreckage. New drone attacks in Blue Nile and on the power grid, and where they are launched from. The Tigray offensive and the role, if proven, of fighters coming from Sudan. Sudan, war by remote: who supplies, who pilots, who should stop it

More than a thousand civilians killed by drones in five months, by both sides. A UN report reconstructs the network supplying the RSF across the Emirates, Chad, Libya and Puntland, and the Colombian contractors at the controls. By 9 October it will be decided whether the Mission continues.

In brief Between January and May 2026 drones killed more than 1,000 civilians in Sudan, according to the UN Human Rights Office. Both sides use them: the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the regular army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF). The UN Fact-Finding Mission concluded that there are "reasonable grounds" to believe that a transnational network, with bases and routes across the United Arab Emirates, Chad, Libya and Puntland, has supplied the RSF with weapons, drones, fuel and personnel. The Emirates deny it. Up to 2,000 Colombian contractors, according to the Mission, have piloted and maintained the RSF's drones, in some cases without ever handing control over to the Sudanese militiamen. The army too strikes hospitals and markets with foreign drones, consistent with Turkish-made models. On who supplies them, the Mission's investigation is still preliminary. By 9 October the Human Rights Council must decide whether to renew the mandate of the Mission, the only independent international body documenting these crimes. Sudan has been at war since April 2023. On one side is the army, led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan; on the other the Rapid Support Forces, a militia born from the Janjaweed of Darfur and led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. Until 2021 they had governed together. Today the RSF control almost all of Darfur, which they finished conquering with the fall of El Fasher in October 2025, and parts of Kordofan. The army holds the centre, the east and Khartoum. Caught in between are 8.8 million internally displaced people, 4.3 million refugees abroad and 19.5 million people in acute food insecurity, more than four Sudanese in ten. This war is no longer fought only with rifles and pick-ups. It is fought with drones launched hundreds of kilometres from their target, and with weapons that come from much further away. This piece tries to follow that chain. The facts On 1 September 2026 the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan, set up by the UN Human Rights Council in 2023, presented its report to the Council's 63rd session ( A/HRC/63/23 ). The report focuses on two things: the drone war and the external networks that feed it. On drones, the report cites a figure from the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights: more than 1,000 civilians killed in drone attacks between January and May 2026. Some of the incidents documented by the Mission: Date Place Target Dead Attributed to 4/12/2025 Kalogi, South Kordofan Nabaa al-Hanan kindergarten and hospital 114, about 60 of them children RSF 15/1/2026 Dilling market at least 12 RSF 20/3/2026 Ad-Da'ein, East Darfur teaching hospital at least 70, 146 injured SAF 29-30/3/2026 Yabus, Blue Nile market at least 13 SAF 8/4/2026 Kutum, North Darfur wedding party about 30 SAF 6/6/2026 Abu Zaima, North Kordofan market at least 12 SAF Source: UN Fact-Finding Mission, A/HRC/63/23, September 2026, paragraphs 28-51. Hospitals, markets, a kindergarten, a wedding party. These are not isolated incidents, and both sides are responsible for them. On 4 September the Emirates, through their UN mission in Geneva, replied that they are not involved in the war and have not supplied weapons or materiel to either party since April 2023 ( Khaleej Times ). They called for an immediate and unconditional ceasefire. The RSF network To understand what the Mission has established, the degree of certainty matters. A UN fact-finding mission is not a court: when it writes that there are "reasonable grounds to believe" something, it means it has gathered enough evidence to support it, not that it has handed down a verdict. With this degree of certainty, the Mission concludes that the RSF's military operations have been sustained by a transnational network of air, land and sea routes, linking people and entities located in the United Arab Emirates, Chad, south-eastern Libya and Puntland, in Somalia. The weapons. Since April 2025, Chinese 155-millimetre howitzers, air-defence systems, radars, armoured vehicles and reconnaissance and attack drones have arrived. Verified images show them in the hands of the RSF and then, in some cases, captured by the army. The routes. Witnesses describe recurring cargo flights from locations in the Emirates to Chad. In Libya, Benghazi, Kufra and Jufra act as hubs for weapons, vehicles, fuel and personnel, with the support of battalions of General Haftar's Libyan National Army. In Somalia, the port and airport of Bosaso, in Puntland, are identified as a recurring transit point, with a military base run by entities based in the Emirates. The men. The Colombian contractors are said to number between 350 and 2,000; the Mission believes the number is close to 2,000. They were recruited in Colombia, trained in the Emirates among other places, and moved to Darfur via Bosaso, Benghazi or Chad. On 28 April 2026 the Security Council sanctions committee targeted two of the recruiters: a retired Colombian colonel based in Abu Dhabi and his wife, who organised the recruitment in Colombia. The most serious point concerns their role. According to the Mission, the Colombian contractors piloted and maintained the RSF's drones, including those used in the attacks, and in some cases never transferred control of them to the militiamen. The one flying the drone is not always the one fighting the war. The army's drones The same Mission documents the Sudanese army's attacks. Since the end of 2023, it writes, the SAF have greatly expanded their capabilities with systems supplied from abroad. Technical analysis identified features consistent with Turkish-made Bayraktar Akıncı combat drones in footage from Nyala and Al-Farshaya in January 2026. Among the remains of the attack on the Yabus market, components consistent with a Yiha III loitering munition were found. Here the Mission stops: its investigation into external support for the army is described as "preliminary", and the report does not attribute the supply of these systems to any state. We report it as such, without going beyond what has been established. Legal analysis 1. Striking civilians. International humanitarian law applies to all parties to an armed conflict, regular armies and militias alike. It prohibits attacks on civilians and civilian objects, and gives special protection to hospitals and schools (Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions; Additional Protocol II, to which Sudan has been a party since 2006). The Mission concludes that there are reasonable grounds to believe that both the RSF and the SAF have committed serious violations, and that intentionally directing attacks against hospitals, schools and civilian objects may constitute a war crime. For El Fasher, in earlier reports, the Mission had already documented war crimes, crimes against humanity and conduct bearing the hallmarks of genocide, which we wrote about in the manifesto on Sudan . 2. The arms embargo. Since 2004 the Security Council has prohibited the supply of weapons to Darfur (resolution 1556, extended by resolution 1591 of 2005). The obligation applies to all UN member states. The RSF fight and resupply precisely in Darfur. The Mission writes that the nature, scale and persistence of external support raise "serious concerns" about compliance with the embargo, and recommends that the Security Council extend it to the whole of Sudan: today, weapons reaching the army outside Darfur are not covered by it. 3. The responsibility of those who help. A state that knowingly aids another state in committing an internationally wrongful act is responsible for it (International Law Commission Articles on State Responsibility, article 16). And Common Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions obliges all states not only to respect humanitarian law, but to ensure respect for it. International criminal law goes in the same direction for individuals: anyone who provides the means to commit a crime, knowing they will be used for that purpose, is an accomplice (Rome Statute, article 25, paragraph 3, letter c). This is why the Mission calls for the whole chain to be prosecuted: those who commit, those who order, those who finance, those who supply. 4. The limit of justice. The International Criminal Court has jurisdiction over Sudan only for Darfur, because Sudan has not ratified the Rome Statute and the Court's jurisdiction derives from the Security Council referral of 2005 (resolution 1593). Crimes committed in Kordofan, in Khartoum or in Blue Nile remain outside it. In 2025 the International Court of Justice dismissed, for lack of jurisdiction, Sudan's case against the Emirates, as we reconstructed in an earlier piece . The Mission recommends extending the ICC's jurisdiction to the whole of Sudan and creating a special tribunal. 5. Who sells weapons to the suppliers. The Arms Trade Treaty, to which Italy is a party, prohibits the export of weapons when the exporting state knows they will be used for war crimes (article 6), requires an assessment of the risk of serious violations (article 7) and obliges states to prevent their diversion to other recipients (article 11). In January 2021 Italy had suspended exports of missiles and bombs to the Emirates over the war in Yemen; in April 2023 the government lifted the suspension ( Al Arabiya ). We have no evidence that Italian weapons have reached Sudan. But the risk of diversion to a conflict under embargo, after a UN report like this one, is exactly what the Treaty requires to be assessed before every new licence. The symmetry test The same questions, turned around. A hospital hit by a drone is a crime because of what it does to the patients, not because of who pressed the button. The hospital in Ad-Da'ein, hit by the army, weighs as much as the kindergarten in Kalogi, hit by the RSF. That is why the table in this piece puts them side by side. If it were Iran, or Russia, supplying drones and mercenaries to the RSF, would the international reaction be the same? The Emirates are a strategic partner of the United States and Europe, Italy included. The standard we apply to the Emirates must apply to anyone who supplies weapons used against civilians, and it is the same one we have applied elsewhere to Western states that supply armies accused of crimes. And it applies to the Sudanese army and its suppliers. That the Mission has not yet attributed the army's drones to a state does not mean there are no suppliers. It means the investigation is not finished. It is one more reason not to shut it down. Editorial judgment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. The war in Sudan is often told as an African war, distant and incomprehensible, between two generals. The Mission's report tells something else: a globalised war, with Chinese and Turkish weapons, routes running through four countries and two continents, pilots recruited in South America and trained in the Gulf. It is distant only for those who watch it. For those who fight it, it is very close to the international markets. This changes the question. It is not enough to ask the two generals to stop. Those who make the war possible must be asked to stop making it possible. The embargo has existed for more than twenty years, and it is a list of prohibitions that almost no one enforces. Then there is an imbalance that is not about Sudan, but about us. More than 1,000 civilians killed by drones in five months, a kindergarten with about 60 children dead, a hospital with 70: in Europe this news rarely gets beyond a short item. The figure does not prove an intention. It proves a choice of attention, and it is the same choice this site has decided not to make. Finally, the Mission. By 9 October the states of the Human Rights Council decide whether to renew it, in the middle of the UN's financial crisis. Switching off the only independent body documenting this war, just as it has begun to put a name to the chain of suppliers, would be the simplest way to avoid having to answer its report. Update, 6 October 2026. On Monday 5 October the Human Rights Council renewed the Mission's mandate, with 28 votes in favour, 10 against and 9 abstentions ( Al Jazeera , Darfur24 ). According to the Syrian news agency SANA , the renewal is for one year, not the two requested by 68 civil society organisations, and those voting against included Egypt and Qatar: Egypt objects that the resolution puts the Sudanese army and the RSF on the same footing. The Sudanese government protested that its reservations had not been taken into account. The resolution also calls for an immediate and complete ceasefire, without preconditions. When this update was published, the official text was not yet available. Correction, 22 October 2026. The first version of this piece said “14.7 million displaced people”, an overall figure that did not distinguish between those who fled within Sudan and those who are refugees abroad. According to IOM there are 8.8 million internally displaced people (May 2026, IOM data via UNHCR ), and according to UNHCR there are 4.3 million Sudanese refugees in the region ( UN Geneva ). We have corrected the text. What to watch The Human Rights Council vote on renewing the Mission, by 9 October: length of the mandate and resources. The responses of Chad, Libya, Somalia and Ethiopia, which according to the Mission have not cooperated. The Mission's investigation into external support for the Sudanese army. The proposal to extend the arms embargo to the whole of Sudan and the ICC's jurisdiction beyond Darfur. The investigations in Colombia into the recruitment of the contractors. Italian export licences to the Emirates in the next annual report to Parliament under law 185/1990. Airport for airport: how the war between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia came back, and what each side wants
Twelve dead at Riyadh airport. The news bulletins condemn it but do not explain where this war comes from or what each side is asking for. We reconstruct it.

In brief On the evening of 10 October an attack on King Khalid airport in Riyadh killed 12 people, including 8 foreigners, and injured 309, according to the Saudi civil aviation authority. It is the deadliest in an escalation that began in July. The trigger: on 13 July a strike hit the runway of Sanaa airport to stop an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. Yemen's government, allied with Riyadh, claimed it; the Houthis blame Saudi Arabia. Since then the two sides have been hitting each other's airports. But the war was not born in July: it has been open since 2014, with Saudi intervention since 2015, frozen by a truce in 2022 and never closed by a peace agreement. The Houthis demand an end to the air and sea blockade, public-sector salaries, the withdrawal of foreign forces and control of the country's resources. Saudi Arabia wants to defend its territory and restore the recognised government. Washington has so far refused to intervene. It concerns people far away too: with Hormuz down to a fraction of its traffic, Gulf oil increasingly leaves through the Red Sea, and the Houthis are striking precisely those ports. On the evening of Saturday 10 October, at King Khalid airport in Riyadh, Terminal 3 was evacuated amid ambulances and helicopters. The next day the Saudi civil aviation authority gave the figures: 12 dead, four Saudis and eight foreigners including an American, and 309 injured, some seriously ( ANSA ). The news bulletins condemned the attack, as they should. Almost no one explained why a Yemeni armed movement fires missiles at the Saudi capital, or what it asks for in order to stop. We try to do that. The facts It is the third attack on Saudi airports in a week. On 6 and 7 October strikes on Riyadh and Abha had killed a Sudanese man, a Moroccan woman and an Algerian woman and injured 36 people; on 8 October three Saudis died in Riyadh, including a Saudia airline captain ( Khaleej Times ). The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Saree, claimed those attacks and warned airlines that every aircraft in Saudi airspace is a target, except those bound for Mecca and Medina ( Al Jazeera ). For 10 October the Houthis claimed strikes on "sensitive sites" in Riyadh and on Aramco facilities in Yanbu, without naming the airport, as a response to Saudi attempts to hit Sanaa ( AFP, via TNND ). The type of missile and Terminal 3 as the point of impact come from anonymous sources quoted by AFP and the Wall Street Journal ( ANSA ): they are not officially confirmed. How we got here The Houthis ( who they are, in our Glossary ) are an armed movement born in the 1990s in northern Yemen. Since 2014 they have controlled the capital, and since then the war has never ended ( Council on Foreign Relations ). Date Event 2004-2010 Six wars between the Houthis and the government of President Ali Abdullah Saleh. September 2014 The Houthis take Sanaa. March 2015 A coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervenes on behalf of the recognised government. In April UN Security Council resolution 2216 demands that the Houthis withdraw and imposes an arms embargo on them ( UN ). End of 2021 According to the UN Development Programme, the war has caused 377,000 deaths, 60% from hunger and disease ( Al Jazeera ). April 2022 UN-brokered truce. It expires in October but holds in practice: the Houthis stop striking Saudi Arabia ( DAWN ). December 2023 The UN envoy announces the parties' commitments to a "roadmap": ceasefire, public-sector salaries, oil exports, reopening of roads, ports and the airport ( UN News ). The plan stalls with the Houthi attacks on ships in the Red Sea, launched over the war in Gaza. US strikes follow in 2025 ( here ). The trigger of 13 July. That day a strike hits the runway of Sanaa airport and prevents an Iranian plane carrying a senior Houthi delegation from landing; after Omani mediation the plane lands in Hodeidah ( AP, via Al-Ahram ). Who struck is disputed. AP speaks of a Saudi strike and the Houthis blame Riyadh; the defence ministry of Yemen's government, in Aden, says instead that its own forces did it. Saudi Arabia has not commented ( Al-Monitor ). The government says the flight was carrying personnel and dual-use equipment: an accusation not independently verified, to which Tehran has not replied ( The National ). From there the spiral: missiles on Abha airport, the naval blockade declared by the Houthis on 20 July ( here ), offensives towards Taiz and Bab el-Mandeb, then the airports. By early October more than 200,000 people had been displaced in this new phase, according to the International Organization for Migration ( Al Jazeera ). Why it concerns everyone: two straits Before the war with Iran, which began on 28 February, about 125 large commercial vessels passed through Hormuz every day; on Tuesday 6 October, according to Kpler data, there were seven commercial vessels, the lowest number since July ( Reuters, via AAP ; here our piece on the strait). Oil has found other outlets: 6.7 million barrels a day leave from the Gulf of Oman coast and the Red Sea, more than double the pre-war level ( Reuters, via AAP ). For Saudi Arabia the outlet is Yanbu, on the Red Sea. According to Kpler data, between March and July 2026 an average of 3.8 million barrels a day left Yanbu, about five times the earlier level; in August, as Houthi attacks resumed, 1.5 million ( AFP, via Al-Ahram ). In September an attack halted exports from Yanbu for a week. General traffic in the Red Sea, on the other hand, is holding up: 280 ships a week at Bab el-Mandeb in the month to 27 September, against 316 in June ( Lloyd's List Intelligence ). The Houthis deny wanting to close the strait; according to the Institute for the Study of War their target is Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil ( AFP, via Al-Ahram ). The risk, then, is not a total blockade today. It is that both outlets for Gulf oil remain under threat at the same time. What the parties want We report the declared positions, not attributed motives. Party What it says it wants Houthis On 19 August they said the only way out for Riyadh is to lift the blockade, implement the measures already agreed to end the conflict, pay salaries, withdraw foreign forces and leave natural resources to Yemenis ( Shafaq News ). The statement does not say which measures: the only agreed measures made public are those of the 2023 UN roadmap. According to the International Crisis Group, they have moved from asking for confidence-building measures, such as salaries, to presenting the conflict as a question of sovereignty over airspace, ports and waters ( AP, via Al-Ahram ). Saudi Arabia and the coalition To defend Saudi territory and "Yemen's sovereignty", meaning that of the recognised government. Riyadh rejects the accusation of a siege and says it let more than 300 ships through to Houthi ports in the first half of 2026 ( here ). In September Mohammed bin Salman asked Trump, in two phone calls in a single day, to strike the Houthis ( Axios ). Yemen's recognised government The restoration of its authority over the country, on the basis of resolution 2216. It is divided: between December 2025 and January 2026 southern separatists attempted a secession that Riyadh attributes to support from the Emirates ( here ). Iran An ally of the Houthis. We found no official statements from Tehran on the attacks on the airports. The Houthis present the escalation as a Yemeni war, not as a front of the Iran war ( AP, via Al-Ahram ). United States No intervention so far: Trump offered only intelligence and targeting data, fearing, according to a former Pentagon official, a Houthi reaction at Bab el-Mandeb and a rise in oil prices ( Axios ). After 10 October he called the attack "not acceptable": "We'll make a decision" ( ANSA ). Pakistan Islamabad's foreign ministry spokesman said Pakistani troops will not cross the border to attack the Houthis but will act in defence of the territory ( Al Jazeera ). Legal reading and symmetry test Airports are civilian objects, in Riyadh as in Sanaa. International humanitarian law requires states and armed groups always to distinguish between military objectives and civilian objects ( ICRC, rule 7 ). A civilian airport loses protection only if it is used for military purposes, and even then an attack must not cause civilian harm that is excessive in relation to the expected advantage. A missile on a terminal, with 12 dead and 309 injured, is hard to justify by this standard; the same goes for the threat against any civilian aircraft in Saudi skies. But the rule also applies to the runway in Sanaa. Yemen's government says the flight was carrying military equipment: if this were proven, the embargo in resolution 2216 would give the action a basis. But there is no public evidence, and an unproven accusation does not turn a civilian airport into a target. The blockade. The one declared by the Houthis and the one the Houthis attribute to Riyadh follow the same rules: a blockade is unlawful if it starves civilians or if the harm to civilians is excessive in relation to the military advantage. For both, independent verification is lacking. The condemnations. The October attacks were condemned by the United Nations and by many governments ( Aviation Week ), including Qatar, Oman, Egypt ( Al Jazeera ) and the Emirates ( Khaleej Times ); after 10 October the UN envoy Hans Grundberg spoke of a grave escalation ( ANSA ). Saudi Arabia and Yemen's government asked the Security Council to act ( Al Jazeera ). The strike on the Sanaa runway was not explicitly condemned by anyone at the Security Council on 14 July: the UN warned that unilateral measures do not bring peace closer, the United States blamed Iran ( The National ). And the same yardstick applies to the whole war: more than 25,000 coalition air strikes since 2015, with nearly 19,000 civilians killed according to the Council on Foreign Relations ; the Houthi siege of the city of Taiz, which began in 2016 ( AFP, via Naharnet ). Editorial judgement This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Condemning a missile on an airport is a duty, and we reaffirm it. But a condemnation without context makes the war look like an outburst of madness. This war has a long history and precise demands, many of which were already written into the UN roadmap of 2023: salaries, ports, the airport, oil. The parties had said yes to it, and in August the Houthis asked for the measures already agreed to be implemented. Then Gaza, then the war with Iran, then a runway hit to stop a flight. There is also a lesson about selective memory. Hitting the runway in Sanaa and hitting the terminal in Riyadh are acts of the same kind, even if with very different consequences: using a civilian airport to punish the adversary. Al Jazeera's correspondent in Sanaa summed up the logic declared by the Houthis like this: "airport for airport". Whoever condemns one and stays silent about the other is not defending the law: they are choosing a side. One question remains about Washington. Trump said no to Riyadh for months, out of fear of a new front and of the price of oil, according to the sources. The midterm elections in November may be another reason, but no source we have read documents it: we flag it only as a hypothesis. After 10 October that caution could end. If the United States enters this war, it is worth remembering that a document already exists to which both sides had said yes. What to watch Trump's decision on an intervention alongside Saudi Arabia. An explicit Houthi claim for 10 October and the official Saudi report on Terminal 3. Exports from Yanbu and traffic at Bab el-Mandeb. The fighting around Taiz and Mokha and the number of displaced people. The initiatives of the UN envoy and of Oman to reopen negotiations. Yemen, the war is back in full: four thousand dead in a month and a number no one can give

The Houthis have taken the Red Sea coast and cut off Taiz; the government wants to retake the whole country. ACLED's death count has tripled in a year, but in the north no one verifies it. And the Houthis are not just "pro-Iranian".

In brief Since September Yemen has been at war again on every front. On 9 October the UN envoy Hans Grundberg told the Security Council that the country has "slid back into full-scale war". ACLED, the monitor we use for our Map, counts 8,804 deaths in 2026 as of 23 October: four weeks earlier there were 4,689, and 2,940 in the whole of 2025. The WHO counts at least 1,574 since August, but receives no data from Houthi-held areas. The numbers do not contradict each other: they count different things, in different places. Taiz, the most populous governorate, is again besieged by the Houthis. For Human Rights Watch the siege may amount to a war crime: starving civilians as a method of warfare. On the other side, Saudi-led coalition strikes on Sanaa and the north also hit factories and telephone networks. There, no one independently verifies who dies. The Houthis are neither Iran's puppet nor an independent movement: they depend on Tehran for their most advanced weapons, but on choices that touch their survival they decide for themselves. In 2026 the bond is the closest ever documented, and the two agendas coincide. No court and no international commission is investigating the crimes of this war today. Until the summer, Yemen was a mid-sized bubble on our Map: fewer deaths than Sudan, far fewer than Ukraine. Then, when we updated the ACLED data at the end of October, the bubble almost doubled in four weeks. A jump like that can mean one of two things: either the war has changed, or the way it is counted has changed. We went to look. The war has changed. But the way it is counted explains why so little is said about it outside Yemen. The facts The coast and the strait (September). On 3 September the Houthis launched an offensive in Taiz governorate, to cut the road between the city and the coast. On 10 September they took Mokha, the historic port on the Red Sea about eighty kilometres from the Bab el-Mandeb ( AFP, via Al-Monitor ). In the following days they occupied the rest of the western coast and the Hanish islands ( Long War Journal ). For the first time they control a stretch of coast directly overlooking the strait. The strait matters more than usual today: with Hormuz almost closed by the war between the United States, Israel and Iran, in June more than 7 million barrels of oil and products a day passed through the Bab el-Mandeb (same source, on shipping data). Taiz cut off (October). On 4 October the Houthis took al-Turbah and with it the last main road between the city of Taiz and Aden ( Al Jazeera ). Taiz had been under siege since 2015, but one route had stayed open. On 23 October the UN humanitarian agency (OCHA) counted twenty days of isolation. The World Food Programme says it cannot reach more than 600,000 people who depend on aid; the UN humanitarian coordinator, Laurent Bukera, said the city's water production has halved and the health system is "close to collapse" ( Human Rights Watch, 29/10/2026 ). The counter-offensive (October–November). On the same day, 4 October, the head of the Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, announced an offensive to retake all Houthi territory, Sanaa included ( AAP, via Illawarra Mercury ). The Saudi-led coalition said it was taking part with a hundred fighter jets ( Al Jazeera, 7/10/2026 ). In early November the hardest fighting was in al-Jawf, to the north-east, around Taiz and in northern Lahij, on the line between Taiz and Aden ( Al Jazeera, 4/11/2026 ). The deadliest attacks. On 19 October three Houthi ballistic missiles hit a security forces training camp in Shabwa, in the south: 73 dead, all recruits aged 18 to 20, and more than 200 wounded, according to the governor of the province ( AP, via Korea Times ). The Houthis say the camp was run by the Saudis ( Reuters, via Express Tribune ). Since the start of October the Houthis have struck Saudi airports and oil facilities almost daily; we wrote about it in "Airport for airport" . The Houthis say Saudi strikes on their territory have numbered more than 2,700 ( dpa, via Qatar Tribune ); the figure cannot be verified. Those who flee. Between 1 August and 12 October the International Organization for Migration counted 217,303 displaced people ( IOM, via UNI ), the highest number since the 2022 truce ( The National ); at the end of October the UN spoke of more than 250,000 ( L'Orient-Le Jour ). More than 3,800 have crossed the sea to Djibouti ( UN, via Al Jazeera ). The numbers: why they don't add up There are three counts, and none of them is wrong. Who counts What they count How many Where they reach ACLED deaths from all political violence, fighters included, from news and local partners 8,804 in 2026 as of 23 October; more than 6,400 since the war resumed ( ACLED, via dpa ) the whole country, with the most conservative figures available WHO dead and wounded recorded by health facilities at least 1,574 dead and 6,939 wounded since August only where hospitals report: not from Houthi-held areas UN human rights office civilian casualties verified one by one at least 125 civilians killed or injured from August to 24 September ( AFP, via Dhaka Tribune ) where it can verify, that is mostly in government areas ACLED counts all deaths, soldiers included, and October's war is above all a war of soldiers: both sides announce hundreds of enemies killed every day. ACLED says it always uses the most conservative estimate available ( ACCORD, methodology note ); we do not know how much of its total comes from the parties' own figures. There is also a declared limit: since 2025 ACLED has expanded its coverage of Yemen with a local partner, and warns that data from before 2024 are not comparable with today's ( ACLED ). The comparison between 2025 and 2026, however, holds. The point that matters for the reader is a different one. The WHO says it receives no figures from Houthi-held areas, where most Yemenis live. In August the UN counted 17 civilian casualties of Houthi attacks in government areas and 2 in Houthi areas ( Volker Türk, High Commissioner for Human Rights, via TRT ). This does not mean Saudi strikes do not kill: it means there is no one there to count them independently. Missing data is not data worth zero. Who's who Who What they want Who backs them Houthis (Ansar Allah) An end to the air and sea blockade, public salaries, the withdrawal of foreign forces, recognition of their power in the north. Iran: weapons, components and advisers (see below). Who they are, in our Glossary . Presidential Leadership Council (recognised government, in Aden) To retake the whole country, Sanaa included. Saudi Arabia: aircraft and money for salaries. UN resolution 2216 recognises it. Saudi Arabia To defend its territory and its oil routes, and keep the government standing. The United States, politically. Southern separatists A southern state. The Southern Transitional Council, backed by the Emirates, dissolved in January after a defeat by pro-Saudi forces; its supporters say the decision was taken under pressure. Partly the Emirates, until January. Houthis and Iran: ally or puppet? In the news the Houthis are almost always "the Iran-backed rebels", and Yemen's war becomes a front in the war against Iran. That is part of the truth. To see how large a part, it helps to separate three things: the weapons, the people, the decisions. Weapons: a strong dependence. Since 2018 UN experts have found in Houthi missiles and drones features of Iranian weapons and components made in Iran, in breach of the embargo of resolution 2216 ( AFP, via Arab News ). Conflict Armament Research, a British centre that examines seized weapons, studied more than 800 missile and drone components intercepted in the Red Sea in 2024 and 2025: the assembly labels use the Iranian names of the missiles, not the Houthi ones, and for the centre external support remains decisive ( Conflict Armament Research ; Jerusalem Post ). The same study, however, shows that only 5% of those components were produced in Iran: the rest bear the marks of companies from 15 other countries, China and Europe included. Iran, in other words, acts mainly as a supply network and a source of designs. The Houthis also assemble and experiment on their own ( The National ). People: in 2026, the most direct role ever documented. According to two anonymous Iranian sources quoted by Reuters, the 13 July 2026 flight from Tehran, the one the Yemeni government tried to stop by bombing the runway at Sanaa, carried between 10 and 21 members of the Revolutionary Guards, including senior officers, and missile and drone components. The Houthis say only civilians were on board; Tehran says the flight was bringing home a delegation and patients ( Reuters, via bdnews24 ). On the coastal offensive, five Yemeni government military sources told Reuters that the Revolutionary Guards directed it, and two Iranian sources that Tehran asked the Houthis to step up attacks on Saudi Arabia, promising money, weapons and officers ( Reuters, via The New Arab ). An AP investigation, based on ten officials and soldiers, describes Revolutionary Guards advisers in the field who helped plan operations and analyse intelligence: the most direct Iranian involvement since the war began in 2014 ( AP, via Iran International ). These are mostly anonymous sources, and many belong to the Yemeni government, that is to a party to the war: we report them as unverified. Tehran denies directing the Houthis and says they are an ally, "not a proxy". Decisions: more autonomy than is often said. An Iranian official, in the same Reuters report, says the taking of Mokha was a Houthi decision, not Iran's, even if it suited Iran. In 2014, according to US officials and later President Obama himself, Iran advised the Houthis against taking Sanaa; they took it anyway ( HuffPost, 2015 ). In March 2026, when the United States and Israel attacked Iran, Hezbollah and the Iraqi militias entered the war within the first weeks ( Reuters, via ARY ); the Houthis held back for weeks, and analysts at ACLED and the Arab Gulf States Institute read this as a calculation about their own survival, not as an order received ( ACLED ; AGSI ). Other analysts think instead that Tehran was holding them in reserve (same source). And the Houthis' story, the six wars with Saleh, the rivalry with Saudi Salafism, the power over Sanaa, began before Iranian support became important. How we see it. "Iran's puppet" is wrong; "independent movement" is wrong too. The Houthis are an ally that depends on Iran for its most advanced weapons and decides on its own when what is at stake is its survival or power in Yemen. In 2026 the bond is the closest ever documented, and the two agendas coincide: Iran, under attack, has an interest in leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb and Saudi oil; the Houthis have an interest in taking the coast and making Saudi Arabia pay for the blockade. Those who read this war only as a proxy war forget that it is Yemenis who fight it, and die in it, for Yemeni reasons. Those who read it only as a civil war forget where the missiles that hit Riyadh come from. The same yardstick. The question applies to the other side too. The government in Aden depends on Saudi Arabia for salaries, 346.6 million dollars in February 2026 alone ( Arab News ), for aircraft and for its very composition: in January 2026 Riyadh broke up the Emirati-backed separatists by force and replaced their members on the Presidential Council ( TRT World ). If the Houthis are "pro-Iranian", the government is, by the same measure, "pro-Saudi". Neither label is enough on its own. Legal commentary Taiz and hunger as a weapon. Besieging a city defended by soldiers is not prohibited in itself. Using the starvation of civilians as a method of warfare is prohibited, and so is blocking aid without military necessity. It is a rule of customary international law, which applies in civil wars too and to an armed group such as the Houthis; Yemen, moreover, has been a party since 1990 to the Second Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, which sets it out in Article 14 ( ICRC, International Review of the Red Cross ). For Human Rights Watch the siege of Taiz "may amount" to that crime; intent can be inferred from the circumstances, and people do not have to die of hunger to prove it. The Houthis reply that it is government forces that are closing the roads; residents, civil society workers and UN officials say the opposite. The Shabwa camp. Were the 73 recruits a military target? It depends on what they were. A soldier in training is a combatant; a police officer, under humanitarian law, is a civilian, unless he is part of the armed forces or takes part in the fighting. The governor says they were training for security in the province, not for the front; the Houthis say the camp was Saudi. No one has yet verified it. It is the first question an investigation should ask. The Saudi airports. A civilian airport full of passengers is a civilian object. Warning the airlines, as the Houthis did, does not make striking it lawful: it only makes it predictable. The strikes on the north. The same rules apply to the coalition. Every strike on a factory, an antenna or a neighbourhood of Sanaa must hit a military objective and not cause civilian harm that is excessive in relation to the expected advantage. Whether it has done so or not, today no one knows, for the reason given above: in the north there is no one to verify. Who judges. No one, for now. Yemen signed the Statute of the International Criminal Court in 2000 but never ratified it ( Parliamentarians for Global Action ); nor have Saudi Arabia and Iran. The UN group of experts that investigated crimes by all parties was shut down in 2021 by a vote of the Human Rights Council ( International Commission of Jurists ). Meanwhile 72 UN staff remain detained by the Houthis ( Grundberg to the Security Council, 9/10/2026 ). Symmetry test The yardstick. If a regular army closed the last road into a city of hundreds of thousands of people and halved its water, this site would speak of starvation as a method of warfare. We say it here in the same words, for an armed group that the government would like the UN to declare "terrorist" ( Al Jazeera, 20/10/2026 ) and that its supporters call resistance. The numbers. The data verified by the UN lean one way: almost all the civilian casualties counted were caused by the Houthis. But they lean that way because the UN works mostly on one side. In the years of the air war, between 2015 and 2019, ACLED attributed about two thirds of directly killed civilians to air strikes ( ACLED, 2019 ). Reading the asymmetry of the data as an asymmetry of conduct would be a mistake, in either direction. The truce. 2022 had stopped the war; no one had ended it. The demands of the Houthis and of the government were already written into the UN "roadmap" of December 2023. Neither side today seems to think it can get more at the table than on the battlefield. Our view This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Yemen's bubble on our Map has grown because the war really is back in full, not because of a counting error. But the most important figure is not the number: it is the hole in the number. In half the country the dead are counted from the communiqués of those who fight, and a war that is not counted is a war that is not judged. Grundberg put it another way: gains on the battlefield cannot replace the negotiations that will in any case be needed to end the war. As long as no one investigates, each side can tell its own war as the only true one. What to watch Whether the UN manages to open a humanitarian route to Taiz, as governor Nabil Shamsan asks. Grundberg's next briefing to the Security Council and any resolution on the Bab el-Mandeb. Whether anyone verifies the status of the Shabwa recruits and the coalition strikes in the north. ACLED's November data and the next UCDP release, to see whether the two sources converge. The fate of the 72 detained UN staff. Yemen: war intensifies again and fuels child recruitment, as the UN warns of famine risk
Over 100 killed since last week between Taiz and Hodeidah, 62 new child-recruitment cases documented in the second quarter of 2026 alone, 6 million people on the edge of famine.

«This reflects a systematic policy of child recruitment.» — Ali Hazazi, Human Rights Office of the Presidency, Aden The facts Over the past week, more than 100 fighters from both sides have been killed in clashes between Houthi forces and government/pro-Saudi forces along the western Taiz and southern Hodeidah fronts (Kadha front) — the most intense escalation in years along the same frontline already reported on this site in July 2026. Over the same period, Hazazi documented 62 new child-recruitment cases in the second quarter of 2026 in Houthi-controlled provinces, calling them "only a fraction" of the real phenomenon, since most cases go unreported. SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, which monitors human rights violations in the country, recorded 11,310 children recruited or used across 19 governorates between 2014 and 2023, including 6,269 aged 8 to 11. Individual cases collected by Al Jazeera show explicit financial compensation for enlistment: around 50,000 Yemeni rials (210 dollars) as a one-off payment, or a monthly wage of around 45,000 rials (80 dollars) — slightly above the local average wage, in a country where more than four in five rural children live in poverty. Pro-government forces have captured numerous Houthi child soldiers, including on the al-Dhale front; the sources consulted for this cycle show no comparable cases of recruitment on the government side (see the symmetry test below). In the background, UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher told the Security Council in mid-August 2026 that 6 million people face "emergency" levels of deprivation bordering on famine. A joint report by ACAPS/FAO/UNICEF/World Bank/WFP/WHO from early 2026 ranks Yemen fourth worldwide for food insecurity, with 18.3 million people projected to be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse. The UN Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP) 2026, published by OCHA on 18 March 2026, estimates 22.3 million people in need of assistance and protection in the country, including 5.2 million internally displaced people. Yemen also appears on the International Rescue Committee's 2026 Emergency Watchlist, published in December 2025 — that is, before any of this week's news. On 20 July 2026 the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, calling it an "eye for an eye" response to what they describe as a Saudi land, sea and air siege lasting around 12 years — a declaration that came after a Saudi strike on Sanaa airport, amid renewed regional tensions over Iran's role. Saudi Arabia rejected the siege accusation the following day, saying more than 300 ships carrying food, goods, fuel and construction materials had passed through the ports of Hodeidah, Salif and Ras Isa in the first half of 2026, and announced measures to protect maritime traffic in the Bab al-Mandab strait. Neither side has so far provided independent verification of how the Houthi-declared blockade is actually being enforced. Legal commentary Recruiting and using children under 15 in combat is a war crime under the Rome Statute, art. 8(2)(b)(xxvi) and (e)(vii); the Optional Protocol to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, to which Yemen is a state party, extends the recruitment ban up to age 18. It should be noted that some of the documented cases involve 17-year-olds: an age bracket where international law still bans use in combat, but not under the same absolute threshold set for under-15s — a legal distinction that should not be flattened. Both the Yemeni government (with a UN action plan signed in 2014) and the Houthis (with a similar agreement in 2022) had committed to ending the practice; the evidence gathered in this cycle shows the Houthi commitment remains largely unmet. Implications — the symmetry test The principle — no recruitment of children, by any actor — would apply equally to Houthi forces as to government or pro-Saudi forces: this is not a judgment reserved for one side. But applying it honestly here also means saying what this cycle's sources do not show: unlike the case already covered on this site in July (where the Saudi coalition, the UAE and the US/UK shared comparable, documented responsibility), the sources available for 2026 child recruitment are concentrated almost entirely on the Houthi side — pro-government forces appear to be capturing children recruited by the Houthis, not recruiting them in turn in this cycle. A known precedent (recruitment also by the Yemeni army during the 2011 uprising against Saleh) shows the phenomenon has never been exclusive to one actor in the past — but applying that to the present without a comparable 2026 source would be a manufactured symmetry, not a found one. The asymmetry is therefore stated rather than papered over. On humanitarian access, by contrast, the picture remains two-sided, as in the July case already published on this site: the Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of a years-long siege, Riyadh denies it and claims hundreds of ships transited Houthi ports in the same period — neither version has been independently verified, and both should be reported as competing claims, not as an established fact favouring either side. Judgment Stated as such, separate from the facts above: poverty does not justify child recruitment — it remains a crime regardless of who commits it or the economic conditions of those who consent to it — but it explains why the "choice" keeps presenting itself as one. A payment of 80 dollars a month, in a country where four in five rural children live in poverty, is not a neutral incentive: it is the difference between a meal and no meal for a family. Poverty does not help families choose otherwise when the immediate alternative is hunger — it does not absolve those who recruit, but it narrows the real space of choice for those who consent. Yemen: 73 UN staff still arbitrarily detained by the Houthis, as Hodeidah bleeds again

73 UN staff remain arbitrarily detained by Houthi authorities as of June 2026, one died in custody; on 5 July the fiercest clashes in years killed 16 government soldiers in Hodeidah. Legal analysis under ICCPR art. 9 and the Geneva Conventions.

«These actions violate international law, cause deep suffering to families.» — António Guterres, UN Secretary-General, 12 June 2026 The facts On 5 July 2026, Houthi fighters attacked Yemeni government force positions in the Hodeidah region (Hays area), on the Red Sea coast, using mortars, drones and sniper fire: 16 soldiers killed and 22 wounded, according to medical and military sources cited by Al Jazeera — the fiercest clashes in years along a frontline frozen since 2022. The same day, a commercial vessel was attacked off Hodeidah, with no claim of responsibility. In parallel, and over a longer period: as of 12 June 2026, 73 United Nations staff — all Yemeni nationals — remained arbitrarily detained by the Houthi de facto authorities, as part of an arrest campaign that began in May 2024 and has never concluded; one World Food Programme worker died in Houthi custody on 11 February 2025. On 29 January 2026 the WFP announced it was terminating the contracts of all 365 of its staff in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen — where 70% of the country's humanitarian need is concentrated — explicitly citing the operating environment made unsafe by arbitrary detentions. On 27 January 2026 the UN Security Council voted a final extension, to 31 March, of the mission supporting the Hodeidah Agreement (UNMHA), which was then shut down: the United States pushed for its closure, arguing Houthi obstruction had made it ineffective; China and Russia voted to keep it. In the background, 21.6 million people remain in need of assistance (11 million children), 4.5 million are displaced, and the 2026 UN humanitarian appeal of $2.16 billion was only 29% funded in 2025. Legal commentary The arbitrary detention of UN staff — often without a warrant, with cases of enforced disappearance lasting months and one death in custody never clarified — violates Article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (no one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest or detention), to which Yemen has been a state party since 1987, as well as the immunities recognised for UN personnel acting in their official capacity. The systematic obstruction of humanitarian access — which already forced the WFP to suspend operations in Saada governorate — falls instead within the scope of the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocol II, which prohibit impeding humanitarian relief to civilians in non-international armed conflicts. The two violations are distinct but reinforce one another: those who should guarantee access to aid are detained, and in doing so the very crisis that access should relieve is worsened. Implications — the symmetry test The principle — humanitarian personnel are not arbitrarily detained, relief access is not obstructed — applies to the Houthis exactly as it would to any other actor this site has already covered. But Yemen has no single culprit, which is what makes it a textbook case for symmetry: the Saudi-led coalition has conducted more than 25,000 air strikes since 2015 and caused nearly 19,000 civilian casualties according to the Council on Foreign Relations; the United Arab Emirates is accused by Riyadh of having armed the Southern Transitional Council's secessionist bid between December 2025 and January 2026, later repelled by pro-Saudi forces; the United States and the United Kingdom have struck Houthi targets directly since 2024. Applying the criterion only to the Houthis because they are the most visible actor at this moment — while staying silent on the coalition, the Emirates, and the Anglo-American strikes — would not pass the test. Appendix: the "Rough Rider" campaign and the Sa'ada strike (March-April 2025) An earlier episode, documented but not yet covered on this site, deserves reconstruction here because it sheds direct light on the symmetry principle applied above. Between March 15 and May 6, 2025, the United States conducted a campaign of air and naval strikes against Yemen, codenamed "Operation Rough Rider," in response to Houthi attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea: according to estimates by the independent organization Airwars, the US strikes killed at least 224 civilians. On April 28, 2025, a US air strike hit a migrant detention centre in Sa'ada, north-western Yemen, killing and injuring dozens of African migrants held there by Houthi authorities. An Amnesty International investigation concluded that the strike constitutes an indiscriminate attack, to be investigated as a possible war crime. Asked by Amnesty, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it was "assessing all reports of civilian harm" from that period; by the end of 2025 the results of that assessment had not been made public. In the same timeframe, the Houthis resumed missile and drone attacks on Israel — a missile injured 4 people near the main terminal of Ben Gurion airport (May 4, 2025), a drone injured over 20 people near a hotel in Eilat (September 24, 2025) — alongside attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea, sinking two vessels (Greek-owned, Liberian-flagged) and killing at least three crew members. Extended symmetry test: a US strike on a migrant centre that no public assessment has ever clarified; Houthi attacks on civilian shipping and a third country (Israel) unrelated to the arbitrary detention of UN staff discussed above, yet compounding the same climate of widespread impunity. None of the three actors — Washington, Sana'a, the coalition — comes out absolved. Mali: army and Russian Africa Corps mercenaries arrange a corpse into a swastika after killing four civilians

On June 23, 2026, near Timbuktu, a joint patrol of the Malian army and Russia's Africa Corps kills four civilians and arranges one victim's dismembered body into a swastika — while Mali has already withdrawn from the Rome Statute.

«When you find a human being cut up to form a Nazi symbol, by a regular army, it's truly shocking.» — local witness quoted by RFI The facts On June 23, 2026, near Timbuktu, a joint patrol of the Malian army and Russia's Africa Corps (the organization that replaced the Wagner Group after Yevgeny Prigozhin's death) passed through the villages of Zarho and Abakoïra, at the border of the Timbuktu and Gao regions. After the patrol passed, residents found four civilians killed: two Tuareg at Zarho and two Songhai at Abakoïra, the latter struck by a drone attack while riding a motorbike. The dismembered body of one of the Tuareg men was arranged into the shape of a swastika on the sand, his severed head placed at the center of the limbs. Local sources and the Malian human rights collective CD-DPA confirmed that the victims were herders known in the community, with no ties to armed groups. CD-DPA's secretary general, Tilla Ag Zeini, described the incident as a violation of humanitarian law designed to terrorize the population. Neither the Malian army nor the Africa Corps has publicly commented on the incident, despite the latter posting regularly on social media after other operations. The same day, the al-Qaeda-linked jihadist group JNIM claimed a separate attack on a joint army-Africa Corps convoy in the Kayes region, reporting six dead — a distinct episode but indicative of the intensity of the conflict on multiple fronts in the same country on the same day. The political context: the military junta led by Colonel Assimi Goïta expelled French forces and ended the UN peacekeeping mission MINUSMA, replacing them with Russian mercenaries — a choice presented to the population as a recovery of sovereignty. As this site already reported in Burkina Faso leaves the International Criminal Court while remaining the world's country most affected by terrorism , Mali withdrew — together with Burkina Faso and Niger — from the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (September 2025), explicitly removing itself from the jurisdiction of the very court that could investigate episodes like this one. Legal commentary The outrage upon the personal dignity of corpses and the killing of civilians without distinction from military targets violate Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law applicable to non-international armed conflicts. The staging would fall under "outrages upon personal dignity," prosecutable as a war crime under Article 8 of the Rome Statute — a statute from which Mali has just withdrawn, making the risk of impunity concrete. Implications — symmetry test This site has already condemned elsewhere the presence and conduct of Russian-linked paramilitary forces; the same standard applies here, with no discount for the fact that the victim is a Malian herder rather than an internationally prominent figure. But responsibility is not one-directional: the patrol was joint — regular Malian army and Africa Corps together — and neither has commented on or condemned what happened. Mali's withdrawal from the Rome Statute, precisely as episodes like this multiply, is itself a political act that deserves condemnation regardless of who physically carried out the killing. Haiti: its people, its history, who is shooting and why

Country profile on Haiti: a people born of a slave revolt, the ransom paid to France, the US occupation, the Duvalier dictatorship, the coups, the earthquake, the assassination of the president and the gangs that now control the capital, who gains from it and what international law says. An entry we keep up to date.

News from Haiti talks about gangs, kidnappings, foreign forces arriving and leaving, postponed elections, but rarely explains how the poorest country in the Americas ended up with neither an elected president nor an elected parliament, or who armed the gangs. In Haiti, unlike the other countries in these profiles, the war does not pit different peoples against each other: the fault lines are class, skin colour, language, town and countryside. This entry tries to provide that background. We keep it up to date: every change is logged at the bottom, with date and source. In brief Haiti has about 11.6 million inhabitants. Almost all are descended from Africans brought as slaves; a small mixed-race minority and a few families of Middle Eastern origin long dominated politics and the economy. Almost everyone speaks Creole; French, the language of power, is spoken well by perhaps one person in ten. In 1804 Haiti became the first republic born of a slave revolt. To win recognition, in 1825 it had to promise France a huge indemnity, paid off with interest until 1947. Then came the US occupation (1915-1934), the Duvalier dictatorship (1957-1986), coups and foreign missions. Since the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in July 2021, no one in Haiti has been elected: there is no president and no parliament. Power has passed to transitional authorities; the vote has been postponed to July 2027. In the vacuum the gangs have grown. In 2025 violence killed almost 6,000 people, according to the UN, mostly at the hands of the gangs but also in security-force operations. Almost one and a half million people have fled their homes. The weapons come mainly from the United States. Land and people Haiti occupies the western third of the island of Hispaniola, in the Caribbean Sea; the rest is the Dominican Republic. It is a mountainous country, with little farmland and forests that have almost disappeared. The capital, Port-au-Prince, is in the Ouest department; the Artibonite valley, north of the capital, is the country's breadbasket. Haiti is divided into 10 departments.
