We do not draw the areas held by individual gangs, which change from month to month. The square marks the capital. Boundaries: Natural Earth (10 departments). The inhabitants. Freedom House estimates about 11.6 million inhabitants ( Freedom House ). A very large share of Haitians live abroad, mainly in the United States, Canada, France and the Dominican Republic. A word of caution about the numbers. Haiti publishes no recent official data on the origins of its inhabitants, and the percentages in circulation are rounded estimates. For religion, different sources give very different figures, and we say so. Afro-Haitians — about 95% of the population ( Minority Rights Group ). They are descended from the more than 500,000 enslaved Africans who worked the plantations of the French colony in 1790 (same source). They are the great majority of farmers and of the urban poor. Mixed-race Haitians — most of the remaining 5% (same source). They are partly descended from the free gens de couleur of the colonial era, about 28,000 in 1790. For much of the country's history a small urban mixed-race minority held political and economic power and did not identify with the black rural majority (same source). In Haiti skin colour has long also been a matter of class; the Duvaliers built their power by presenting themselves as defenders of the black majority. Haitians of Syrian and Lebanese origin — a few thousand people, with no reliable figure. They arrived between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and today are very present in trade and industry (same source). Other small minorities — descendants of Europeans, including a community of Polish origin, and Dominicans (same source). The languages. There are two official languages, Haitian Creole and French ( Minority Rights Group ). Almost everyone speaks Creole; French is spoken well, according to scholars' estimates, by about 10% of Haitians, usually the most educated and the wealthiest ( University of Alabama ). For many Haitians school, the courts and official documents remain in a language they barely understand. Religion. In 2018 the US government estimated 55% Catholics and 29% Protestants, with a small share identifying only as Vodou ( US State Department, via ecoi.net ); a 2024 survey instead shows more Protestants (37%) than Catholics (29%) ( via Wikipedia ). Vodou, a religion born from the meeting of African religions and Catholicism, has been officially recognised since 2003 and is practised by many Haitians alongside another faith, often in secret because of the stigma attached to it ( Minority Rights Group ). As in South Sudan, religion is not what separates those who shoot from those who die. The economy. Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas and, according to Minority Rights Group, the most unequal in Latin America and the Caribbean (same source). It has no great resources to fight over, such as oil or mines: whoever controls the roads, the ports, the customs posts and the fuel supply controls the economy. That is exactly where the gangs concentrate. A short history From the Taíno to the richest colony in the world. When Columbus arrived in 1492, the island was inhabited by the Taíno, who within a few decades were wiped out by the violence and diseases brought by the Spanish. In 1697 Spain ceded the western part to France, which became Saint-Domingue. In the eighteenth century it was the richest colony in the world, thanks to sugar and coffee produced by hundreds of thousands of slaves: in 1790 there were more than 500,000 of them, against about 30,000 Europeans who held all power ( Minority Rights Group ). The revolution and independence (1791-1804). In August 1791 the slaves of the north rose up. Under the leadership of Toussaint Louverture they forced France to abolish slavery in 1794. In 1802 Napoleon sent an army to restore it; Toussaint was captured and died in a French prison. His successor Jean-Jacques Dessalines defeated the French and on 1 January 1804 proclaimed the independence of Haiti, the first republic born of a slave revolt ( The Nation ). The ransom (1825-1947). For twenty years the European powers and the United States refused to recognise the new state. In 1825 King Charles X of France sent warships and demanded 150 million francs to recognise independence and compensate the former plantation owners, for their slaves too ( Collège de France ). In 1838 the sum was reduced to 90 million, but to pay it Haiti had to borrow from French banks. According to a 2022 New York Times investigation, Haiti paid about 112 million francs in all, and the interest on the loans kept it tied until 1947; the economists consulted by the paper estimate that the country lost between 21 and 115 billion dollars in growth ( The Nation ; El Caribe ; New York Times data ). These are estimates, and they are debated, but no one disputes that the debt deprived Haiti of the resources to build a state. The US occupation (1915-1934). Between 1911 and 1915 seven Haitian presidents were killed or overthrown ( Office of the Historian, US State Department ). After the lynching of President Vilbrun Guillaume Sam in July 1915, US President Wilson sent in the Marines. The United States took control of finances and customs, created a gendarmerie, abolished the ban on foreigners owning land and crushed the resistance of the cacos led by Charlemagne Péralte; they left in 1934 ( CRS, US Congress ; History Matters ). The Duvaliers (1957-1986). In 1957 François Duvalier, "Papa Doc", a country doctor, was elected. He proclaimed himself president for life, created a personal militia, the Tontons Macoutes , and ruled by terror; in 1971 his son Jean-Claude, "Baby Doc", succeeded him. In almost thirty years the regime killed about 30,000 people, according to the most widely cited estimates, and hundreds of thousands of Haitians emigrated ( Business Recorder, from AFP ). On 7 February 1986 Baby Doc fled to France on a US military plane ( Human Rights Watch ). He returned in 2011 and died in 2014 without ever being tried. The 1987 Constitution and the coups. In 1987 Haitians approved a new Constitution, written to prevent the return of a dictatorship. In 1990 the priest Jean-Bertrand Aristide won the first free elections; in 1991 a military coup overthrew him. He returned in 1994 with a multinational force led by the United States, was re-elected in 2000 and left the country again in 2004, in the midst of an armed revolt. A UN mission, MINUSTAH, arrived and stayed until 2017. The earthquake and cholera (2010). On 12 January 2010 a magnitude 7 earthquake destroyed Port-au-Prince. The death toll has never been established: the government set it at 316,000, other estimates range from fewer than 100,000 to about 160,000 ( Britannica ). A few months later a cholera epidemic broke out, a disease not seen in the country for more than a century: it killed almost 10,000 people. Investigations pointed to waste from a base of Nepalese peacekeepers as the source; in 2016 Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon apologised for the UN's role, without explicitly acknowledging that its soldiers had brought the disease ( IPS ; WBUR ). Martelly, Moïse and the assassination (2011-2021). From 2011 to 2016 Michel Martelly governed, then Jovenel Moïse, from the same party. Legislative elections were not held, and parliamentarians' terms expired one after another. On 7 July 2021 a commando of former Colombian soldiers killed Moïse in his bedroom. In May 2026 a federal court in Miami convicted four men who organised the plot from Florida, but who ordered and paid for it is still unclear ( AP, via Washington Times ; Haiti Liberté ). A state with no elected officials (since 2021). After the assassination Prime Minister Ariel Henry governed; in January 2023 the last ten senators' terms expired, and Haiti was left without a single elected official at national level ( Freedom House, 2025 ). In 2024 the gangs attacked prisons and the airport, Henry resigned and a nine-member Transitional Presidential Council was formed. A Kenyan-led police mission arrived; in September 2025 the Security Council replaced it with a larger "Gang Suppression Force" (GSF) ( analysis on this site ). Since 7 February 2026 Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé has governed alone. The elections, set for 13 December 2026, have been postponed to 18 July 2027 ( analysis on this site ). Who governs, and how On paper Haiti is a semi-presidential republic: a president elected for five years and a prime minister who must have the confidence of parliament. Today there is neither. An unelected prime minister governs, on the basis of a pact signed with parties and civil society, with no deadline set ( analysis on this site ). In its 2026 report Freedom House rates Haiti "not free", with 22 points out of 100: violence has repeatedly pushed back the vote, and the gangs also restrict freedom of movement with their paid roadblocks ( Freedom House ). We explain what distinguishes an autocracy from a democracy in the entry Autocracy ; Haiti is not a dictatorship, but a state in which no one any longer has a popular mandate. The Constitution to be changed. For the 2027 vote the government is also planning a "popular ratification" of amendments to the 1987 Constitution, which have not yet been published. The Constitution itself forbids amending it by referendum; the Council of Europe's Venice Commission nonetheless recommended a referendum, warning that amendments decided by unelected authorities have "very limited" legitimacy. We explained this in our analysis of the postponed vote . Who's who Who Led by Position Transitional government Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé Sole head of the executive since 7 February 2026, unelected. Says the vote will be held as soon as security allows ( analysis on this site ) National Police (PNH) and army — The police fight the gangs with few resources; the army, disbanded in 1995 and re-established in 2017, is small. A task force linked to the prime minister uses armed drones ( Jurist, on Human Rights Watch ) Viv Ansanm ("Living together") Among others Jimmy Chérizier, known as "Barbecue" Coalition formed in September 2023 from the alliance between the capital's two big gang federations, G9 and G-Pèp. Designated a terrorist organisation by the United States in May 2025 ( Guardian Trinidad, from CMC ). Controls much of Port-au-Prince Gran Grif — The strongest gang in Artibonite, active since 2016; also designated a terrorist organisation by the United States (same source) Self-defence groups and "Bwa Kalé" No central command Groups of citizens who arm themselves against the gangs and lynch suspected members: the UN attributes to them about 6% of the dead and injured in 2025 ( BINUH ) Gang Suppression Force (GSF) Authorised by the Security Council, not commanded by the UN On 12 October 2026 it had 1,563 troops of the 5,550 planned; mandate until 31 March 2027 ( analysis on this site ) El Salvador Pres. Nayib Bukele More than two thousand soldiers arrived from late October 2026 after the abduction of four of its servicemen; who commands them and under what rules has not been said (same source) Vectus Global Erik Prince, founder of Blackwater US private military company working for the government since March 2025 under a ten-year contract of undisclosed value ( Al Jazeera ) The candidates Among others former president Michel Martelly Registered for the 2027 vote. Martelly is sanctioned by the United States and Canada, accused of financing gangs; he has not been convicted by any court ( analysis on this site ) UN Integrated Office BINUH Counts the victims and documents violations; the Security Council maintains sanctions against those who lead and finance the gangs (same source) Where the crisis comes from We use the four levels of our piece "Are the world's wars 'Muslim'?" . In Haiti there is no religion or people to defend: there is a hollowed-out state and power to be seized. The ground: a state never built for everyone. For more than a century the debt to France took away the resources for roads, schools and courts; the US occupation concentrated power in the capital; the Duvaliers governed with a militia instead of institutions. A small elite, largely urban and French-speaking, kept control of the economy, while the Creole-speaking rural majority was left out ( Minority Rights Group ). The spark: the vacuum of 2021. Gangs had existed for decades, often in the service of politicians and businessmen. With the assassination of Moïse and the end of the last parliament, anyone with a mandate to govern disappeared. The gangs united, in 2023, and went from being tools to being masters ( analysis on this site ). The banner: the gangs' "revolution". Some leaders, such as Chérizier, present themselves as defenders of the poor against the elites and demand a seat at the political table. But their victims are the poorest: in 2025 the gangs used gang rape as a weapon, with 1,753 documented cases, and abducted hundreds of people ( Dominican Today, on BINUH ). No political demand makes it lawful to kill, rape or kidnap. The outside multiplier: weapons, money, deportations. Most of the gangs' weapons and ammunition come from the United States, especially Florida, hidden in shipping containers ( UN, UNODC report to the Security Council ). A pistol bought in a US gun shop for 400-500 dollars can be resold in Haiti for up to 10,000 ( Ahram, from AFP ). Meanwhile the Dominican Republic sent 265,000 people back to Haiti in 2025 alone, to a country that cannot protect those who already live there ( IOM, via ReliefWeb ). Who gains We document declared or verifiable interests, not motives. If an actor denies something, we say so. The gangs. They live off kidnapping, extortion, road tolls and control of ports and fuel depots. The weaker the state, the more they earn. Those who have used the gangs. The experts appointed by the UN Secretary-General write that the links between gangs, politicians and businessmen are being reactivated ahead of the vote: the gangs offer territory, access to voters and "security" at polling stations in exchange for protection ( analysis on this site ). In 2022 Canada sanctioned three of the country's richest businessmen, Gilbert Bigio, Reynold Deeb and Sherif Abdallah, accusing them of providing funds and weapons to the gangs ( Government of Canada ); Canada and the United States have also sanctioned politicians, including Martelly. Sanctions are not judgments: none of them has been convicted, and those concerned reject the accusations. Those who govern without a mandate. Every postponement of the vote prolongs a power no one voted for. The reasons for the postponement, violence and lack of money, are real; but the postponement also suits those in government ( analysis on this site ). Those who sell weapons and security. Arms traffickers profit from the price difference between Florida and Haiti. Private companies profit from the war on the gangs: Vectus Global's contract runs for ten years and its value has not been made public ( Al Jazeera ). Who intervenes from outside United States. Two military occupations (1915-1934 and 1994), sanctions on politicians and gangs, designation of Viv Ansanm and Gran Grif as terrorist organisations; they are also the country most of the weapons come from. They flew part of the Salvadoran soldiers in on military aircraft ( analysis on this site ). France. The former colonial power; in 2025, two hundred years after the indemnity, it set up a commission to study its consequences ( via Wikiwand ). UN. Peace missions from 1993 to 2017, including MINUSTAH; today the political office BINUH, the office that supplies the GSF and a sanctions regime against those who lead and finance the gangs, renewed in October 2026 ( analysis on this site ). Kenya. From June 2024 it led the police mission that preceded the GSF ( analysis on this site ). El Salvador. More than two thousand soldiers since October 2026 (same source). Dominican Republic. It has partly closed the border, is building a wall and has stepped up expulsions: 98% of forced returns to Haiti in 2025 ( IOM, via ReliefWeb ). Canada. Sanctions on politicians and businessmen accused of supporting the gangs ( Government of Canada ). The human cost. In 2025 the UN counted at least 5,915 dead and 2,708 injured from armed violence ( BINUH ). Almost one and a half million people are displaced, about half of them children ( analysis on this site ). In 2023 there had been 4,789 deaths, more than double the year before ( Freedom House, 2024 ). Documented violence. We recall some cases, attributed to different parties: Duvalier, 1957-1986 : about 30,000 killed by the regime and the Tontons Macoutes ( Business Recorder, from AFP ). Cholera, 2010-2016 : almost 10,000 dead, starting from a UN base; UN apology in 2016 ( IPS ). Pont-Sondé, October 2024 : the Gran Grif gang kills more than 100 people in Artibonite ( BINUH ). The gangs, 2025 : 1,753 documented cases of sexual violence, hundreds of kidnappings ( Dominican Today, on BINUH ). Security operations : in the first quarter of 2025, 802 dead in security-force operations, about a fifth of them passers-by hit in the street or at home, and 65 summary executions attributed to police officers ( BINUH ). Between March 2025 and January 2026 the government task force's armed drones killed at least 1,243 people, including children and passers-by ( Jurist, on Human Rights Watch ). International law The treaties. Haiti: has been a party to the Geneva Conventions since 1957 and to the two Additional Protocols since 2006 ( ICRC ); has been a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights since 1991 ( analysis on this site ) and to the American Convention on Human Rights since 1977; since 1998 it has accepted the jurisdiction of the Inter-American Court ( OAS ); signed the Rome Statute in 1999 but has never ratified it: the International Criminal Court can step in only with a Security Council referral or if Haiti accepts its jurisdiction ( PGA ). Gangs or war? Whether gang violence amounts to an armed conflict, to which humanitarian law applies, is disputed: it depends on how intense the fighting is and how organised the groups are. Either way, human rights apply: the state must protect its citizens' lives and may use lethal force only when strictly necessary. A drone exploding in a crowded neighbourhood, or the summary execution of a suspected gang member, does not become lawful because the target was a criminal. Foreign forces. The GSF's legal basis lies in the Security Council resolutions, which require participating states to set up mechanisms to prevent and investigate abuses. A foreign contingent outside the GSF can be in Haiti only with the government's consent, and its soldiers answer to their own country's courts ( analysis on this site ). The right to vote. Article 25 of the Covenant on Civil and Political Rights guarantees periodic and genuine elections. Postponing a vote in the midst of violence may be necessary, but the longer the postponement lasts, the more public reasons and a plan are needed ( analysis on this site ). Justice denied. Baby Doc Duvalier died without a trial. The victims of cholera have received no individual compensation: the UN invokes its immunity ( Arab Times, from agencies ). For the assassination of Moïse the convictions came from a US court, not a Haitian one. For the gang massacres and for the killings in security operations, trials in Haiti are extremely rare. Mozambique: its peoples, its history, who is fighting and why

Country profile on Mozambique: its peoples and their numbers, four centuries of Portuguese rule, the war of independence and the civil war between Frelimo and Renamo, the Rome peace, the hidden debts, the war in Cabo Delgado and the gas, who gains from it and what international law says. An entry we keep up to date.

News from Mozambique talks about an armed group linked to the Islamic State, about gas, Rwandan soldiers and disputed elections, but rarely explains who the peoples of the north are, why one party has governed without interruption since 1975, and why a province so rich in resources is among the poorest in the country. This entry tries to provide that background. We keep it up to date: every change is logged at the bottom, with date and source. In brief Mozambique has about 36.6 million inhabitants, and they are very young: the median age is under 17. The largest people are the Makua, in the north: about a quarter of the population speaks their language. In the Cabo Delgado conflict three peoples matter most: the Makua, the Makonde and the Mwani. After almost five centuries of Portuguese presence, Frelimo fought for ten years for independence, starting precisely in Cabo Delgado, and won it in 1975. A civil war against Renamo, backed first by Rhodesia and then by apartheid South Africa, began soon after: about a million dead, ended in Rome in 1992 through the mediation of the Community of Sant'Egidio. Frelimo has governed for fifty years. The 2024 elections, won by Daniel Chapo, were contested in the streets: the crackdown killed about 400 people, according to a Mozambican civic platform. The research centre Freedom House rates the country "partly free". Since 2017, in Cabo Delgado in the north, an armed group now affiliated with the Islamic State has been fighting the army, which is helped by Rwandan soldiers. More than 6,600 people have been killed and more than a million have fled. Beneath the sea off the same province lie some of Africa's largest gas reserves, which TotalEnergies, ExxonMobil and Eni are developing. Land and peoples Mozambique is a long strip of coast on the Indian Ocean, about 2,700 kilometres, cut in two by the Zambezi River. The south, with the capital Maputo, is more urban and more closely tied to South Africa; the centre and north are more rural. Cabo Delgado is the northernmost province, on the border with Tanzania. The country is divided into 11 provinces. Names in italics show where some of the peoples mentioned in this entry live: they are only a rough guide, because many peoples live in more than one province. We do not draw the areas held by the armed group, which change from month to month. The square marks the capital. Boundaries: Natural Earth (10 provinces; Maputo city is merged with its province). The inhabitants. According to UN estimates, in 2026 Mozambique has about 36.6 million inhabitants, with a median age of 16.6; 42% live in towns and cities ( Population Pyramid, on UN data ). The last census, in 2017, counted 28.9 million people ( INE, via GHDx ). A word of caution about the numbers. Mozambique's census does not ask which people you belong to: it asks for your mother tongue. The percentages below are therefore those of the languages, the closest we can get to counting peoples, and they refer to the population aged five and over ( INE, 2017 census, via Wikipedia ). For some small peoples we only have old figures or conflicting estimates, and we say so. Makua (Emakhuwa language) — about 26%, almost 6 million people. The largest people, in the northern provinces: Nampula, Niassa, Zambézia and also Cabo Delgado, where they are the majority ( Minority Rights Group ; ISS ). In Cabo Delgado province many Makua are Muslim. Changana, or Tsonga (Xichangana) — about 9%. The main people of the south, around Maputo and in Gaza province. Many of Frelimo's historic leaders come from the south. Nyanja (Cinyanja) — about 8%, in the west, along the borders with Malawi and Zambia. Lomwe (Elomwe) — about 7%, in Zambézia and Nampula; they are close relatives of the Makua. Sena (Cisena) — about 7%, in the Zambezi valley and Sofala. The centre of the country was Renamo's heartland during the civil war ( Springer ). Chuwabo, Ndau, Tswa and many others — between 3.5 and 4.5% each (same INE source). Makonde (Shimakonde) — about 2%, 371,000 people according to the 2007 census ( via Wikipedia ). Few, but very influential. They live on the Mueda plateau, inland in Cabo Delgado, and are mostly Catholic. They were the first to fight the Portuguese with Frelimo and have been rewarded with pensions and positions of power: former president Filipe Nyusi, many generals and at least three former defence ministers are Makonde from Cabo Delgado ( ISS ). Mwani (Kimwani) — the figures differ: about 30,000 people with Kimwani as their mother tongue in the 2007 census, between 120,000 and 200,000 according to other estimates ( via Wikipedia ; Intelyse ). They are the people of the Cabo Delgado coast, of Swahili culture, Muslim, mostly fishermen, and poorer than the Makonde ( Mining.com, from Bloomberg ). During the war of independence many of them did not side with Frelimo, and after 1975 they were sidelined ( Good Governance Africa ). According to several scholars, many of the armed group's first fighters came from here (see "Where the conflict comes from"). Portuguese is the only official language, but it is the mother tongue of fewer than one Mozambican in five, mostly in towns (INE, cit.). Religion (2017 census): Catholics 27.2%, Muslims 18.9%, Zionist churches (African Christian churches) 15.6%, Evangelicals and Pentecostals 15.3%, no religion 13.9% ( CIA World Factbook, via IndexMundi ). Christians are more numerous in the south and centre, Muslims in the north ( Afrobarometer ). In Cabo Delgado, in 2017, 53% said they were Muslim and 36% Catholic ( Open University, on INE data ). Cabo Delgado's resources. Off the province, in the Rovuma basin, there are proven gas reserves of more than 85 trillion cubic feet, among the largest in Africa ( Ecofin, on Mozambican ministry data ). Three large projects have been approved: TotalEnergies' project, restarted in January 2026 after a five-year halt; the one led by ExxonMobil, which is aiming for a final investment decision by the end of 2026 ( Lusa, 12/8/2026 ); and the floating platforms of Italy's Eni, which have been producing since 2022 ( analysis on this site ). Inland lies Montepuez, the largest known ruby deposit: the mine is 75% owned by Britain's Gemfields and 25% by the Mozambican company Mwiriti ( 360 Mozambique ). There is also graphite at Balama. Yet Cabo Delgado remains one of the poorest provinces in the country. A short history Before the Portuguese. On the coast, Swahili port towns traded for centuries with Arabia, Persia and India; that is how Islam arrived, on the northern coast. In 1498 Vasco da Gama reached the Island of Mozambique ( DC Stamps ): this began a Portuguese presence that for centuries was limited to the coast and to trade, including the slave trade. The companies and forced labour (1891-1929). At the end of the nineteenth century Portugal, fearing it would lose the territory to the British and Germans, handed a third of it to private companies. The Niassa Company governed today's provinces of Cabo Delgado and Niassa for 38 years: it imposed a hut tax and chibalo , forced labour on plantations and public works ( Wikipedia, on Neil-Tomlinson, Journal of African History ; Max Planck Institute ). Historians describe the north as the most neglected part of the colony, a "chronic periphery" ( Africana Studia, University of Porto ). Mueda and the war of independence (1960-1975). On 16 June 1960 in Mueda, on the Makonde plateau, farmers gathered to demand independence and better living conditions; the colonial police opened fire on the crowd. Estimates of the dead range from a few dozen to about 500 ( University of Central Arkansas ). On 25 June 1962 three nationalist movements merged in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, and founded Frelimo, led by Eduardo Mondlane. On 25 September 1964 Frelimo attacked the administrative post of Chai, in Cabo Delgado: the armed struggle had begun (same source). Mondlane was killed by a parcel bomb in 1969; Samora Machel succeeded him. After the Carnation Revolution in Portugal, the Lusaka agreements of September 1974 opened the way to independence, proclaimed on 25 June 1975. Machel was the first president. The civil war (1977-1992). Frelimo built a Marxist-inspired one-party state and supported liberation movements in neighbouring countries. Against it rose Renamo, armed first by white-ruled Rhodesia and, from 1980, by apartheid South Africa ( Better Evidence Project, George Mason University ). The war devastated the country: about a million dead, from fighting and hunger, and about five million displaced people and refugees ( Conciliation Resources ; Radio Netherlands ). On 19 October 1986 Machel died when his plane crashed at Mbuzini, on South African territory: the South African commission of inquiry blamed the Soviet crew, Mozambique and the USSR rejected its findings, and in 2001 South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found no conclusive evidence either way ( South African History Online ; Nelson Mandela archive ). Joaquim Chissano succeeded him. The Rome peace (1992). After 27 months of negotiations at the headquarters of the Community of Sant'Egidio, with the Italian government, on 4 October 1992 Chissano and Renamo leader Afonso Dhlakama signed the General Peace Agreement in Rome ( Sant'Egidio ). Renamo became a party; in 1994 the first multiparty elections were held, won by Frelimo, which has won every one since ( Freedom House ). The hidden debts (2013-2016). Between 2013 and 2016 three state companies run by the intelligence services secretly obtained more than two billion dollars in loans from Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB, guaranteed by the state without parliament or the International Monetary Fund knowing. The companies went bankrupt almost immediately; when the scandal broke in 2016, the Fund suspended its support and the country plunged into a financial crisis ( AIM ). Former finance minister Manuel Chang was sentenced in the United States to eight and a half years; at least ten people were convicted in Mozambique, including the son of former president Armando Guebuza; Credit Suisse paid at least 475 million dollars to British and US authorities ( ABC News, from AP ). Chang returned to Maputo in April 2026, having served his sentence ( AIM ). Renamo takes up arms again (2013-2019). In 2013 Dhlakama withdrew to the Gorongosa mountains and Renamo resumed a low-intensity guerrilla war. Dhlakama died in 2018; his successor Ossufo Momade signed agreements with President Nyusi on 1 and 6 August 2019. The disarmament of 5,221 former guerrillas ended in June 2023 with the closure of the last base, at Vunduzi ( Club of Mozambique, from Lusa ; UN Mozambique ). Cabo Delgado (since 2017). On 5 October 2017 an armed group attacked Mocímboa da Praia. People call it al-Shabaab, but it has no links with the Somali group of the same name; since 2019 the Islamic State has claimed it as one of its "provinces". In March 2021 it attacked Palma, next to the gas site, and TotalEnergies stopped everything. In July 2021 Rwandan soldiers arrived and, soon after, those of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), which would leave in 2024 ( ADF ). The war is not over: we have reported on recent years in our analysis of Cabo Delgado . The 2024 elections. On 9 October 2024 the Frelimo candidate Daniel Chapo won with 65.17% according to the Constitutional Council; Venâncio Mondlane, who came second with 24%, did not accept the result and called people onto the streets ( Club of Mozambique, from Lusa ). Between October 2024 and March 2025 the civic platform Decide counted about 388 dead, more than 800 people hit by gunfire and thousands of arrests; the government acknowledges at least 80 deaths ( Club of Mozambique ). Amnesty International has called for an independent investigation ( The Citizen, from AFP ). Chapo took office on 15 January 2025. Who governs, and how Mozambique is a presidential republic with multiparty elections, but the same party, Frelimo, has governed since independence. In its 2026 report Freedom House rates it "partly free", with 42 points out of 100 (13 out of 40 for political rights, 29 out of 60 for civil liberties), and points to corruption and to attacks on journalists who cover it ( Freedom House ). We explain what distinguishes a democracy from a hybrid regime in the entry Hybrid regime . One party, one state. Since 2024 the largest opposition party in parliament has been Podemos, which had backed Mondlane, while Renamo has been cut down to size ( Freedom House, 2025 ). Mondlane founded his own party, Anamola, registered in August 2025 ( RTP, from Lusa ); he has been charged with "incitement to terrorism" over the protests ( Club of Mozambique, from AIM ). In May 2026 he said that 56 members of his movement had been killed ( Sábado, from Lusa ): these are his accusations, not the findings of a court. The "Inclusive National Dialogue" to reform the state, launched with a law of April 2025 agreed with the parties in parliament ( RTP, from Lusa ), has not yet given Anamola a seat on its technical commission ( AllAfrica, February 2026 ). Who's who Who Led by Position Government and Frelimo (Mozambique Liberation Front) Pres. Daniel Chapo In power since 1975. Asks for international help against "terrorism" in Cabo Delgado and rejects the accusations against its soldiers ( analysis on this site ) FADM (armed forces) General staff Fight the armed group; a special unit protected the gas area. Accused of abuses, which they deny (same source) "Força local" (local militia) Veterans of the war of independence Made up mostly of Makonde veterans and their sons, active inland in Cabo Delgado. For years it operated without any law authorising it ( ISS ) Islamic State Mozambique (known as al-Shabaab; Ahlu Sunnah wal Jama'a) No publicly acknowledged leader Active since 2017. Of about 2,400 violent events recorded by ACLED, more than 2,200 involve it ( Club of Mozambique, from Lusa ) Renamo (Mozambican National Resistance) Ossufo Momade The former guerrilla movement of the civil war, now a party. Disarmament completed in 2023 Podemos and Anamola Venâncio Mondlane (Anamola) The opposition that emerged from the 2024 elections. Mondlane does not recognise Chapo's victory and is asking to join the national dialogue Rwanda Pres. Paul Kagame About 2,000 soldiers in Cabo Delgado since July 2021, at Mozambique's invitation, largely around the gas area. Since May 2026 Mozambique has been paying for them ( analysis on this site ) Tanzania — About 300 soldiers in Nangade district, on the border, under a bilateral agreement ( ADF ) European Union EUMAM mission, led by Portugal Trains and equips army units. Mandate until 31 December 2026 ( EEAS ) The gas companies TotalEnergies, ExxonMobil, Eni Developing the fields off Cabo Delgado. TotalEnergies is under investigation in France over Palma and the subject of a complaint for complicity in war crimes; it rejects the accusations ( analysis on this site ) Where the conflict comes from We use the four levels of our piece "Are the world's wars 'Muslim'?" . In Cabo Delgado religion is the banner the armed group has chosen, but on its own it does not explain why so many young men followed it. The ground: the forgotten periphery. Cabo Delgado was neglected by the colony and remained poor after independence. Over the past fifteen years rubies, graphite and gas have been discovered there, but the wealth went elsewhere: concessions displaced communities and artisanal miners, and those who lived there saw companies and soldiers arrive more than jobs ( Daily Maverick, from ISS ). According to the scholars who follow it most closely, the armed group grew mainly out of local causes: young men without work, land and resources taken from communities, a distant government ( analysis on this site ). The fault line: Makonde and Mwani. On the coast the Mwani, Muslim and poor, live alongside the Makonde, Catholic and tied to Frelimo's power since the war of independence. Several researchers read the revolt, at least at the beginning, as a rebellion of the Mwani against the advance of the Makonde and their interests on Mwani land ( ISS ; Kronos ). In the early attacks, journalists on the ground reported, only the houses of the Makonde were burned in one mixed village ( Mining.com, from Bloomberg ). It is a contested reading and does not explain everything: today the group also recruits among the Makua and kills Muslims as well as Christians. The banner: radical Islam. Radical preachers trained abroad gave the anger a religious language and a goal, Islamic law against the state; then came affiliation with the Islamic State ( Good Governance Africa ). But Mozambicans themselves see it differently: in an Afrobarometer survey, fewer than one in ten say people join the group for religious reasons ( Afrobarometer ). None of these reasons makes it lawful to behead a civilian, abduct a child or burn a church. The outside multiplier: gas and foreign soldiers. Gas has brought huge investment and a heavy military presence to Cabo Delgado. Many troops, Rwandan and Mozambican, are deployed around the construction sites; for those who live there, the security of the gas and their own do not always coincide ( analysis on this site ). A militia made up mostly of Makonde also risks giving the conflict an even more ethnic face ( ISS ). Who gains We document declared or verifiable interests, not motives. If an actor denies something, we say so. Those who control the party and the state. Fifty years of uninterrupted power have made it hard to tell Frelimo and the state apart. The hidden-debts scandal showed where this can lead: two billion dollars borrowed in citizens' names, more than 200 million of it paid in bribes to officials and bankers, according to US prosecutors ( Daily Maverick ). Those close to the resources. The Montepuez ruby mine has earned almost a billion euros since 2012 ( 360 Mozambique ). In 2019 Gemfields paid 5.8 million pounds, without admitting liability, to settle the case brought by 273 Mozambicans who accused the mine's security of beatings, shootings and abuse ( Creamer Media ). Analysts often point out that Frelimo's Makonde veterans have access to land and concessions in the north; it is one of the reasons for the resentment on the coast ( ISS ). The gas companies. They need security for investments worth tens of billions. For years TotalEnergies supported the army unit that protected the site; since October 2023 it has paid a contribution to the state instead of paying the soldiers directly ( analysis on this site ). The company rejects any accusation of complicity in abuses. The armed group. It lives off looting, kidnapping and control of some routes; its strength also depends on how absent the state remains. Rwanda. It has gained prestige as a force that "works", and for two years part of its mission was paid for by the EU. The same army is sanctioned by the United States for supporting the M23 rebels in Congo, accusations Rwanda rejects ( analysis on this site ; Country profile: DR Congo ). Who intervenes from outside Rwanda. About 2,000 soldiers since July 2021 ( analysis on this site ). SADC. The regional SAMIM mission from 2021 to April 2024; the largest contingent was South African, about 1,500 soldiers ( ADF ). Tanzania stayed on with about 300 soldiers. European Union. A military training mission since 2021, now EUMAM, with more than 40 courses for 1,200 Mozambican soldiers since September 2024 ( Lusa, 15/5/2026 ); equipment worth 89 million euros; 40 million for the Rwandan mission between 2022 and 2024 ( analysis on this site ). The mandate expires on 31 December 2026. Private military companies. In the early years Russia's Wagner and South Africa's Dyck Advisory Group fought for the government ( Daily Maverick, from ISS ). Gas financiers. The United States confirmed a 4.7 billion dollar loan to the TotalEnergies project; the United Kingdom and the Netherlands withdrew ( analysis on this site ). The human cost. In Cabo Delgado more than 6,600 people have been killed since 2017, according to ACLED ( analysis on this site ); more than a million have fled their homes, and many have done so several times ( AllAfrica ; Club of Mozambique, from OCHA ). About 670,000 displaced people are recorded as having returned home ( analysis on this site ). The Norwegian Refugee Council has placed Mozambique among the world's ten most neglected displacement crises two years running (same source). Documented violence. We recall some cases, attributed to different parties: Mueda, 1960 : the Portuguese colonial police fire on a crowd of Makonde farmers ( University of Central Arkansas ). Civil war, 1977-1992 : about a million dead, from fighting and hunger; massacres of civilians are attributed to both sides ( Conciliation Resources ). Palma, March 2021 : the armed group attacks the town; a journalist counted 1,402 dead or missing, the government about thirty ( analysis on this site ). Afungi, summer 2021 : according to an investigation by Politico, found credible overall by a Dutch institute, Mozambican soldiers locked between 180 and 250 civilians in shipping containers; many were killed or disappeared. The government and TotalEnergies reject the accusations (same source). Protests, 2024-2025 : about 388 dead, most of them hit by gunfire ( Club of Mozambique ). Mocímboa da Praia, March 2026 : the navy fires on six fishing boats, killing at least 13; local commanders apologise, while the official version still denies it ( analysis on this site ). International law The treaties. Mozambique: has been a party to the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol I since 1983, and to Protocol II, on internal conflicts, since 2002 ( University of Minnesota ); ratified in 2004 the UN Protocol that bars armed groups from recruiting under-18s ( analysis on this site ); signed the Rome Statute in 2000 but has never ratified it: the International Criminal Court can step in only if Mozambique accepts its jurisdiction or if the Security Council refers the case to it (same source). The internal conflict. The Geneva Academy, which classifies conflicts, considers Cabo Delgado a non-international armed conflict ( Geneva Academy, RULAC ). Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and Protocol II therefore apply: they prohibit killing or torturing those who are not fighting, enforced disappearances, rape and the recruitment of children. They apply equally to the armed group, the army, the local militia and the foreign troops. Calling enemies "terrorists" does not suspend these rules. Companies. The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights ask companies not to contribute to violations, including through those who protect them. In France this duty has been law since 2017, and it underpins one of the complaints against TotalEnergies ( analysis on this site ). Justice denied. For the container killings and for the fishermen who were shot, no soldiers are known to have been put on trial. For the deaths during the 2024-2025 protests, Amnesty International is still calling for an independent investigation ( The Citizen, from AFP ). In the hidden-debts case, by contrast, justice did come, in part, thanks to a foreign court. Haiti's vote slips to 2027. Meanwhile, two thousand of Bukele's soldiers arrive

Haiti was due to vote on 13 December, for the first time since 2016. The vote has been postponed to July 2027, together with changes to the Constitution that nobody has published yet. Meanwhile El Salvador has sent as many soldiers as the UN-authorised force has, without anyone saying who commands them.

In brief Haiti was due to vote again on 13 December. On 6 October the electoral council postponed everything indefinitely; on 28 October it set the first round for 18 July 2027. In early October one voter in eight was on the rolls. On the same day voters are supposed to approve some changes to the Constitution, which nobody has published yet. The 1987 Constitution expressly forbids amending it by referendum. The Council of Europe's experts accept this route as an exception, because there is no parliament, but warn that changes decided by unelected authorities have "very limited" legitimacy. The new electoral decree removed the rule excluding candidates sanctioned by foreign countries. Among those registered for the presidency is former president Michel Martelly, sanctioned by the United States and Canada on accusations of financing armed gangs. Since 18 October, after four of its servicemen were abducted, El Salvador has brought more than two thousand soldiers to Haiti: as many as the entire UN-authorised international force. Who commands them, how long they will stay and under what rules has not been said. The context Haiti has had no president since July 2021, when Jovenel Moïse was assassinated, and no elected parliament since January 2023. The last national elections were held in 2016. Since then the country has been governed by transitional authorities that nobody voted for. The gangs filled the vacuum. The strongest coalition, Viv Ansanm, controls almost the whole capital and has spread towards the centre of the country. Nearly one and a half million people have fled their homes, and about half of them are children ( UN, 19/10/2026 ). On this site we covered the international force against the gangs as it was about to go into action, in June ( Haiti: a "suppression force" ), and its six-month renewal at the end of September, with the question of who investigates if one of its soldiers kills a civilian ( Who controls who shoots? ). Here we look at the other half of the problem: the vote, that is the way Haitians should take back the right to choose who governs them, and the new foreign soldiers who arrived just as that vote slipped away. Who is who Who What it is What it says or wants The gangs (Viv Ansanm and others) A coalition formed in 2023, led among others by Jimmy Chérizier, known as "Barbecue". According to UN experts it is now riven by "violent fractures". They live off kidnapping, extortion and control of the roads. Ahead of the vote, according to the UN, each leader is seeking political deals on his own. The government Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, unelected, has been sole head of the executive since 7 February 2026, under a pact signed with parties and civil society. The pact has no end date. Says elections will be held as soon as security allows and has asked ministers to stay neutral. The Provisional Electoral Council (CEP) The body that organises the vote. It is called "provisional" because the permanent one provided for by the Constitution has never been created. Says the dates depend on security and funding. The international force (GSF) Authorised by the UN Security Council, but not commanded by the UN. On 12 October it had 1,563 troops out of the 5,550 planned. Mandate until 31 March 2027. To fight the gangs together with the Haitian police and army. El Salvador Had just over a hundred servicemen in the GSF. Since 21 October it has sent more than two thousand. President Nayib Bukele says he only wants to bring his four technicians home, "the easy way or the hard way". The candidates As of 24 October at least sixteen presidential candidates, including former president Michel Martelly and former prime minister Claude Joseph. The CEP has yet to decide who is admitted. The UN In Haiti it has a political office (BINUH), which counts victims and documents violations, and an office that supplies the GSF. Warns that setting new dates without assessing their feasibility is not enough. The facts A vote that keeps receding. At the end of July the electoral council had set the first round of the presidential and legislative elections for 13 December 2026 ( France 24, 27/7/2026 ). On 6 October it postponed it without giving a new date. On 28 October it published a new calendar: first round on 18 July 2027, second round and local elections on 4 October 2027 ( Juno7, 28/10/2026 ). It is the third calendar in less than a year. The International Observatory for Democracy and Governance, a Haitian think tank, writes that the calendar was published without any explanation and that the string of missed dates amounts to a de facto extension of the transition ( OIDG, via Le National, 29/10/2026 ). Who can vote. As of 5 October there were 759,257 people on the electoral rolls, out of an estimated electorate of 6.5 million ( UN, 19/10/2026 ). The reason is not just lack of interest. In several gang-controlled municipalities there is not even a registration centre, and gangs often close the roads ( AFP, via Jamaica Observer, 29/10/2026 ). Displaced people often no longer have their documents, or an address. The CEP has also opened online registration. A Constitution to change. On 18 July voters are also supposed to vote on a "popular ratification" of some changes to the Constitution, provided for by the electoral decree ( HPN, 28/10/2026 ). The problem is twofold. First: the 1987 Constitution, written after the fall of the Duvalier dictatorship, in Article 284-3 explicitly forbids any popular consultation that amends the Constitution by referendum ( Venice Commission of the Council of Europe ). The drafters wanted it because in 1964 François Duvalier had himself proclaimed president for life through a rigged referendum ( US Library of Congress, Haiti: a country study ). Second: the text of the changes has not yet been published. At the end of September a civic association, ITIYAyiti, asked the government to make public both the changes and the legal reasoning by which it intends to distinguish this "ratification" from a prohibited referendum ( ITIYAyiti, 28/9/2026 ). We found no reply. A year ago the transitional government had abandoned the plan for a new Constitution precisely because of criticism of its legality ( ConstitutionNet, 13/10/2025 ). Now the idea is back, smaller and under another name. There is, however, an authoritative opinion that complicates the picture. In 2024 the Venice Commission, the Council of Europe's body of constitutional experts, consulted through the Organization of American States, wrote that in Haiti the ordinary amendment procedure cannot be followed until elected institutions return. If it is decided to change the Constitution before the vote, it concluded, the changes should be approved by the people in a referendum, even though the current Constitution does not provide for it. But it added two conditions: changes decided by authorities that nobody elected would have "very limited" democratic legitimacy, and for that reason they must be kept to what is necessary and discussed as openly as possible ( Venice Commission, opinions CDL-AD(2024)017 and CDL-AD(2024)042 ). The candidates and the gangs. On 6 October the government published the third version of the electoral decree in four months. Among other things, the new text removed the rule excluding candidates sanctioned by foreign governments: only those sanctioned by the UN remain excluded ( AP, via La Nación, 9/10/2026 ). On 23 October former president Michel Martelly filed his candidacy, followed by hundreds of supporters ( AP, via Africanews, 24/10/2026 ). Canada sanctioned him in 2022 and the United States in 2024, accusing him of facilitating drug trafficking and sponsoring several gangs ( US Treasury, 20/8/2024 ). Martelly has not been convicted by any court, and sanctions are not a judgment. The same applies to former Senate president Youri Latortue, sanctioned by the United States, Canada and the EU. In early October the final report of the panel of experts assisting the UN sanctions committee on Haiti was made public: 94 pages on the ties between gangs, politicians and businesspeople ( UN, S/2026/714 ). According to the experts, as the vote approaches those ties are being reactivated: gangs can offer territory, access to voters and "security" at polling stations in exchange for protection and rewards after the vote. The report accuses former deputy Alfrédo Junior Antoine of supplying weapons, ammunition and money to Viv Ansanm ( AP, via Washington Times, 7/10/2026 ). Bukele's soldiers. On 18 October in Croix-des-Bouquets, north-east of the capital, an armoured vehicle carrying Salvadoran GSF servicemen was attacked ( UN, 19/10/2026 ). Four air force technicians went missing. On 21 October Salvadoran president Nayib Bukele threatened the gangs, in Creole, on X: if they do not release them, he will destroy them. On 24 October he said the human remains handed to his troops were not those of his men ( CBC Barbados, 30/10/2026 ). Before the ambush El Salvador had at least 124 servicemen in Haiti, according to a UN report. On 27 October it had about a thousand, carried in part by US military aircraft ( Reuters, 27/10/2026 ). On 28 October the Salvadoran government announced more than two thousand soldiers, "as part of a large-scale operation supported by various countries and international organisations". Bukele says El Salvador will pay 90% of the costs and that this is not an invasion. Two thousand soldiers are more than the entire Haitian army and about as many as the entire UN-authorised international force ( CNN, 29/10/2026 ). But who commands them has not been said, nor how long they will stay ( Reuters, 27/10/2026 ). It is unclear whether they will join the GSF or operate on their own ( Al Jazeera, 29/10/2026 ). The Haitian government has said only that the two countries will strengthen cooperation. A Salvadoran analyst interviewed by Reuters expects at least some of the soldiers to operate outside the GSF chain of command and to coordinate with Erik Prince's private military company, which already works for the Haitian government. In El Salvador, since March 2022, the state of exception imposed by Bukele against the gangs has led to the arrest of tens of thousands of people, many with no established link to gangs. Socorro Jurídico Humanitario, a Salvadoran organisation that assists detainees' families, has counted at least 554 deaths in prison up to August 2026, almost all of people awaiting trial ( EFE, via Diario Libre, 3/8/2026 ). The Salvadoran government has not commented. Pierre Espérance, who heads Haiti's main human rights network (RNDDH), welcomed the rapid arrival of the Salvadorans, but pointed out that not everyone living in gang-held neighbourhoods is a gang member ( Reuters, 27/10/2026 ). Who is shooting. Between July and early October gang-related violence killed 1,123 people. In the West and Artibonite departments gangs killed 241 people accused of resisting their control, and in July and August they raped 689 women and girls. But more than half of those killed and injured (52%) fell during operations by the security forces, and 148 of them had no links to gangs ( UN, 19/10/2026 ). The UN experts' report also reports summary executions of children accused of being with the gangs, by security forces and self-defence groups ( Security Council Report, 2026 ). This is the figure to keep in mind as new soldiers arrive. Legal commentary The right to vote. Haiti acceded in 1991 to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Article 25 guarantees every citizen the right to vote in periodic and genuine elections. The UN Human Rights Committee, which interprets the Covenant, asks states to take effective measures so that those entitled can actually vote, to facilitate registration and to overcome obstacles such as impediments to freedom of movement ( General Comment No. 25, § 11 ). Postponing a vote amid violence is not in itself a violation: voting under gang control would not be a free vote. But the longer the postponement, the more it needs public, verifiable reasons and a plan. Ten years without elections, and three calendars in a year without explanation, are not that. The Constitution. Article 284-3 is clear: any popular consultation that amends the Constitution by referendum is prohibited. The Constitution provides another route, long and difficult: two successive legislatures, two-thirds majorities in both chambers. Today there is no parliament, and that makes the ordinary route impossible. This is the argument of necessity, which the Venice Commission accepted: when institutions do not exist, one may step outside the Constitution to rebuild them. But necessity justifies only what is truly needed, and whoever invokes it must prove it. The Haitian government has not done so: it has published neither the text of the changes nor the legal reasoning. Calling the vote a "ratification" instead of a "referendum" does not change its substance. Without a public, limited and debated text, a Constitution amended by a government nobody elected would be contestable from birth, and so would the power of whoever is elected under it. Foreign soldiers. A state may send soldiers onto another's territory in three cases: if the Security Council authorises it, if the receiving state consents, or in self-defence. For Salvadorans who join the GSF the basis is clear: Security Council resolutions 2793 and 2829. For those who stay outside it, the only possible basis is the consent of the Haitian government. The Fils-Aimé government is not elected, but it is the one the UN and other states recognise, and under international law its consent counts. Consent, however, is not a blank cheque: it covers what the government has accepted, and nobody has made that public. It also matters where the rules end. Resolution 2793 asks states taking part in the GSF for a mechanism to prevent, investigate and publicly report abuses. A contingent outside the GSF is not covered by it. Its soldiers answer to their own country's courts. El Salvador nonetheless remains bound by the human rights treaties it has signed, including the American Convention on Human Rights, even when its soldiers operate abroad, in the places and over the people they control. If a Salvadoran soldier kills a civilian in Port-au-Prince outside the GSF, today the question "who investigates?" has only one answer: Salvadoran justice, that is, the justice of the state of exception. The gangs. Kidnapping, rape, killing those who resist, recruiting children: these are crimes under Haitian law and grave human rights violations. The UN has a sanctions regime against those who lead and finance them, renewed on 14 October by resolution 2831: 14 votes in favour and Russia abstaining ( Security Council Report ). It is the only one the new electoral decree considers for excluding a candidate. Symmetry test The gangs. They are the primary cause of all this: they have killed, raped and driven hundreds of thousands of people from their homes, and today they prevent many from registering to vote. Nothing we say about the others makes them less guilty. The security forces. They are fighting a real enemy. But according to the UN more than half of the victims in recent months fell in their operations. The same yardstick applies to everyone who shoots: gangs, police, GSF, contractors, and from now on the Salvadorans. The government. The reasons for the postponement are real: violence, the money that is lacking. But the postponement also suits those who govern without a mandate and without an end date. And the government has changed the voting rules three times in four months, once removing a filter against candidates tied to gangs. Bukele. He has a duty to search for his men, and the speed of the response has convinced even some Haitian human rights defenders. But a rescue operation does not need two thousand soldiers, and if it becomes a campaign against the gangs it must have a public mandate and rules of oversight. We used the same yardstick for the Rwandan soldiers in Mozambique, who arrived at the government's invitation and were praised for their effectiveness ( Mozambique, Cabo Delgado ). The United States and the other partners. They sanctioned Martelly and designated the two main gang coalitions as terrorist organisations. They also provided the aircraft for the Salvadoran soldiers, without it being said under what mandate. Those who call for credible elections in Haiti must also demand clear rules from those who send or carry soldiers. What has worked The electoral council has registered more than 35 parties and groupings and some 3,500 candidates for the various offices, and has opened online registration. Registration on the rolls, though low, has grown: from about half a million in early September to just under nine hundred thousand at the end of October, according to the Miami Herald as cited by Al Jazeera. The UN experts' report named those accused of arming the gangs. And the UN sanctions regime has been renewed. These are small steps, but in the right direction. What we do not know Who commands the Salvadoran soldiers, under what rules of engagement and until when they will stay. Neither the Haitian nor the Salvadoran government has said. What has happened to the four Salvadoran technicians. Which changes to the Constitution are to be voted on 18 July. Which of the registered candidates the electoral council will admit. What will happen to the GSF after 31 March 2027, almost four months before the vote. Our judgement This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Haiti is a country where for ten years nobody has chosen who governs it. In that vacuum others have decided in the place of Haitians: the gangs with weapons, politicians with the gangs, foreign governments with their soldiers. The vote is the only way to put the choice back in Haitians' hands. That is why the way it is reached matters as much as the date. Postponing may be necessary. Voting at a gang's gunpoint is not voting. But those who postpone without explaining, change the rules every season, remove the filter on candidates tied to gangs and meanwhile prepare a change to the Constitution without publishing a single line of it, are not preparing an election. They are extending a transition that nobody voted for. And if Haiti cannot yet choose, those who decide for it must answer more, not less. That applies to the Haitian government, which must publish the text of the constitutional changes and the terms of the agreement with El Salvador. It applies to Bukele, who has brought two thousand soldiers into a foreign country saying only that it is not an invasion. And it applies to the Security Council, which in March must decide whether to renew the GSF: it cannot pretend that a second foreign army, with no public mandate, has not sprung up beside it. What to watch The final list of admitted candidates and the decision on Martelly's candidacy. Publication of the text of the constitutional changes and of their legal basis. The status of the Salvadoran soldiers: agreement with Haiti, integration into the GSF, rules of engagement, duration. The fate of the four Salvadoran technicians. The next UN (BINUH) report on victims, with the share attributed to the security forces. The renewal of the GSF by 31 March 2027.
