Haiti: the UN renews the anti-gang force for six months. But who controls those who shoot?

The Security Council has renewed the international force against Haiti's gangs until March 2027. The resolution requires abuses to be investigated and publicly reported, but after a year no public report can be found.

— Haiti (Port-au-Prince, Artibonite) “[Participating States are to] establish a robust compliance mechanism […] to prevent, investigate, address and publicly report violations or abuses of human rights.” — UN Security Council, resolution 2793 (2025), para. 18 For a year Haiti has had an international armed force that does not wear the blue helmet. It is called the Gang Suppression Force. The UN Security Council authorised it but does not command it. Its task is to fight the gangs that hold the capital hostage, and it may do so on its own, without the Haitian police. Its mandate was due to expire on 30 September: the day before, the Council renewed it, but only for six months, until 31 March 2027, while the force had asked for two years. The new resolution contains no external oversight mechanism; it does, however, encourage States to grant its soldiers privileges and immunities. This site wrote about it in June, when the force was about to go into action . Here we look at its first year and at a question that remains open: if a soldier of this force kills a civilian, who investigates? Who is involved At least five different actors carry weapons in Haiti today, and each answers to a different authority. To understand who controls whom, one must first tell them apart. The gangs. The strongest is Viv Ansanm (“Living Together”), a coalition of armed groups that controls most of Port-au-Prince. Among its leaders is Jimmy Chérizier, known as “Barbecue”. In May 2025 the United States designated it a terrorist organisation. The gangs live off kidnapping, extortion and control of the roads, and they recruit many children. The Haitian State. Haiti has had no elected president since 2021, when Jovenel Moïse was assassinated, and since then it has had no elected parliament either. Since 7 February 2026, when the mandate of the Transitional Presidential Council ended, the sole executive authority has been Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, who is unelected and backed by the United States. The State fights the gangs with the National Police and with a small army rebuilt only a few years ago. The task force and Vectus Global. This is where things become less clear. Since March 2025 a special anti-gang “task force”, set up by the Haitian government, has been operating together with an American private military company, Vectus Global. It was founded by Erik Prince, the former soldier who in the 2000s ran Blackwater, the contractor firm behind the Nisour Square massacre in Baghdad, Iraq, in 2007; the contractors convicted for that massacre were later pardoned by Donald Trump. In practice Vectus supplies the government with what the Haitian police lack: armed drones, helicopters, snipers, intelligence and communications specialists, with planned personnel of around two hundred people from the United States, Europe and El Salvador. Vectus works for the government in Port-au-Prince, not for the UN: it is not part of the international force and no Security Council resolution authorises it. To export these services to Haiti it needs a licence from the US State Department, and it obtained one. In August 2025 Prince spoke of a ten-year contract. The details are not public: what is known comes from the press (Wall Street Journal, Miami Herald, Le Nouvelliste), as pieced together by the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime, a research centre on organised crime. According to these accounts there are two agreements. The first, for one year, concerns security: instructors, coordination of drone strikes, direct participation in combat, helicopters and boats. The second, for ten years, would entrust Vectus with modernising customs, that is, collecting duties on the border with the Dominican Republic, which before the gangs advanced accounted for more than half of the country's tax revenue. For this part Vectus would be paid a percentage: 20% of the increase in customs revenue in the first three years, then 15%, plus a fixed fee of 3% on import volumes. The Haitian government has never confirmed this second agreement. If these accounts are accurate, a foreign private company is waging war on the gangs on behalf of the State and is also paid with a share of the taxes it helps to collect. Its men are neither Haitian soldiers nor peacekeepers: who judges them if they do wrong depends on Haitian and American law, and so far no one has put that to the test. The international force (GSF). It was created on 30 September 2025 by resolution 2793, adopted with 12 votes in favour and 3 abstentions: China, Russia and Pakistan. It replaced the Kenyan-led mission, which had never received enough troops or funding; Kenya left the country in April 2026. It may number up to 5,550 people. On 8 July it had 1,083 military personnel and 16 civilians, according to the UN Secretary-General's report, and at the end of September around 1,500, less than a third of its planned strength. Its contingents come from Chad, Jamaica, Mongolia and Sri Lanka. Operations began on 1 June 2026 and full capacity is expected between October and December. The force commander and the special representative are not chosen by the UN but by a “Standing Group of Partners” made up of the United States, Canada, the Bahamas, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica and Kenya. The United States was its main driving force. The UN. It is present on the ground in two ways, neither of them armed. BINUH is the political office: it follows the transition and documents human rights violations, and almost all the figures in this article come from it. UNSOH is the logistical support office created alongside the force, to which it provides equipment and services. Above it all sits the Security Council, where the United States and Panama draft the resolutions on Haiti. Facts In August the force's Sri Lankan soldiers were the first to operate outside the capital, in the Artibonite region. Its operational record is still limited: on 21 June, for example, the force detained 14 suspected gang members, and 13 were released for lack of evidence. On 28 September a Sri Lankan unit attacked the illegal checkpoints of a gang, Kokorat San Ras, in the Artibonite and killed three of its members without suffering losses, according to the Reuters and AP news agencies. A few hours later the soldiers returned to their base in Gonaïves. In retaliation the gang attacked residents: at least eleven people were killed and homes burned, according to the local mayor. The episode shows another limit of a force that is still too small: it can strike, but it cannot stay to protect the people who live there. No one asked for it to be shut down. The Haitian government requested its renewal, and on 26 September 32 member States of the Organization of American States did the same in a joint statement. The force itself presented a plan running to September 2028 and asked to be extended until then. The first round of presidential and legislative elections, together with a constitutional referendum, is set for 13 December 2026. Meanwhile the violence has not stopped. Between April and June 2026 the UN office in Haiti (BINUH) counted 1,408 people killed and 656 injured. More than half of the victims were harmed by gangs, which in the same period committed 796 acts of sexual violence, almost all of them gang rapes. Around 40% of the victims, by contrast, fell during security force operations: 584 people were killed, 33 of whom, including seven children, had no links to the gangs. In the same quarter explosive drone strikes killed or injured nine civilians, six of them children. Nearly one and a half million people are displaced. Those drones are not used by the international force but by the government's task force with Vectus Global. Human Rights Watch counted 141 drone operations between March 2025 and January 2026, with 1,243 dead, including 17 children. The authorities have opened no investigation into the victims of these operations, the UN writes in its August report. The renewal On 29 September the Security Council adopted resolution 2829 with the same vote as a year ago: 12 in favour, none against, and abstentions by China, Russia and Pakistan. The force remains authorised until 31 March 2027, as the UN support office announced. According to the Caribbean National Weekly, the Secretary-General will have to report every six months on progress against the set benchmarks, and the text reaffirms that operations must respect international law, including human rights. According to the AP news agency, the resolution also expresses “grave concern” about the forced recruitment of children by the gangs. For the question this article asks, one novelty matters most, reported by China's Xinhua news agency and by the Caribbean National Weekly: the Council takes note of a 27 July agreement on the force's legal status and encourages States to grant its members the necessary privileges and immunities. At the time of publication we were unable to consult the full text of resolution 2829. A power the force already had since 2025, and which can be read in resolution 2793, is instead confirmed, according to Xinhua: to adopt, on an exceptional basis and to save lives, “urgent temporary measures” to help the police maintain order, including arrest and detention. The 2025 resolution required these measures to be limited, proportionate and reported to the Council, and children who are apprehended not to be detained with adults. US Ambassador Mike Waltz, who sponsored the text with Panama, defended the project before the Council: “We're trying to do something genuinely different” from the missions that came before it, Al Jazeera reports. The Haitian government called it “an important step forward”, according to the AP news agency. China and Russia, Al Jazeera and the Caribbean National Weekly report, said they were sceptical about the mission's effectiveness, and China recalled that the crisis is also one of governance, not only of security. The sources consulted do not explain why the renewal was for six months rather than two years. The oversight gap On paper the rules exist, and they are detailed. In paragraph 18, resolution 2793 asks the States taking part in the force to establish a “robust compliance mechanism” to “prevent, investigate, address and publicly report” human rights violations, including sexual exploitation. It also asks for an oversight mechanism, dedicated child and women protection advisers, safe complaint channels, timely investigations, accountability for perpetrators and the repatriation of units when there is credible evidence of abuse. The problem lies in who has to do it: it is not the UN that checks, but the very States that send the soldiers. And the resolution requires violations to be made public, yet a year on we have found neither any public trace of this mechanism nor a single report on its work. Security Council Report, which follows the Council's work, also reports criticism that the force lacks adequate oversight and accountability mechanisms. The case of Sri Lanka shows why the question matters. It is now the largest contingent, with 900 soldiers and 189 paramilitary police. In 2007 more than a hundred Sri Lankan peacekeepers were repatriated from Haiti after credible allegations of sexual exploitation of children, and there is no record of anyone ever being prosecuted. According to a PassBlue investigation of 8 September, the selection of soldiers for the new force relied partly on information supplied by the Sri Lankan authorities themselves and on self-declarations; the US embassy rejected at least one candidate. The previous mission had also faced four allegations of sexual exploitation that were later substantiated, three of them involving child victims, as seven US senators recalled in June when they asked their government what independent accountability mechanisms exist. The UN has only one tool of its own, and it is indirect. It is called the Human Rights Due Diligence Policy: it bars the UN from supporting non-UN forces that commit grave violations, and the resolution applies it to all the support the support office gives to the force, the police and the Haitian army. According to the Secretary-General's July report, at the end of May the office presented the force's leadership with an initial risk assessment and the measures to mitigate those risks. It is a serious tool, but it has a limit: it allows the UN to suspend its own support, not to investigate a killing or punish whoever committed it. In other words, the Council can decide whether to keep providing fuel and logistics, but it has no tool of its own to judge the force it has authorised to fight. The renewal does not change this picture; if anything, it makes it more visible. Immunities for the soldiers of a foreign force are normal practice: they usually mean that they are tried not by the courts of the country where they operate but by those of the country that sent them. That is exactly why control by the sending States becomes the only safeguard. Under resolution 2829 the force keeps its powers, including arrest and detention, and receives more legal protection; it does not, however, receive an external body to check how it uses them. Legal reading The first question is which law applies. Most human rights organisations, including Human Rights Watch, regard operations against gangs as law enforcement. In that case international human rights law applies, which allows lethal force only when it is strictly unavoidable to protect life. A force created to “neutralize” the gangs, with an offensive mandate, pushes instead towards the rules of war, that is, humanitarian law, which allow combatants to be targeted even when they are not an immediate threat. The text of resolution 2793 does not settle the question. It authorises the force to use “all necessary measures”, the formula by which the Council authorises the use of armed force, but it never mentions humanitarian law: it cites only human rights, and with the caveat “as applicable”. The rules of engagement, that is, when one may shoot, are drafted by the force's special representative, its commander and the Haitian government, and they are not public. This ambiguity is not a detail: whether a killing is lawful or not depends on it. The second question is accountability. When a force is authorised by the Security Council but is not a UN operation, it is the States that sent the soldiers who answer for a violation, and it is up to them to try them. Haiti's history shows how easily this chain of accountability breaks down. In 2007 there was the abuse of children. In 2010 peacekeepers brought cholera into the country, which killed more than 9,000 people; only in December 2016 did Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon apologise to Haitians, and the UN acknowledged that it had played “a role” without, however, accepting full legal responsibility. The Council itself knows this: in paragraph 19, resolution 2793 asks the force's States to manage waste and wastewater to prevent water-borne diseases. For the gangs the rule is the same: murder, rape and the recruitment of children are crimes under international law, and the Haitian State is obliged to prosecute them. Implications — symmetry test There must be only one standard. It applies to the gangs, responsible for most of the victims. It applies to the Haitian police, to whom the UN attributes 14 executions or attempted executions in the same quarter. It applies to the drone task force and to the private company working with it, whose victims no one investigates. And it applies to the international force, whose operational record is still limited today, but which is expected to triple by the end of the year and which can arrest and detain. The six-month renewal at least provides a close deadline: in March the Council will have to vote again, and it will be able to ask how the force has used its powers. This site's judgement is that the renewal measures something broader than Haiti. It is a new model: the Council authorises the force, does not command it, and delegates oversight to those who exercise it. If it works without credible oversight, it becomes a precedent for other crises. Haitians are demanding security and they have a right to it. But security for which no one is accountable does not restore the rule of law: it replaces it. Update, 1 November 2026. On 6 October the electoral council postponed the 13 December elections; on 28 October it set the first round for 18 July 2027 ( Juno7 ). Since 18 October, after four Salvadoran technicians of the force were abducted, El Salvador has brought more than two thousand soldiers to Haiti, without saying who commands them. We cover this in " Haiti's vote slips to 2027. Meanwhile, two thousand of Bukele's soldiers arrive ". Haiti: a UN-authorized “suppression force” against gangs half made of children
On 30 September 2025 the UN Security Council adopted resolution 2793, transforming the Multinational Security Support mission (MSS, Kenyan-led, authorized

“Security enforcement alone will not be enough to resolve the governance problems.” — António Guterres, UN Secretary-General The fact On 30 September 2025 the UN Security Council adopted resolution 2793, transforming the Multinational Security Support mission (MSS, Kenyan-led, authorized in 2023 by resolution 2699) into a “Gang Suppression Force” of up to 5,550 personnel, mandated to conduct “counter-gang operations to neutralize, isolate and deter” the gangs. It is a UN-authorized force but not a UN operation; the United States was its main architect, and China, Russia and Pakistan abstained over concerns about rules of engagement, funding, oversight and accountability. The first contingents from Chad are expected in April 2026. On the ground, the Viv Ansanm gang coalition controls up to 90% of Port-au-Prince and is expanding into the Artibonite and Centre departments. The humanitarian crisis is among the world's gravest and least-funded: 6.4 million people — over half the population, including 2.8 million children — need assistance, and more than one Haitian in ten is displaced; by the end of 2025 the humanitarian response was only 24% funded. According to ACLED, more than 4,500 people were killed in 2025, among the highest tolls in the world; intentional homicides in Artibonite and Centre rose 210% between January and August 2025. Deaths from drone and air strikes rose 120% in the first quarter of 2026: according to the IRC and Médecins Sans Frontières, government forces and the private military company Vectus Global carried out drone strikes in residential areas, with civilian casualties. Legal commentary Here the law applies in three directions. Towards the gangs: the recruitment and use of minors in hostilities is prohibited by the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (2000), which classifies it as a war crime, and abuses against civilians — killings, rapes, kidnappings — violate the Convention on the Rights of the Child itself and the principles of humanitarian law. Towards the Haitian State: the use of drones in inhabited areas tests the principle of distinction and the protection of civilians (Fourth Geneva Convention ), and the High Commissioner for Human Rights has called the use of force “unnecessary or disproportionate,” with operations that “could be described as targeted killings.” Towards the UN-authorized force: resolution 2793 itself invokes respect for human rights and the protection of minors, but — according to Council sources — several States have criticized a US directive focused on “killing” gang members, in a country where, according to UN and UNICEF estimates, 30 to 50% of the fighters are minors. The sanctions regime and the arms embargo (resolution 2653) have so far hit very few individuals, while most of the weapons fuelling the gangs come from the United States. Implications This is the symmetry test pushed to its limit: the same standard must apply to those who commit the violence and to those who claim to come to stop it. A force named “suppression,” with a posture oriented towards the lethal use of force against an armed population half composed of minors, raises a question the law has always posed: a child with a rifle remains, in legal terms, first of all a victim to be protected and reintegrated, not a target — and UNICEF itself recalls that recruited minors must be treated first as children. And yet Haiti remains one of the planet's most forgotten crises, its humanitarian response funded at a quarter and its suffering off the radar. The law applies to those who shoot and to those who say they come to restore order, or it applies to no one. Mozambique, Cabo Delgado: the gas has restarted, the war has not

Northern Mozambique has been at war for nine years with a group linked to the Islamic State. TotalEnergies' gas project has restarted, guarded by soldiers accused of grave abuses. Europe trains and funds them, and in December decides whether to carry on.

— Cabo Delgado, Mozambique In brief Northern Mozambique has been at war for nine years. On one side is an armed group linked to the Islamic State; on the other, the Mozambican army, helped by Rwandan troops. More than 6,600 people have died. In all, more than a million people have fled their homes. In the middle of the war lies one of Africa's largest gas fields. The project led by France's TotalEnergies, halted since 2021, restarted in January. It is guarded by a military force that the company itself helped to fund. Those soldiers face grave accusations: a massacre of civilians locked in shipping containers in 2021, sexual violence documented in a UN report that was never published, fishermen killed at sea this year. In France, TotalEnergies faces a judicial investigation and a complaint for complicity in war crimes. The company rejects every accusation. Europe trains and equips this army. Until May it also paid part of the cost of the Rwandan troops, the same troops the United States has sanctioned over the war in Congo. By 31 December the EU must decide whether to renew its military mission in Mozambique. Background Cabo Delgado is Mozambique's northernmost province, on the border with Tanzania. It is one of the poorest in the country. Beneath its sea lie huge gas reserves, and inland there are ruby and graphite mines. On 5 October 2017 an armed group attacked Mocímboa da Praia, a port on the coast. People call it al-Shabaab, but it has nothing to do with the Somali group of the same name. Since 2018 it has pledged allegiance to the Islamic State, which now calls it "Islamic State Mozambique". According to the researchers who follow it closely, the group grew mainly out of local causes: young people without work, land and resources taken from communities, a distant government accused of shutting the north out of the country's wealth ( ISS, October 2025 ). Jihadist ideology came later, and served to recruit. It is a crisis almost nobody reports. The Norwegian Refugee Council has placed it, two years running, among the ten most neglected displacement crises in the world ( NRC, June 2025 ; June 2026 ). For 2026 the UN asked for 348 million dollars to help 1.1 million people, and by the end of March it had received about a third of that ( UN humanitarian plan, reported by ACLED, 8/4/2026 ). Who's who Who What it is What it says or wants Islamic State Mozambique (al-Shabaab) Armed group active since 2017, affiliated with the Islamic State. Wants to impose its religious law. Attacks villages, churches, soldiers. Government of Mozambique President Daniel Chapo, since January 2025. The Frelimo party has governed since independence (1975). Asks for international help against "terrorism"; rejects the accusations against its soldiers. Mozambican armed forces (FADM) Fight the group; a special unit guards the gas area. Deny the abuses. Rwandan army About 2,000 soldiers, in Cabo Delgado since July 2021 at Mozambique's invitation. Says it defends African security; asks those who benefit to pay for the mission. TotalEnergies Leads the Mozambique LNG consortium (26.5%): about 20 billion dollars, among the largest private investments in Africa. Rejects every accusation; says it had no staff on site in the months of the alleged events. European Union Has trained and equipped units of the Mozambican army since 2021. Says it supports the protection of civilians and respect for humanitarian law. The facts Palma, March 2021. The armed group attacks Palma, the town next to the gas site. The government speaks of some thirty dead. The journalist Alex Perry, after five months of research, counted 1,402 dead or missing, including 55 workers of the site's contractors ( AFP, 15/3/2025 ). TotalEnergies evacuates its staff and in April halts everything, declaring "force majeure". The containers of Afungi, summer 2021. Since 2020 an agreement between TotalEnergies' subsidiary and the government had entrusted the protection of the site to a special army unit, the Joint Task Force, to which the company provided material and logistical support ( ECCHR, 18/11/2025 ). In September 2024 Perry wrote in Politico that, between July and September 2021, those soldiers locked between 180 and 250 men in metal shipping containers at the entrance to the site. They were civilians fleeing the war, accused of siding with the rebels. Many were beaten, starved, killed or disappeared. In September Rwandan soldiers found 26 of them alive and freed them ( Politico, 26/9/2024 ). In October 2023, on the advice of a report commissioned by TotalEnergies itself, the agreement had been changed: no more direct payments to the soldiers, but a contribution to the State ( Clingendael, November 2025 ). What they say. TotalEnergies says that between April and November 2021 none of its employees was on site, and that its internal checks found nothing to confirm the account ( Mozambique LNG, November 2024 ). It asked the Mozambican authorities to investigate. Mozambique's attorney general opened a criminal inquiry in March 2025. The National Human Rights Commission, in a statement on 17 March 2026, wrote that so far it had found no evidence of torture or executions within the project's perimeter, and that the inquiry continues ( Lusa, 17/3/2026 ). President Chapo denies there were any violations. On the other side is the report by the Dutch institute Clingendael, commissioned by the Dutch Ministry of Finance, which guaranteed the loan through its export credit agency. The researchers conducted more than 80 interviews in the districts of Palma and Mocímboa da Praia. They do not establish the individual details, but they judge the account credible as a whole: four independent local sources confirm that many civilians were detained and mistreated by the security forces in front of the site ( Clingendael, November 2025 ). TotalEnergies objected that the authors did not go to the site in person and relied on information gathered by third parties ( TotalEnergies, 2/12/2025 ). In France. Two proceedings concern TotalEnergies. The first, opened by investigating judges in Nanterre in March 2025, stems from a complaint by survivors and relatives of the victims of Palma: involuntary manslaughter and failure to assist the contractors' workers ( Reuters, 15/3/2025 ). The second is a complaint filed on 17 November 2025 by the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR), a German organisation: complicity in war crimes, torture and enforced disappearances over the container events. We have found no report of an investigation opened on this second complaint. TotalEnergies "categorically" rejects the accusations. The gas restarts. On 7 November 2025 the consortium lifted force majeure, and on 29 January 2026 it fully resumed work ( TotalEnergies, 29/1/2026 ). First gas is expected in 2029. Not all the lenders stayed. On 1 December 2025 the United Kingdom withdrew a public loan of 1.15 billion dollars, saying the risks had grown ( statement by minister Peter Kyle, 1/12/2025 ). The Dutch export credit agency did the same. The United States, by contrast, had approved a 4.7 billion loan in March 2025 ( EXIM, 19/3/2025 ). Off the same coast, Italy's Eni has produced gas from a floating platform since 2022, and in October 2025 it decided to build a second one ( Eni, 2/10/2025 ). Some UN human rights experts criticised the African Development Bank's loan to this second project, because it risks worsening human rights violations and the climate crisis ( OHCHR, March 2026 ). The report the UN did not publish. In June 2026 Forbidden Stories, a network of investigative journalists, revealed a 2024 report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) that had been left in a drawer. It gathers testimony from women and girls in Cabo Delgado. It describes rape and sexual violence by the armed group and also by army soldiers, even against minors, almost always unpunished. It describes women forced to trade sex for humanitarian aid. And it reports that some men linked to the gas site, including employees and subcontractors, allegedly sexually exploited women who had come to Palma looking for work ( Forbidden Stories and Zitamar, 18/6/2026 ). In the report, TotalEnergies' name was almost always replaced with the phrase "a multinational energy company". The UN says conditions on the ground did not allow the text to be brought up to the standards required for publication. TotalEnergies rejects the accusations and says its reporting system has never received such complaints. An internal project report obtained by the Italian organisation ReCommon shows, however, that in 2022 the project had been informed of "several cases" of misconduct by the Joint Task Force in nearby villages. The fishermen. To fight the rebels, who also move by sea, the army has banned fishing along some stretches of coast. Many fishermen go out anyway, because they have nothing else. On 15 March 2026 a navy patrol boat opened fire on six boats off Mocímboa da Praia: at least 13 dead ( Zitamar, March 2026 ; Human Rights Watch, 30/3/2026 ). According to ACLED, similar incidents have killed about 70 fishermen since 2024. On 25 March, at a meeting with the community of Mocímboa da Praia, military and police commanders admitted responsibility and apologised ( Zitamar, 26/3/2026 ). The armed forces' official position, however, has not changed: they deny it, and blame the killings on rebels in uniform ( Zitamar, 19/10/2026 ). And the rebels. The armed group remains the main perpetrator of the violence: of about 2,400 incidents recorded by ACLED since 2017, more than nine in ten involve it ( ACLED, June 2026 ). It beheads civilians, burns villages and churches, abducts children. In 2025 Human Rights Watch counted at least 120 abducted children, used as porters, forced labourers, fighters or brides ( HRW, 24/6/2025 ). In August and September this year it targeted civilians more and more often, in the districts of Mocímboa da Praia, Muidumbe and Macomia ( ACLED and Zitamar, 6/10/2026 ). Between late September and early October another 4,445 people fled the districts of Macomia and Mocímboa da Praia (IOM, 6/10/2026). Who pays the soldiers. Rwanda sent its troops in July 2021, at Mozambique's invitation. They are considered the most effective force on the ground, and many are deployed around the gas area. Since 2022 the European Union has paid part of the mission: 40 million euros in two tranches, through the European Peace Facility ( EU Council, 2024 ). On 2 March 2026 the United States sanctioned the Rwandan army and four of its generals for supporting the M23 rebels in eastern Congo ( US Treasury sanctions, 2/3/2026 ), whose background we set out in the DR Congo country profile . Rwanda rejects the sanctions as "unjust". In May the European funds ran out, without renewal. Since then, Rwanda has said, Mozambique pays ( Lusa, 29/5/2026 ). The EU, meanwhile, has spent 89 million euros to equip eleven rapid reaction companies of the Mozambican army, trained by an EU military mission led by Portugal ( Lusa, 2/9/2026 ). That mission's mandate expires on 31 December 2026 ( Lusa, 14/5/2026 ). Legal commentary It is a war, not just terrorism. The government speaks of a fight against terrorism. For international law, what counts is something else: how intense the fighting is and how organised the armed group is. The Geneva Academy's research centre that classifies conflicts (RULAC) considers Cabo Delgado a non-international armed conflict ( Geneva Academy, RULAC ). The rules of humanitarian law therefore apply, in particular Article 3 common to the Geneva Conventions. They protect those who do not fight and those who have been captured: no killing, no torture, no cruel treatment, no disappearances. The rules bind all parties, the armed group and the army alike. Calling the enemy "terrorists" does not suspend them. The children. In 2004 Mozambique ratified the UN Protocol that forbids armed groups from recruiting anyone under 18. Conscripting or using children under 15 in hostilities is a war crime. The first duty to protect them, search for them and reintegrate them lies with the State. The fishermen. A State may restrict fishing in a war zone. It may not fire on unarmed civilians simply because they broke a ban. The right to life, protected by the UN Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and by the African Charter, also requires an investigation into every suspicious death. The apology is a step. An investigation with public results would be the next one. Who can judge. Mozambique signed the Rome Statute in 2000 but has never ratified it ( PGA ). So the International Criminal Court cannot investigate, unless Mozambique accepts its jurisdiction or the Security Council refers the case. That leaves Mozambican courts: for the containers and for the fishermen, no soldiers have been tried so far. It also leaves the courts of other countries, where there is a link to them. France is such a case: TotalEnergies is a French company, and the Paris anti-terrorism prosecutor's office also has jurisdiction over war crimes. Companies. A company is not an army. But the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011) ask companies not to contribute to violations, including through those who protect them. If a company pays or equips an armed force, it must know how that force behaves and react when serious warning signs arrive. In France this duty has been law since 2017: the law on the "duty of vigilance" of large companies. The ECCHR complaint claims that TotalEnergies knew of the accusations against the Mozambican army as early as 2020. The company says it did not. A judge will decide, if someone opens an investigation. Europe. The decisions by which the EU funded the Rwandan soldiers require the beneficiary to respect humanitarian law and human rights, and to report regularly on how it uses the support ( CFSP Decision 2022/2354 ). The problem is checking it. According to the Institute for Security Studies, the EU has no concrete way of making sure that the money does not also help Rwanda's operations in Congo ( ISS, April 2026 ). The same goes for the Mozambican army: equipping it only makes sense if those who do wrong are held to account. Symmetry test The armed group. It is the main party responsible for the deaths and the mass flight. It beheads, abducts children, attacks people of other faiths. None of the accusations against the soldiers makes it any less guilty. The government. It has a real enemy and a population to protect. It accepted 284 of the 292 recommendations of its latest UN human rights review (Zitamar, 19/10/2026). But on the container events it denies everything. On the fishermen, local commanders apologised, while the official version still denies. We have found no report of soldiers convicted for abuses against civilians in Cabo Delgado. TotalEnergies. It is entitled to the presumption of innocence. The gravest accusations come from journalistic investigations and from a complaint, not from a verdict. But whoever pays an army for its own security must answer for how that army provides it. Those who want the gas. The African Energy Chamber called the British withdrawal an example of Western priorities overriding the needs of Africa, where many people have no electricity ( bne IntelliNews, 3/12/2025 ). It is a serious argument: Mozambique has the right to use its resources to grow. But Cabo Delgado's gas is destined mainly for export, to Europe and Asia. Rwanda. The same army that is praised in Cabo Delgado for bringing back some security is sanctioned in Congo for supporting an armed group. Rwanda rejects the sanctions. But Europe cannot judge it differently depending on the country. Europe. In Ukraine it demands that those who commit war crimes answer for them. In Mozambique it pays and equips armies accused of abuses, without publicly asking for an account of those accusations. And it needs the gas from that coast. What has worked Rwandan troops and the trained units have retaken many areas the rebels had occupied, and in Cabo Delgado alone about 670,000 displaced people are recorded as having returned home (IOM, June 2026). Part of the truth has come out thanks to local and foreign journalists, Human Rights Watch, ACLED and Zitamar, who count the incidents one by one. And in the case of the fishermen, the community's protests led the commanders to apologise in front of the families, and according to ACLED the navy then scaled back its operations against boats ( ACLED, 8/4/2026 ). It is little, but it is not nothing. What we don't know How many men really died in the containers of Afungi. The figures come from a journalistic investigation and from testimony. No authority has confirmed them. What TotalEnergies knew, and when. Only an independent investigation or a trial can establish that. Who will pay for the Rwandan troops, and for how long. Mozambique has said it will, but not how. Whether the EU will renew its military mission after 31 December. Our judgement This section states the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. In Cabo Delgado the word "security" has two meanings. For the gas site it means fences, soldiers, protected investments. For those who live there it means being able to go back to their village, go out to sea to fish, and fear neither the rebels nor those who are supposed to defend them. So far the first meaning has fared better than the second. Nobody here defends the armed group. It has killed thousands of people and abducted children. Fighting it is the government's duty. But an army fighting terror cannot become another terror for those around it. And whoever pays it, arms it or trains it, be it a company or the European Union, cannot say they did not know. By 31 December the EU will decide whether to keep training that army. We are not asking for Mozambique to be left alone. We are asking for one simple condition: that every euro spent comes with a public question about what happened in the containers of Afungi and at sea off Mocímboa da Praia. And that the question gets an answer. What to watch The EU Council's decision on the military mission in Mozambique (mandate expiring on 31/12/2026). The ECCHR complaint in Paris: whether the anti-terrorism prosecutor opens an investigation. The Nanterre investigation into Palma. The final findings of the National Human Rights Commission and of Mozambique's attorney general. New population movements recorded by IOM and ACLED's monthly data. A door handle held for hours on 7 October. A key from 1948 carried from tent to tent in Gaza. Two fears that look alike, and a first meeting point: listening to them.

The safe room door does not lock. You find this out that Saturday morning, when the shooting starts outside and you realise that the only thing between you and them is your hand on the handle. Your daughter is under the bed; you told her not to make a sound. Messages from the neighbours arrive on your phone: they are in the house, they hear footsteps, they are afraid. Then the messages stop. You hold the handle for an hour, then two, then six. Your arm shakes and you do not let go. You do not know if anyone is coming to save you. You do not know if anyone is still alive on the other side of the wall. It is 7 October 2023, in a kibbutz near Gaza. Many families have told it this way, with a hand on a door handle. Now another home, a few kilometres away. In fact, not a home: a tent, because the home is gone. For two years, at night, you heard the drones, and you learned to tell the sound that passes from the sound that stops. They told you to move, and you moved, once, then again, then again, and each time you carried fewer things. But one thing you always carried. It is a big iron key that your grandmother put in your hand before she died. It opens the door of a house near Jaffa that your family left in 1948 and could never return to. That door may no longer exist. The key does. Many families in Gaza have carried it like this, from one displacement to the next. Two doors. One to be held shut with all your strength. One that could never be opened again. When I talk about Israel with Jewish friends, the first word is always the same: security. Some go as far as saying that the only way to be safe is for no one to be left on the other side. For a long time I thought it was enough to disagree. Then I tried to put myself in the place of the one holding the handle. And also of the one holding the key. What history has taught The one holding the handle has a long history. Grandparents who survived the Shoah, a state born so as never again to ask anyone's permission to exist. And then the lessons of the last twenty-five years. In 2000 Israel leaves southern Lebanon, and Hezbollah arrives at the border. In the Oslo years, while there is talk of peace, buses explode in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv. In 2005 it leaves Gaza, pulls out soldiers and settlers, and Gaza passes to Hamas. The rockets increase. Until that Saturday. For the one holding the handle there is only one lesson: every time we gave up land, the land came back as a threat. The one holding the key also has a long history. 1948, which Palestinians call the Nakba, the catastrophe: hundreds of thousands of people who left or were driven out, and never returned. 1967, and since then the occupation, for almost sixty years. The checkpoints, the permits for everything, the family land that sometimes cannot be reached. And then the lessons of the last thirty years. In the Oslo years, while there is talk of peace, the settlements in the West Bank grow. There are negotiations, and meanwhile the hills fill up with houses that are not theirs. For the one holding the key there is only one lesson: every time we negotiated, the land shrank. Two different lessons. They are built the same way. Where fear leads Fear, when it lasts long enough, changes people. The polls say so, on both sides, and they please no one. In Israel two people in three do not want a Palestinian state , and in the 27 October election not even Netanyahu's main challengers proposed one . And there is worse: in a Penn State poll a large majority of Jewish Israelis said they supported expelling the inhabitants of Gaza . Twenty years ago there were far fewer. Among Palestinians half still think armed struggle has worked , even after what happened in Gaza. And the majority do not believe that Israelis really want peace . And here is the point. Each of the two fears is fed by what the other side does. A rocket on Sderot strengthens those who want to bomb Gaza. A house destroyed in Gaza, an olive grove burned in the West Bank, strengthen those who want to fire the next rocket. It is a machine. It runs on its own, and every turn proves right those who keep it turning. And yet, underneath, there is something else. Most Israelis want neither to withdraw nor to annex : they are stuck, waiting. Most Palestinians would accept a state born of an agreement : they just do not believe they will see it. Two majorities that wait. Each waits for the other to move. Opening If security is a closed door, the first step cannot be to break it down. No one opens it because someone outside tells them they must. The harder you push, the tighter the other holds the handle. The first step is to listen. Listening does not mean agreeing. It means recognising that on the other side there is a real fear, born of a real history. That the one holding the handle and the one holding the key are afraid of the same thing: of being erased. From there comes the second step: the land belongs to those who live on it. Whoever lives on that land, Jew or Palestinian, has the right to stay there and to live there safely. Neither people is going to leave. No one can build their own future on the idea that the other will disappear. The principle does not solve everything, and it is right to say so. It does not say what to do about the settlements in the West Bank, which under international law are illegal . It does not say what to do about the keys: about the refugees of 1948 and their descendants, who no longer live on that land. These are the two hardest questions, and they remain to be negotiated. But they are better negotiated between two peoples who have stopped fearing they will disappear. Those who have already opened it After much reflection and many pieces written, I have become convinced of one thing. Hope will not come from governments. It will come from people. In my experience, taken one by one, people are almost all good people. The truly bad ones, inside, are few. I know the polls above seem to say the opposite. Perhaps they do not. Perhaps they say that fear can lead decent people to accept terrible things. If so, the enemy is not people. It is fear. And fear can be reduced. There are those who are doing it. Rami Elhanan is Israeli. In September 1997 his daughter Smadar, fourteen, was in central Jerusalem buying her school books when three suicide bombers blew themselves up . Bassam Aramin is Palestinian. In January 2007 his daughter Abir, ten, had left school with her sister and two friends to buy sweets when she was hit in the head by a rubber bullet fired by the Israeli Border Police: an Israeli court ruled so . Two fathers who would have every reason in the world to hate. Today they work together in the Parents Circle, which brings together more than 850 Israeli and Palestinian families who have lost someone in the conflict and have chosen not to take revenge. They go into schools and talk about their daughters, side by side. It is not easy. Israel's Ministry of Education has tried several times to remove their programme from schools, and in June a court put it back . Their joint ceremony for the dead of both sides was held this year at an undisclosed location . For security. People can live with little. They do it every day, in a kibbutz as in a tent. What they cannot do without is feeling safe and having rights. The one holding the handle is right to be afraid. The one holding the key is right to be afraid. But a door, sooner or later, has to be opened, knowing that on the other side there is someone as afraid as you. Rami and Bassam opened it. They were the two people who had the most reasons to keep it shut. On 7 October 2023 about 1,200 people were killed in Israel and 251 were taken to Gaza as hostages. Three years on, a remembrance.

On 7 October 2023, armed groups led by Hamas attacked Israel. They killed about 1,200 people: civilians in their homes, in the kibbutzim and in the towns of the south, young people at a festival where they were dancing, soldiers and police officers. Whole families were wiped out. They took 251 people to Gaza as hostages ( The Times of Israel ). A United Nations mission found reasonable grounds to believe that rape, including gang rape, took place that day in at least three locations, and clear and convincing information of sexual violence against hostages ( UN, Special Representative on Sexual Violence in Conflict ). Today I remember them, and everyone who has lived with an empty chair at the table since that day. Editorial note: this site applies the same yardstick to all parties. The crimes of 7 October are in the preamble of the manifesto on Israel , which also documents what happened afterwards in Gaza. Pakistan versus Afghanistan: a year of strikes "in self-defence" and a massacre at a treatment centre in Kabul

Islamabad strikes the Pakistani Taliban, whom, according to the UN, Kabul continues to support. In a year more than five hundred Afghan civilians have been killed; on 16 March, at a drug treatment centre in Kabul, at least 269. What self-defence allows, and what it does not.

In brief For a year Pakistan has been bombing Afghanistan. It says it is defending itself against the Pakistani Taliban (TTP), who strike Pakistan's soldiers and cities from Afghan territory. A UN report in August proves it right on one point: the Taliban government in Kabul continues to support them. According to the UN mission in Afghanistan, from October 2025 to September 2026 cross-border attacks killed 512 Afghan civilians. The worst strike came on 16 March: a drug treatment centre in Kabul, at least 269 dead. Pakistan denies targeting it. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International say it may be a war crime. No investigation is known to have been opened. Self-defence has rules: an armed attack, a necessary and proportionate response. And even when it is lawful, civilians remain protected. The background The Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in August 2021. Since then Pakistan has accused their government of sheltering the Pakistani Taliban, a different movement that fights the Pakistani state. Kabul denies it and says terrorism is Pakistan's internal problem. In September we covered the other side of this rupture: the forced returns of Afghans from Pakistan . Who is who Who What it is What it says or wants Afghan Taliban They have governed Afghanistan since 2021. Russia recognised them in July 2025. They deny hosting armed groups and accuse Pakistan of aggression. TTP (Pakistani Taliban) A Pakistani armed group. According to the UN, it also operates from Afghanistan. It fights the Pakistani state. Pakistan's government and army They carry out the strikes in Afghanistan. They ask Kabul for "concrete and verifiable" action against the armed groups. Baloch separatists (BLA) An armed group in Balochistan, a Pakistani province bordering Afghanistan and Iran. Pakistan accuses the Taliban and India of backing them. Islamic State Khorasan The Afghan branch of the Islamic State, an enemy of the Taliban. It claimed the Islamabad bombing of 6 February 2026. The facts 2025. In October, the first serious clashes along the border. Qatar and Turkey broker a truce in Doha. In November, the Istanbul talks fail ( Al Jazeera, 16/10/2026 ). 2026, open war. On 6 February a suicide bomber kills 31 people in a Shia mosque in Islamabad. The Islamic State claims it, not the TTP ( Arab News, 7/2/2026 ). On 16 February a car bomb kills eleven soldiers and a child in Bajaur: according to the UN, the TTP claims it and reportedly acted from Afghanistan ( Security Council, S/2026/651 ). On 21 February the first Pakistani strikes in the provinces of Nangarhar and Paktika kill 13 civilians, according to the UN. On the 26th the Taliban attack Pakistani border posts. The next day Pakistan declares that it is acting "in exercise of its right to self-defence" ( Pakistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 27/2/2026 ). The strikes reach as far as Kabul. 16 March. Shortly before nine in the evening three bombs hit the Omid centre in Kabul, where more than a thousand men are being treated for drug addiction. They are leaving evening prayers. The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) has verified at least 269 dead and 122 injured, and writes that the real number may be higher because patient records were destroyed ( UNAMA, civilians January-March 2026 ). The Kabul authorities speak of more than 400 dead. Pakistan says it hit drone and ammunition depots and that "no hospital" was a target. Afterwards. On 18 March, at the request of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Turkey, the two sides agree to a pause for the end of Ramadan ( Al Jazeera, 18/3/2026 ). The war does not end, but the strikes thin out: June, September, October. On the night between 30 September and 1 October they hit homes in the provinces of Helmand and Kunar: at least ten civilians killed, almost all of them children, according to the UN ( AFP via Oman Observer, 1/10/2026 ). Mediation by China, Turkey and Russia has not produced an agreement. The toll. From October 2025 to September 2026 UNAMA counted 512 Afghan civilians killed and 1,236 injured in the cross-border fighting, almost three deaths in four in the first three months of 2026 ( Outlook, 17/10/2026 ). It attributes almost all of them to Pakistani forces ( UNAMA, April-June 2026 ). UNAMA does not count victims in Pakistan, and no one else counts them independently. Pakistan's government speaks of more than 1,300 citizens killed in a year in attacks launched, it says, from Afghanistan ( Afghanistan International, 26/10/2026 ). According to PICSS, a research centre in Islamabad, attacks by armed groups in Pakistan in September were the most numerous in twelve years ( PICSS ). What they reply. The Pakistani army spokesman called UNAMA's July report "baseless": those killed, he says, were militants ( Amu TV, 1/8/2026 ). The Foreign Ministry also rejects Kabul's accusations as "baseless" ( The Nation, 27/10/2026 ). The Taliban deny hosting the TTP and accuse UNAMA of propaganda. Legal commentary The rule. The UN Charter prohibits the use of force against another state (Art. 2(4)). The exception is self-defence: a state may respond "if an armed attack occurs", in a necessary and proportionate way, and must immediately report it to the Security Council (Art. 51). We explained this in the Glossary, under Use of force and self-defence . Pakistan has invoked self-defence in its statements and at the Council, on 9 March and 16 September ( Dawn, 17/9/2026 ). We have not found a formal letter from it to the Council, as Article 51 requires. Afghanistan's mission to the UN told the Council it had lodged a formal complaint on 22 February. The crux: the attack comes from a group, not a state. The attacks in Pakistan are not carried out by the Afghan army but by the TTP. In 1986, in the Nicaragua case, the International Court of Justice said that sending armed bands against another state can be an armed attack; arming or helping them is not. In 2005 it rejected the self-defence claimed by Uganda in Congo, because the rebels' attacks were not attributable to the Congolese government. And it left open whether force may be used in response to an armed group acting on its own ( ICJ, Congo v. Uganda ; ASIL ). Pakistan's argument. Without using the formula, Pakistan reasons like those who hold that one may strike on the territory of a state "unwilling or unable" to stop the attacks. It is the argument the United States used in Syria in 2014. Some states support it; many do not. What the UN says about the Taliban. The panel of experts that monitors the Security Council's sanctions writes that the Taliban "continued their support" to the TTP. It adds that they moved about 2,000 fighters and their families away from the border, and that their leader reportedly asked the TTP to stop the attacks ( S/2026/651, paras 91 and 99 ). This is Pakistan's strongest argument. It does not settle the question: for the Court, supporting an armed group is unlawful, but on its own it does not amount to an armed attack. Even when self-defence is lawful, the means have rules. The law that says when war may be waged and the law that says how it is fought are separate. The second always applies: distinguish between military and civilians, do not strike if the harm to civilians is disproportionate, take every feasible precaution. Hospitals and treatment centres lose their special protection only if used for military purposes and after a warning has gone unheeded. On Omid, Human Rights Watch found no evidence of military use and speaks of an unlawful attack and a possible war crime ( HRW, 27/3/2026 ). Amnesty reached the same conclusion: it identified at least one precision-guided bomb, a sign of a deliberate choice of target, and no warning ( Amnesty International, 21/7/2026 ). UNAMA gives no formal finding and calls for an investigation. Who could investigate. The UN Secretary-General called for an independent and impartial investigation ( UNAMA, 19/3/2026 ). We have found none. One route remains: Afghanistan has been a party to the Rome Statute since 2003, and the International Criminal Court is investigating crimes committed on its territory ( ICC, situation in Afghanistan ). The Court can try those who commit them there even if they are nationals of a state that, like Pakistan, has not joined ( Rome Statute, Art. 12 ). It is the same investigation that led to the arrest warrants against the Taliban leaders . Symmetry test Pakistan. The threat it denounces is real and documented by the UN. Its soldiers and civilians really are dying. But it has rejected the UN's figures, and on Omid there is no sign that it has accepted an independent investigation. The Taliban. They deny supporting the TTP, but the UN writes the opposite. On 26 February, after the first strikes, it was they who attacked Pakistani border posts. UNAMA also asks them to stop firing mortars and rockets into populated areas, and has documented military use of a school and a hospital by their forces. Pakistan's own yardstick. In January 2024 Iran struck an armed group in Balochistan which, it said, was attacking it from Pakistani territory. Two children died. Islamabad spoke of an "illegal act" and of a violation of its sovereignty that was "completely unacceptable" ( Dawn, 17/1/2024 ). Two days later it struck inside Iran in turn, against militants it said were preparing attacks from Iranian territory ( Dawn, 19/1/2024 ). For Islamabad the same argument was illegal when its neighbour used it, and legitimate when it used it itself. And what if it were the other way round? On 22 October the New York Times reported that Pakistani army and intelligence officials have met leaders of armed groups fighting the Taliban to discuss possible support. The sources are anonymous: a Pakistani intelligence official and a member of the Afghan resistance ( Afghanistan International, 22/10/2026 ; Long War Journal, 26/10/2026 ). Pakistan denies arming Afghans against Kabul. If the report were true, Pakistan would be doing what it reproaches the Taliban for, and by its own rule Kabul could strike it. For now it is not an established fact. The others. China, Turkey, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Russia have mediated. We have not found a Security Council statement on this war. What worked The truces reduced the death toll: after March civilian deaths fell from hundreds to a few dozen per quarter, then to a dozen. UNAMA has kept counting and publishing, despite protests from both sides. It is the only independent count we have. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Pakistan has a real problem. Someone killed in a bombing in Bajaur or in a mosque in Islamabad is no less a victim than someone killed in Kabul. And a government that lets an armed group strike a neighbour from its own territory cannot ask the world to defend its sovereignty without answering for whom it shelters. But self-defence is not a general licence. It is a narrow exception, with three conditions: an attack, a necessary response, a proportionate response. Two hundred and sixty-nine men leaving prayers in a treatment centre are not a proportionate response to anything. If Pakistan has evidence that the site was a military depot, it has a simple way to prove it: let someone independent look at it. In 2024 Islamabad knew how to explain, in clear words, why a cross-border strike against an armed group is illegal. They were the right words. They still apply. What to watch Whether anyone opens an independent investigation into Omid: Pakistan, the UN or the International Criminal Court. UNAMA's next quarterly report. The mediation efforts: Turkey, China, Russia, Qatar. The New York Times report on Pakistani contacts with anti-Taliban groups. A year ago the RSF took El Fasher, in Sudan. The earthen wall they used to seal off the city is still there. The world saw it, and kept on watching.

There is a wall around El Fasher. It is not made of concrete: it is earth piled up by bulldozers, an embankment more than fifty kilometres long. The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) raised it during the siege to close off the city: no food and no medicine in, no one out ( AFP, via Kuwait Times ). Two months before the city fell, on 26 October 2025, UNICEF estimated that 260,000 civilians were still behind that wall, half of them children ( UNICEF, 26/8/2025 ). A year later, the wall is still there. In September witnesses said the RSF were still reinforcing it. In October people who went back to see their homes were arrested and accused of spying for the army; a source close to the RSF confirms the arrests and calls them security measures ( Darfur24, 6/10/2026 ). And here is the point. That wall could be seen from space. Yale University's Humanitarian Research Lab followed it on satellite images as it grew ( allAfrica, 1/9/2025 ), and its director, Nathaniel Raymond, later described what followed to the British Parliament as a collective failure to prevent the massacre ( written evidence, 23/6/2026 ). Behind the wall In the 48 hours after the fall, according to monitoring groups, at least 1,500 people were killed. The same Yale lab documented house-to-house killings and, in the weeks that followed, a systematic campaign to make the bodies disappear: buried, burned, removed ( Al Jazeera, 16/12/2025 ). In February the UN fact-finding mission concluded that in El Fasher the RSF committed at least three of the acts listed in the Genocide Convention against the Zaghawa and the Fur ( UN Geneva ). It is the finding of a commission, not a judgment. The RSF deny large-scale killings. Those who managed to get out reached Tawila, sixty kilometres away, often on foot, after days of walking ( MSF ). Many did not make it: far fewer people reached Tawila than had been in the city ( Al Jazeera, 3/11/2025 ). There is no way of telling this that makes it lighter, and I am not looking for one. The Sudanese government objects to putting the army on the same level as a militia accused of such grave crimes ( SUNA, via allAfrica ). It is a serious argument: El Fasher has no equivalent on the other side. But this war does not have only one culprit. In the first three weeks of October drones killed at least 306 civilians in Sudan, and the UN human rights office attributes the strikes to both sides: the RSF and the army ( UN News, 23/10/2026 ). On 19 October a drone hit the Amiet market, in Abyei, killing more than eighty people according to the UN. South Sudan blames the Sudanese army; a Sudanese officer, speaking anonymously, said the target was fuel tankers heading to the RSF ( Al Jazeera, 21/10/2026 ). On 23 October army drones struck El Fasher, the market included ( Darfur24, 23/10/2026 ). A market is still a market, whoever hits it. On 7 October the army chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, rejected negotiations and promised to retake "every inch" of the territory held by the RSF ( Al Jazeera ). Two weeks later, in Geneva, representatives of 27 countries repeated that there is no military solution ( The National, 23/10/2026 ). What I think What follows is my assessment, not a fact. The day after El Fasher fell, Trump's envoy for Africa, Massad Boulos, said the world was watching with great concern ( allAfrica ). He was right. The world was watching. We watched the wall grow for months, in public images. The problem was never seeing. It is what you do afterwards. Afterwards came the reports, the condemnations, the one-year renewal of the fact-finding mission, with 28 votes in favour, 10 against and 9 abstentions ( allAfrica, 6/10/2026 ). Then the sanctions by the United States, the European Union and the United Kingdom against individual RSF commanders ( Arab News, 19/2/2026 ). Then the "breakthrough" announced in July by the prosecutor's office of the International Criminal Court, which says it can link the crimes to the leadership ( Reuters, via NBC ). Then the Geneva meetings. No arrest warrant made public for the crimes of this war ( Middle East Eye ). And the UN humanitarian plan for Sudan, in early October, was less than half funded ( Sudan Tribune, 13/10/2026 ). Why? Perhaps because Sudan is far away. Perhaps because the arms suppliers of both sides are countries nobody wants to quarrel with. Perhaps because a massacre without cameras makes less news. I do not know for certain: we looked for part of the answer by comparing what Europe does for Ukraine with what it does for Sudan ( Why Ukraine and not Sudan ). I know that the wall around El Fasher could be seen, and that seeing it stopped no one. And one siege teaches the next. In July the mission warned that around El Obeid, a city of half a million people, the RSF were using the tactics of El Fasher ( Al Jazeera, 9/7/2026 ). When a siege costs little to those who carry it out, it becomes a method. The sanctions hit assets those commanders are unlikely to hold in the West ( Sudan War Monitor ). There have been no arrests. There is a part that concerns us too. According to the mission there are "reasonable grounds" to believe that the United Arab Emirates are a hub of the network supplying the RSF; the Emirates deny any role. And the Emirates also buy weapons from Italy. It is not proven that Italian weapons have reached Sudan, and I do not write that. I write that the law requires those who sell weapons to assess the risk that they end up being used against civilians, and that after El Fasher nobody can claim not to know that risk ( Sudan, war by remote ). The wall of El Fasher is still there. It can be seen from above, as it could a year ago. The world is watching with great concern. I will not look away. But watching, on its own, has never saved anyone. South Sudan: its peoples, its history, who is fighting and why

Country profile of South Sudan, the world's youngest State: its peoples and their numbers, the Anglo-Egyptian condominium and the wars with Khartoum, independence in 2011 and the civil war between Kiir and Machar, oil, who benefits and what international law says. Updatable entry.

News from South Sudan talks about Kiir and Machar, a treason trial, elections postponed for years, famine and clashes in Jonglei, but rarely explains who the peoples involved are, why a State born to applause in 2011 was at war two years later, and why the peace signed in 2018 never worked. This profile tries to provide the background. It is updatable: every change is recorded at the bottom, with date and source. In brief South Sudan has about 12.4 million inhabitants, and a very young population: the median age is 19. The largest peoples are the Dinka, between 35 and 40%, and the Nuer, about 15%; dozens of smaller peoples follow, such as the Shilluk, Azande, Bari and Murle. For more than half a century the South fought the governments in Khartoum: two civil wars, from 1955 to 1972 and from 1983 to 2005, the second with about two million dead across Sudan. In 2011, 98.83% voted for independence. In December 2013 the power struggle between President Salva Kiir, a Dinka, and his deputy Riek Machar, a Nuer, became a civil war fought also along ethnic lines. Until 2018 it caused about 383,000 more deaths than normal, half of them violent. The 2018 peace agreement was never really implemented. Machar has been detained since March 2025 and is on trial; in 2026 fighting has resumed, 7.8 million people are going hungry and the government is preparing the first elections in the country's history for 22 December. The country lives on oil: according to the World Bank it accounts for 99% of exports and 85-90% of State revenue. It flows through a pipeline across Sudan, which is at war, and a huge share of that money, as the UN and several research centres document, ends up off-budget. Land and peoples South Sudan is landlocked. The oil wells are in the north, in Upper Nile and Unity States ( The Conversation, via allAfrica ); the south, Equatoria, borders Uganda. Since 2020 the country has been divided into 10 States and 3 "administrative areas" (Ruweng, Greater Pibor and Abyei), after years in which the number of States had been raised first to 28 and then to 32 ( Eye Radio ). The dashed circle marks Abyei, an oil-rich area disputed with Sudan. Names in italics show where some of the peoples mentioned in this entry live; the Dinka and the Nuer live in many States. We do not draw front lines, which change from week to week. The square marks the capital. Boundaries: Natural Earth, which draws the 10 States but not, separately, the administrative areas of Ruweng and Greater Pibor or the Abyei area. The population. According to UN estimates reported by Worldometer , in 2026 South Sudan has about 12.4 million inhabitants, with a median age of 19; 28% live in towns. The last census dates back to 2008, when the country was still part of Sudan. A warning about the numbers. There are no recent, reliable data on ethnic groups. The percentages below are 2011 estimates taken from different sources: read them as orders of magnitude. For the smaller peoples there is no reliable figure, and we say so. Dinka (who call themselves Jieng) — between 35 and 40% of the population ( OSAR ; CNN, via ABC17 ). The largest people. President Salva Kiir is a Dinka (OSAR, cit.). Nuer (Naath) — about 15% (same sources). Riek Machar is a Nuer (OSAR, cit.). The so-called "White Army" grew out of the self-defence groups of young Nuer men (see below). Shilluk — the country's third people, with no reliable figure. They live along the Nile and the Sobat, in Upper Nile, and have a hereditary kingdom led by the reth . For years they have accused the Dinka leadership of occupying part of their land; in 2017 an offensive by the government and Dinka militias against the Shilluk armed group Agwelek forced tens of thousands of civilians to flee ( Minority Rights Group ). Azande, Bari, Kakwa, Murle, Acholi and many others — no reliable figure (OSAR, cit.). Many live in Equatoria, the southern region where the NAS rebel movement operates (see below). Religion (2020 estimates): Christians 60.5%, traditional religions 32.9%, Muslims 6.2% ( CNN, via ABC17 ). In a country that is overwhelmingly Christian or of traditional religion, religion is not what separates the warring parties. Oil. South Sudan produces oil in Upper Nile and Unity, but it has no access to the sea: crude reaches the Red Sea through a pipeline to Port Sudan, crossing Sudan, which charges for transit ( The Conversation, via allAfrica ). According to the World Bank, oil accounts for 99% of exports, 85-90% of State revenue and between 50 and 60% of gross domestic product ( World Bank, January 2026 ); the International Monetary Fund gives similar figures: nearly 90% of fiscal revenue and about 95% of exports ( IMF, 2024 ). In the 2026-27 budget presented in September, oil covers about 79% of expected revenue ( The Rio Times ). Depending on a single product and a single pipeline makes the State fragile: in February 2024, while fighting raged in Sudan, the pipeline ruptured, production fell from about 150,000 to under 50,000 barrels a day and the economy contracted; exports resumed in April 2025, with new interruptions, and in fiscal year 2025 oil revenue fell by about two thirds (World Bank, cit.). A short history The Anglo-Egyptian condominium (1899-1955). Formally Sudan, the South included, is governed jointly by the United Kingdom and Egypt; in practice the British are in charge ( Fanack ). From 1922 the "closed district ordinances" bar northern Sudanese from entering and trading in the South (Fanack, cit.); from 1930 the "Southern Policy" prepares the South for a separate future, with Christian missionaries instead of an Arab administration ( Library of Congress ). In the end, however, the South is left inside independent Sudan. The two wars with Khartoum (1955-2005). In August 1955, five months before Sudan's independence, southern soldiers mutiny: the first civil war begins ( Refworld ). In 1972 the Addis Ababa Agreement gives the South autonomy, with Juba as capital ( CNN, via ABC17 ). In 1983 President Nimeiri abolishes it and imposes sharia on the whole country; in May of that year John Garang founds the Sudan People's Liberation Army, the SPLA (Refworld, cit.; CNN, cit.). The second war lasts until 2005 and kills about two million people across Sudan ( CFR ). The 1991 split. During the war the southern movement splits. In 1991 Riek Machar breaks with Garang: he calls for the South's independence, while Garang wants a united "New Sudan". Machar's forces, helped by Khartoum, attack Bor and kill about 2,000 people, mostly Dinka civilians; Machar publicly apologised in 2012. In 1997 he allies with the Khartoum government, then in 2002 returns to the SPLA ( Al Jazeera ). The memory of Bor still weighs on relations between Dinka and Nuer. Peace and independence (2005-2011). On 9 January 2005 the Comprehensive Peace Agreement ends the war and promises the South a referendum within six years. From 9 to 15 January 2011 the South votes: 98.83% choose separation. On 9 July 2011 the Republic of South Sudan is born ( CNN, via ABC17 ). Salva Kiir is president, Riek Machar vice-president (Al Jazeera, cit.). The civil war (2013-2018). In July 2013 Kiir removes Machar from the government; Machar announces that he will challenge him for the party leadership (Al Jazeera, cit.). On 15 December fighting breaks out in Juba between Dinka and Nuer soldiers; Kiir accuses Machar of an attempted coup, Machar denies it. In the following days hundreds of Nuer men in Juba are rounded up and killed: for the African Union Commission of Inquiry it was "an organised military operation". After Machar flees, his forces in turn commit massacres of Dinka in Bor, Bentiu and Malakal ( Al Jazeera, 2015 ). A peace agreement signed in 2015 collapses in July 2016, when fighting breaks out again in Juba and Machar flees once more; Kiir replaces him with Taban Deng Gai ( CNN, via ABC17 ). Between December 2013 and April 2018 the war causes about 383,000 more deaths than normal, of which about 190,000 violent, according to an estimate by the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine ( LSHTM ). Peace on paper (2018-2024). On 12 September 2018 Kiir and Machar sign the Revitalised Agreement (R-ARCSS). In February 2020 the country returns to 10 States ( Eye Radio ) and a unity government is formed, with Machar as first vice-president (CNN, cit.). The agreement provided for a unified army, a constitution, a census, a war crimes court and elections: in August 2026, 46.4% of its provisions had still not been implemented ( analysis on this site ). In May 2024 Kenya launches the "Tumaini Initiative" in Nairobi to bring in the groups left out of the agreement; the strongest, Thomas Cirillo's NAS, does not take part ( PeaceRep ). War returns (2025-2026). In March 2025 in Nasir, in Upper Nile, the White Army overruns an army base and kills a general; the government arrests ministers and officers close to Machar, and Uganda sends special forces to Juba ( Al Jazeera ). Machar has been under house arrest since March 2025 and since September 2025 has been on trial for treason, murder and crimes against humanity, charges he denies ( International Crisis Group ). Since late 2025 there has been fighting in Jonglei between the army and Machar's forces: in the first quarter of 2026 the UN mission counted 767 civilians killed ( UNMISS ). On 22 September 2026 Kiir dissolves the unity government and calls elections for 22 December ( analysis on this site ). Who governs, and how South Sudan has never held elections since independence: the first are called for 22 December 2026. Salva Kiir has been president since 2011. In its 2026 report, the research centre Freedom House rates the country "not free", with 0 points out of 40 for political rights: elections have been postponed since 2018, the press and civil society are restricted, and the first vice-president has been suspended and put on trial ( Freedom House ). We explain what distinguishes an autocracy from a democracy in the entry Autocracy . The succession. Kiir is 74, has governed for about twenty years and has never named a successor. According to the Swiss research centre Small Arms Survey, his method is to build up potential rivals and get rid of them when they show ambition ( Small Arms Survey ). The latest case is Benjamin Bol Mel: a businessman sanctioned by the United States for corruption since 2017, appointed vice-president in February 2025 and seen as the "crown prince", he was dismissed on 12 November 2025, demoted to private and placed under arrest; meanwhile the weight of Kiir's daughter, Adut Salva Kiir, has grown ( Eye Radio ; Small Arms Survey, cit.).
