Here religion plays no role: the parties are largely Christian, and the war is fought over power, land and oil money. The ground: a State born from an army. South Sudan was born after fifty years of war, led by the party and the army that had fought Khartoum, the SPLM and the SPLA, but that had also split internally, as in 1991. It has a single large source of money, oil. And in herding communities the defence of cattle and pastures coexists with raiding and inter-communal violence ( allAfrica ). The spark: the 2013 power struggle. The war does not stem from ancient hatred, but from a clash within the ruling party: Kiir removes Machar in July 2013, Machar wants to challenge him, and in December the two camps open fire on each other in Juba (Al Jazeera, cit.). The flag: ethnic belonging. After the killings of Nuer in Juba and the massacres of Dinka in Bor, Bentiu and Malakal ( Al Jazeera, 2015 ), a clash between two men becomes for many a clash between two peoples. Pospisil notes that many Nuer fighters say they took up arms precisely after the Juba killings ( allAfrica ). None of these identities makes it lawful to kill a civilian for being Dinka, Nuer or Shilluk. The external multiplier: the neighbours. Uganda openly defends Kiir. Sudan controls the pipeline on which the State depends, and since 2023 has itself been at war: hundreds of thousands of Sudanese have fled to South Sudan (UNHCR, see below). According to Small Arms Survey, Bol Mel also had business ties with the United Arab Emirates and with Sudan's RSF, who were irritated by his fall (cit.). Who profits We document declared or verifiable interests, not motives. If an actor denies, we say so. Whoever controls the oil. The World Bank lists among the problems of public finances non-transparent oil advances, oil-backed loans and off-budget transactions ( World Bank, January 2026 ). According to an analysis published by The Conversation in 2025, the accounts of the State oil company Nilepet rarely appear in official records and are often managed off-budget, and the fees for protecting the oil fields go directly to the National Security Service, the NSS, without passing through the budget ( allAfrica ). The "oil for roads" programme paid about 2.2 billion dollars to companies linked to Bol Mel by the end of 2024, according to UN human rights reports cited by Small Arms Survey; almost none of the roads were built ( Small Arms Survey ). The president. The dissolution of the unity government leaves all power in Kiir's hands until his successor is sworn in, and some South Sudanese jurists fear the new law will let him postpone the vote again ( analysis on this site ). The government presents the elections as the fulfilment of the peace agreement. The armed opposition. The SPLM-IO draws from Machar's trial and from its rejection of the vote a reason not to disarm; local armed groups control territory, pastures and cattle. The opposition too has ordered forced evacuations of civilians in its areas ( analysis on this site ). Uganda. Kampala has declared it is defending Kiir's government ( Al Jazeera ). It also hosts over a million South Sudanese refugees (UNHCR, see below). Who intervenes from outside Uganda. Special forces in Juba since March 2025 ( Al Jazeera ). Kenya. Mediating since 2024 through the Tumaini Initiative, at Kiir's invitation ( PeaceRep ). UN. The UNMISS mission protects civilians and monitors violations ( UN ). The Security Council maintains an arms embargo, renewed on 29 May 2026 until 31 May 2027 with 9 votes in favour and 6 abstentions, including China and Russia ( Petra ). Sudan. Controls the pipeline, whose rupture in 2024 caused Juba's revenue to collapse ( World Bank, January 2026 ). The border remains disputed in the Abyei area, rich in oil and claimed by both countries: in September 2026 clashes between Ngok Dinka and Misseriya Arab herders killed at least 26 people; a UN force of about 3,000, UNISFA, operates there ( Al Jazeera ). United States. Sanctioned Bol Mel for corruption in 2017 ( Eye Radio ). The human cost. The 2013-2018 war caused about 383,000 more deaths than normal ( LSHTM ). Internally displaced people number over 1.9 million ( IOM, via ReliefWeb ). South Sudanese refugees in neighbouring countries number about 2.48 million: over a million in Uganda, about 690,000 in Sudan, 470,000 in Ethiopia, 215,000 in Kenya ( UNHCR ). At the same time South Sudan hosts about 660,000 refugees, 95% from Sudan ( UNHCR, via The Star ). In April 2026, 7.8 million people were in severe food insecurity, more than half the population ( analysis on this site ). Documented massacres. We recall some of them, attributed to different parties: Bor, 1991 : about 2,000 dead, mostly Dinka civilians, killed by Machar's forces ( Al Jazeera ). Juba, December 2013 : hundreds of Nuer men rounded up and killed by government forces or their allies, in what the African Union Commission calls an organised operation; Bor, Bentiu and Malakal, 2014 : revenge attacks on Dinka by Machar's forces, with rapes and killings even in churches and hospitals ( Al Jazeera, 2015 ). Upper Nile, 2017 : an offensive by the government and Dinka militias in Shilluk lands, tens of thousands displaced ( Minority Rights Group ). Jonglei, 2026 : 767 civilians killed in the first quarter alone ( UNMISS ); the order to evacuate Akobo county forced about 270,000 people to flee ( analysis on this site ). International law Treaties. South Sudan: has been a party to the Geneva Conventions and both Additional Protocols since January 2013 ( International Commission of Jurists ); ratified in 2015 the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the Convention against Torture and the Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women ( UN Geneva ); is not a party to the Rome Statute: the International Criminal Court can act only through a Security Council referral, which has never happened ( analysis on this site ). The missing court. The 2018 peace agreement provided for a hybrid court with the African Union for crimes committed since 2013. It has never been set up ( analysis on this site ). Machar's defence argues that this court, and not the special court created by the president, should try the charges of crimes against humanity ( analysis on this site ). The internal conflict. Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and the Second Protocol apply: they prohibit attacking civilians, summary executions, rape and the use of starvation as a method of warfare. They apply equally to the army, to Machar's forces, to the White Army and to every other armed group. Missing justice. For the major massacres listed above, the court envisaged by the 2018 peace has never come into being. The most important trial under way is that of the president's main political rival. Use of force and self-defence: what the UN Charter prohibits, the two exceptions, and who decides whether an attack was lawful

Since 1945 the UN Charter has prohibited States from using force against another State. There are two exceptions: authorisation by the Security Council and self-defence against an armed attack. What they mean, where they end, and why almost every war today is presented as self-defence.

Almost every State that attacks another says it is defending itself. Russia said so in Ukraine in 2022, the United States and Iran said so in the 2026 war, Ethiopia and Eritrea are saying so this year. To understand when the argument holds, you need two articles of the Charter of the United Nations: Article 2, paragraph 4, and Article 51. What it is The Charter, signed in 1945, prohibits all States from threatening or using force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another State (Art. 2(4)) ( Charter of the United Nations ). Before, war was a lawful tool of politics; since then, it no longer is. The prohibition applies even to those who feel threatened or are right in a dispute. The two exceptions Authorisation by the Security Council. The Council can determine that there is a threat to the peace or an act of aggression (Art. 39) and, if other measures are not enough, authorise the use of force (Art. 42). It takes nine votes out of fifteen and no vote against from any of the five permanent members: that is why the Security Council rarely authorises force. Self-defence. Article 51 recognises the right of a State to defend itself, alone or with its allies, "if an armed attack occurs". The response must be necessary and proportionate, must be reported immediately to the Security Council, and lasts only until the Council acts. What counts as an "armed attack" The International Court of Justice clarified this in 1986, in the case of Nicaragua v. United States. An armed attack is one of the most grave forms of the use of force: an invasion, or the sending of armed bands with comparable effects. Supplying weapons or support to rebels is unlawful, but it is not an armed attack and does not entitle the victim to respond with war ( ICJ, Nicaragua v. United States ; extract of the judgment ). In 1974 the General Assembly had already defined aggression: invasion, bombardment, blockade of ports, sending armed bands. The list is not closed, and the Security Council decides case by case ( resolution 3314 ). The grey areas Defending first. An imminent attack may justify anticipatory self-defence. The most cited test comes from an 1841 letter by US Secretary of State Daniel Webster on the Caroline case: a necessity "instant, overwhelming", leaving no choice of means and no moment for deliberation ( Avalon Project, Yale ). Preventive war against a future, uncertain threat is something else: for most States and legal scholars it is prohibited. Armed groups. The Charter was written with States in mind. In 2004 the International Court of Justice ruled out Israel invoking Article 51 for the wall in the West Bank, because the attacks did not come from a foreign State but from territory Israel itself controlled ( ICJ, advisory opinion of 9 July 2004 ). In 2014 the United States struck the Islamic State in Syria, arguing that one may act on the territory of a State that is "unwilling or unable" to stop the attacks ( US letter to the Council ). It is the position of some States, not a rule accepted by all. Humanitarian intervention. In 1999 NATO bombed Yugoslavia to stop the repression in Kosovo, without authorisation from the Council. A resolution by Russia, Belarus and India to stop the bombing was rejected by 12 votes to 3 ( UN, 26 March 1999 ). An independent international commission later concluded that the intervention was illegal, though politically and morally justified ( Kosovo Commission, 2000 ). The Charter provides no humanitarian exception. The limit, in practice It should be the Security Council that decides whether a war was self-defence. But when the attack comes from one of the five permanent members or one of its allies, the veto blocks everything. Since 17 July 2018 the International Criminal Court can try leaders for the crime of aggression, but for States that are not members of the Court a referral by the Council is needed, that is, once again the consent of the five ( Coalition for the ICC ). The General Assembly can condemn, not compel. Cases already cited on this site Russia–Ukraine, 2022. Moscow told the Council it was acting under Article 51 ( letter S/2022/154 ). Ukraine had not attacked Russia; the General Assembly condemned the aggression with 141 votes ( What Europe could do ). United States–Venezuela, January 2026. The fight against drug trafficking, the American justification, falls under neither of the two exceptions ( Interests first, order second ). United States, Israel and Iran, 2026. Washington and Tehran both invoked Article 51; a preventive attack on a nuclear programme is the most contested claim ( Iran: the unresolved question of the use of force ). Ethiopia and Eritrea, October 2026. Each of the two States accuses the other before the Council and invokes the Charter ( Ethiopia, a guide to the war ). If every State can call its own war self-defence, the prohibition in Article 2 remains a dead letter. That is why the yardstick must be the same for everyone. Firing squads are back in Libya: in Benghazi, Haftar's military courts decide

After fifteen years without executions, eastern Libya has put dozens of detainees to death in two months, after secret military trials and confessions the condemned say were extracted under torture. Fifty more are waiting. What happened, who protested and what the law says.

In brief Since 23 August the forces of General Khalifa Haftar, the de facto rulers of eastern Libya, have resumed carrying out death sentences. On 14 October the UN envoy told the Security Council that 58 people convicted of terrorism had been executed in Benghazi in two months. Human rights organisations denounce trials before military courts, behind closed doors, based on confessions the detainees say they gave under torture. At least two men were reportedly shot after their sentence had been reduced to life imprisonment. Libya had not carried out a death sentence since 2010. In the Gernada military prison at least fifty condemned men risk being next. International law does not forbid Libya from having the death penalty. It forbids applying it after unfair trials and on the basis of extracted confessions. The background Libya has the death penalty in its code, but for fifteen years it did not apply it: a de facto moratorium, never written down, that survived the fall of Gaddafi and the civil war. Since 2014 the country has been split between the government in Tripoli, recognised by the UN, and the east controlled by Haftar and the House of Representatives in Benghazi (we covered this in October, in our analysis of the Tripoli agreement ). Libya did not appear in our piece on the countries that still execute : now it does. Many of the condemned had been arrested in Benghazi and Derna between 2014 and 2018, during the war between Haftar's forces and rival armed groups. Between 2018 and 2021 the military courts in the east tried hundreds of civilians ( Human Rights Watch ). The facts The first executions. On 23 August the eastern military prosecutor announced that ten people convicted of murder and terrorism had been shot. On 29 August six more were killed ( Amnesty, ICJ, Libya Crimes Watch and OMCT ). Two weeks earlier, on 10 August, a car bomb in Benghazi had killed Haftar's head of military intelligence, General Fawzi al-Mansouri ( Al Jazeera ). No source links the two. How many. The counts keep rising and do not match. Local organisations had documented 31 by 10 September, 23 in Benghazi and 8 in Derna ( JURIST ). On 14 October the UN envoy Hanna Tetteh spoke of 58 executions in Benghazi over the previous two months ( UNSMIL ). In the Gernada military prison at least fifty men sentenced to death risk being next ( Amnesty International ). How. According to Human Rights Watch and Amnesty, the trials took place before military courts, without notice and without the public: no families, no journalists. Some defendants could not choose their lawyer or see the evidence. The judgments carry no written reasons. Several of the condemned say they confessed under torture, after their arrest, to armed groups linked to Haftar. Families were not informed, bodies were not returned, funerals were banned. At least two men were shot even though a military appeals court had commuted their sentence to life imprisonment. What they answer. The eastern authorities announced the executions by listing the charges, but we found no response from them to the criticism of the trials. On 14 October, before the Council, the UN envoy reported a first step: the east has agreed to open the death penalty case files to the mission and to allow visits to its prisons. Who protested. On 16 September the UN mission called for executions to be suspended and procedures reviewed. The Tripoli government condemned them. On 30 September the European Union called for them to stop and for the trials to be reviewed by the UN mission ( EEAS ). In the Council, Denmark called for an official moratorium as a first step towards abolition ( Denmark at the UN ). The United States' statement at the same meeting, as published by its mission, speaks of the electoral agreement, drones and oil, but not of the executions ( US Mission to the UN ). Legal commentary The death penalty as such. Libya has not signed the protocol to the UN Covenant on Civil and Political Rights that abolishes the death penalty. International law therefore does not forbid it from having one. It forbids applying it like this. The Covenant. Libya has been a party to the Covenant since 1970 ( Human Rights Library, University of Minnesota ). Article 6 allows capital punishment only for the most serious crimes and only after a final judgment by a competent court. Article 14 guarantees a fair and public trial. The UN Committee that interprets the Covenant is explicit: a death sentence handed down after an unfair trial violates the right to life ( General Comment No. 36 ). The same Committee regards military trials of civilians as an exception to be justified case by case, not a rule (General Comment No. 32). And it regards keeping the date of execution and the place of burial secret as inhuman treatment of the family. Torture. Libya ratified the UN Convention against Torture in 1989. A confession obtained by torture cannot be used as evidence in any proceedings (Article 15). Libyan law. On 2 November 2025 the constitutional chamber of the Supreme Court in Tripoli declared unconstitutional the 2017 law that placed civilians accused of terrorism before military courts ( Libya Herald ). The east, however, disputes that chamber: the House of Representatives has created its own Constitutional Court in Benghazi, which has declared the Tripoli chamber abolished ( Asharq Al-Awsat ). The country's division reaches all the way to the question of which judge can say what is lawful. On one point, though, there is no need to choose a judge: a man whose sentence has been commuted no longer has a death sentence to carry out. Who is responsible. The obligations under the Covenant belong to Libya. In the east they are exercised, in practice, by whoever controls the territory and the courts: Haftar's command. Symmetry test The east. The executions were decided and announced by its military institutions. The condemned were accused of serious crimes, some linked to a war in which the east suffered bombings and killings: the latest, that of al-Mansouri, in August. The seriousness of the charges, however, does not change the rules of the trial: it is precisely for the most serious crimes that the Covenant makes them stricter. Tripoli. The UN-recognised government condemned the executions. But for the Mitiga prison in Tripoli, the International Criminal Court has confirmed charges of torture and killing of detainees against its former head, Khaled El Hishri, who will stand trial. The problem of detainees without guarantees is not the east's alone. The outsiders. The European Union and Denmark spoke. The statement published by the United States, which through its envoy Massad Boulos negotiates directly with the Haftar family, did not. Human Rights Watch is asking the governments that back Haftar's forces to intervene: as of 25 October we found no public statement from them. The yardstick. If a government hostile to the West shot dozens of opponents after secret military trials, would the reactions be louder? We cannot prove it. We can record that here, so far, they have been few. What worked The UN mission has obtained access to the death penalty case files and to the prisons. It is little, but it is the first door to open. The case reached the Security Council in the month in which it must renew the mission's mandate. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Fifteen years without executions were not a law. They were a choice, repeated every day by those who could have signed an order and did not. That is why they can be broken in a single day. We do not know why the east started again now. Perhaps to answer the Benghazi car bomb. Perhaps to show strength while talks go on about who will govern the country. We do not know. We know that the trials were secret, that the confessions are disputed and that at least two men died with a sentence that was no longer a death sentence. "Every execution carried out under these conditions is an irreversible injustice," Human Rights Watch wrote. That is the word that matters: irreversible. A wrong trial can be held again. A firing squad cannot. Fifty men are still in Gernada. The Security Council, which is writing the mission's new mandate these days, has the chance to ask for one simple thing: that none of them be killed before someone has read their file. What to watch The renewal of the UN mission's mandate by 31 October: whether the text mentions the executions and the access to the files. What the mission finds in the files and in the eastern prisons. The fate of the Gernada detainees. The General Assembly vote on a moratorium on the death penalty, at the end of the year, and how Libya will vote. Dozens dead in one cell: in Minna, Nigeria, the State is the accused

In September dozens of people arrested in a raid on illegal gold mines died in a cell of Nigeria's paramilitary corps, many of them teenagers. The commander admits "a very costly mistake", the guard says he heard the screams and did not open the door. The government report was due on 21 October and has not been published. What happened, and what the law says when someone dies in custody.

In brief On 16 September Nigeria's paramilitary corps NSCDC arrested dozens of unlicensed gold miners near Minna, the capital of Niger State. On the night of the 17th, in the command's cell, 37 of them died according to the government; the mortuary received 33 bodies. According to the governor, many were between 14 and 18 years old. The guard in charge of the cell admitted before the state commission of inquiry that he heard people screaming about the heat and the overcrowding, and did not open the door. The regional commander, suspended along with twenty-three other officers, speaks of "a very costly mistake". The official cause of death has not yet been established. The federal government reacted quickly: suspensions, an inquiry, President Tinubu calling for prosecutions. But the federal panel's report, due on 21 October, has not been made public, and a human rights group is demanding its release. Under international law a death in custody creates a presumption that the State is responsible, until a genuine investigation proves otherwise. Nigeria has had a law against torture since 2017, but so far it does not appear to have led to the conviction of any officer. Stopping illegal mining is legitimate: in the north of the country lead from gold mining has killed hundreds of children. The way it was done in Minna is not. The background This is the site's second piece on Nigeria. The first, Nigeria: who is killed, who tells the story, who should prosecute , described the violence of armed groups and the clash of narratives about the dead. It also explained that part of that violence is sustained by gold mined in secret in the north of the country. This piece looks at the same economy from the opposite side: what happens when the State tries to stop it. In Nigeria thousands of people dig for gold without a licence, by hand, in pits and tunnels. Many are teenagers. The work is dangerous even for those who live next to the mines: since 2010, in Zamfara State, lead released by gold processing has killed more than 400 children ( Human Rights Watch ). In 2024 the government created a dedicated unit against illegal mining, the "Mining Marshals", placed under the civil defence corps NSCDC ( Voice of Nigeria ). The NSCDC is an armed paramilitary corps under the Ministry of the Interior. It was created to protect infrastructure and public property, but it has powers of arrest and its own cells. The facts The raid. Residents of a housing estate on the outskirts of Minna, M.I. Wushishi, had long complained about miners digging close to their homes. On 15 September the NSCDC commander for Niger State, Suberu Aniviye, visited the site; on the evening of the 16th his men arrested dozens of people between Wushishi and Lukoto ( TheCable ). Who carried out the raid is already disputed. The commander says he sent the Mining Marshals. Their national commander denies it: the unit answers only to headquarters in Abuja, none of its men were in Minna, and he learned of the operation from the newspapers ( Naija News ). The figures on the number of detainees do not match either: 67 according to the governor, Umaru Bago ( Sahara Reporters ), 58 according to the cell guard, including 25 women, in a facility meant for 28 to 30 people ( THEWILL ). The night in the cell. On 17 September, at the NSCDC command in Minna, dozens of detainees were found dead. According to the governor many were between 14 and 18 years old and worked in the mines instead of going to school ( Reuters ). Survivors interviewed by the Nigerian daily Premium Times describe a small, windowless room with up to 65 people inside. They say that towards evening they began banging on the door asking for water, that they lifted the youngest up towards a vent so they could breathe, and that when the door was opened many were already dead ( Premium Times ). Among the survivors is a nine-year-old boy ( Sahara Reporters ). One mother told Reuters that officers were asking for 100,000 naira, about 75 dollars, to release the detainees. What the guard says. Before the state commission of inquiry, chaired by Justice Mohammed Mohammed, the officer in charge of the cell, Usman Isah Ndamaka, confirmed the core of those accounts. He said he heard the detainees screaming about the heat and the crush, and did not open because he was alone and feared being overpowered. He apologised in tears: "I admit my mistake" ( THEWILL ). Still to be verified is the claim by some survivors that in the days before, officers had sprayed a substance in the cell presented as mosquito repellent. How many died. The state government and almost all media report 37 dead. Before the state commission, however, the head of the Minna hospital mortuary said he received 33 bodies, brought in two ambulance trips, and could not account for bodies that never arrived ( Leadership via allAfrica ). The list of 37 names, released by a human rights association, started from the 33 registered at the hospital; four more names were added after families reported missing relatives ( TheNigeriaLawyer ). Where those four bodies are, and how they died, no one has yet explained in public. The cause of death. It has not been established. The NSCDC first spoke of a possible disease outbreak. The governor did not rule out exposure to toxic substances from the mines. According to an intelligence report cited by AFP, overcrowding and lack of air may have contributed ( CrispNG ). The victims were buried quickly, according to Islamic tradition. Toxicology tests require the families' consent and the samples are going to a laboratory in Lagos; so far the commission has not received conclusive forensic evidence ( THEWILL ). The anger. The next day hundreds of people took to the streets in Minna, some with sticks, machetes and hunting rifles; some tried to set fire to public buildings. Security forces fired live rounds ( Reuters ). A 24-year-old told AFP he was shot while returning from the funeral of one of the miners ( Africanews ). A curfew was imposed. The State's response. It was quick. The government suspended the commander and some twenty officers, later rising to 24: those who made the arrests, those who investigated, the cell guards and the legal office. President Bola Tinubu ordered an inquiry and said that suspensions are no substitute for justice: those responsible must be prosecuted. The Minister of the Interior appointed a ten-member panel, including a doctor, a human rights activist and a representative of the miners. Niger State opened its own commission, chaired by a judge. The vice-president announced 250 million naira for the families. What has emerged so far. On 6 October the chairman of the federal panel, Jonathan Kure, spoke of "elements of institutional breakdown" and "overzealousness", and asked for two more weeks, until 21 October, pending the test results ( Vanguard ). On 17 October, before the state commission, the suspended commander apologised to the families: "A mistake was made, but a very costly one". He said the detainees were due to appear before a judge precisely on the 17th. The head of his legal office said he had advised him to release the minors to their parents, and did not know why that was not done ( Channels TV ). 21 October passed without the federal report being made public. On the 22nd a Nigerian diaspora human rights group, NDOCHR, called for its immediate release and announced a protest outside NSCDC headquarters in Abuja ( The Guardian Nigeria ). Legal commentary Whoever dies in custody dies in the hands of the State. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which Nigeria has ratified, protects the right to life. The UN Committee that monitors it puts it plainly: a death in custody in unnatural circumstances creates a presumption that the State has arbitrarily deprived someone of life, and the presumption falls only if a proper investigation proves otherwise ( General Comment No. 36, para. 29 ). It is not for the families to prove the officers' guilt: it is for the State to prove it did everything to keep alive those it had locked up. Whether the cause was asphyxia, a substance or a disease, those shut in that cell depended on the State for air and water. The guard who hears the screams and does not open is the textbook case: the duty to protect does not depend on how many officers are on duty that night. The teenagers. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, ratified by Nigeria, allows the detention of a minor only as a last resort and for the shortest possible time, and requires that children be separated from adults (art. 37). In Minna, according to the accounts, 14-year-olds were in the same cell as adults, and the advice to release them to their parents was not followed. That they worked in the mines instead of going to school is not their fault: it is one more thing the State should have prevented. Before a judge within a day. The Nigerian Constitution requires that anyone arrested be brought before a judge within one day, if there is a court within 40 kilometres (s. 35). The commander says the hearing was set for the 17th, the day after the arrest. Some survivors speak instead of three days in detention. It is one of the points the commissions must clarify. Torture. Nigeria ratified the UN Convention against Torture in 2001 and its Optional Protocol, which provides for inspections of places of detention, in 2009. Since 2017 it has had a national law against torture: it provides for up to 25 years in prison and, if torture causes death, a murder charge ( UNCAT ). Denying water and air to people locked in an overcrowded room can amount to cruel and inhuman treatment, even without intent to kill. But the law has a difficult precedent: in 2020 Amnesty International documented 82 cases of torture and killings by the SARS police unit, disbanded the same year after mass protests, and no officer had been prosecuted ( Amnesty International ). Who investigates. The UN rules for investigating suspicious deaths, the so-called Minnesota Protocol , require that the investigation be independent of the body involved, prompt, transparent and open to the families. The federal panel was appointed by the Ministry of the Interior, the same ministry the NSCDC answers to, and so far it has published nothing. The public hearings of the state commission, chaired by a judge, are instead where the admissions have come from. Symmetry test Illegal mining is a real problem. Minna residents had asked for the digging near their homes to be stopped, and gold mined in secret also finances the armed gangs of the north-west. Lead from the mines has killed hundreds of children. The State has the right, and the duty, to intervene. The problem is not the raid, it is what happened afterwards. The protest was not peaceful. Some protesters were armed and tried to set fire to public buildings. This does not justify firing live rounds into the crowd, but it explains why a curfew was imposed. The government did more than usual. Within 24 hours came the suspensions, the president called for prosecutions, the commander and the guard admitted their mistakes in public. In the SARS cases none of this happened. It remains to be seen whether words turn into trials. It does not happen only in Nigeria. In Italy Stefano Cucchi died in 2009 a week after his arrest. It took more than twelve years and several trials, including for the cover-ups, before the Court of Cassation convicted two Carabinieri of manslaughter ( Il Fatto Quotidiano ). Deaths in custody happen in democracies too. What makes the difference is what happens next. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. In Minna there was no war, no jihadist attack, no bandit raid. There were teenagers digging for gold and a State that wanted to stop them. They died in a room locked by those who were supposed to bring them before a judge, while the man holding the key heard the screams. That is why this case says more about Nigeria than many massacres: it measures not the strength of armed groups, but the State's ability to respect the rules it asks others to respect. The government's reaction deserves credit: immediate suspensions, a president calling for prosecutions, officers admitting their mistake in public. That is more than was seen after the SARS cases. But the first deadline has already passed: the federal report was due on 21 October and is not public. Nigerian commissions of inquiry have a long history of reports delivered and never published. The test remains simple: whether the report is published in full, whether anyone is tried under the anti-torture law or for murder, and whether the families receive compensation decided by a judge and not just a donation. In our first piece on Nigeria we wrote that violence in the country is told above all through the religion of the victims. These deaths fit neither narrative: they were not killed by jihadists or armed herders. They died in a prison, in the hands of State officers. In Europe they have barely been mentioned. That too is a way of looking away. What to watch Whether and when the federal panel's report is published, and whether in full. The results of the autopsies and toxicology tests. The conclusions of the Niger State judicial commission: who ordered the raid, how many detainees there were, the gap between 37 and 33 dead. Whether the suspended officers are charged, and with what offence. Compensation for the families, and new rules for NSCDC cells. Ethiopia: its peoples, its history, who is fighting and why

Country profile on Ethiopia: its peoples and their numbers, the empire, the Italian occupation and the Derg, ethnic federalism, who governs and who fights, who profits and what international law says. An entry we keep updated.

The news from Ethiopia talks about Tigray, the TPLF, Fano, Eritrea and access to the sea, but rarely explains who the peoples involved are, why a country that came out of a war in 2022 is at war again, and who profits from it. This profile gathers the essential background. We keep it updated: every change is logged at the bottom, with its date and source. In brief Ethiopia has about 135 million inhabitants and is the second most populous country in Africa. It is a federation of regions drawn largely along ethnic lines: the largest peoples are the Oromo and the Amhara; the Tigrayans, at the centre of the war, are about 6%. In 1896 it defeated Italy at Adwa and remained independent. Fascist Italy invaded it in 1935 and occupied it until 1941, using gas and massacring civilians. From 1974 to 1991 the military junta known as the Derg ruled; then, for 27 years, a coalition dominated by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). In 2018 Abiy Ahmed came to power; he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 and in 2020 took the country to war against Tigray. The 2020-2022 war was one of the deadliest of the century: estimates range from fewer than 100,000 to about 600,000 dead. Since 23 September 2026 there has been fighting again: the government against an alliance of Tigrayan, Amhara, Oromo and Afar armed groups. On 4 October the army retook Mekelle. Behind the internal war lies a regional confrontation: Ethiopia wants an outlet to the sea and has built the great dam on the Nile; Eritrea, Egypt, Sudan and Somalia have lined up against it. Addis Ababa accuses Eritrea of sending troops into Tigray; Asmara denies it. Land and peoples Ethiopia is a highland plateau crossed by the Rift Valley and surrounded by arid lowlands to the east and west. The Blue Nile rises on the plateau and carries most of the Nile's water to Egypt. The country has had no outlet to the sea since 1993, when Eritrea became independent and took the whole coastline with it ( Britannica ). The capital, Addis Ababa, in the centre, is also the seat of the African Union. Tigray is in the far north, on the border with Eritrea; Amhara lies west and south of Tigray; Oromia, the largest region, surrounds the capital; the lowlands of Afar and the Somali region are in the east. Oromo Amhara Tigrayans Somali Afar Sidama Peoples of the south Eritrea Somaliland Somalia Kenya South Sudan Sudan Yemen Red Sea Gulf of Aden Addis Ababa Mekelle Gondar Bahir Dar Asmara Assab Djibouti GERD dam Open war: Tigray and Amhara Insurgency: Oromia In dark red, the regions where open war is being fought, Tigray and Amhara; in light red, Oromia, where the OLA insurgency has been active since 2018. Names show where the peoples mentioned in this entry live. We do not draw front lines, which change from week to week. Squares mark capitals; the triangle marks the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile. Assab is the Eritrean port Ethiopia lost in 1993. Boundaries: Natural Earth, which still shows the regions as they were before 2020: Sidama and the new southern regions are not drawn. A warning about the numbers. Official data on the country's peoples still come from the 2007 census, which counted 95 ethnic groups ( IRB Canada, via ecoi.net ). The percentages below come from that census, as reported by Minority Rights Group ( MRG ), and should be read as orders of magnitude: the population has since grown to about 135 million ( UNFPA ), and not every people has grown at the same rate. More recent estimates from other sources give similar shares: Oromo between 34% and 35%, Amhara between 26% and 27%, Tigrayans around 6% (Britannica and the Bertelsmann Stiftung, as reported by IRB Canada, cited above). For some small peoples there is no reliable figure, and we say so. Oromo — 34.4% (2007 census), the largest people. They live mainly in Oromia, the largest region, with about 40 million inhabitants ( AP, via UNB ), and speak Oromo. They have long complained of marginalisation by a government dominated by Tigrayans; from 2015 they protested against plans to expand Addis Ababa onto their farmland (MRG, cited above). Since 2018 the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) has been fighting in Oromia (AP, cited above). Amhara — 27% (2007 census). They live on the north-central plateau. Their language, Amharic, is the federal official language. Together with the Tigrayans they historically dominated politics: under Haile Selassie, Amhara language and culture were the model of Ethiopian identity, at the expense of other peoples. Under ethnic federalism they have demanded more autonomy for their region, with protests in Gondar in 2016 (MRG, cited above). Since 2023 the region has been the scene of a war between the army and the Fano militias ( our analysis ). Somali — 6.2% (2007 census). Muslim herders of the eastern lowlands, in the Somali region (the Ogaden), which Somalia contested in the war of 1977-1978 (MRG, cited above). The Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) fought there for many years. Tigrayans — 6.1% (2007 census). They live in Tigray, which has about 7 million inhabitants ( our analysis ), and speak Tigrinya, like most Eritreans. Most are Orthodox Christians. Although a small minority, through the TPLF they led the federal government from 1991 to 2018, and their presence in the security forces fed the idea of a "Tigrayan" government (MRG, cited above). Sidama — 4% (2007 census). They live in the south. For decades they demanded a region of their own and obtained it in 2020 after a referendum marked by delays and clashes ( Rift Valley Institute, via ecoi.net ). After them, other southern peoples demanded and obtained new regions (same source). Afar — 1.7% (2007 census). They live in the Afar lowlands, in the east, crossed by the road to Djibouti, through which almost all the country's trade passes ( our analysis ). Under the Derg the government exploited divisions between the Afar and the Somalis (MRG, cited above). Gurage, Wolayta, Hadiya, Gamo, Gedeo and the other peoples of the south — between 1.3% and 2.5% each (2007 census). They are dozens of peoples speaking different languages. Kunama, Irob and the other small peoples — together, 8.8% (2007 census). No reliable estimate for the individual groups. In the Gambella region and the Lower Omo, indigenous peoples have been displaced by villagisation programmes, plantations and dams (MRG, cited above). Religion : about 43.5% are Orthodox Christians and 33.9% Muslims; the rest are Protestants, Catholics or followers of traditional religions (MRG, cited above; 2007 census). Ethiopian Christianity is among the oldest in the world: in the fourth century King Ezana of Aksum proclaimed it the state religion ( National Geographic ). Resources and economy : agriculture, coffee, gold, river water. Between July and December 2025 gold exports reached $2.56 billion, and coffee $1.3 billion in a single quarter ( UNDP ). Public debt stands at $68.8 billion, which the IMF considers unsustainable; according to the World Bank, poverty rose from 33% in 2016 to 39% in 2021 (same source). In September 2025 Ethiopia inaugurated the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile: 5,150 megawatts at full capacity, $5 billion, financed almost entirely at home ( Khaleej Times ). More than 95% of imports and exports pass through Djibouti, at a cost of over $1 billion a year ( IBA ). A short history The empire. In the first century AD the kingdom of Aksum arose on the northern plateau; in the fourth century, under King Ezana, it became Christian, and between the third and sixth centuries it was one of the powers of the Red Sea (National Geographic, cited above). The Ethiopian empire descends from that Christian core on the plateau, and remained a monarchy until 1974. Adwa (1896). Italy, which had held the colony of Eritrea since 1890 (Britannica, cited above), tried to extend its rule. On 1 March 1896, at Adwa, Menelik's army defeated it: it was "the first crushing defeat of a European power by African forces during the colonial era" ( Britannica ). Ethiopia remained independent. The Italian occupation (1935-1941). In October 1935 Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia; on 5 May 1936 it took Addis Ababa. Mussolini and Badoglio authorised the use of gas ( The Reporter, drawing on Richard Pankhurst ). Emperor Haile Selassie appealed to the League of Nations, which did nothing (same source). On 19 February 1937, after an attack on the viceroy Rodolfo Graziani, the Italians laid waste to Addis Ababa for three days: estimates of the dead range from about 3,000 (Del Boca) to about 19,200 (Ian Campbell) to 30,000 (Ethiopian sources) ( Domani ). On 20 May 1937, on Graziani's orders, the monks of the Debre Libanos monastery were shot: 297 monks and 23 lay people according to Fascist records, up to 1,500-2,000 according to other estimates. In Italy, a bill to create a day of remembrance for the African victims of Italian colonialism has been stuck in parliament for years (Domani, cited above). On 5 May 1941 the British army and Ethiopian partisans liberated the country (The Reporter, cited above). Haile Selassie (1941-1974). The emperor returned to the throne. In 1952 the former Italian colony of Eritrea was federated with Ethiopia; in 1962 it became an Ethiopian province, and a guerrilla war for independence began that would last thirty years (Britannica, cited above). The Derg (1974-1991). In 1974 a communist military junta, the Derg, led by Mengistu Haile Mariam, overthrew the emperor ( Al Jazeera ). From 1976 the "Red Terror" targeted opponents ( HRW ): up to 30,000 dead according to the most conservative estimates by Africa Watch ( University of Pennsylvania ). The famine of 1983-1985 killed hundreds of thousands of people, worsened by the war and by government policies (Al Jazeera, cited above); the regime forcibly moved hundreds of thousands of peasants from north to south, and Médecins Sans Frontières, which reported at least 50,000 deaths during the transfers, was expelled ( MSF ). According to Human Rights Watch, the Derg's actions caused 500,000 or more civilian deaths (HRW, cited above). The TPLF in power (1991-2018). In 1991 the EPRDF coalition, led by the TPLF, entered Addis Ababa; Mengistu fled to Zimbabwe (HRW, cited above). The Tigrayan leader Meles Zenawi governed until his death in 2012. In 1993 Eritrea became independent (Al Jazeera, cited above). The 1995 Constitution created a federation of ethnically based regions and recognised the peoples' right to self-determination, including secession (Article 39); but power remained highly centralised in the EPRDF, which in 2015, with its allies, won every seat in parliament (MRG, cited above). From 1998 to 2000 Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a border war around the village of Badme, with tens of thousands of dead (Al Jazeera, cited above); the commission set up under the Algiers agreement awarded Badme to Eritrea, but Ethiopia did not accept the decision and the two countries remained for eighteen years in a state of "no war, no peace" ( Gulf News ). Abiy Ahmed and the Tigray war (2018-2022). After years of Oromo and Amhara protests, Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in April 2018. Within months he accepted the agreement with Eritrea and travelled to Asmara; in 2019 he received the Nobel Peace Prize (Gulf News, cited above). The TPLF lost federal power and remained in government in Tigray ( our analysis ). In November 2020 Abiy ordered an offensive against Tigrayan forces, after an attack on a federal military base ( Eye Radio ). Eritrean troops and Amhara militias fought alongside the army; in Axum, at the end of November 2020, Eritrean soldiers killed hundreds of civilians according to Amnesty International, in a massacre that may amount to a crime against humanity ( Amnesty International ). A joint investigation by the UN and the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission documented violations by all parties ( OHCHR ). On 2 November 2022 the Pretoria agreement ended the war ( our analysis ). The African Union mediator, Olusegun Obasanjo, spoke of around 600,000 dead; the head of the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission urged caution about all estimates (Eye Radio, cited above). After Pretoria (2023-2026). In 2023 the government tried to dissolve the Amhara regional special forces: the Fano militias, which had fought alongside the army, rebelled ( our analysis ). On 1 January 2024 Abiy signed a memorandum with Somaliland, Somalia's breakaway region, to lease about 20 km of coastline for fifty years in exchange for future recognition; Somalia considers it a violation of its sovereignty (IBA, cited above). In 2025 the TPLF lost its registration as a party; in April 2026 it removed the interim administration created by Pretoria and reinstated Debretsion Gebremichael at the top ( our analysis ). In the June 2026 elections, which were not held in Tigray, the Prosperity Party won 438 seats ( Reuters, via Polity ). The new war (since September 2026). On 20 September seven armed groups announced an alliance to overthrow the government. From 23 September the TPLF took the airports of Mekelle, Axum and Shire and attacked towards Amhara and Afar ( our analysis ). On 1 October Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and Eritrea broke off diplomatic relations ( Political.org ). On 4 October the federal army re-entered Mekelle without a fight ( Al Jazeera ); on the 5th Abiy was sworn in for a second term ( our analysis ). From 7 October the monitoring centre ACLED reported Eritrean troops entering Tigray at Zalambessa; Ethiopia struck them with drones and demanded their withdrawal; Eritrea neither confirmed nor denied it (Political.org, cited above). On 16 October Abiy appointed a caretaker administration for Tigray for six months, with the aim of holding elections ( Reuters, via Daily Maverick ), entrusted to men close to Getachew Reda and the Tigray Peace Force ( Critical Threats ). Tigrayan forces have announced a counteroffensive in central Tigray; in Amhara, the Fano are advancing in northern Shewa (same source). No ceasefire has been announced. Who governs, and how Ethiopia is a federal parliamentary republic: power lies with the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, in office since 2018, and his Prosperity Party. In the June 2026 elections the party won 438 seats, about 90% of those declared; there was no vote in Tigray, nor in at least eight constituencies in Amhara. The opposition accuses the government of arresting its leaders; the government denies it. In February the authorities did not renew the accreditation of Reuters journalists in Addis Ababa ( Daily Monitor, from Reuters ). The Swedish institute V-Dem , in its 2026 report, classifies Ethiopia as an "electoral autocracy": people vote, but elections are neither free nor fair ( V-Dem ). We explain what distinguishes an autocracy from a democracy in the entry Autocracy . The Constitution is federal and the federalism is ethnic: each region has its own government, its own police and, until 2023, its own special forces. In Tigray, since 16 October 2026, the federal government has installed a caretaker administration, while the TPLF continues to claim authority over the region (Critical Threats, cited above). Accuses Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of backing the rebels ( Reuters, via Daily Maverick ). Calls access to the sea an "existential" issue ( IBA ) National Defence Force (ENDF) Under the prime minister's command The federal army, with air force and drones. Calls the new war "defensive". They were the first to enter Mekelle and lead the new caretaker administration ( Critical Threats ) Fano (Fano National Movement) Zemene Kassie Amhara nationalist militias: allies of the army against Tigray in 2020-2022, at war with the government since 2023. Egypt and Sudan deny backing the rebels (same source) Where the conflict comes from We use the four levels of our piece "Are the world's wars 'Muslim'?" . Here religion is not the front line: the Tigrayans, Amhara and most of the Oromo who are fighting one another are mostly Christian. The ground: an empire turned federation. The empire governed from the centre, making Amhara language and culture the model of Ethiopian identity; the Derg recognised regional autonomy only on paper (MRG, cited above). The TPLF turned that model upside down with ethnic federalism: each people its own territory, with the right, on paper, to secede. But the boundaries between regions left contested lands between Tigray and Amhara, which remained under Amhara control even after Pretoria ( our analysis ); and those who live in "someone else's" region feel like foreigners in their own home. This does not absolve those who govern today. The TPLF governed for 27 years with a centralised system that won every seat (MRG, cited above). Abiy's government took the war to Tigray with the help of a foreign army, Eritrea's, and then broke with the Amhara militias that had helped it. All armed parties are accused by the UN of crimes against civilians. The spark: the succession of 2018. The war stems from the TPLF's loss of power. In 2018 the party that had governed for almost three decades was left in control of Tigray alone; in November 2020 the war began. The Pretoria agreement stopped the fighting but did not resolve the core issues: disarmament, the return of the displaced, the contested lands ( our analysis ). The flag: unity versus autonomy. The government fights for the unity of the state and calls the war in Amhara a "security problem" (same source). The opposition alliance says it is fighting for the "survival" of the peoples it represents and demands Abiy's fall. Both flags are political; neither makes it lawful to strike a school or recruit a child. The external multiplier: the sea and the Nile. The internal war has fused with a regional confrontation. Ethiopia wants an outlet to the sea, and its neighbours fear it will seek one by force, at Assab or in Somaliland; Egypt, which depends on the Nile for about 90% of its fresh water, considers the Ethiopian dam an existential threat (Khaleej Times, cited above). Every enemy of Addis Ababa has an interest in weakening it, and Addis Ababa has an interest in presenting every rebellion as directed from abroad. Who profits We document declared or verifiable interests, not motives. If an actor denies something, we say so. Abiy's government. Retaking Tigray allows it to install a friendly administration and to settle accounts with the TPLF, whose registration as a party it had already revoked. Abiy was sworn in for his second term promising to work towards an outlet to the sea ( our analysis ); a war with Eritrea, if it comes, would revolve around that port. The government denies having military designs on Eritrea: in March Abiy said Ethiopia would not go to war over the sea ( Africanews ). The TPLF. It is fighting to return to power in Tigray, from which it was excluded by the elections and now by the caretaker administration. In its alliance with Fano and the OLA it has sought allies among peoples who were until recently its adversaries. Eritrea. It fought against TPLF-led Ethiopia in 1998-2000, remained for eighteen years in a state of "no war, no peace", and in 2020 sent its troops into Tigray alongside Abiy (Gulf News, cited above). Today, according to the Ethiopian government, it finances the rebel alliance; Asmara denies it ( Reuters, via Daily Maverick ). Its declared interest is to prevent Ethiopia from gaining "sovereign access to the sea" at its expense (Political.org, cited above). On 13 October the Ethiopian army showed foreign diplomats weapons it says it seized from the TPLF, including Iranian-made and Turkish-Pakistani drones, as well as Eritrean uniforms and documents (Critical Threats, cited above). Egypt and Sudan. For Cairo, a weak Ethiopia is an Ethiopia less able to manage the Nile dam on its own; together with Sudan it has for years demanded a binding agreement on the filling and operation of the dam (Khaleej Times, cited above). Both deny backing the rebels. Ethiopia and Sudan accuse each other of interfering in each other's wars ( Al Jazeera ). Those who sell weapons. During the 2020-2022 war the United Arab Emirates organised an air bridge of more than 90 flights to Ethiopia, and satellite images showed Chinese Wing Loong drones at an Ethiopian base; in August 2021 Ethiopia signed a military cooperation agreement with Turkey ( Al Jazeera ). Since then the government has used drones, above all Turkish Bayraktar TB2s but also Chinese and Iranian models, in Tigray, Amhara and Oromia, with hundreds of civilian victims ( The New Humanitarian ). Somalia and Somaliland. The 2024 memorandum with Somaliland pushed Mogadishu towards Cairo and Asmara. Today the Somali president says he does not object to Ethiopia having commercial access to Somali ports, provided it is agreed with Mogadishu (same source). Who intervenes from outside The African Union. It mediated the Pretoria agreement in 2022 ( our analysis ); its headquarters are in Addis Ababa. The United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Canada. On 13 October 2026 Abiy's adviser Getachew Reda met the EU special envoy for the Horn of Africa; on the 14th US Secretary of State Rubio asked Abiy to respect sovereignty and end cross-border incursions; on the 15th Canada and the United Kingdom called for restraint ( Critical Threats ). The UN. Ethiopia has asked the Security Council to respond to the presence of Eritrean troops; Eritrea has asked the same against Ethiopia ( Al Jazeera ). The human cost. There is no death toll for the current war. About 750,000 Tigrayans were still displaced in February 2026 from the previous war (UNHCR, cited by Reuters, via Daily Maverick ). Across the country there are 1.9 million internally displaced people, and Ethiopia hosts 1.1 million refugees; malnutrition affects 4.4 million children and pregnant or breastfeeding women, and because of funding shortfalls emergency food aid covers 60% of the ration ( WFP ). In Tigray the regional administration has been unable to pay the salaries of about 137,000 civil servants since March, and the region also faces drought ( Al Jazeera ). International law The treaties. According to the University of Minnesota database ( HRL Minnesota ) and the UN ( OHCHR ), Ethiopia: has been a party to the Genocide Convention since 1949; has been a party to the Geneva Conventions since 1969 and to the two Additional Protocols since 1994; has been a party to the Convention against Torture since 1994 and to the Protocol on children in armed conflict since 2014; has not signed the Rome Statute : the International Criminal Court can act only on a referral from the Security Council , where such a decision can be blocked by the veto of a permanent member. Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan are bound by international law just as Ethiopia is; the TPLF, the Fano and the OLA, as armed groups, are bound by humanitarian law just as the army is. The internal conflict. Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and the Second Protocol apply: they prohibit attacks on civilians and on civilian objects such as schools and hospitals, require that aid be allowed through, and prohibit recruiting children under 15; the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child raises the limit to 18 for armed groups ( our analysis ). Eritrea. If Eritrean troops operate on Ethiopian territory without the consent of the government in Addis Ababa, that is a use of force between states, prohibited by the UN Charter except in self-defence. Likewise, an Ethiopian attack on Eritrea to obtain a port would be an act of aggression. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea recognises a right of access to the sea for landlocked states, but the terms of transit must be agreed with the transit states (IBA, cited above): the sea is negotiated, not conquered. Justice denied. No one has been tried internationally for the crimes of the 2020-2022 war. The Pretoria agreement, as we have written, is not a treaty with a judge but a political commitment (same source). Myanmar: its peoples, its history, who is fighting and why
Country profile on Myanmar: its peoples and their numbers, British colonial rule, who governs and who fights, who profits, and what international law says. An updatable entry.

News about Myanmar talks of the junta, of rebels, of the Rohingya, but rarely explains who these peoples are, where the war comes from and who profits from it. This entry gathers the essential background. It can be updated: every change is recorded at the end, with its date and source. In brief Myanmar (formerly Burma) has about 54 million inhabitants and more than a hundred different peoples. The Bamar majority lives in the central plain; minorities live in the mountains along the borders. The military has ruled almost without interruption since 1962. In 2021 it overthrew Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government. Since then the country has been at civil war, and the army has lost control of most of its borders. In April 2026 the head of the junta, Min Aung Hlaing, became president after elections from which the main opposition was excluded. Myanmar is accused of genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority, before the International Court of Justice (ICJ). Hearings closed on 29 January 2026; as of 22 October no date for the judgment had been announced. The conflict is also a war over resources: jade, rare earths, gas, gold and opium. About half of the world's heavy rare earths, used in electric cars and wind turbines, come from mines in the north. Land and peoples Myanmar is shaped like a horseshoe. In the centre lies a great plain along the Irrawaddy River, home to the majority; all around it, towards Bangladesh, India, China, Laos and Thailand, are mountains home to the minorities. This geography explains much of the country's history: the centre rules, the periphery resists. Bamar Kachin Chin Rakhine Shan Karenni Karen Mon Rohingya Wa Kokang Ta'ang India Bangladesh China Laos Thailand Bay of Bengal Andaman Sea Naypyidaw Yangon Mandalay Kyaukphyu Lashio States (minority peoples) Regions (Bamar majority) The states in red are named after a people, but other peoples live there too; the regions are mostly Bamar. Italic names with a red dot mark where the smaller peoples mentioned in this entry live. The square marks the capital. Boundaries: Natural Earth. A warning about the numbers. In 2014 Myanmar held its first census in thirty years. Almost all the results were published in 2015, showing a population of more than 51 million, and the data on religion in 2016. The data on ethnicity, however, have never been made public ( The Irrawaddy ); when the UN closed the project, it too noted that they were the last data still withheld ( UN Myanmar ). The issue is political: some argue that, if all minorities were counted, the Bamar might not be an absolute majority. That is why the figures below are of three kinds, always labelled: estimate : the percentages of the CIA World Factbook, the only widely used and consistent series ( CIA ), which other sources consider too favourable to the majority; census : the share of the population living in the state named after a people, from the 2014 results ( UNFPA ). States are mixed, so the number does not match the people; UN and NGOs : for the Rohingya, data from the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and Human Rights Watch. The total population is estimated today at about 54 million ( Freedom House ). Bamar (Burmans) — about 68% (estimate), more than 35 million people. They live in the central plain, speak Burmese and are largely Buddhist. Almost all army and political leaders come from among them. The name "Burma" comes from them. Shan — about 9% (estimate), almost 5 million. They live on the eastern plateau, bordering China, Laos and Thailand; Shan State, the largest in the country, was home in 2014 to 11.3% of the population, about 5.8 million people (census). They are linguistic relatives of the Thais and Buddhist. This is where the opium "Golden Triangle" lies and where several armed groups operate. Karen — about 7% (estimate), more than 3.5 million. They live in the south-east, on the Thai border, and partly in the delta plain; Karen (Kayin) State had 1.57 million inhabitants in 2014 (census). Many are Christians, converted by missionaries in colonial times. Their armed organisation, the KNU, has fought the central government since 1949: it is one of the longest-running insurgencies in the world. Rakhine (Arakanese) — about 4% (estimate), about 2 million. They live on the west coast, on the Bay of Bengal, and are Buddhist. Until 1784 they had an independent kingdom, Arakan, later conquered by the Burmans. Today their army, the Arakan Army, controls almost all of Rakhine State (see "Who's who"). Rohingya — Muslims of northern Rakhine, on the border with Bangladesh. The 1982 citizenship law does not include them among the recognised peoples, so they are stateless; the government calls them "Bengalis", meaning illegal immigrants. In the camps in Bangladesh UNHCR counts about 1.2 million ( Daily Observer, on UNHCR data ); in Rakhine, according to Human Rights Watch, about 630,000 remained in 2024 ( HRW ). They have fled in waves: in 1978, in 1991-92 ( HRW ) and in 2017, the worst. This is the case before the ICJ. Chinese of Myanmar — about 3% (estimate). Communities that arrived mostly in colonial times, today very present in trade. Not to be confused with the Kokang (see below). Indians of Myanmar — about 2% (estimate). They arrived in colonial times as officials, traders and workers; many were expelled after the 1962 coup. Mon — about 2% (estimate); Mon State was home in 2014 to 4% of the population (census). They live in the south, around Mawlamyine, and are Buddhist. Theirs is an ancient civilisation that helped bring Buddhism to the region; their kingdom fell in 1757, conquered by the Burmans. Kachin — no reliable estimate. Kachin State, in the far north on the border with China, was home in 2014 to 3.3% of the population, about 1.7 million people (census), not all of them Kachin. Most are Christians. Their land holds the great jade mines of Hpakant and the mines that produce about half of the world's heavy rare earths ( Reuters, via Mining.com ). Their army is called the KIA. Chin — no reliable estimate. Chin State, in the western mountains on the border with India, was home in 2014 to 0.9% of the population, fewer than half a million people (census). Most are Christians and they are among the poorest in the country; many have fled to India. Karenni (Kayah) — no reliable estimate. Kayah State, in the east, is the smallest: 286,738 inhabitants in 2014 (census). In 1875 an agreement between the British and the Burmese king recognised the independence of the Karenni states, which is why the Karenni claim never to have been part of Burma. Wa — no reliable estimate. They live in the north-east, on the Chinese border. They have the largest non-state army in the country, the UWSA, closely tied to China, and a de facto autonomous region. Kokang — no reliable estimate. They are ethnically Chinese and speak Mandarin; they live in northern Shan State. Their armed group, the MNDAA, played a key role in the 2023 offensive. Ta'ang (Palaung) — no reliable estimate. They live in northern Shan State, are Buddhist and grow tea. Their armed group is the TNLA. Religion (2014 census, data published in 2016): about 88% Buddhist, 6% Christian, 4% Muslim. The census did not count most of the Rohingya, so the real Muslim share is higher. Resources : jade, rubies, gold, rare earths, natural gas, oil, timber, tin. Myanmar is also the world's main known source of illicit opium: in 2025 cultivation rose to 53,100 hectares, its highest level in ten years, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, UNODC ( Anadolu ). A short history Before colonisation. For centuries different kingdoms rose and fell in the region: Burman, Mon, Shan, Arakanese. The first great Burman kingdom, Pagan, emerged in the 11th century. In the 18th century the Burman Konbaung dynasty conquered the Mon (1757) and Arakan (1784) and pushed as far as Assam and Manipur, in India. That is where it clashed with the British Empire. British colonisation (1824-1948). The British conquered the country in three wars, between 1824 and 1885, and ran it as a province of British India until 1937 ( CIA ). Two colonial choices still weigh today: Two Burmas. The plain, "Burma proper", was ruled directly; the minorities' mountains were administered separately, through local chiefs. The two parts grew apart. An army without Bamar. Colonial troops were recruited mainly among the Karen, Kachin and Chin, many of them converted to Christianity, while the Bamar were almost excluded. For Burmese nationalists, the minorities thus became "the soldiers of the British". Because Burma was a province of India, hundreds of thousands of workers and traders also arrived from the rest of the empire, including Muslims from Bengal into Arakan. At the time this was internal movement; today the government treats it as illegal immigration ( HRW ). It is one of the roots of the dispute over the Rohingya (see "Where the conflict comes from"). War and independence (1942-1948). In 1942 Japan invaded Burma. The young nationalist Aung San, father of Aung San Suu Kyi, first fought alongside the Japanese and then, in 1945, went over to the Allies. Many Karen instead stayed loyal to the British, and there were massacres between the two sides. In February 1947, at Panglong, Aung San signed an agreement for a federal union with Shan, Kachin and Chin leaders. In July he was assassinated. Independence came on 4 January 1948, but Panglong's federal promise was not kept: within a year the Karen, the communists and other groups took up arms. The military in power (1962-2011). In 1962 General Ne Win seized power in a coup and ruled for 26 years with an isolationist military regime, the "Burmese Way to Socialism". In 1988 a popular uprising was crushed in blood; Aung San Suu Kyi emerged. In 1990 her party, the National League for Democracy (NLD), won the elections, but the military refused to recognise them. Under that junta she spent a total of 15 years under house arrest ( Daily Mirror, from Reuters ). In 2007 the monks' "Saffron Revolution" was crushed. In 2008 the military pushed through a Constitution that reserves a quarter of parliamentary seats for them, and therefore the power to block any amendment, together with the ministries of Defence, Home Affairs and Border Affairs. The civilian interlude (2011-2021). From 2011 a government led by former officers opened up the economy and politics. In 2015 the NLD won the elections and Aung San Suu Kyi became de facto head of government, but the army kept control of security. In August 2017, after attacks by a Rohingya armed group (ARSA) on police posts, the army launched "clearance operations" in northern Rakhine: more than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. In 2019 Aung San Suu Kyi defended her country before the ICJ, and her international standing collapsed. The coup and the civil war (since 2021). On 1 February 2021, after another NLD victory, commander Min Aung Hlaing seized power. Peaceful protests were crushed; many young Bamar fled to minority areas and took up arms. For the first time Bamar and minorities fought on the same side. In October 2023 three armed groups (the Kokang, the Ta'ang and the Arakan Army) launched "Operation 1027" and took dozens of towns. In 2024-25 the army lost most of the borders. On 28 March 2025 a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck the centre of the country, near Mandalay: the official toll is 3,768 dead ( ReliefWeb ). The elections and the presidency (2025-2026). Between December 2025 and January 2026 the junta held elections without the NLD, which it had dissolved in 2023, and without voting in many war zones. The military's party, the USDP, won by a landslide. On 3 April 2026 the new Parliament elected Min Aung Hlaing president, with 429 votes out of 584; command of the army passed to General Ye Win Oo, a former intelligence chief ( Al Jazeera ; CNBC ). On 30 April the junta announced that Aung San Suu Kyi would serve the rest of her sentence under house arrest. Her son says he has no proof she is alive, and no one has been able to verify it ( Il Post ; Daily Ittefaq, from the BBC ). Who governs, and how Formally, Myanmar today is a presidential republic with an elected Parliament. In practice power remains with the military: the president is the former head of the junta, a quarter of the seats are reserved for the army by the Constitution, and the pro-military bloc holds almost 90% of the seats, according to India's public broadcaster ( All India Radio ). Of the 30 ministers in the new government, 28 are serving or retired generals, lawmakers of the military's party or members of the previous junta (same source). Two independent institutes, from two different countries, reach the same conclusion: Freedom House (United States), 2026 report: 4 points out of 100, "not free". The score fell from 7 in 2025 because the junta's laws prevented a genuine opposition from standing and some minority voters could not vote ( Freedom House ). V-Dem (Sweden), 2026 report: "closed autocracy", the category of regimes in which people do not freely elect those who govern ( V-Dem ). What distinguishes an autocracy from a democracy is explained in our entry Autocracy . Western governments and many observers criticised the elections as not free ( CNBC ). China, by contrast, promptly congratulated the new president ( Al Jazeera ).
