In 2024 they fought alongside the army against the Arakan Army, and according to Human Rights Watch they helped forcibly recruit young Rohingya ( HRW ) Where the conflict comes from We use the four levels of our piece Are the world's wars "Muslim"? . The ground: a country drawn by others. Myanmar's borders are the ones drawn by the British, who joined into a single state kingdoms and peoples that had never had a common government. The border mountains, rich in jade, timber and opium, have always been hard to control, and whoever controls the resources can pay for an army. After independence no government managed to build the federal state promised at Panglong. This does not absolve later governments. The colonisers left the ground, but the choice to govern through the army, to deny the minorities autonomy and to strip the Rohingya of citizenship was made in Rangoon and Naypyidaw, after 1948. The spark: the 2021 coup. The border wars had been going on for seventy years. The coup turned them into a national war, because for the first time the Bamar of the plain rebelled too. The flag: Buddhist-Burman nationalism. The junta presents its war as a defence of national unity and of Buddhism. The most extreme case is that of the Rohingya. For the junta and for many Burmese they are Bengali immigrants who arrived in colonial times; the Rohingya answer that they have lived in Arakan for centuries. The historical sources partly support both: Muslim traders were present on the Arakan coast from the 8th century, and in the 15th century Arakan's Buddhist kings had Muslim officials at court; then, under British rule, strong immigration from Bengal followed ( HRW ). Neither story justifies denying citizenship to people born in the country. The external multiplier: weapons, protection and business. A war of this length cannot be fought without supplies. The next section documents who sells weapons, who buys resources and who protects the junta at the UN. Who profits We document declared or verifiable interests, not motives. When an actor denies, we say so. The junta and its conglomerates. The armed forces control two large business groups, MEHL and MEC, active in mining, banking and construction. The United States and the United Kingdom sanctioned them in March and April 2021, Canada already in 2007 ( Gibson Dunn ), and the European Union on 19 April 2021 ( GlobalSecurity, from an EU statement ). For the military, the war is also the defence of a fortune. China is the junta's main ally. Its documented interests: energy : a gas pipeline (operating since 2013) and an oil pipeline (since 2017) run from Made Island, off Kyaukphyu in Rakhine, to Yunnan in China ( GlobalSecurity ). They allow part of the oil bound for China to avoid the Strait of Malacca; the port of Kyaukphyu , part of the Belt and Road: in April 2026 Beijing congratulated Min Aung Hlaing, promising "high-quality" cooperation on exactly these projects ( Al Jazeera ). The Arakan Army is fighting a few kilometres from the port; rare earths : in 2025 Myanmar supplied about 53% of China's rare-earth imports, according to S&P Global as cited by Geopolitical Monitor ( Geopolitical Monitor ). The mines are in KIA areas; the KIA took control of them in October 2024. According to Reuters, China threatened to stop buying unless the KIA gave up its assault on the town of Bhamo; China's foreign ministry replied that it was not aware of the details ( Reuters, via Mining.com ); jade : the mines of Hpakant, in Kachin State, supply China every year with jade worth billions of dollars ( Crisis Group ). China, however, talks to all sides, and when needed it also puts pressure on the rebels. In November 2024, according to The Irrawaddy, it held the Kokang leader, Peng Daxun, in Kunming to persuade him to leave Lashio; Beijing said he was in China for medical treatment ( The Irrawaddy ). In April 2025 the city returned to the army, with Chinese observers present at the handover ( RFA ). Russia is the main arms supplier. According to the UN special rapporteur Tom Andrews, between February 2021 and December 2022 the junta imported weapons and materials worth at least one billion dollars: 406 million from Russian entities, including the state agency Rosoboronexport (Su-30 and MiG-29 fighters); 267 million from China; 254 million from entities based in Singapore; 51 million from India; 28 million from Thailand ( The Irrawaddy ; UN ). Andrews specifies that he has no evidence that the governments of Singapore and Thailand approved those transfers, unlike Russia, China and, to a lesser extent, India. Special rapporteurs are independent experts and do not speak for the UN. India built the port of Sittwe, in Rakhine, as part of the Kaladan project, a trade route towards its north-eastern states. Since 2024 the port has been idle because of the fighting, and the route crosses areas controlled by the Arakan Army ( BNI ). India is also seeking access to Kachin rare earths: according to Reuters, in 2024 it sent officials of a state-owned company to KIA areas ( Reuters, via Mining.com ). Thailand buys much of Myanmar's gas: about 70% of the gas from the Yadana field goes to the Thai company PTT ( Oil & Gas Journal ). It also hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees and workers from Myanmar. The United States and Europe. They have sanctioned the junta and its conglomerates. In January 2022 France's TotalEnergies and America's Chevron announced their withdrawal from the Yadana field, citing worsening human rights (same source). According to Geopolitical Monitor, the Trump administration has received proposals to gain access to Myanmar's rare earths, including by dealing with the junta or the KIA ( Geopolitical Monitor ): an interest to watch. For symmetry: the West has given Myanmar far less attention and far less aid than other crises. The UN humanitarian plan for 2026 aims to help 4.9 million people, 27% fewer than the year before, for lack of funds ( OCHA ); more than 16 million people need help ( OCHA, July 2026 ). The armed groups. The militias too are financed by resources: taxes on the trade route to China (at least 40 toll gates and checkpoints, ISP-Myanmar ), jade, gold in Sagaing and rare earths. Along the borders online scam centres have grown, run by local clans linked to pro-government militias. China has begun to prosecute them: in January 2026 it executed 11 members of the Ming family, which ran scam centres in the Kokang region ( CNN, via ABC17 ). Who intervenes from outside ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations). On 24 April 2021 ASEAN leaders and the junta agreed on a "five-point consensus": an immediate end to violence, dialogue among all parties, an ASEAN special envoy, humanitarian aid, and a visit by the envoy to meet all parties ( Malay Mail ). The junta did not implement it and was excluded from summits. Since the elections Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to return; the 2026 Philippine chairmanship has asked that the ASEAN envoy be allowed to meet Aung San Suu Kyi ( Newcastle Herald, from AAP ). UN. In December 2022 the Security Council adopted resolution 2669, the first on Myanmar according to the British representative: 12 votes in favour, none against, with China, Russia and India abstaining. It calls for an end to violence, the release of political detainees, including Aung San Suu Kyi, humanitarian access and the safe return of the Rohingya ( UN ). The Secretary-General's special envoy is Julie Bishop ( The Star, from AFP ). An independent UN investigative mechanism (IIMM) collects evidence for trials. Bangladesh. It hosts about 1.2 million Rohingya in the camps of Cox's Bazar and on the island of Bhasan Char. Since December 2024 another 150,000 have arrived ( Daily Observer, on UNHCR data ). The human cost. According to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP), a Burmese organisation close to the opposition that counts only verified cases, the junta and allied militias have killed at least 8,211 people since the coup, as of 28 July 2026 ( AAPP ); more than 22,000 people are detained for political reasons ( AAPP ). The count does not include fighters or the victims of other armed groups. Internally displaced people number almost 3.8 million, the highest figure ever recorded in the country ( UNICEF ). International law The treaties. According to treaty databases ( HRL Minnesota ; Guide to humanitarian law ), Myanmar: has been a party to the Genocide Convention since 1956, with a reservation to Article VIII, which concerns recourse to UN organs; has been a party to the Geneva Conventions since 1992, but not to their Additional Protocols; is not a party to the Rome Statute , that is, to the International Criminal Court; has not signed the UN Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The ICJ case (The Gambia v. Myanmar). On 11 November 2019 The Gambia, mandated by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), accused Myanmar of violating the Genocide Convention against the Rohingya. The stages: 23 January 2020: provisional measures, that is, the Court's unanimous order to Myanmar to protect the Rohingya; 22 July 2022: the Court rejects Myanmar's objections, including the one claiming that the real applicant was the OIC and not The Gambia, and declares itself competent ( ICJ ); eleven states intervene to explain how the Convention should be read: Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, the Maldives, Slovenia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Belgium and Ireland; 12-29 January 2026: hearings on the merits ( ICJ ); judgment: as of 22 October 2026 the Court has not announced the date. The ICJ judges states, not people: a conviction would send no one to prison, but it would oblige Myanmar to make reparation and to punish those responsible. What the Court must decide, and what it can order, we explain in The Rohingya verdict that has not come . **The International Criminal Court .** Myanmar is not a member, but Bangladesh is. The judges have ruled that the ICC can try crimes begun in Myanmar and completed in Bangladesh, such as deportation ( FIDH ). On 27 November 2024 the prosecutor requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing for the deportation and persecution of the Rohingya in 2017 ( UN Geneva ). As of 22 October 2026 the judges have not yet decided, a delay that several organisations and jurists consider unusual ( CSW ; Opinio Juris ). The Court has stated that his new office as president gives him no immunity ( DVB ). The case is on our ICC Fugitives page. Universal jurisdiction. In February 2025 an Argentine federal court issued international arrest warrants for Min Aung Hlaing and others, for genocide and crimes against humanity ( DVB ). Universal jurisdiction allows a state to try the gravest crimes wherever they are committed. Other parties' responsibilities. International law does not concern the junta alone: the Arakan Army is accused by Human Rights Watch of killings and arson against the Rohingya in 2024 ( HRW ); armed groups are bound by humanitarian law just as states are; according to the UN special rapporteur, Russian arms transfers after the coup violate international humanitarian law ( Bangkok Post ): the Geneva Conventions (common Article 1) oblige states not to help those who violate them. DR Congo: its peoples, its history, who is fighting and why

Country profile on the Democratic Republic of the Congo: its peoples and their numbers, Leopold II's Congo and the Belgian colony, who governs and who fights in the east, who profits from cobalt and coltan, and what international law says. An entry we keep updated.

The news from the Democratic Republic of the Congo talks about the M23, Goma, Rwanda and coltan, but rarely explains who the peoples of the east are, where a war that has lasted thirty years comes from and who profits from it. This profile gathers the essential background. We keep it updated: every change is logged at the bottom, with its date and source. In brief DR Congo has about 112 million inhabitants, divided into some 250 peoples. It should not be confused with the Republic of the Congo, the neighbouring country whose capital is Brazzaville. From 1885 to 1908 it was the personal property of King Leopold II of Belgium; then a Belgian colony until 1960. After independence its first head of government, Patrice Lumumba, was killed, and Mobutu ruled for 32 years. The wars in the east began in 1994, when, after the genocide of the Tutsi in Rwanda, hundreds of thousands of Hutu, among them many of those responsible for the genocide, took refuge in Congo. From 1996 to 2003 two wars drew in up to nine African countries. Since 2021 the M23 armed group, backed by Rwanda according to the UN, has taken most of North and South Kivu, including Goma and Bukavu. In October 2026 former president Joseph Kabila, sentenced to death in absentia, put himself at the head of the rebellion. Congo produces more than three quarters of the world's cobalt and a large share of its coltan: the batteries and electronics of half the world depend on its mines. The United States, China, the European Union and the neighbouring countries all have documented interests in these resources. Land and peoples Congo covers almost the whole basin of the Congo River, most of it rainforest. In the west it has an outlet to the Atlantic only a few kilometres wide. The capital, Kinshasa, is on the river, in the west; the copper and cobalt mines are in the south-east, in former Katanga; the most fertile and most contested land is in the east, on the highlands of the Great Lakes, on the borders with Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania. For many people in the east, Kigali and Kampala are closer than their own capital. Kongo Mongo Luba Zande, Mangbetu, Ngbandi Rep. of the Congo Central African Rep. Boundaries: Natural Earth, which does not yet show the borders of Ituri province. A warning about the numbers. DR Congo's last census dates from 1984, when the country was still called Zaire; a new census is being prepared in 2026 ( Al Jazeera ). Even the population is an estimate: about 112 million according to the World Bank (same source). There are no recent official data on the country's peoples. The figures below are of two kinds, always indicated: estimate : the percentages compiled by the language research centre of Université Laval, in Canada ( CEFAN, Université Laval ), which does not give the year of the survey; they should be read as orders of magnitude; description : for the peoples of the east, where the fighting is, independent sources describe where they live and how they relate to one another, but give no reliable numbers. The country has some 250 peoples and more than 200 languages. The official language is French, but only a minority speaks it; the four national languages are Lingala (west and north, the language of the army and of music), Swahili (east and south-east), Kikongo (west) and Tshiluba (south-centre) (same source). Luba — about 18% (estimate). They live in Kasai and northern Katanga, in the south-centre, and speak Tshiluba. They descend from a great pre-colonial empire. Mongo — about 17% (estimate). They live in the great forest of the central basin, in the former Équateur province. They are a cluster of many groups related by language. Kongo — about 12% (estimate). They live in the west, between Kinshasa and the Atlantic, and across the borders with Angola and the Republic of the Congo. They descend from the Kingdom of Kongo, one of the great pre-colonial states of Central Africa. Banyarwanda (Congolese Hutu and Tutsi) — about 10% (estimate). They are the Kinyarwanda-speaking people who live in Kivu, mostly Hutu, with Tutsi and Batwa minorities. Some have lived there since before colonisation; others were moved there by the Belgians, who after 1922 also governed Rwanda and transferred tens of thousands of workers to the plantations of North Kivu; others still came as refugees. According to Minority Rights Group they came to make up about half the population of North Kivu ( Minority Rights Group ). Their citizenship has been granted, revoked and redefined by law several times: it is one of the roots of the war (see "Where the conflict comes from"). Banyamulenge — no reliable estimate. They descend from Tutsi herders who settled on the Mulenge highlands, in South Kivu; today the name generally refers to the Congolese Tutsi of the south (same source). They are often treated as "Rwandans" and are attacked by the army and by pro-government militias ( HRW, via our analysis ). The M23 says it defends them. Nande, Hunde, Nyanga, Shi and the other peoples of Kivu — no reliable estimate. They are farmers and traders in North and South Kivu. The Hunde claim customary rights over the land against the Banyarwanda farmers who came later; in 2013 a Hunde militia forced at least 3,000 people to leave Kitchanga (Minority Rights Group, cited above). Hema and Lendu — no reliable estimate. They live in Ituri, in the north-east. From 1999 a conflict over land between the two peoples spread to other groups and ethnic militias; the Ugandan army, which occupied the region for about four years, armed several factions ( HRW ). Today the CODECO militia, linked to the Lendu, operates in Ituri. Pygmies (Mbuti, Twa, Baka) — no reliable estimate. They are the oldest peoples of the forest; they live by hunting and gathering and are among the most discriminated against in the country (CEFAN, cited above). Peoples of the north (Zande, Mangbetu, Ngbandi) — no reliable estimate. They speak non-Bantu languages (CEFAN, cited above). Religion (estimate, CEFAN, cited above): Catholics about 40%, Protestants 35%, Kimbanguists (a church born in Congo) 10%, Muslims 9%. The Catholic Church is one of the main actors in civil society and has led protests over elections. Resources : cobalt, copper, coltan (from which tantalum is extracted), gold, tin, diamonds, timber, the rainforest, the river's potential for energy. In 2024 Congo supplied 77% of the cobalt mined in the world ( Cobalt Institute ). Mining accounts for about 26% of gross domestic product and more than 92% of exports; the leading buyer is China ( IISD ). The Rubaya mine in North Kivu alone produces about 15% of the world's coltan ( Daily Maverick ). Yet most of the population lives in extreme poverty: 64% on less than $2.15 a day ( ALNAP, on FSIN data ). A short history Before colonisation. Large states arose in the Congo basin, such as the Kingdom of Kongo on the Atlantic coast and the Luba and Lunda empires in the south-east. For centuries the region was struck by the slave trade, both towards the Atlantic and, in the nineteenth century, towards the Indian Ocean. Leopold II's Congo (1885-1908). At the Berlin Conference of 1885 the European powers recognised the "Congo Free State". It is not a Belgian colony: it is, in practice, the personal property of King Leopold II ( San José State University ). His private army, the Force Publique, imposes rubber quotas on villages, to be delivered without pay; those who fail to meet them are punished, and soldiers must account for every bullet by showing a severed hand, sometimes cut from living people (same source). How many died is not known precisely, because nobody counted the population before 1924. According to the Encyclopaedia Britannica the population fell from about 20 million to 8 million ( Britannica ); scholars' estimates of the victims range from 1 million to more than 10 million, and the debate is open ( review of the estimates, Lenz ). The scandal, raised above all in Britain, forces the king to hand Congo over to the Belgian state (Britannica, cited above). The Belgian Congo (1908-1960). The Belgian Congo is governed by the parliament in Brussels (Britannica, cited above), together with the big mining companies of Katanga and the Catholic missions. In 2020 and 2022 King Philippe expressed his "deepest regrets" and acknowledged that colonial rule was based on racism, but without making a formal apology ( The East African ). Independence and Lumumba (1960-1965). On 30 June 1960 Congo becomes independent: Joseph Kasa-Vubu is president, Patrice Lumumba prime minister. A few days later the army mutinies and Katanga, the mining province, declares independence with the support of Belgian interests. In January 1961 Lumumba is killed in Katanga ( The East African ). In 2001 a Belgian parliamentary commission concluded that some Belgian ministers and officials bore "moral responsibility" for his death, and in 2002 Belgium apologised ( Brussels Times ). Until 1965 secessions and rebellions kill at least 500,000 people (The East African, cited above). Mobutu (1965-1997). On 24 November 1965 General Joseph-Désiré Mobutu takes power in a coup; in 1971 he renames the country "Zaire" ( Mail & Guardian ). A one-party, anti-communist state, it is an ally of the West during the Cold War; his critics call the regime a "kleptocracy", and in the 1970s and 1980s the country goes bankrupt ( EBSCO ). 1994 and the two Congo wars (1996-2003). In July 1994, at the end of the genocide of the Tutsi in Rwanda, between 500,000 and 850,000 refugees, almost all Hutu, enter Goma in five days; in the camps the former Rwandan army and the Interahamwe militias responsible for the genocide regroup ( National Academies Press ). In 1996 Rwanda and Uganda back a rebellion led by Laurent-Désiré Kabila, who overthrows Mobutu on 17 May 1997 (Mail & Guardian, cited above). In August 1998 Kabila breaks with his allies: the second Congo war begins, with Rwanda and Uganda backing the rebels and Angola, Zimbabwe, Namibia and Chad defending the government ( EBSCO ). The foreign armies exploit gold, diamonds and coltan. In January 2001 Kabila is killed by one of his bodyguards and is succeeded by his son Joseph. The agreements of 2002-2003 formally end the war, but not in the east (same source). How many people died, mostly of hunger and disease, is disputed: the International Rescue Committee estimated 5.4 million deaths between 1998 and 2007; a review by the Human Security Report argues the figure could be up to 60% too high ( Congo Research Group ). Joseph Kabila (2001-2019). In 2006 the first free elections since independence are held and Joseph Kabila wins them (Mail & Guardian, cited above). In the east the wars continue: in May 2012 mutinous Tutsi officers found the March 23 Movement, the M23 (same source). Kabila's second term expires in 2016, but the elections are postponed until December 2018. Félix Tshisekedi officially wins them and in January 2019 becomes president in the first peaceful transfer of power in the country's history ( Al Jazeera ). The M23's new war (since 2021). In 2021 the M23 takes up arms again ( Al Jazeera ). In April 2024 it takes the Rubaya mining area (Daily Maverick, cited above); on 27 January 2025 it enters Goma, where according to the UN almost 3,000 people die ( VOA ); in February it takes Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu ( All India Radio ). In 2025 agreements multiply: on 27 June DR Congo and Rwanda sign a peace agreement in Washington; on 15 November the government and the M23 sign a framework agreement in Doha; in December presidents Tshisekedi and Kagame sign the "Washington Accords" with Trump, together with a mining partnership between Congo and the United States dated 4 December ( Al Jazeera ; IEA ). Six days later, on 10 December, Rwanda and the M23 take Uvira ( HRW ). On 30 September 2025 a military court in Kinshasa sentences Joseph Kabila to death in absentia for treason and war crimes, accusing him of supporting the M23 ( AP, via KSAT ). 2026. In August 2026, after talks in Switzerland with the United States, Qatar, Togo and the African Union, the government and the M23 agree on a roadmap for negotiations and a ceasefire verification mission ( Al Jazeera ). The fighting goes on all the same. In mid-October Kabila announces in Goma the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), which replaces the M23's political-military alliance and calls for resistance against Tshisekedi "by all means, including force" ( Al Jazeera ). Meanwhile in Ituri an Ebola epidemic that began in May 2026 had killed 2,911 people by 29 August, the worst ever recorded in the country ( Africa Rivista ). Who governs, and how DR Congo is a presidential republic. Félix Tshisekedi has been president since 2019; his second and, under the Constitution, last term ends at the end of 2028. The Constitution states that the number and length of terms cannot be changed. In July 2026, however, the Constitutional Court approved a law that allows the president to change the Constitution through a constituent assembly and a referendum in case of a "serious dysfunction" of the institutions: the opposition sees it as the road to a third term ( Africanews ). Two independent institutes, in two different countries, reach similar conclusions: Freedom House (United States), 2026 report: 18 points out of 100, "not free", as the year before. The political system is "paralysed by elite manipulation of the electoral process" ( Freedom House ). V-Dem (Sweden), 2026 report: "electoral autocracy", the category of regimes in which people vote but elections are neither free nor fair ( V-Dem ). We explain what distinguishes an autocracy from a democracy in the entry Autocracy . In the east, in Goma and Bukavu, the administration of the M23, now the FRN, governs in practice, with its own taxes and officials ( our analysis ). In 2026 it gave logistical support to the ceasefire verification mission ( Al Jazeera ) Where the conflict comes from We use the four levels of our piece "Are the world's wars 'Muslim'?" . Here religion plays almost no part: the great majority of the fighters are Christian, and the only group that flies a religious flag, the ADF, is fighting a separate war. The ground: a large, absent state. Congo's borders are those drawn in Berlin in 1885. The country was born as an extraction business: rubber and ivory for Leopold, copper and diamonds for the Belgian companies, cobalt and coltan today. In such a vast territory the state never really reached the east: whoever controls a mine can pay a militia. The border with Rwanda, moreover, divides peoples who speak the same language, and the Belgians moved tens of thousands of Rwandans into Kivu (Minority Rights Group, cited above). This does not absolve the governments that followed. Mobutu emptied the state to enrich himself; for decades Kinshasa's governments treated the citizenship of the Banyarwanda as a political weapon: granted in 1972, revoked by the 1981 law, redefined on ethnic grounds in 2004 and 2006 (same source); and today they arm militias that, according to the UN, commit crimes in their turn. The spark: 1994. The genocide of the Tutsi in Rwanda exported the war to Congo. The refugee camps of Goma housed civilians and perpetrators of the genocide together; the new Rwandan government saw them as a threat and invaded Congo in 1996. Since then every cycle of war in the east has returned to the same themes: Congolese Tutsi who feel threatened, armed Hutu whom Rwanda wants to neutralise, local peoples who see both as foreigners taking their land. The flag: self-defence and sovereignty. Everyone fights in the name of protection. The M23 says it defends the Congolese Tutsi; Rwanda says it is defending itself against the FDLR; Kinshasa and the Wazalendo militias say they are defending national sovereignty against an invader. According to UN experts, however, Rwanda's aim in 2025 was to conquer territory rather than to neutralise the FDLR (Africanews, cited above); and according to the UN fact-finding mission all parties, including the Congolese army, have committed possible war crimes ( our analysis ). The external multiplier: minerals. A war that has lasted thirty years needs money and weapons. In Kivu the money comes above all from the mines. The next section documents who buys, who transports and who negotiates access to these minerals. Who profits We document declared or verifiable interests, not motives. If an actor denies something, we say so. Rwanda and the M23. According to UN experts, military involvement has given Rwanda access to minerals, farmland and political influence in eastern Congo (Africanews, cited above). The M23 levies a 15% tax on the value of the coltan bought from the miners of Rubaya; according to UN investigators the mineral travels through Goma and Bukavu to Rwanda, where it is mixed with Rwandan coltan to hide its origin before being exported to Asia (Daily Maverick, cited above). Rwanda's mineral exports rose from $772 million in 2022 to $1.1 billion in 2023, and a researcher at the International Peace Information Service argues that Rwanda's geology does not allow it to mine as much as it exports ( Euronews ). Kigali denies supporting the M23. The government in Kinshasa uses the same resources as diplomatic currency. In December 2025 it signed a strategic partnership with the United States that gives American companies a right of first offer on strategic mining projects and on exported minerals, and plans to send a growing share of copper and cobalt exports towards the Lobito corridor, in Angola ( IEA ). Congolese lawyers have filed a constitutional challenge against the deal, which they say should have required parliamentary approval ( our analysis ). The United States mediated the peace agreements and, alongside them, the mining one: Trump said the United States would get "a lot of the mineral rights" from Congo (same source). It also sanctioned the Rwandan army, on 2 March 2026 (HRW, cited above). China is the leading buyer of Congolese minerals: cobalt from Chinese-owned mines is refined in China (IISD, cited above). The large "infrastructure for minerals" deal of 2008, renegotiated in 2024, provides for about $7 billion of roads and public works in exchange for copper and cobalt from the Sicomines joint venture, 68% controlled by Chinese companies ( Mining.com, from Reuters ). According to an independent analysis, China sells weapons both to Rwanda and to the Congolese army (see "Minerals for security" ). The European Union signed a memorandum with Rwanda in February 2024 to secure supplies of critical raw materials, including tantalum, and has earmarked more than €900 million from the Global Gateway programme for Rwanda. Belgium asked for the deal to be suspended; the Commission replied that its very purpose is to make minerals traceable (Euronews, cited above). Uganda and Burundi. During the second war Uganda occupied Ituri and its gold exports more than doubled (HRW, cited above); today it fights the ADF on Congolese territory together with Kinshasa's army. Burundi fights in South Kivu partly to strike at its own rebels (EWN, cited above). Kabila and the armed opposition. Kabila ruled for 18 years; today, sentenced to death, he has joined the armed rebellion. His party calls the sentence political (AP, cited above). The war will also help decide who governs Kinshasa after 2028. Who intervenes from outside The United States and Qatar. Two parallel processes: in Washington between DR Congo and Rwanda (neutralising the FDLR and withdrawing Rwandan troops), in Doha between the government and the M23 (ceasefire, prisoners, return of refugees) ( Al Jazeera ). On 13 October 2026 the UN envoy for the Great Lakes, Huang Xia, told the Security Council that diplomacy had made "notable progress" but that the situation on the ground "has continued to deteriorate" ( Al Jazeera ). The African Union. A group of facilitators, including former presidents Uhuru Kenyatta (Kenya) and Mokgweetsi Masisi (Botswana), met the parties in Goma and Kigali on 5 and 6 October 2026 ( Al Jazeera ). The UN. The peacekeeping mission was provided for by the 1999 Lusaka agreements (EBSCO, cited above) and is now called MONUSCO. The Security Council has extended it to 20 December 2026 (Le360, cited above). The human cost. Nobody counts the dead of the current war. In the capture of Goma alone, in January 2025, almost 3,000 people died (VOA, cited above). There are 5.6 million internally displaced people and 1.25 million Congolese refugees in African countries ( UNHCR , February-March 2026 data). More than 26.5 million people, almost one Congolese in four, cannot meet their basic food needs, according to the IPC ( FAO and WFP ). The UN humanitarian plan for 2026 asks for $1.4 billion for 7.3 million people, out of almost 15 million who need help ( OCHA ). International law The treaties. According to the University of Minnesota database ( HRL Minnesota ) and the International Criminal Court, DR Congo: has been a party to the Genocide Convention since 1962; has been a party to the Geneva Conventions since 1961 and to the two Additional Protocols since 1982 and 2002; has been a party to the Rome Statute since 2002: the International Criminal Court can therefore try crimes committed on its territory; has been a party to the Convention against Torture since 1996. Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi are bound by international law just as Congo is; the M23, the ADF and the militias, as armed groups, are bound by humanitarian law just as armies are. **The International Criminal Court .** Congo referred its own situation to the Court in 2004. The convictions so far all concern Ituri in 2002-2003: Thomas Lubanga (2012, 14 years, for child soldiers), Germain Katanga (2014, 12 years) and Bosco Ntaganda (2019, 30 years). The warrant against Sylvestre Mudacumura, military commander of the FDLR, issued in 2012, has never been executed ( ICC ). On crimes in North Kivu since 2022 the prosecutor has opened an examination at the request of the Congolese government itself ( our analysis ). **The International Court of Justice .** There is a direct precedent. In 2005 the Court ruled that Uganda had violated the prohibition on the use of force by occupying Ituri and supporting armed groups; in 2022 it ordered Uganda to pay $325 million, in five instalments of $65 million: 225 for harm to people, 40 for damage to property, 60 for looted natural resources, including gold, diamonds and timber ( UN Geneva ). On 26 June 2026 DR Congo brought Rwanda before the Court, accusing it of thirty years of abuses in the east, from 1996 to the present ( Jurist ). The case has only just begun: no responsibility has been established. We wrote about it in "The DRC takes Rwanda to the International Court of Justice" . The responsibilities of others. International law does not concern only those who fight: common Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions obliges all states to ensure respect for humanitarian law: this applies to those who arm the M23 as much as to those who arm the FDLR and the Wazalendo militias; a people's permanent sovereignty over its natural resources, affirmed by the UN in 1962 and by Article 1 of the two human rights Covenants, is the yardstick for judging agreements that trade minerals for security (see "Minerals for security" ); those who buy minerals from war zones have a duty to check where they come from: according to the Commission this is the point of the EU-Rwanda memorandum, and it is exactly the point on which critics challenge it (Euronews, cited above). The Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger): its peoples, its history, who is fighting and why

Regional country profile on the central Sahel, that is Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger: the peoples and their numbers, the empires and the French colony, the coups and the juntas, the jihadist groups and the Tuareg rebels, Russia, who profits and what international law says. An updatable entry.

The news from the Sahel talks about juntas, jihadists, Wagner and the Africa Corps, Kidal and blockades around Bamako, but rarely explains who the peoples involved are, why three countries threw out France and the UN, and why the war, instead of ending, has spread. This profile covers Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger together, the "central Sahel": three countries that share the same colonial history, are ruled by military juntas allied with one another and fight the same armed groups, across borders those groups ignore. It can be updated: every change is logged at the bottom, with date and source. In brief Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have about 79 million inhabitants between them. They are landlocked countries, largely desert or semi-arid, with dozens of peoples: the largest are the Bambara and the other Mande peoples in Mali, the Mossi in Burkina Faso and the Hausa in Niger. The Fulani (Peul) and the Tuareg live in all three. They were French colonies and became independent in 1960. Since 2012, with the Tuareg revolt and the advance of jihadist groups in northern Mali, the war has spread to the whole region. Between 2020 and 2023 the military seized power in all three countries. The juntas expelled French troops and the UN mission, turned to Russia, left the Economic Community of West African States and dissolved the political parties. The region is the world centre of jihadist terrorism: Burkina Faso is the most affected country in the world. But the armies and their allies are also accused of massacring civilians, as in Moura, in Mali, in 2022 (more than 500 dead according to the UN). In 2026 the war got worse: on 25 April the jihadists of JNIM and the Tuareg rebels of the FLA struck Bamako, Kati and northern Mali together, killing the defence minister; the FLA held Kidal until 6 October. Land and peoples The Sahel is the semi-arid belt south of the Sahara that crosses Africa from west to east. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have no access to the sea. The north of Mali and Niger is desert; the south is savannah, where most people live. The Niger river crosses Mali and Niger and flows past Bamako, Timbuktu, Gao and Niamey. The heart of the war is Liptako-Gourma, the border zone between the three countries ( CFR ). Names in italics show where some of the peoples mentioned in this entry live; the Fulani and the Tuareg live in all three countries. We do not draw front lines, which change from week to week. Squares mark capitals; the triangle marks Arlit, the uranium-mining town. Boundaries: Natural Earth, which shows the old subdivisions: in Mali, the regions of Ménaka and Taoudénit are not drawn; in Burkina Faso, provinces are drawn. The population. According to UN estimates (World Population Prospects 2024, reported by Worldometer ), in 2026 Niger has about 28.8 million inhabitants, Mali 25.9 million and Burkina Faso 24.6 million. A warning about the numbers. None of the three countries publishes recent, reliable data on ethnic groups. The percentages below come from different estimates, from different years, and should be read as orders of magnitude; for many small peoples there is no reliable figure, and we say so. Mali (estimates reported by Minority Rights Group, MRG ): Bambara, Malinke and the other Mande peoples — almost half the population. Bambara is spoken by about 80% of Malians as a common language (MRG, cited above). Fulani (Peul) — 14.7%. Herders and livestock breeders. In central Mali they have been accused as a group of supporting the jihadists and targeted by militias from other peoples: in March 2019, in the village of Ogossagou, about 160 Fulani were killed (MRG, cited above). Senufo — 10.5% (MRG, cited above). Dogon — 8.9%. They live in the centre of the country, where Dogon militias and Fulani armed groups fight each other; in 2020 violence in central Mali killed at least 400 people (MRG, cited above). Tuareg — 7.7%. A Berber people of the Sahara, in the north, who speak Tamasheq. Since the 1990s Tuareg movements have demanded independence or autonomy for "Azawad", the north of the country (MRG, cited above). Bozo — 2.9%; Songhai — 1.6% (MRG, cited above). Burkina Faso (2021 estimates reported by EBSCO ): Mossi — 53.7%. The largest people, on the central plateau around Ouagadougou. Their roots go back to the 10th century, and before the French arrived they were the undisputed rulers of the region (EBSCO, cited above). Fulani (Peul) — 7.8%. They live mainly in the north and east, the areas hit hardest by the war. Together with the Tuareg they were pushed to the margins as the Mossi came to dominate the state ( MRG ); today they are the main victims of reprisals by the army and the militias, as in Solenzo in 2025 (see below). Gurunsi 5.9%, Dioula 5.7%, Gurma 5.2%, Bobo 3.4%, Bissa 3.3%, Senufo 2.2%, Lobi 1.5% (EBSCO, cited above). For the other peoples there are no reliable figures (MRG, cited above). Niger (estimates reported by MRG , based on 2006 data): Hausa — 53.1%. They live in the south, along the border with Nigeria. Zarma-Songhai — 21.2%. They live in the west, around Niamey. Tuareg — about 11% (other estimates give 8.3%). In the desert north, where the uranium mines are. They rebelled in 1990 and again in 2007-2009, with the Niger Movement for Justice, which also demanded a share of uranium revenues (MRG, cited above). Fulani (Peul) — 6.5%; Kanuri — 5.9% (MRG, cited above). Descent-based slavery still exists in Niger, affecting mainly people of slave descent in Tuareg, Arab and Fulani communities: it has been a crime only since 2003 (MRG, cited above). Religion : the great majority is Muslim: about 95% in Mali (MRG, cited above), 98% in Niger (MRG, cited above), 64% in Burkina Faso, where Catholics are 20% and Protestants 6% (EBSCO, cited above). In a region that is almost entirely Muslim, the victims of the jihadists are also overwhelmingly Muslim. Resources and economy : farming and herding, gold, uranium. In 2023 Mali was Africa's second-largest gold producer: gold accounts for about three-quarters of exports and a quarter of state revenue ( The East African ). In Burkina Faso industry, mostly mining and mostly gold, accounts for about 30% of gross domestic product (EBSCO, cited above). Niger has uranium: the Somair mine, 63% owned by French capital, was taken over by the junta (The East African, cited above) in June 2025 ( our analysis ). Artisanal gold areas are also a source of income for the armed groups ( Anadolu ). A short history The empires. For centuries the Sahel was the region of trade across the Sahara, of gold and salt. In the 15th and 16th centuries the Songhai empire flourished there, one of the great trading states of West Africa, centred on the middle Niger, in today's Mali, and stretching into today's Niger and Nigeria ( Britannica ). Further south, on the plateau of today's Burkina Faso, the Mossi kingdoms remained independent until the French arrived (EBSCO, cited above). The French colony (1895-1960). At the end of the 19th century France conquered the region and brought it into French West Africa, the grouping of colonies that existed from 1895 to 1958. Today's Mali was then called French Sudan; Upper Volta, the future Burkina Faso, was created as a colony in 1909, broken up among the neighbouring colonies in 1932 and re-established in 1947 ( Britannica ). In 1960 the three countries became independent (same source). From independence to 2012. The three countries went through single parties, military regimes and democratic openings. In Burkina Faso, in 1983, Captain Thomas Sankara took power and in 1984 renamed the country "Burkina Faso", "land of upright people"; in 1987 he was assassinated, and his deputy Blaise Compaoré, "closely implicated", took power ( MRG ). Compaoré ruled for twenty-seven years, until the protests of October 2014 (EBSCO, cited above). In Mali and Niger the Tuareg rebelled several times, in the 1990s and the following decade (MRG, cited above). The war in Mali (since 2012). In 2011 the collapse of the Libyan state spread weapons and fighters across the region. In 2012 the National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad (MNLA) rebelled in northern Mali; a coup overthrew the government in Bamako; the jihadist groups pushed the Tuareg aside and took control of the north ( CFR ). In all, the rebels came to control about two-thirds of the country (MRG, cited above). In 2013 France intervened with Operation Serval, later Barkhane, which reached about 5,100 troops; the UN deployed the MINUSMA peacekeeping mission (CFR, cited above). In 2015 the Algiers agreement between the government and the armed groups of the north promised local autonomy and the integration of fighters into the army ( Africanews ), but left out the jihadist groups (CFR, cited above). In 2017 the main groups linked to al-Qaeda merged into JNIM ( Anadolu ); the Islamic State has its own branch in the region (CFR, cited above). The war spread to Burkina Faso and Niger and became entangled with conflicts between communities, such as the one between Fulani and Dogon in central Mali (MRG, cited above). The coups (2020-2023). In Mali the military seized power in 2020 and again in 2021; in Burkina Faso twice in 2022, in January and in September, when Captain Ibrahim Traoré took power (EBSCO, cited above); in Niger, on 26 July 2023, the military overthrew the elected president Mohamed Bazoum (CFR, cited above). The juntas broke with France, which withdrew its troops; in June 2023 Mali demanded the departure of MINUSMA (CFR, cited above). From late 2021 the Russian mercenaries of the Wagner Group arrived in Mali ( Arab News ). On 16 September 2023 the three countries signed a mutual defence pact, the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), and in January 2025 they left the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) (CFR, cited above). Mali without an agreement (2023-2025). In November 2023 the Malian army and Wagner retook Kidal, the stronghold of the Tuareg rebels ( ACAPS ). On 25 January 2024 the junta declared the "immediate" end of the Algiers agreement, accusing Algeria of hosting groups it calls "terrorists" ( Africanews ). In June 2025 Wagner left Mali and in its place the Africa Corps stayed, the paramilitary force under the direct command of the Russian defence ministry (Arab News, cited above). Since September 2025 JNIM has been blocking the roads around Bamako, causing a fuel crisis across the country ( Anadolu ). The 2026 offensive. On 25 and 26 April 2026 JNIM and the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), the Tuareg separatist movement, struck together at Bamako and Kati, Gao, Sévaré, Mopti, Bourem and Kidal. Defence Minister Sadio Camara was killed in Kati; on 26 April the FLA announced it had taken Kidal, while the army and the Africa Corps withdrew; on 29 April JNIM announced a new blockade around Bamako ( ACAPS ). On 6 October the Malian army and the Africa Corps re-entered Kidal without a fight; the FLA spoke of a "controlled withdrawal" ( The Sahel Brief ). On 18 October 2026 an attack that local leaders attributed to the Islamic State killed at least 40 people in a village in the Menaka region (CFR, cited above). In Burkina Faso, in February 2026, a series of JNIM attacks in the north and east killed more than 130 soldiers, auxiliaries and militants in a few days ( Arab News ). In Niger, on 29 January 2026, the Islamic State attacked Niamey airport with drones ( ADF ). Who governs, and how All three countries are ruled by military juntas, which have postponed elections and dissolved the political parties. The Swedish institute V-Dem , in its 2026 report, classifies all three as "closed autocracies", that is, countries where no multi-party elections are held for the head of government ( V-Dem ). We explain what separates an autocracy from a democracy in the entry Autocracy . Mali. General Assimi Goïta has been in power since the coups of 2020 and 2021. In May 2025 the junta dissolved all political parties and banned meetings; in July 2025 the transitional parliament gave him a five-year term, renewable "as many times as necessary", without elections ( Al Jazeera ). Burkina Faso. Captain Ibrahim Traoré has ruled since September 2022. In May 2024 the transition was extended by 60 months from July 2024, and Traoré will be allowed to stand in future elections ( Al Jazeera ). In February 2026 the junta dissolved all political parties ( our analysis ). Niger. General Abdourahamane Tiani (Tchiani) was sworn in as transitional president on 26 March 2025, for five "flexible" years that can be extended depending on security; the junta dissolved all political parties; former president Bazoum is still detained ( IDEA ). In December 2025 the junta decreed a "general mobilisation", with broad powers to requisition people and property ( ADF ). Who's who Who Led by Position Mali's junta Gen. Assimi Goïta In power since 2020-2021. Expelled France and the UN, ended the Algiers agreement, brought in Wagner and then the Africa Corps. Presents its policy as the recovery of sovereignty ( our analysis ) Burkina Faso's junta Capt. Ibrahim Traoré In power since 2022. Relies on the Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland (VDP), civilian militiamen armed by the state ( our analysis ) Niger's junta Gen. Abdourahamane Tiani In power since 2023. Expelled the French and the Americans, turned to Russia and keeps up its cooperation with Italy ( our analysis ) Alliance of Sahel States (AES) The three junta leaders Mutual defence pact of 16 September 2023; the three countries left ECOWAS in January 2025 ( CFR ) JNIM (Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims) Iyad Ag Ghaly, according to the UN Affiliated with al-Qaeda, formed in 2017 from the merger of five groups. About 6,000 fighters according to an estimate reported by the Washington Post. Funds itself through kidnapping, smuggling, cattle theft and control of artisanal gold; has spread towards Côte d'Ivoire, Benin, Togo and Nigeria ( Anadolu ) Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) — The Islamic State's branch in the region (CFR, cited above). In Niger's Tillabéri region it is the group that has killed the most civilians ( ADF ). It also fights JNIM Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) — Tuareg separatist movement of northern Mali. In April 2026 it attacked together with JNIM and held Kidal until October ( ACAPS ) Africa Corps (formerly Wagner) Russian defence ministry In Mali since 2021 as Wagner, since June 2025 as the Africa Corps; about 2,000 men according to US estimates ( Arab News ). Accused, together with the Malian army, of summary executions and killings of civilians, as near Timbuktu in June 2026 ( our analysis ) VDP (Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland) Under Burkina Faso's government A militia of armed civilians. Together with the special forces, according to Human Rights Watch, it killed at least 100 Fulani civilians in Solenzo in March 2025 ( Africanews ) Where the conflict comes from We use the four levels of our piece "Are the world's wars 'Muslim'?" . Here religion is the banner of the jihadist groups, but the victims are overwhelmingly Muslim, and the war is fought among Muslims. The ground: weak states over huge territories. The borders drawn by France put together desert peoples and savannah peoples, herders and farmers, governed from capitals far from the north. The Tuareg have rebelled in every generation since independence (MRG, cited above); the Fulani, mobile herders, were pushed to the margins in Burkina Faso as the Mossi came to dominate the state ( MRG ). The jihadist groups recruit on these injustices and on conflicts between communities over land and water. This excuses no one. No government, civilian or military, has resolved the rebellions of the north; the juntas, which took power promising security, have not delivered it, as ADF writes about Niger ( ADF ); the jihadist groups kill civilians and extort them; and the armies, with their Russian allies and the militias, punish entire villages for the crime of belonging to the "wrong" people. The spark: Libya, 2011. The collapse of the Libyan state spread weapons and fighters across the Sahel; the following year came the Tuareg rebellion, the coup in Bamako and the jihadist takeover of the north ( CFR ). The banner: sovereignty against terrorism, jihad against the state. The juntas present their war as a fight against terrorism and the break with France as the recovery of sovereignty. The jihadist groups present it as a war on "apostate" governments and their foreign allies. The Tuareg separatists fight for Azawad. None of these banners makes it lawful to kill a herder because he is Fulani or because he is Tuareg. The outside multiplier: Russia, gold, the neighbours. France and the UN have left; Russia came in with Wagner and then with the Africa Corps. Algeria, which had mediated the 2015 agreement, was accused by Mali of hosting the rebels ( Africanews ), and broke with Niger in 2025 before mending ties ( The Sahel Brief ). Gold and uranium give the juntas resources to fight over with multinationals, and the armed groups resources to fight over with the state. Who profits We document declared or verifiable interests, not motives. If an actor denies something, we say so. The juntas. The war justifies suspending elections: in all three countries the transitions have been extended and the parties dissolved, on security grounds (see above). The juntas have also rewritten their relations with foreign mining companies. Mali's 2023 mining code allows the state to take up to 30% of new mines ( The East African ); after a standoff that included seized gold and detained employees, in February 2025 Canada's Barrick signed an agreement to pay about $438 million ( Daba Finance ). In Niger the junta took over the Somair uranium mine, controlled by French capital (The East African, cited above). Russia. With Wagner and then the Africa Corps, Moscow has taken France's place alongside the juntas. According to the monitoring centre ACLED, the switch from Wagner to the Africa Corps gives the Kremlin more control and fewer legal and reputational risks, with the aim of stabilising the regimes, protecting infrastructure and gaining influence ( ACLED ). The jihadist groups. JNIM controls smuggling routes, artisanal gold-mining areas and livestock, and with the blockade around Bamako it uses fuel shortages as a weapon ( Anadolu ). The north and east of Burkina Faso, where it attacks most, are home to gold sites and smuggling routes ( Arab News ). The United States and Italy. They have declared interests in staying: for Washington, the uranium stuck in Niamey and containing Russia; for Rome, migration control, with the MISIN mission in Niger, authorised for up to 550 troops ( our analysis ). Cooperation continued even after a Nigerien army drone struck the market in Kokoloko, killing 17 civilians in January 2026 (same source). Who intervenes from outside France. With Serval and Barkhane it deployed up to about 5,100 troops from 2013; it left after the coups ( CFR ). UN. The MINUSMA mission left Mali after the junta demanded its departure in June 2023 (CFR, cited above). Russia. Wagner in Mali from late 2021, then the Africa Corps from June 2025 ( Arab News ), also present in Burkina Faso ( our analysis ) and in Niger ( ADF ). United States. After the coup in Niger it suspended more than $500 million in aid (CFR, cited above) and in 2024 left the drone base in Agadez; in 2026 it resumed non-lethal supplies to Niger's army ( our analysis ). Italy. It stayed in Niger with the MISIN mission and about 350 Carabinieri (same source). Algeria. Mediator of the 2015 agreement, accused by Mali of hostility ( Africanews ). ECOWAS. The three countries left it in January 2025 (CFR, cited above). The human cost. According to the CFR, the Liptako-Gourma border zone accounts for more than half of the world's terrorism deaths and about 2.6 million displaced people; in the first seven months of 2023 ACLED counted at least 7,800 civilians killed in the region ( CFR ). Burkina Faso is, for the second year running, the country most affected by terrorism in the world ( our analysis ). In Niger, in 2025, the Tillabéri region alone accounted for more than 1,200 of the 1,939 deaths recorded in the country ( ADF ). In the area the UN refugee agency calls the "Sahel Plus" there are about 2.9 million internally displaced people, three-quarters of them in Burkina Faso, and about 1.1 million refugees; Mali hosts more than 251,000 refugees, nearly twice as many as in 2024, most of them fleeing Burkina Faso ( UNHCR ). Documented massacres. We recall some of them, attributed to different sides: Moura, Mali, March 2022 : according to the UN human rights office, over five days the Malian army and "foreign military personnel" killed more than 500 people, almost all summarily executed, and raped at least 58 women and girls; the Malian authorities denied investigators access ( UN ). Solenzo, Burkina Faso, March 2025 : at least 100 Fulani civilians killed by the special forces and the VDP, according to Human Rights Watch; the government denied it. After the soldiers withdrew, JNIM reportedly killed residents it accused of collaborating with the army ( Africanews ). Kokoloko and Tillabéri, Niger, January 2026 : 17 civilians killed by an army drone in a market; in the same month the Islamic State executed 30 civilians in the same region ( our analysis ). Mali, 2023-2026 : on 29 September 2026 Amnesty International accused Malian soldiers and Wagner men of killing at least 34 civilians, between June 2023 and December 2025, in seven incidents in the Mopti, Ségou and Timbuktu regions: war crimes, according to Amnesty. On 19 October Human Rights Watch documented indiscriminate drone strikes by Malian forces and the Africa Corps ( CFR ). International law The treaties. The three countries: are parties to the Geneva Conventions (Burkina Faso since 1961, Niger since 1964, Mali since 1965) and to both Additional Protocols (Niger since 1979, Burkina Faso since 1987, Mali since 1989) (list of states parties, Wikipedia, based on data from the Swiss depositary ); Mali (since 1974) and Burkina Faso (since 1965) are parties to the Genocide Convention ; Niger is not ( UN Treaty Collection ); joined the Rome Statute and in September 2025 announced their withdrawal from the International Criminal Court ( Jurist ). They deposited their notifications with the UN between 18 and 24 June 2026: the withdrawal will take effect on 23 June 2027 ( Amnesty International ). The International Criminal Court. Withdrawal does not erase the Court's jurisdiction over crimes committed while the three countries were members, that is, until June 2027. In Mali the Court has been investigating since 2013, and the investigation continues (Amnesty International, cited above). The internal conflict. Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and the Second Protocol apply: they prohibit attacks on civilians, summary executions, collective punishment and outrages on personal dignity, including that of the dead. They apply equally to the armies, to their Russian allies, to militias such as the VDP and to armed groups such as JNIM, the Islamic State and the FLA ( our analysis ). Striking a crowded market with a drone without distinguishing between fighters and civilians violates the principle of distinction ( our analysis ). The mercenaries. The Africa Corps reports to the Russian defence ministry ( Arab News ): its acts, if committed by forces under Moscow's control, can engage the responsibility of Russia, as well as that of individuals. Justice denied. No one has been tried for Moura: more than a year later the Malian authorities were still denying any responsibility pending an internal inquiry ( UN ). For Solenzo, Burkina Faso's government denied it ( Africanews ). For Kokoloko, Niger's junta did not reply to Human Rights Watch ( our analysis ). Timeline Year Event 15th-16th c. Sudan: its peoples, its history, who is fighting and why
Country profile on Sudan: its peoples and their numbers, Turco-Egyptian and British colonial rule, who governs and who fights, who profits, and what international law says. An entry we keep updated.

The news from Sudan talks about "two generals", the RSF, Darfur and El Fasher, but rarely explains who the peoples involved are, where the war comes from and who profits from it. This profile gathers the essential background. We keep it updated: every change is logged at the bottom, with its date and source. In brief Sudan has about 50 million inhabitants, most of them Sunni Muslims. Alongside the Sudanese Arabs, the largest group, live many non-Arab peoples: the Fur, Zaghawa and Masalit in Darfur, the Beja in the east, the Nuba in the centre-south, the Nubians in the north. Since independence (1956) the country has almost always been ruled by soldiers or by regimes backed by the army. The wars against the peripheries – the South, Darfur, the Nuba Mountains and Blue Nile – began before independence. The South left in 2011. Since 15 April 2023 the regular army (SAF) of General al-Burhan has been fighting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of General Dagalo, known as Hemedti. Until 2021 they ruled together. Today there are two rival governments: one in Khartoum, the other in Nyala, in Darfur. It is the largest displacement crisis in the world: about 8.8 million people displaced inside the country and 4.3 million refugees abroad, and 19.5 million people in acute food insecurity. A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the RSF assault on El Fasher in October 2025 bears the "hallmarks of genocide". Both sides are accused of war crimes. Behind them stand foreign states, and beneath them lies gold. Land and peoples The Nile crosses Sudan from south to north: at Khartoum the White Nile, which comes from Uganda, meets the Blue Nile, which comes from Ethiopia. Along the river and in the plain between the two Niles, the Gezira, lives the richest and best-represented part of the country. All around lie the peripheries: the desert in the north, the Red Sea hills in the east, the savannahs of Kordofan and Darfur in the west, the Nuba Mountains and Blue Nile in the south. As in many African countries, the centre governs and the peripheries resist. Italic names show where the peoples mentioned in this entry live; the red dot marks the Masalit around El Geneina. We do not draw front lines, which change from week to week. The square marks the capital. Boundaries: Natural Earth. A warning about the numbers. Sudan has counted ethnic groups in only one census, that of 1956 ( Human Rights Watch ). The last general census, in 2008, still included the South but did not ask about ethnicity; the count was disputed and has never been repeated. Moreover, "Arab" in Sudan is not a biological category: it means someone who speaks Arabic as a first language and identifies with an Arab genealogy. A Fur who became a nomadic herder could be regarded as Baggara, that is, as an Arab ( Library of Congress ). That is why the figures below are of three kinds, always labelled: 1956 census : the shares at the time, which however also included the South, today South Sudan; 2008 census : the population of the states where a people lives, which is not the same as the people itself ( Central Bureau of Statistics ); estimate : assessments by independent organisations, such as Minority Rights Group. The total population today is estimated at about 50 million ( The National ). All the peoples below are African; the distinction that matters in this war is between those who call themselves Arab and those who do not. Sudanese Arabs — the largest group. In 1956 they were 39% of all Sudan, South included (1956 census); in 1983 they were almost 55% of the northern provinces ( Library of Congress ). They are not a single bloc. The river tribes , such as the Ja'aliyin, live along the Nile north of Khartoum: this is the world from which much of the elite that has governed since independence comes, because the political system has always favoured the Arab and Muslim groups around the capital ( Freedom House ). The Baggara ("cattle people") and the Abbala ("camel people") are herders of Kordofan and Darfur: among them the Rizeigat, Hemedti's tribe, and the Misseriya. It was from these herders that the government recruited the Janjaweed militias in the 2000s. Fur — the largest people of Darfur, which bears their name: "Dar Fur" means "land of the Fur". No reliable estimate. They are settled farmers around the Jebel Marra massif, Muslim but not Arabised, and until 1916 they had an independent sultanate ( Library of Congress ). In 2008 about 7.5 million people lived in the five states of Darfur (2008 census), and according to the EU asylum agency non-Arab groups make up between two thirds and three quarters of the region's population ( EUAA ). Zaghawa — no reliable estimate. Semi-nomadic herders of northern Darfur, they live on both sides of the border with Chad, where many hold important positions in the army ( Library of Congress ; Al Jazeera ). The leaders of two of the main armed movements of Darfur, today allies of the army, are Zaghawa (see "Who's who"). Masalit — about 350,000 speakers according to Ethnologue (2011), cited by Canada's refugee board ( IRB Canada ). Farmers of western Darfur, around El Geneina. In 2023 they were among the first targets of the RSF: according to a UN panel of experts, between 10,000 and 15,000 people were killed in El Geneina ( Justice Info ). Beja — about 2-3 million (estimate, Minority Rights Group ). They live in the east, between the Red Sea hills, Port Sudan and Kassala, and lived there before the Arabs arrived. They speak their own language, Bedawiye, and are Sufi Muslims. They are among the poorest people in the country (same source), even though Port Sudan, the main outlet to the sea, lies on their land. Nuba — about 3.7 million (estimate, Minority Rights Group , 2018); in 1956 they were 6% (1956 census). They are not a single people but more than fifty different communities living in the Nuba Mountains, in South Kordofan, and speaking different languages. They are Muslim, Christian or follow traditional religions. In 1992 the governor of Kordofan declared jihad against them (same source). Their armed movement, the SPLM-N, controls part of the mountains. Nubians — in 1956 they were 3% (1956 census). They live along the Nile in the far north and in southern Egypt, and descend from the ancient Nubian civilisations. In the 1960s Egypt's Aswan Dam flooded their land: between 35,000 and 50,000 were moved to Khashm al-Qirbah, in the east ( Library of Congress ). Peoples of West African origin (called "Fallata" in Sudan) — in 1990 they numbered almost a million, about 6.5% of the population, nearly 60% of them of Nigerian origin (same source). They are mostly Hausa and Fulani, who arrived at different times. Peoples of Blue Nile — no reliable estimate. In 2008, 832,112 people lived in Blue Nile state, on the border with Ethiopia and South Sudan (2008 census). It is a region of many small peoples, some of them Christian or following traditional religions, where the SPLM-N has been fighting since 2011. Religion : according to the government, about 91% of the population is Muslim, almost all Sunni and with a strong Sufi tradition; Christians live mainly in the cities, in the Nuba Mountains and in Blue Nile; less than 1% follow traditional religions ( US State Department, 2019 ). Resources : gold, oil, fertile land and Nile water, livestock, the Red Sea coast. Sudan is Africa's third-largest gold producer ( Al Jazeera ). With the independence of the South in 2011 it lost about three quarters of its oil output ( The New Humanitarian ), and gold became its main export: in 2024 it accounted for almost half of recorded exports ( Steptoe ). A short history Before colonisation. Along the Nile arose one of the oldest kingdoms in Africa, Kush. In the 8th century BC its kings conquered Egypt and ruled it for almost a century, as the 25th dynasty of pharaohs. In the 6th century AD the three kingdoms of Nubia became Christian, and remained so for almost a thousand years. In 1504 the Muslim Funj sultanate was founded on the Blue Nile, with Sennar as its capital ( Embassy of Sudan in the Netherlands ); in the 17th century, in the west, the Fur founded the sultanate of Darfur ( Macquarie University ). The Turco-Egyptian conquest (1821-1885). In 1821 the army of Muhammad Ali, the pasha of Ottoman Egypt, invaded the country. The stated aim was to seize "the gold and slaves" needed to build the Egyptian state ( Fanack ). Heavy taxes and repression provoked continual revolts (same source). In 1874 Darfur too was annexed (Macquarie, cited above). The Mahdi (1881-1898). In 1881 a preacher, Muhammad Ahmad, proclaimed himself the Mahdi, the redeemer awaited in Islam, and led the revolt against Turco-Egyptian rule. In 1885 his forces took Khartoum and killed the British general Gordon. His state lasted thirteen years: on 2 September 1898, at Omdurman, Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army destroyed it ( National Army Museum ). The Anglo-Egyptian condominium (1899-1955). Formally Sudan was governed jointly by Britain and Egypt; in practice the British were in charge ( Fanack ). Darfur became independent again under Sultan Ali Dinar and was conquered only in 1916 (Macquarie, cited above). Three colonial choices still weigh today: A developed centre, neglected peripheries. The British invested along the Nile: Port Sudan in 1906, the great Gezira cotton scheme from 1911, the Sennar dam in 1925 (Fanack, cited above). Darfur, Kordofan, the east and the South were left almost without schools and roads. Two Sudans. From 1922 the "Closed District Ordinances" barred northern Sudanese from entering and trading in the South (Fanack, cited above); from 1930 the "Southern Policy" prepared the South for a separate future, with Christian missionaries in place of the Arab administration ( Library of Congress ). Power to those on the river. With independence, power stayed with the Arab and Muslim groups around Khartoum, whom the political system has always favoured at the expense of Darfur, South Kordofan and Blue Nile ( Freedom House ). Independence and the wars with the South (1955-2005). In August 1955, five months before independence, southern soldiers mutinied: the first civil war began. Independence came on 1 January 1956. Two years later, in 1958, General Abboud seized power; in 1964 a popular uprising drove him out; in 1969 Colonel Nimeiri staged a new coup. In 1972 the Addis Ababa agreement gave the South autonomy and ended the first war. In 1983 Nimeiri scrapped it and imposed sharia on the whole country, with the "September laws": the second civil war began, led in the South by John Garang and his SPLA ( Refworld ). It would last until 2005 and kill about two million people ( CFR ). Bashir (1989-2019). On 30 June 1989 General Omar al-Bashir seized power with the backing of Hassan al-Turabi's Islamists (Refworld, cited above). In the 1990s Sudan was put on the American list of state sponsors of terrorism, where it would stay for 27 years ( Africanews ). In 2000 a group of Darfuri intellectuals secretly circulated the "Black Book", which argued that the Nile elites held 95% of the country's power and wealth ( Al Jazeera ). In 2003 Darfur's armed movements, the SLA and JEM, rebelled. The government responded by arming the Janjaweed militias, recruited among Arab herders: burned villages, rapes, mass expulsions of Fur, Zaghawa and Masalit. The United States confirmed the destruction of 2,964 villages between 2003 and 2009 ( IRB Canada ). About 300,000 people died ( CFR ). In 2005 the Security Council referred Darfur to the International Criminal Court, which in 2009 sought Bashir's arrest and in 2010 added the charge of genocide against the Fur, Masalit and Zaghawa ( ICC ). Also in 2005, the peace agreement with the South provided for a referendum: in 2011 the South voted and became independent. In 2013 Bashir turned the Janjaweed into an official force, the Rapid Support Forces, under Hemedti's command and reporting directly to him (CFR, cited above; BBC, via allAfrica ). The revolution and the transition (2018-2021). In December 2018 protests broke out across the country. On 11 April 2019 the army and the RSF, together, deposed Bashir ( HRW ). On 3 June forces led by the RSF broke up the sit-in outside army headquarters in Khartoum: according to the doctors' union, 124 people were killed between 3 and 18 June (same source). In August soldiers and civilians signed a power-sharing agreement; the prime minister was the economist Abdalla Hamdok, Burhan chaired the Sovereignty Council and Hemedti was his deputy. In December 2020 the United States removed Sudan from the list of state sponsors of terrorism, after the country agreed to pay 335 million dollars to the victims of the 1998 attacks and to normalise relations with Israel ( Africanews ). The coup and the war (since 2021). On 25 October 2021 Burhan and Hemedti, together, overthrew the civilian government. In December 2022 a framework agreement provided for a return to civilian rule, but set no date for integrating the RSF into the army. The two generals split over this point: on 15 April 2023 fighting broke out in Khartoum ( CFR ). The government fled to Port Sudan. The RSF occupied much of the capital and, in western Darfur, El Geneina. In March 2025 the army retook Khartoum; on 26 October 2025, after an eighteen-month siege, the RSF took El Fasher, the last big city in Darfur still held by the army. According to the UN, more than 6,000 people were killed in those days ( People Daily, citing the ICC and the UN ). Two governments (2025-2026). In July 2025 the RSF and its allies announced a parallel government, de facto based in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur ( Sudan War Monitor ). On 11 January 2026 the army's government returned to Khartoum after almost three years in Port Sudan ( Al Jazeera ). In 2026 the army advanced in Kordofan: in February it broke the siege of Kadugli ( Anadolu ), in October it took al-Mazroub and moved on En Nahud ( Al Jazeera ). The RSF holds almost all of Darfur and strikes the army's cities with drones, as far as Blue Nile. Who governs, and how Today Sudan has two governments, and neither was elected. There have been no elections since Bashir's fall, and there is no parliament ( Freedom House ). The army's government , based in Khartoum, is the one that holds Sudan's seat at the UN ( The National ). At the top is the Sovereignty Council chaired by Burhan; since May 2025 the prime minister has been the jurist Kamil Idris (same source). The RSF government , called the government "of peace and unity", grew out of the Tasis ("foundation") alliance and is led by a fifteen-member presidential council chaired by Hemedti; the prime minister is Mohamed Hassan al-Ta'aishi ( Sudan War Monitor ). Two independent institutes, in two different countries, reach the same conclusion: Freedom House (United States), 2026 report: 1 point out of 100, "not free". It lost a point compared with the previous year because of ethnically based killings and expulsions ( Freedom House ). V-Dem (Sweden), 2026 report: "closed autocracy", the category of regimes in which people do not vote for who governs them ( V-Dem ). What distinguishes an autocracy from a democracy is explained in our entry Autocracy . On 22 September 2026 the US State Department declared that neither the army nor the RSF, nor their leaders, represent legitimate governance: both rule "through force of arms alone" ( The National ). The Khartoum government rejected the statement. Who's who Who Who leads it Position Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Sovereignty Council, Khartoum Gen. Sanctioned by the US in January 2025, when Washington determined that the RSF had committed genocide ( CBC ) SPLM-N (Sudan People's Liberation Movement–North), Nuba Mountains Abdelaziz al-Hilu Has fought for the Nuba since 2011. Since 2025 it has been allied with the RSF and al-Hilu is vice-president of the Tasis government ( Sudan War Monitor ) Darfur Joint Forces Minni Minnawi (SLA) and Jibril Ibrahim (JEM), both Zaghawa The former rebels of 2003, today allied with the army against the RSF ( Asharq Al-Awsat ).
