On 9 March 2026 the US designated them a terrorist organisation ( CSW ) SLM-AW (Sudan Liberation Movement), Jebel Marra Abdel Wahid al-Nur Controls much of the Jebel Marra massif and shelters hundreds of thousands of displaced people in Tawila. Fights with neither side. In September 2026 its administration declared famine ( Sudan Tribune ) Sumud (Civil Democratic Alliance of Revolutionary Forces) Abdalla Hamdok, former prime minister The civilian coalition born in 2025 out of the 2019 revolution. Refuses to side with either party ( Sudans Post ) Where the conflict comes from We use the four levels of our piece Are the world's wars "Muslim"? . Here almost all the fighters are Sunni Muslims: religion does not divide the sides. The ground: a centre and its peripheries. Sudan was born of a conquest, the Turco-Egyptian one of 1821, and its borders are those set by Cairo and London. For two centuries the centre on the Nile took slaves, soldiers, gold and livestock from the peripheries, and gave little back. The British reinforced the imbalance, investing along the river and isolating the South. After independence the Arab elites of the Nile kept that model: this is the charge of the 2000 "Black Book". The wars of the South, Darfur, the Nuba Mountains and Blue Nile all start here. This does not absolve the governments that followed. Colonialism left the imbalance; arming one part of the population against another was a choice made in Khartoum, by Nimeiri, by Bashir and by the generals who succeeded him. The spark: two armies for one state. Bashir had created the RSF as a personal army, separate from the regular army and loyal to him. After his fall the two armies found themselves sharing the country's power and wealth. The December 2022 agreement asked for them to be merged, but without a date; neither general wanted to give up command. On 15 April 2023 the dispute became a war. The banner: Arabs and non-Arabs. Neither side fights in the name of ethnicity. But in Darfur the war has followed the lines of the 2003 one. The RSF and allied militias have systematically attacked the Masalit, Fur and Zaghawa: for the UN fact-finding mission, in El Fasher this violence "was not random excesses of war" but a planned operation ( UN Geneva ). On the other side, the army has enlisted militias on tribal and Islamist lines, and civilians from Arab tribes are accused of siding with the RSF. Behind ethnicity there is also land: the herders' pastures and the farmers' fields, which drought has made ever scarcer ( HRW ). The external multiplier: weapons, gold and ports. A war of this length cannot be fought without supplies. The next section documents who supplies the two sides, who buys the gold and who wants a port on the Red Sea. Who profits We document declared or verifiable interests, not motives. When an actor denies something, we say so. The two generals and gold. Even before commanding the RSF, Hemedti took control of Jebel Amer, Darfur's largest artisanal gold mine. His family's company, al-Junaid, became the country's largest gold exporter ( BBC, via allAfrica ); the United States sanctioned it in June 2023 ( Steptoe ). In 2015 Hemedti also sold his men to Saudi Arabia and the Emirates to fight in Yemen (BBC, cited above). But gold also funds the army: in 2024 the Port Sudan government officially exported gold worth 1.97 billion dollars, almost half of all recorded exports, and according to the state mining company 80% of the gold leaves the country as contraband (Steptoe, cited above). In July 2026 the European Union banned the purchase of Sudanese gold, accusing both sides of financing the war this way; the United Kingdom sanctioned an RSF financier and three state mining companies (same source). The United Arab Emirates. According to the UN fact-finding mission there are "reasonable grounds" to believe that a network with bases in the Emirates, Chad, Libya and Puntland supplied the RSF with weapons, drones, fuel and mercenaries. The Emirates deny any involvement (we wrote about it in "Sudan, war by remote" ). Their documented interests: gold : in 2024 the Emirates imported 29 tonnes of gold directly from Sudan, up from 17 in 2023, according to UN data compiled by the NGO Swissaid ( Swissaid ). The Emirates buy the gold exported by the army's government, and the United States, the United Kingdom and the EU have sanctioned traders based in the Emirates for buying gold from RSF mines ( Steptoe ). The Emirati authorities said those companies were operating without an active licence (same source); the Red Sea : in 2022 two Emirati companies signed a 6-billion-dollar project for a port and an agricultural zone at Abu Amama, north of Port Sudan. In November 2024 the army's government cancelled it, accusing the Emirates of backing the RSF ( The New Arab ). Egypt is the army's main regional backer: aircraft, ammunition and intelligence ( CFR ). It wants a friendly government to its south, on the Nile on which its water depends, while its dispute with Ethiopia over the great GERD dam remains open. According to press investigations, including one by the New York Times, Egypt has moved from support to direct intervention, with drones launched from a base in the Egyptian desert; Cairo denies it and says it has only trainers in Sudan ( Horn Review ). Saudi Arabia declares itself neutral and hosted the 2023 Jeddah talks, but backs the army's legitimacy ( CFR ). According to the African business press, a 1.5-billion-dollar contract for Pakistani weapons for the army, paid for by Riyadh, was linked to a deal on Sudanese gold with the Saudi refinery; Reuters reported that it was cancelled in April 2026 after protests from Western governments ( Steptoe ). Turkey and Iran. Iran has supplied the army with Mohajer-6 drones ( CFR ). The UN mission recognised, in footage of army attacks, drones consistent with Turkish models, but did not attribute their supply to any state (we reported it in "Sudan, war by remote" ). Russia has switched horses. From 2017 the company Meroe Gold, which according to the US Treasury was a front for the Wagner group, mined gold in Sudan; Wagner later forged ties with Hemedti ( Al Jazeera ). Today Moscow backs the army ( CFR ), and the interest is a port: a 2020 agreement provides for a Russian naval base in Port Sudan for 25 years, with up to four ships and 300 personnel. It has never been ratified, and in November 2025 the Russian ambassador said it was "halted" because of the war ( Kyiv Post ); according to the Wall Street Journal, in December the army offered it again in exchange for weapons ( The New Arab ). In November 2024 Russia vetoed a Security Council resolution calling for a ceasefire ( Al Jazeera ). The neighbours. Chad and the eastern Libya of General Haftar are named by the UN mission as hubs for supplies to the RSF; satellite imagery and press investigations link Ethiopian military facilities to the supply and training of the RSF ( CFR ). Kenya hosted in Nairobi, in February 2025, the signing of the parallel government's charter (same source). The United States and Europe. They have sanctioned the leaders of both sides and their companies. The United States determined in January 2025 that the RSF had committed genocide, and in May 2025 that the army had used chemical weapons in 2024, a charge the government rejects ( Justice Info ). But the Emirates, Egypt and Saudi Arabia, the main external backers of the two sides, are also strategic partners of Washington and of European countries, Italy included. And Europe's attention remains far smaller than for other wars, as we documented in "Why Ukraine and not Sudan" . The Islamists. Pushed out of power by the 2019 revolution, they are back on the front line fighting alongside the army ( Asharq Al-Awsat ). For civilian groups their presence is one of the reasons the army refuses to negotiate; the army replies that the militias are under its command. Who intervenes from outside The "Quad" (United States, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, the Emirates). On 12 September 2025 it approved a roadmap: a three-month humanitarian truce, then a permanent ceasefire and a transition to civilian government ( Sudan Tribune ). As of 22 October 2026 the truce has never taken effect. According to Reuters, the United States denied Burhan a visa for the UN General Assembly after he rejected a 90-day truce ( Sudan Tribune ). The UN. Since 2004 the Security Council has banned the supply of weapons to Darfur (resolutions 1556 and 1591). On 12 September 2026 it renewed the embargo but kept it limited to Darfur, while the United States and the UN mission were asking for it to be extended to the whole country ( allAfrica ). The Secretary-General's personal envoy is the former Finnish foreign minister Pekka Haavisto, appointed in February 2026 ( UN ). On 5 October 2026 the Human Rights Council renewed the fact-finding mission for one year; the Sudanese government rejects it and refuses visas to its members (allAfrica, cited above). The host countries. Of the 4.3 million Sudanese refugees in the region, about 1.4 million are in Egypt; the others mainly in Chad and South Sudan ( UN Geneva, citing UNHCR ). The human cost. No one knows how many have died. ACLED, an organisation that counts only documented killings in the fighting, has recorded at least 59,000 ( AP, via AJC ). Studies that also estimate unrecorded deaths give much higher numbers: for the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, in Khartoum state alone more than 61,000 people died of all causes in the first fourteen months of the war ( LSHTM ); for the Norwegian institute PRIO, deaths in 2025 may have reached 100,000 ( PRIO ). Internally displaced people number 8.8 million ( UNHCR, on IOM data, May 2026 ), refugees abroad 4.3 million. In May, 19.5 million people, more than four in ten, were in acute food insecurity; on 19 October the IPC, the international system that measures hunger, warned that areas at risk of famine are growing in Darfur and Kordofan, also because of drought linked to El Niño ( AP, via AJC ). International law The treaties. According to the humanitarian law database ( Guide du droit humanitaire ), Sudan: has been a party to the Genocide Convention since 2003; has been a party to the Geneva Conventions since 1957 and to both Additional Protocols since 2006: the second protects civilians in internal wars like this one; has been a party to the Chemical Weapons Convention since 1999 and to the Convention against Torture since 2021; signed the Rome Statute in 2000 but has not ratified it. The RSF is an armed group, not a state, but it is bound by humanitarian law just like the army. **The International Criminal Court .** Sudan is not a member, but in 2005 the Security Council referred to it the crimes committed in Darfur (resolution 1593). That is why the Court can judge Darfur but not Khartoum, Kordofan or Blue Nile. The arrest warrants for Bashir, issued in 2009 and 2010, have never been executed. On 6 October 2025 came the first conviction for Darfur, that of the former Janjaweed leader Ali Kushayb, and on 9 December the sentence: 20 years ( ICC ). On today's war, the prosecutor's office is investigating the massacres of El Geneina and El Fasher and says it has "concrete evidence" against the RSF leaders, but has not yet announced charges ( People Daily ). The Sudanese suspects are on our page ICC Fugitives . Genocide. On 19 February 2026 the UN fact-finding mission concluded that in El Fasher the RSF committed at least three of the acts listed in the Genocide Convention against the Zaghawa and Fur: killings, serious bodily and mental harm, and conditions of life imposed to destroy the group ( UN Geneva ). It is a finding by a commission of inquiry, not a judgment; the same applies to the American determination of January 2025. The RSF denies large-scale killings. We wrote about it in our manifesto for Sudan . **The case at the International Court of Justice .** In March 2025 Sudan accused the Emirates of complicity in the RSF's genocide ( CFR ). On 5 May 2025 the Court dismissed the case without examining the merits: when they joined the Convention, the Emirates excluded the Court's jurisdiction over disputes concerning them (a reservation to Article IX) ( The East African ). The decision says nothing about whether the accusations are well founded. The responsibilities of others. International law does not concern only the two generals: common Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions obliges all states to ensure respect for humanitarian law, and a state that knowingly helps another to violate it is responsible too. We explained this in "Sudan, war by remote" ; the UN embargo on Darfur binds all member states; whoever supplies weapons to the RSF in Darfur violates it; the Genocide Convention obliges states to prevent it, not only to punish it. In 2007, in the Bosnia v. Serbia judgment, the International Court of Justice held that every state must use "all means reasonably available", all the more so the greater its capacity to influence those committing it ( Opinio Juris ). Cameroon, one year after the vote: protesters before a military court, those who fired before no one

On 12 October 2025 Paul Biya, in power since 1982, was re-elected for the eighth time. A year later, dozens of protesters have been convicted by a military court, while no trial is on record for the deaths during the protests. In the Anglophone regions the war goes on, and almost no one talks about it.

In brief On 8 October 2026 the military court in Yaoundé convicted 66 people arrested during the protests after the vote. The charges: false news, rebellion, unlawful assembly. About a hundred other detainees are awaiting trial. No trial is on record for the deaths during the protests. The government speaks of 16 dead, Human Rights Watch of 48 to 55; a coalition of Cameroonian associations puts the figure at 706, with a method it has not made public. Opposition leader Anicet Ekane died in detention on 1 December 2025. The inquiry announced by the government, according to his family, has stalled. The complaint filed in Paris in June against Biya and some twenty officials still has no public response from the prosecutor. Fighting has gone on in the Anglophone regions since 2016. In 2026 separatists killed Mbororo civilians in Gidado and imposed a new lockdown to stop schools from reopening. The UN Security Council has held only one informal meeting on Cameroon, in 2019. The background In July we reported on the complaint filed in Paris by opposition leader Issa Tchiroma Bakary against President Paul Biya ( Cameroon: election crackdown lands in a Paris court ). A year has passed since the vote, and this piece looks at what happened next: who has been tried, who has not, and the war that continues in the Anglophone regions. On 12 October 2025 Cameroon voted for president. On 27 October the Constitutional Council declared Paul Biya, aged 92, the winner with 53.66%, against 35.19% for Tchiroma; fewer than one voter in two turned out ( Hespress ). Tchiroma declared himself the winner and left the country. The protests that followed were put down. The facts The protests and the dead. On 30 October 2025 the UN Human Rights Office said it was alarmed by reports of people killed during the protests. It urged the security forces not to use lethal force and called for prompt and impartial inquiries into all election-related violence ( OHCHR, via GlobalSecurity ). According to Human Rights Watch, the security forces used tear gas and live ammunition; the dead were between 48 and 55, and lawyers estimated up to 2,000 arrests. HRW also notes that some protests turned violent, with roadblocks and buildings ransacked ( JURIST ). Figures that do not match. The government speaks of 16 dead and more than 800 arrests. A coalition of some thirty Cameroonian associations led by the NGO Un Monde Avenir presented a toll of 706 dead, 40 summary executions and 1,494 arbitrary arrests to the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights in May 2026. The method has not been made public, and the NGO itself admits it could not access hospitals ( Camer.be, via allAfrica ). The gap between 16 and 706 is huge, and it is exactly what an independent inquiry should clear up. Who has been tried. On 8 October 2026 the military court in Yaoundé tried 66 people arrested after the vote and convicted all of them of spreading false news, rebellion, unlawful assembly and failing to carry an identity card. Sentences range from six months suspended to fifteen months in prison; the last should be released in February. About a hundred other detainees represented by the same defence team are awaiting trial ( RFI, via allAfrica ). Who has not been tried. No trial is on record for the deaths during the protests. Anicet Ekane, 74, leader of the opposition party Manidem, died on 1 December 2025 at the gendarmerie's medical centre in Yaoundé, where he had been held since 24 October without being brought before a judge. His family says the oxygen concentrator he needed had been taken from him. The Defence Ministry says he suffered from chronic illnesses and was properly cared for. The government announced an inquiry; the family asked for an independent commission and, as of January, had received no answer ( Camer.be ). The Paris complaint. The two complaints Tchiroma filed in June with the Paris court, under universal jurisdiction, have received no public response. In August a diaspora association sent the prosecutor a memorandum urging that they be examined; there is no record of an investigation being opened ( Camer.be, via allAfrica ). The war in the Anglophone regions. Since 2016, in the North-West and South-West, the army has been fighting armed groups that want independence for the two English-speaking regions, which they call Ambazonia. More than 6,500 people have been killed, at least 334,000 are internally displaced and more than 76,000 have fled to Nigeria ( Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect ). On 14 January 2026, in Gidado, in Donga-Mantung division, fighters identified by the authorities as separatists killed 14 civilians from the Mbororo herding community, almost all women and children, according to the regional governor ( Journal du Cameroun ). From 7 September 2026 separatists imposed a week-long lockdown to stop the school year from starting, threatening to kill anyone who left their home ( IANS/Xinhua, via NewKerala ). Attention. In June 2026 the Norwegian Refugee Council again listed Cameroon among the ten most neglected displacement crises in the world; the year before it was ranked first ( Euronews ). Since 2019 the UN Security Council has devoted only one meeting to Cameroon, an informal one on the humanitarian situation. Legal commentary Civilians before military judges. Cameroon is a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which guarantees a fair trial before an independent and impartial tribunal (art. 14). The UN Committee that monitors the Covenant has written that trials of civilians before military courts must be the exception, allowed only when the state shows that ordinary courts cannot handle them. The UN Special Rapporteur on the independence of judges has gone further: as a rule, military jurisdiction over civilians is incompatible with fair and independent justice ( UN, A/HRC/14/26/Add.1 ). A protester accused of spreading false news or of not carrying an identity card has nothing military about him. Why a military court. In Cameroon the law opens the way. The 2017 Code of Military Justice (Law No. 2017/012) states in Article 8 that the military court is "solely competent" for terrorism offences and those "relating to the security of the State", and for "all related offences" ( Law No. 2017/012, UNODC ). The last phrase is the key: a charge of false news or unlawful assembly, if linked to a charge against state security, ends up before military judges. Article 4 also allows the military court in Yaoundé to try cases across the whole country in the event of a "serious threat to public order". After the vote, lawyers told Human Rights Watch that those arrested were also charged with "hostility against the homeland", "insurrection" and "rebellion", offences that in some cases carry the death penalty ( HRW, 12/11/2025 ). In January 142 defendants were tried in summary proceedings before the same court; the October convictions came on much lighter charges. It is not the first time: in 2020, 36 opposition protesters were sentenced by a military court to five to seven years ( Amnesty International, 2025 ), and the American Bar Association notes that the 2014 anti-terrorism law is used to bring human rights defenders and journalists before military judges ( ABA, 2024 ). The duty to investigate. When state agents kill during a protest, or a person dies in state custody, the state is obliged to open a prompt, independent and effective inquiry: this follows from the right to life (art. 6 of the Covenant). In Ekane's case the obligation is stricter, because he was held without a judge and the state was responsible for his health. An inquiry entrusted to the same gendarmerie that held him is not independent. The war. The conflict in the Anglophone regions is a non-international armed conflict: for both sides, Article 3 common to the Geneva Conventions applies, prohibiting the killing of civilians, hostage-taking and attacks on those not taking part in the fighting. The Gidado massacre and the threats against anyone leaving home during the lockdown fall under these prohibitions, as does the destruction of villages attributed to the army in past years. Symmetry test The government tried protesters before a military court and has tried no one for the deaths during the protests or for Ekane's death. Some protesters used violence, with roadblocks and looting: it is right that they answer for it, but before an ordinary judge and on proportionate charges. The opposition's figures must be treated with the same caution as the government's. The toll of 706 dead is far higher than HRW's, and the method is not public. The separatists kill civilians, abduct people and close schools at gunpoint. The Anglophone cause has real roots, but it does not justify the children killed in Gidado or those left without school. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. One year after the vote, justice in Cameroon has worked in one direction only. The protesters were tried by military judges on charges such as false news and unlawful assembly. Those who fired on them have, as far as the record shows, been tried by no one. And the death in custody of a 74-year-old opposition leader has been left to an inquiry by those who held him. Cameroon does not make the news because it never seems to change: the same president for forty-four years, the same war for ten, the same lockdowns every September. But stillness is not neutral. Where there are no trials, the figures stay far apart, from 16 to 706, everyone believes their own and no one can disprove anyone. And where the Security Council does not meet, a war that has killed thousands goes on not existing for the rest of the world. What to watch The other trials before the military court and the appeals of the 66 convicted. The outcome of the inquiry into Anicet Ekane's death. A decision by the Paris prosecutor on Tchiroma's complaints. The reopening of schools in the Anglophone regions and new attacks on civilians. The Rohingya verdict that has not come: what the Court must decide, and what is left for those who wait

Eight months after the last hearings, the International Court of Justice has not yet set a date for its judgment on the Rohingya genocide. Meanwhile, the camps in Bangladesh receive less food, and those who stayed in Rakhine live between the army and the militia that has taken over the region.

— The Hague / Cox's Bazar In brief The case The Gambia v. Myanmar is in its final phase: the hearings on the merits closed on 29 January 2026. The Court has not yet announced the date of the judgment; The Gambia expects it in October. Myanmar does not deny that people were killed. It denies that the army meant to destroy the Rohingya as a group. That question, intent, is what the Court must decide. If the Court finds genocide, it can order more than a condemnation: reparations, guarantees, conditions for a safe return. But it has no means of enforcing them. About 1.2 million Rohingya live in the camps in Bangladesh. Since April, two thirds of them have received less food aid. In Rakhine, the Rohingya who remain also suffer abuses by the Arakan Army, the armed group that now controls almost the entire region. The background In June we reported on the hearings and on the state of the country after the coup ( The International Court of Justice deliberates on the Rohingya genocide ). This piece explains what the Court must decide, what may happen next, and what the Rohingya are living through today. In short: in August 2017 Myanmar's army launched what it called "clearance operations" in Rakhine State, in response to attacks on police posts by a Rohingya armed group, ARSA. Within a few months more than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. In 2019 The Gambia, a distant state but, like Myanmar, a party to the Genocide Convention, brought the case before the International Court of Justice ( what the Court is ). The facts The stages of the case. In January 2020 the Court unanimously ordered Myanmar to take provisional measures to protect the Rohingya. In July 2022 it rejected Myanmar's objections and ruled that it has jurisdiction. Eleven states have intervened to explain how the Convention should be read: Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, the Maldives, Slovenia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Belgium and Ireland. The hearings on the merits were held from 12 to 29 January 2026, with witnesses heard behind closed doors ( ICJ, press releases ). The two cases. The Gambia argues that the violence of 2017 was the peak of a persecution that began at least in the late 1980s, made of restrictions on marriage and movement and of a hate campaign to dehumanise the Rohingya. Myanmar, represented in court by Ko Ko Hlaing, called the report of the UN Fact-Finding Mission a "condemnation without trial". It argues that these were counter-terrorism operations against ARSA, and it does not deny the killings: it denies the intent to destroy the group ( Impunity Watch ). When the judgment comes. No one knows. On the Court's case page the latest press release is the one from late January. The indication "October" comes from The Gambia's Minister of Justice, Dawda Jallow, who gave it in late August to a Bangladeshi minister ( TBS News ). In this case the Court has always announced its decisions one or two weeks in advance: eight days ahead for the 2020 provisional measures, eleven for the 2022 judgment. Seen from above. Some evidence of the 2017 destruction does not depend on witnesses. Using satellite imagery, Human Rights Watch counted 354 Rohingya villages wholly or partly burned after 25 August 2017. At least 118 were burned after 5 September, when the government said the operations were over ( HRW, 18/12/2017 ). The camps. About 1.2 million Rohingya live in the camps of Cox's Bazar, in Bangladesh. Since 2024 about 150,000 more have arrived, fleeing the new fighting in Rakhine ( UNHCR, via Ittefaq ). Since 1 April 2026 the World Food Programme has divided aid into tiers. A third of the people, the poorest, keep 12 dollars a month each; the others receive less, and some go down to 7. For the WFP this is not a cut, because the minimum calorie intake is still guaranteed; for Bangladesh's refugee commissioner it is, and he fears unrest. This year the programmes for the Rohingya are 19% funded ( AP, via NPR ). Rakhine today. The army has lost almost the whole region. The Arakan Army, the armed group of the ethnic Rakhine, controls 14 of the 17 townships and the entire border with Bangladesh. According to Human Rights Watch, the Arakan Army too restricts the Rohingya's movement, confiscates land and houses, and forces them to work and to enlist. A young man abducted in 2024 says he was sent to the front line as a "human shield" ( HRW, 28/7/2025 ). In the same report HRW writes that in 2024 ARSA and other Rohingya armed groups fought alongside the army. The criminal courts. The International Court of Justice judges states, not individuals. For individuals there are two other routes, both stalled. In November 2024 the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court requested an arrest warrant for the army chief Min Aung Hlaing, but the judges have not yet decided. In April 2026 Min Aung Hlaing became president, elected by a parliament that came out of elections organised by the junta; the ICC recalled that the office gives him no immunity ( DVB ). In February 2025 an Argentine court, under universal jurisdiction, issued 25 arrest warrants, one of them for him ( JURIST ). Legal commentary What the Court must decide. That the Rohingya were killed, driven out and stripped of their homes is admitted even by Myanmar. The 1948 Convention, however, asks for more: that these acts were committed with the intent to destroy the group, in whole or in part. When intent is not written in an order, the Court infers it from conduct, but only if it is the only reasonable conclusion. This is the standard set in the judgments on Bosnia (2007) and Croatia (2015), and it is very high: under that standard the Court has recognised only one genocide, Srebrenica. In 2018 the UN Fact-Finding Mission concluded that there was sufficient information to infer intent. The Court may reach the same conclusion or stop short of it. The middle ground. Even without genocide, the Court can find against Myanmar. In the Bosnia case, Serbia was held responsible not for genocide, but for failing to prevent it and to punish those responsible. What it can order. The Gambia asks for a declaration of responsibility, guarantees of non-repetition, reparations and the conditions for a safe return of the Rohingya, including the right to citizenship ( JusticeInfo ). A declaration is the most likely outcome. On reparations there is a precedent: in 2022 the Court ordered Uganda to pay 325 million dollars to the Congo ( UN News ). Citizenship is the hardest point, because judges hesitate to tell a state who must be its citizen. Myanmar also argues that The Gambia, not having suffered direct harm, can obtain only a declaration. The limit. The Court's judgments are binding, but the Court has no force of its own to enforce them. If a state does not comply, the other party can turn to the Security Council, where China and Russia, two of the countries that supply weapons to the junta, hold a veto. Symmetry test Myanmar's army is the accused in the case, and the events of 2017 are documented by witnesses, satellite imagery and the UN Mission. ARSA attacked first in August 2017. In 2024 it allied itself with the army that had persecuted the Rohingya, and today it fights the Arakan Army. Human Rights Watch accuses it, like the Arakan Army, of profiting from the refugees' flight through smuggling networks. The Arakan Army , an enemy of the junta and often described as a force liberating Rakhine, is accused of abuses against the Rohingya. The international community backed the case in The Hague with eleven states, but has not secured the funding for the camps: this year the programmes for the Rohingya are covered for less than a fifth. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. When the judgment comes, it will be news for a day. It deserves to be: it is the first genocide case brought by a state not directly affected to reach a judgment on the merits, and the decision on intent will weigh on the cases concerning Gaza and Ukraine as well. But after that day, little will change for a Rohingya in Cox's Bazar. There will be no less hunger in the camps, he will not get his land back in Rakhine, where a militia rules that no court in The Hague can try as a state, and the accused general will, in all likelihood, remain president. International law has done its part: a small African country brought the case, eleven states supported it, the Court listened. What is missing is what the law cannot do on its own: funding for the camps, real pressure on those who arm the junta, protection for the Rohingya from the militia that has taken their land as well. Without these things, a judgment risks remaining a page of history. What to watch The announcement of the judgment date on the Court's website. The decision of the ICC judges on the warrant for Min Aung Hlaing. Funding for the Rohingya humanitarian plan and the WFP rations. Fighting between the Arakan Army and Rohingya armed groups in northern Rakhine. Immigration: the doors Europe closes and the ones it opens

At the October summit European governments split over Spain's regularisation. Behind the clash are choices that contradict each other: closing irregular routes, returning people to centres abroad, and meanwhile looking for foreign workers. We explain them one by one.

In brief At the summit on 16 October Denmark, Italy and Poland accused Spain of attracting migrants by regularising people already in the country. They did not get the wording they wanted. Irregular arrivals are falling sharply, but more people are dying: on the route to Italy, in proportion to arrivals, deaths have almost tripled. Europe is betting on returns, including to centres outside its borders on the Italian model in Albania. So far that model has cost a great deal and returned very few people. In Italy fear has grown faster than crime. Foreigners are over-represented among those reported for crimes, but the decisive factor is lacking papers: those who get them commit far fewer crimes. Our assessment: immigration is used as a political lever and the fear is real. But laws that produce undocumented people feed the very problem they claim to fight. The question At the European Council of 15 and 16 October immigration divided governments more than any other issue. The target was Spain, which is granting a residence permit to about 600,000 people already living in the country without papers. Denmark, Italy and Poland asked for the conclusions to say that "pull factors" must be reduced. It is a phrase that comes up often: it means anything that, according to those who use it, draws people to a particular country, such as the hope of being regularised. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen put it like this: "You arrive in a country illegally, and suddenly you can obtain permission to stay there legally" ( EU Perspectives, 16/10/2026 ). Madrid replies that regularising people who already work off the books brings work and contributions into the open, and moves no one to other countries. French President Emmanuel Macron closed the discussion like this: when everyone goes back to national solutions, "we are ineffective" ( Euronews, 16/10/2026 ). The request did not pass. Regularisation remains a choice for each government. The conclusions only ask the Commission to prepare rules for emergencies, including cases where a hostile state pushes migrants towards Europe's borders to put them under pressure, as in Ceuta at the end of July ( European Council, 16/10/2026 ; on Ceuta, our piece ). The issue returns in December. Fewer arrivals, more deaths Irregular arrivals in the EU fell by more than a third in the first seven months of 2026; on the Central Mediterranean route, the one to Italy, they more than halved ( Frontex, August 2026 ). Deaths, however, are not falling. On the same route the dead and missing rose from 844 to 996 compared with last year ( UNRIC, on IOM data, 17/9/2026 ). In proportion to arrivals, by our calculation, that is almost three times as many. Fewer people arrive, but for those who set out the journey has become far more dangerous. And according to the IOM, the UN migration agency, "nearly every death and disappearance at sea is preventable". The EU's choices Common rules, little solidarity. Since 12 June the Pact on Migration and Asylum has been in force ( our piece ). For the first time all 27 follow the same rules to examine asylum applications. The Pact also provided for solidarity: the less exposed countries were to take in some of the applicants arriving in Italy, Greece or Spain, or pay. For 2026 states pledged less than half of the places foreseen; Hungary and Slovakia none ( Euronews, 10/6/2026 ). Those on the front line remain, in practice, alone. Returns, including abroad. The new return regulation, agreed in June, allows states to detain for up to two years people who must leave Europe and to send them to "return hubs" in countries outside the EU ( Council of the EU, 1/6/2026 ). The problem it wants to solve is real: today less than a third of those ordered to leave actually do so. Paying those who stop departures. The EU has given Tunisia more than €100 million to stop boats and control its borders. Humanitarian and human rights organisations report violent interceptions, torture and people abandoned in the desert at the border ( Human Rights Watch, 16/7/2026 ). Departures fall, but the human cost moves to where Europe does not look. And meanwhile it looks for workers. Europe is ageing and by 2050 most of its countries will have fewer people of working age ( EUobserver, on Eurostat data ). So the Italian government, one of the toughest on irregular arrivals, has planned almost 500,000 entries of foreign workers over three years, for the "indispensable labour" that companies cannot find ( Sky TG24, 30/6/2025 ). Spain has chosen to give papers to those already in the country ( Euro Weekly News, 17/10/2026 ). They are two different roads towards the same need. Fear and security in Italy In Italy immigration is discussed mainly as a security problem, and fear has grown fast: in four years security has risen from tenth to second place among Italians' concerns. But fear also depends on how people vote: irregular immigration worries more than four in ten centre-right voters and just over one in ten on the centre-left ( Open, on an Ipsos Doxa poll, 11/10/2026 ). The same reality, seen from two camps, produces different fears. The data say two things, and they must be held together. Reported crimes fell in 2025. And foreigners are more than a third of the people reported or arrested, while being less than a tenth of the population: the disproportion exists, especially for theft, robbery and drug dealing ( Open, on Interior Ministry data, 12/10/2026 ). What explains it? Not origin, but condition. In 2007 Italy allocated work permits through a "click day": those who sent the application first got one, those who arrived a few minutes later did not. Two groups of people identical in everything but luck. Economist Paolo Pinotti followed them: those who had obtained the permit had, a year later, committed less than half as many serious crimes as the others ( Cato Institute, summary of the study ). With papers you can work legally, rent a home, have something to lose if you go wrong. Without them, there is undeclared work and often the street. And undocumented people do not only come by sea: laws produce them too. In Italy seven asylum applications out of ten are rejected ( Il Fatto Quotidiano, on ISMU data, 26/2/2026 ). Those who are refused, but not returned because their country will not take them back, stay here without papers. The unease many see in some neighbourhoods of big cities also stems from this: people who can neither work legally nor be sent home. The Albania model The answer governments rely on most is return centres, including abroad. The model is Italian. The two centres built in Albania were meant to examine asylum applications quickly; judges blocked the detentions and since March 2025 one of the two has become a return centre ( Il Post, 11/6/2026 ). The results are far from the promises. The government expected about 3,000 people a month; about 500 have passed through in total, at a cost of more than €670 million ( Euronews, 26/8/2026 ). Returns, according to associations, number about ninety, and all took place after the people had been brought back to Italy; the Interior Ministry does not publish its figures. The reason is the same as for the centres in Italy: to return someone, their country must agree to take them back, and with many countries there are no agreements. The EU Court of Justice has yet to decide whether the model complies with EU law ( our piece ). But Europe has already decided to follow it. "Italy has shown the way and today Europe is following it," said Giorgia Meloni ( Avvenire, 11/6/2026 ). Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece want the first transfers to a country outside the EU in 2027; the press points to Uganda and Rwanda ( Euronews, 4/9/2026 ). The United Kingdom already tried with Rwanda: the plan was abandoned after four voluntary departures. The same yardstick The summit conclusions also recall the extension until 2028 of temporary protection for the 4.4 million Ukrainians living in the EU ( Euromaidan Press, on Eurostat data, 12/8/2026 ). It is a tool that had existed since 2001 and had never been used, not even for Syrians in 2015 ( Verfassungsblog, 10/3/2022 ). It works simply: those fleeing a given war immediately receive the right to live, work and study in the EU, without asylum applications one by one. Those fleeing Sudan, by contrast, find the desert, the sea and interceptions paid for by Europe ( our piece on Ukraine and Sudan ). What worked Temporary protection gave millions of Ukrainians a regular life within days. The Pact provided common rules where before each country went its own way. And legal channels, Italian and Spanish, recognise a fact the debate often hides: Europe's economy needs these people. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Immigration is used as a political lever. The fear is real and must be respected: people living in a run-down neighbourhood need answers, not lectures. But the data say that what produces insecurity is not origin, it is irregular status. Laws that multiply the number of undocumented people without managing to return them feed the very problem they promise to solve. The Albania model shows it: the crux of returns is not where a person is held, but whether their country agrees to take them back. A centre across the Adriatic costs more and does not return more people. That Europe wants to copy it even before the ruling shows how much the message counts for more than the result. Meanwhile arrivals fall, and the price is paid by those who die at sea, far from the cameras. And it is inconsistent to accuse those who give papers to people already working of "attracting migrants", while looking for half a million workers abroad. With Ukrainians Europe showed that welcoming people well is possible. Asking for the same yardstick for those fleeing other wars means applying the rules Europe has given itself: outsourcing does not erase the obligation, it only moves it to where it is harder to enforce ( our manifesto ). What to watch The December summit and the emergency rules the Commission will present by the end of the year. The Court of Justice ruling on the Albania centres and the first agreement for a return hub outside the EU. The figures on deaths at sea at the end of the year. Crime figures for 2026, ahead of the Italian election campaign. What Europe could do: seven proposals

The final piece in the series «Europe's choices». After criticising the choices of Europe's leadership, we try to say what could be done: one goal, coexistence, and seven proposals, each with its historical precedent, its legal basis, who would have to accept it and its weak points.

In brief In nine pieces we have criticised the choices of Europe's leadership. Here we try to say what could be done. The goal is civil coexistence, with three principles: every step towards the other side is rewarded, the reasons of all sides are put on the table, and the compromise leaves no one in ruin. On peace: Europe ties its aid to a seat at the table and an agreed roadmap, starting with the reasons of each side; the contested territories decide through a genuine referendum under international control; Ukraine joins NATO only within an agreement that Moscow also signs. On the tools: it was the Europeans who escalated the sanctions, so it is up to them to take the first step in reviewing them; the assets of the Russian state, not those of private individuals, go into a fund for war damage, with a commission that also judges damage caused by Ukraine; security is built with incentives for transparency, not imposed inspections; peace must pay off for everyone, economically too. Our assessment: no proposal is easy, and for each one we say where it could fail. But they all start from the same principle: diplomacy first, and the same yardstick for everyone, allies included. The question In this series we have tested the choices of Europe's leadership: energy, the electric car, relations with Russia before and after 2022, the weight of the United States, Nord Stream, immigration. The verdict has almost always been harsh. But criticising is the easy part. What could be done instead? This piece is different from the others: it is a proposal, so it expresses the site's position from beginning to end. To avoid writing wishes, we have tested each proposal against four questions: whether there is a historical precedent, what legal basis it rests on, who would have to accept it, and where it risks failing. This piece expresses the site's position. The facts cited are given with their sources. The starting point In mid-October 2026 peace in Ukraine is at a standstill. On 9 October Vladimir Putin told Donald Trump that an immediate resumption of negotiations is unlikely; Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks of a "dangerous stalemate" ( Al Jazeera, 10/10/2026 ). The negotiations, when there are any, go through Washington and Moscow. Europe pays most of the aid to Kyiv, but it does not sit at the table: we described this in the piece on the choices after 2022 . The goal: living together Before the proposals, the goal. Not victory for one side, but civil coexistence: a Europe in which Ukraine and Russia remain neighbours, and must be able to do so without shooting at each other. Getting there takes three principles, which run through all the proposals. Every step towards the other side is rewarded. Whoever makes a concrete gesture gets something in return, and whoever backs out loses what it has gained. It worked in the Cold War: in June 1963 John F. Kennedy announced that the United States would no longer carry out nuclear tests in the atmosphere, as long as others did the same. Nikita Khrushchev responded by accepting, for the first time, a ban limited to atmospheric tests, and within a few weeks the treaty was ready ( Arms Control Association, 2013 ). Understanding the reasons of all sides. A war does not come out of nowhere. The parties must be able to put on the table what each has suffered and what each has done. Understanding the causes does not mean justifying the aggression, which the UN General Assembly condemned with 141 votes in March 2022 ( UN News ). It means knowing what has to be resolved so that the war does not start again. A compromise that leaves no one in ruin. A peace that destroys the economy of one of the parties prepares the next war. And Europe cannot finance indefinitely a war that for years no one has managed to win on the battlefield. 1. A seat at the table, in exchange for aid The proposal. Europe does not ask permission to take part: it sets it as a condition. Aid to Kyiv continues, but tied to two commitments: the Union sits at the negotiations with its own envoy, and the parties follow an agreed roadmap, with stages and deadlines. Whoever pays has the right to say how peace is reached. The first item on the roadmap is a table on the reasons: experts from both sides put in writing their mutual accusations, from NATO enlargement to the war in Donbas since 2014, from the Russian-speaking minorities to the guarantees promised to Ukraine and not kept. For each accusation, a proposed solution. The precedent. European aid to Ukraine is already conditional: the €90 billion loan decided in December 2025 has precise rules on repayment and on the use of frozen Russian assets ( OSW, 19/12/2025 ). It would be a matter of adding a political condition. Further back, the Helsinki Accords of 1975 show that Europe can sit at the table between the blocs. And for the table on the reasons there is a model: the Polish-Russian Group on Difficult Matters, created by the two governments in 2002. Historians from both countries wrote side-by-side chapters on the most painful points of their shared history, from 1918 to 2008, published both in Warsaw and in Moscow ( University of Pittsburgh Press ). The basis. Decisions on aid and on the common foreign policy belong to the 27, by unanimity. Who has to accept it. The 27, Kyiv, and then Moscow and Washington, which today negotiate with each other. Where it could fail. Placing conditions on aid to a country under attack can be read as abandonment, and Moscow could take advantage of it to harden its position. Unanimity is difficult. A roadmap works only if Russia accepts it too. And a table on the reasons can turn into a tribunal of accusations: the Polish-Russian group worked in years of thaw, not during a war. 2. A genuine referendum on the contested territories The proposal. Freezing the front solves nothing: it postpones the problem, as has happened for decades in other conflicts. The principle should be the self-determination of peoples. The fate of the contested territories should be decided by those who live there, with a referendum built into the negotiations. But a genuine referendum, not those organised under occupation: with the withdrawal of troops, a temporary international administration, a vote for those who fled too, and UN observers. The precedent. In 1999 the UN organised in East Timor, then under Indonesia, a consultation under an agreement between Indonesia and Portugal: 98% of those registered voted and 78.5% chose independence. Militia violence followed, then an international force and a UN administration until independence ( UN peacekeeping ). The counter-example is the referendums in Crimea in 2014 and in the other territories in 2022, organised under military occupation and not recognised by the vast majority of states. The basis. The UN Charter recognises the self-determination of peoples. But the Ukrainian Constitution establishes that changes to the territory can be decided only by an all-Ukrainian referendum, and it forbids referendums under martial law ( Washington Law Review, 2022 ). A truce is therefore needed first. Who has to accept it. Kyiv, Moscow and the UN, which would have to organise it. Where it could fail. Who votes? Millions of people have fled, others have arrived. Moscow will not agree to withdraw its troops before the vote; Kyiv fears losing the territories. And Timor teaches that the aftermath of a vote can be violent. 3. NATO only within an agreement that Moscow also signs The proposal. Ukraine's entry into NATO should not be a security problem for Russia. That is why it should happen only within an agreement that Moscow also signs. In return, Ukraine remains armed, free to join the European Union, and obtains written guarantees from countries willing to intervene if it is attacked again. The precedent. In 1955 Austria obtained the withdrawal of all foreign troops, including about 40,000 Soviet soldiers, in exchange for permanent neutrality, later written into its Constitution ( Country Studies, Austria ). And in 2008, in Bucharest, Germany and France slowed down Ukraine's entry precisely so as not to provoke Moscow. The opposite precedent is the Budapest Memorandum of 1994: Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons in exchange for "assurances" that prevented neither 2014 nor 2022 ( our piece from 1990 to 2022 ). The basis. The Charter for European Security signed in Istanbul in 1999, by Russia too, contains two principles together: every state is free to choose its own alliances, and no one should strengthen its own security at the expense of the security of others ( Istanbul Charter, OSCE, 1999 ). An agreement that takes account of both must be written into a treaty. Who has to accept it. Kyiv, Moscow, the NATO countries and the guarantor countries. Where it could fail. Giving Moscow the last word on a neighbour's alliances creates a precedent that other countries, from Moldova to Georgia, fear. The Ukrainian Constitution names NATO membership as a strategic goal. And the lesson of Budapest is that guarantees without concrete commitments are worth nothing. 4. Sanctions: the first step is up to Europe The proposal. Sanctions often also hit people who bear no blame. And since 2022 they have grown, package after package, mostly by European decision, to increase pressure, rather than in response to new Russian actions. If the escalation was a European choice, it is Europe that must take the first step: immediately lift the measures that hit civilians, from food to medicines to everyday goods, and propose a timetable for reducing the others, step by step, tied to progress in the negotiations. With a written rule: if the commitments are broken, the sanctions return. The precedent. The 2015 nuclear deal with Iran provided for exactly this: sanctions lifted in exchange for verified commitments, and a mechanism to reimpose them. In September 2025 that mechanism was used and UN sanctions returned ( Congressional Research Service, 7/7/2026 ). The basis. European sanctions are adopted and lifted by unanimity of the 27. Who has to accept it. The 27. Moscow would have to respond with concrete steps. Where it could fail. Moscow could pocket the gesture without giving anything in return. Some European governments would see it as a surrender. And American sanctions remain outside European control, as we saw in the piece on who really decides . 5. Who pays for the damage: the Russian state, not private individuals, and a judge for both sides The proposal. Two kinds of Russian assets are frozen in the Union, and they must not be confused. There are the assets of the Russian Central Bank, that is, of the state: more than €200 billion. And there are the assets of sanctioned private individuals: about €24 billion in 2023 ( Mind, on Commission data, 25/5/2023 ). Private individuals did not decide the war, and their assets cannot be used for reconstruction without a court conviction. The state's assets, on the other hand, can go into a fund for war damage, provided for in the peace agreement. But the fund must apply the same yardstick to everyone. Whoever started the war pays for its damage. Each party, however, pays for the violations of the laws of war it has committed: Ukraine too, for civilians hit in Russia or for attacks such as the one on Nord Stream, if they are proven. This should be decided by an independent commission, with public accounts and checks on every euro. The precedent. After the war between Eritrea and Ethiopia, an arbitral commission found Eritrea liable for the invasion, but found both countries liable for violations committed during the war, from mistreated prisoners to looting: in 2009 it awarded about $174 million to Ethiopia and about $163 million to Eritrea ( ASIL, 2009 ). And after the invasion of Kuwait, Iraq paid $52.4 billion in compensation from part of its oil revenues, the last instalment in 2022 ( UN News, 9/2/2022 ). The basis. An agreement that Russia signs, or an international decision. In December 2025 the 27 already linked the frozen assets to the payment of reparations ( OSW ). Who has to accept it. The 27, starting with Belgium, where most of the assets are held; Kyiv, which would have to agree to answer for its own damage too; Moscow. Where it could fail. Using the assets without an agreement exposes Europe to lawsuits and financial risks. Kyiv could refuse to be judged alongside the aggressor. And a commission takes years. 6. Security through transparency, not imposed inspections The proposal. No one wants the adversary in their home checking up on them. So instead of imposing inspections, there should be incentives for transparency: whoever publishes data on its own forces, exercises and troop movements near the borders gets something in return, such as a reduction in sanctions or access to trade and joint programmes. More transparency, more benefits. The precedent. The Open Skies Treaty, signed in 1992 and in force since 2002, allowed more than thirty countries, Russia and the United States included, to fly over each other with unarmed aircraft to observe military forces: a less intrusive way of checking than inspections on the ground. The United States withdrew in 2020, Russia in 2021 ( Center for Arms Control ). The 1990 Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces set ceilings on weapons in Europe; Russia withdrew from it in 2023 ( Overt Defense, 7/11/2023 ). The basis. A new agreement between the European states, Russia and the United States, including within the OSCE. Who has to accept it. Everyone: that is why it is the slowest road. Where it could fail. Declared data can be falsified, and without a minimum of verification trust does not grow. But a system of incentives can start with just a few steps, and widen if it works. 7. A compromise that pays off for everyone, economically too The proposal. Peace must pay off for all parties, in the accounts too. For Ukraine, a funded reconstruction and an open road to the Union. For Russia, a gradual reduction of sanctions and the resumption of some trade, tied to respect for commitments. For Europe, the end of spending that weighs on its budgets and its citizens. Trade with Russia could resume, but with new rules: no dependence, as we proposed for gas. The precedent. Five years after the Second World War, France proposed pooling coal and steel with Germany, yesterday's enemy, so that a new war between the two would become "not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible". From that proposal the first European Community was born in 1951 ( Council of the EU, the Schuman Declaration ). The basis. The peace agreement and the Union's trade treaties. Who has to accept it. The 27, Kyiv, Moscow. Where it could fail. Europe has been spending on Ukraine for more than four years and will continue to do so: the €90 billion loan covers 2026 and 2027, and in May and June 2026 alone European institutions allocated nearly €11 billion, mostly through that loan ( Kiel Institute, 13/8/2026 ). But reopening trade with a country that attacked a neighbour divides European governments, and without guarantees it risks financing the next war. The Community of 1951 was born after the war ended, not during it. The lessons of the other pieces The seven proposals concern the war. But the series has also touched on other choices, and each suggests a correction: Energy: no supplier should weigh more than a certain share of Europe's gas, whether Russian, American or Qatari ( the piece ). The electric car: setting a date is not enough; investment in research and batteries is needed, not just tariffs ( the piece ). Sovereignty: use the tools Europe already has, such as the law that protects European companies from foreign sanctions, which today sits in a drawer ( the piece ). The same yardstick: the protection and attention given to Ukraine should also apply to Sudan and the other forgotten wars ( the piece ). Immigration: legal channels and return agreements with countries of origin, instead of costly centres abroad ( the piece ). The rules for everyone: even a country that has been attacked and is supported by Europe must respect the laws of war ( the piece on Nord Stream ). Our assessment None of these proposals is easy. Some may fail, and we have said so. But they all start from the same principle, which runs through the series: diplomacy comes first, always. And they share the same goal: not victory for someone, but civil coexistence. A Europe that chooses does not ask permission to sit at the table: it uses the weight it has, and rewards every step by the other side. It does not freeze conflicts hoping they will resolve themselves: it lets those who live there decide. It does not make one country's security another's insecurity. It acknowledges its own responsibilities, starting with the sanctions it escalated, which also hit people who bear no blame. It applies the same yardstick to everyone: whoever attacked pays, but each answers for its own crimes, allies included. And it seeks a peace that pays off even for today's enemy, because that is the only kind that lasts. What to watch The resumption of negotiations and whether Europe gets a seat at the table. The fate of the frozen Russian assets and of the €90 billion loan. The European Council in December, where Ukraine, sanctions and immigration will return. The dollar and sanctions, bond spreads, taxes, security: the levers used to bend Europe's choices, tested against the facts. Some are American. Others, more than people think, are European.

In brief The dollar is a real lever. In 2014 France's BNP Paribas paid $8.9 billion for breaking US sanctions; in 2023 Europe's vehicle for trading with Iran was shut down after a single transaction. On 9 October 2026 the United States sanctioned the International Criminal Court . Europe protests, but does not use the law that would let it protect its own companies. The bond spread, by contrast, had a European hand. In 2011 the letter to Italy was signed by the ECB of Trichet and Draghi; according to then US Treasury Secretary Geithner, European officials asked Washington to help them bring down Berlusconi, and Washington refused. On taxes , in 2025 the G7 exempted US multinationals from the global minimum tax. But Europe also fined Apple, Meta and Google despite Trump's threats. On security , the European commissioner who negotiated the tariff deal said it openly: "It's not only about the trade, it's about security, it's about Ukraine." The question One claim comes up often: Europe does not really decide. Washington steers it without needing to give orders, through the dollar, interest rates, rating agencies and big funds. A government that gets in the way can be brought to its knees in a few days. In this piece of the series, which follows the one on the choices after 2022 , we test the claim lever by lever. For each one we look for documented cases where it worked and cases where Europe resisted. One rule, as always: a proven interest is not proof of a cause. First lever: the dollar and sanctions The dollar is still the world's leading currency: it makes up 56.7% of central bank reserves ( IMF, 30/9/2026 ). Anyone doing business in dollars passes through the American system, and that is why Washington can punish even those who break sanctions decided by it alone. The best-known case is French. In June 2014 BNP Paribas pleaded guilty before a New York court and paid $8.9 billion for having evaded, between 2004 and 2012, US sanctions on Sudan, Cuba and Iran ( Al Jazeera, 30/6/2014 ). When the United States left the nuclear deal with Iran, France, Germany and the United Kingdom created INSTEX, a company to trade with Tehran without going through the dollar. In four years it made a single transaction, a delivery of medical goods in early 2020. In March 2023 it was wound up; European governments blamed Iran, which had rejected its proposals ( UK Government, 9/3/2023 ). The most recent case concerns international law. On 9 October 2026 Washington sanctioned the International Criminal Court as such, after the arrest warrant for Netanyahu and the investigation into US troops in Afghanistan. European banks and insurers that work with the Court risk secondary sanctions. 58 MEPs asked the Commission to activate the "Blocking Statute", the European law that forbids companies from applying foreign sanctions and allows them to claim damages ( Euronews, 14/10/2026 ). For now the Commission prefers diplomacy ( EUobserver, 14/10/2026 ); on 16 October the European Council said it "deeply regrets" the sanctions, but its conclusions do not mention the Blocking Statute ( European Council, 16/10/2026 ). We have written about the long siege of the Court here . The counter-example. In May 2021 the Biden administration waived sanctions on the Nord Stream 2 company and its chief executive, while acknowledging they had engaged in sanctionable activity, so as not to break with Germany, which wanted the pipeline ( Maritime Executive, 19/5/2021 ). When Berlin holds firm, Washington can give way. Second lever: the bond spread Here the claim needs correcting. In the two hardest European debt crises, the decisive pressure came from Frankfurt and from European capitals. Italy, 2011. On 5 August the European Central Bank, with the signatures of Jean-Claude Trichet and Mario Draghi, wrote to the Berlusconi government demanding precise and immediate measures: cuts, reforms, a balanced budget. ECB support for Italian bonds was tied to those demands. The letter was made public by Corriere della Sera on 29 September; Berlusconi resigned on 12 November ( Wikipedia, Trichet-Draghi letter ). In his memoir, then US Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner wrote that in that autumn "European officials" asked Washington to help them bring down Berlusconi, including by refusing support for an IMF rescue. Washington refused: "We cannot have blood on our hands" ( The Local, 14/5/2014 ). Greece, 2015. On 28 June, on the eve of the referendum on the creditors' plan, the ECB refused to increase emergency liquidity for Greek banks. The Tsipras government closed the banks and imposed limits on withdrawals ( NPR, 28/6/2015 ). The counter-example. The same ECB ended the spread crisis. On 26 July 2012 Draghi said in London: "The ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro." Rates for the weaker countries fell ( Quartz ). And markets do not only punish those who disobey Washington: in September 2022 Liz Truss's United Kingdom, one of America's most loyal allies, announced unfunded tax cuts; sterling hit a record low, the Bank of England had to intervene and Truss resigned after 44 days ( CNBC, 21/10/2022 ). On rating agencies and big investment funds we found no documented evidence of direct pressure on a European government on Washington's behalf. That is why we do not count them among the proven levers. Third lever: taxes On 28 June 2025 the G7 countries, including Germany, France and Italy, agreed to exempt US multinationals from the 15% global minimum tax agreed at the OECD: they will pay only in the United States. The deal came while Congress was debating a "revenge tax" against countries that applied the minimum tax to American companies ( Reuters via Arab News, 28/6/2025 ). But the picture is not one-way. In September 2024 the EU Court of Justice ruled that Ireland had granted Apple illegal state aid and that Apple had to pay back more than €13 billion in taxes. Defending Apple, alongside the company, was the Irish government ( Silicon Republic, 10/9/2024 ). The tax competition that favours multinationals was, in this case, the work of a European country. The counter-example. In April 2025 the Commission fined Apple €500 million and Meta €200 million under the new Digital Markets Act ( AFP via Arab News, 23/4/2025 ). In September 2025 it fined Google €2.95 billion; Trump threatened trade retaliation ( Euronews, 6/9/2025 ). The fines were imposed all the same. Fourth lever: security This is the most explicit lever. On 28 July 2025, defending the deal that accepted 15% US tariffs, EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said: "It's not only about the trade, it's about security, it's about Ukraine" ( IBTimes, 28/7/2025 ). The previous pieces showed the rest: 58% of the weapons imported by European NATO countries come from the United States, and European governments buy American weapons for Kyiv. The counter-example. In 2008, at the NATO summit in Bucharest, Germany and France blocked the membership path for Ukraine and Georgia that Washington wanted to start ( NATO, 3/4/2008 ). And the US debt? It is also said that the United States needs Europe to finance its debt. The numbers say otherwise. In July 2026 US Treasury securities in foreign hands were worth about $9,250 billion ( Trading Economics, on Treasury data ), less than a quarter of a debt that passed $40,000 billion in August ( Africanews, 20/8/2026 ). The largest foreign holders are Japan, the United Kingdom and China. US debt is financed mostly at home. What worked When Europe acts together, with common rules and institutions, it gets results even against American interests: the fines on the big digital platforms were imposed despite the threats, the Apple ruling is final, the ECB stopped speculation against the euro in 2012, and in 2021 Berlin got Washington to waive sanctions on the Nord Stream 2 company. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. The original claim is half true. Washington has real, documented levers: the dollar, with which it punishes those who trade with its enemies, and security, which it openly trades for commercial and tax concessions. The sanctions on the International Criminal Court show it starkly: they hit a court that Europe wanted and funds. But the other half of the claim does not hold. The spread that bent Italy in 2011 and Greece in 2015 had a European address: Frankfurt and the European capitals. And the tax havens that favour multinationals are also inside the Union. Saying that America is in charge is true for one part; for the other part it is a convenient way of absolving Europe's ruling classes. The point, for us, is another. When Europe uses the tools it has, it wins: the ECB and competition policy have shown it. The Blocking Statute has existed since 1996, and it has stayed in a drawer even now that sanctions are hitting the International Criminal Court. Dependence is not only imposed: in large part it is chosen, every time Europe gives up using what it has. What to watch The Commission's decision on activating the Blocking Statute to protect the International Criminal Court. Implementation at the OECD of the exemption for US multinationals from the global minimum tax. Purchases of American weapons with European funds, and the share of European products in rearmament programmes. Per person, Europe gives more humanitarian aid to Gaza than to Ukraine. But only in Ukraine does it send weapons, money for the state and thousands of sanctions. What Ukraine is worth, and to whom.

In brief To help Ukraine, Europe has spent more than €200 billion since 2022, in weapons, money for the state and humanitarian aid. For Sudan, the help is humanitarian only. On humanitarian aid alone, Ukraine is not favoured: in 2026 it receives about €20 per person in need, the Palestinian territories about €60 , Sudan and Yemen about €5 . The difference lies in political choices: only in Ukraine has Europe sent weapons , paid the state budget and listed about 4,600 individuals and entities. Ukraine matters for concrete reasons: it borders four EU countries, used to export 10% of the world's wheat and hosts Europe's largest nuclear power plant. For Washington the aim was stated openly: "We want to see Russia weakened." The question Why Ukraine and not Sudan? In the previous pieces of this series we saw how much Europe has spent after 2022 and how the war came about. Here we put Ukraine next to three other conflicts, Sudan, Gaza and the West Bank, and Yemen, and measure them with the same yardstick. First, though, let us see what Ukraine is worth, and to whom. What Ukraine is worth To Europe. Ukraine borders four EU countries: Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania. Since the Helsinki Final Act of 1975, European security has rested on the principle that borders are not changed by force. Before the war Ukraine exported about 10% of the wheat and 15% of the maize sold worldwide ( farmdoc daily, University of Illinois, 24/2/2023 ). On its territory stands Zaporizhzhia, Europe's largest nuclear power plant, with six reactors: it is in Russian hands and has produced no electricity since 11 September 2022 ( Interfax, 17/4/2026 ). To Russia. In 1997 Zbigniew Brzezinski, a former US national security adviser, wrote in The Grand Chessboard that without Ukraine Russia ceases to be a Eurasian empire. Crimea hosts the base of Russia's Black Sea fleet. Moscow still demands that the "root causes" of the conflict be addressed: NATO enlargement and the protection of Russian speakers ( House of Commons Library, 15/9/2026 ). To the United States. On 25 April 2022, in Poland, Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin said: "We want to see Russia weakened to a degree that it can't do the kinds of things it has done in invading Ukraine" ( Axios, 25/4/2022 ). On 30 April 2025 Washington and Kyiv signed a minerals deal: a joint fund receives half of the revenue from new mining, oil and gas projects, and future US military aid counts as the US share ( CSIS, 1/5/2025 ). The previous pieces showed the rest: American gas and weapons sold to Europe. The same yardstick: humanitarian aid To compare conflicts we need consistent numbers: same source, same year, same unit. The first table compares the needs estimated by the UN for 2026 with the humanitarian aid allocated by the European Commission in the same year. Ukraine Sudan Palestinian territories Yemen People in need of aid in 2026 10.8 million 33.7 million 3.6 million 23.1 million European Commission humanitarian aid in 2026 €220 million €162 million over €217 million €120 million (2025) Euros per person in need about €20 about €5 about €60 about €5 Sources: UN, Global Humanitarian Overview 2026, for Sudan and for the other countries as reported by Concern ; European Commission country pages for Ukraine , Sudan , Palestine and Yemen . For Yemen the 2026 figure has not yet been published; we use 2025. For Sudan we count only aid inside the country, not aid for refugees in neighbouring countries. On humanitarian aid, then, Europe does not favour Ukraine. Those who receive least, by far, are Sudan and Yemen: the two crises with the most people in need. The same yardstick: political choices The difference lies in what Europe does beyond humanitarian aid. Ukraine Sudan Israel and Palestine Yemen Weapons €75.2 billion supplied by the EU and member states EU arms embargo since 1994 member states sell to Israel member states have sold to the Saudi-led coalition Money for the state €43.3 billion in financial assistance, plus the €90 billion loan for 2026-27 none up to €1.6 billion for the Palestinian Authority for 2025-27 about €500 million in development aid since 2015 EU sanctions about 4,600 Russian individuals and entities 18 individuals and 8 entities, from both sides 21 violent settlers and organisations; no measures against the Israeli government; Hamas on the EU list of terrorist organisations the Houthis, under a UN embargo adopted by the EU Sources: Ukraine, Eunews on European Parliament data, 1/6/2026 , AP, 19/12/2025 , Council of the EU, 12/10/2026 ; Sudan, SIPRI and Dabanga, 29/1/2026 ; Israel and Palestine, The New Arab, 1/10/2025 , European Commission, 14/4/2025 , J Street, June 2026 , Lovguiden, 30/7/2026 ; Yemen, Reuters via The New Arab and Council of the EU, 14/3/2022 . Two examples give the measure. Germany had authorised about €251 million in military exports to Israel between early 2024 and mid-2025; in August 2025 it suspended them for a few weeks, then resumed them (The New Arab, cited above). In 2023 Italy lifted the embargo on selling bombs and missiles to Saudi Arabia that it had introduced over the war in Yemen (Reuters, cited above). The European Council of 15 and 16 October 2026 shows the same pattern in words. On Ukraine, the conclusions call for new sanctions against Russia and release €6.6 billion for weapons. On Gaza and the West Bank, they condemn settlement expansion and settler violence, warn companies against bidding for construction in the E1 area and call for Hamas to disarm, but provide for no measures against the Israeli government. On Yemen, they condemn the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia and express solidarity with Riyadh, saying nothing about the Saudi-led coalition. Sudan is never mentioned ( European Council, conclusions of 16/10/2026 ). The dead Death tolls are not in the tables because the sources measure different things. We give them one by one, saying what they count. Ukraine: at least 16,431 civilians killed between February 2022 and June 2026, counting only cases verified one by one by the UN ( UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission, 14/7/2026 ). According to the monitor ACLED, in 2025 alone the war killed about 78,000 people, soldiers and civilians ( Newsweek, on ACLED data ). Sudan: about 80,000 deaths estimated in 2025 alone, according to a model by researchers at Uppsala and at PRIO in Oslo ( The Conversation via Polity, 7/10/2026 ). Gaza: 73,001 dead since 7 October 2023 according to Gaza's health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants; UN agencies consider its records generally reliable ( AP via PBS, 14/6/2026 ). Yemen: 377,000 deaths estimated by UNDP by the end of 2021, including those from hunger and disease ( Al Jazeera, 23/11/2021 ). What worked European humanitarian aid does not follow alliances: per person, the Palestinian territories receive more than Ukraine. In April 2026, in Berlin, the EU and member states pledged more than €812 million for Sudan and its refugees ( European Commission, 15/4/2026 ). And in Sudan, European sanctions hit both sides, the army and the Rapid Support Forces. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. The principles are not false: the UN Charter applies in Ukraine as in Sudan, in Gaza as in Yemen. But Europe enforces them with all its strength only where they coincide with its own interests and with Washington's. In Ukraine they coincide: the Union's borders, grain, nuclear power, a rival to weaken. In Sudan and Yemen they do not, and there Europe sends aid, not policy. In Gaza the interests pull the other way, and European weapons keep reaching one of the parties. International law is not an ideology to be used where it suits. Either it applies to everyone, or it becomes a flag. This site exists to demand that it apply to everyone: the same sanctions for whoever bombs civilians, whoever they are; the same diplomatic effort for every war; the same halt to arms for whoever violates humanitarian law. What to watch The UN Global Humanitarian Overview 2027, in December, and how much of it Europe will fund. New entries in the EU sanctions regime on Sudan, extended on 9 October 2026 until 10 October 2027 with no additions ( Lovguiden, 9/10/2026 ). The proposal to suspend the trade part of the EU-Israel Association Agreement.
