After 2022: what Europe chose and what it cost
Sanctions, loans to Kyiv, rearmament, refugees, a tariff deal with Washington: Europe's choices after the invasion, what they cost and who sits at the peace table.

In brief Since 2022 the Union has adopted 22 sanctions packages against Russia; the latest, on 12 October 2026, targets 1,569 companies and executives in the military industry. In 2025, with US aid almost gone, Europe gave Kyiv about €29 billion in weapons and €39 billion in financial and humanitarian aid. For 2026-27 there is an EU loan of €90 billion . The costs: inflation at 10.6% in October 2022, €540 billion in public support against high energy prices, output of Germany's energy-intensive industries down 15.2% . Meanwhile Europe accepted US tariffs of 15% on its goods, while removing its own on US industrial goods. The peace talks are led by the United States. The Europeans are consulted but do not lead; Moscow, for now, does not want to negotiate. At the summit of 16 October 2026 the 27 criticised Washington for halting sanctions on Russian diesel, but proposed no peace initiative of their own. Kyiv received tens of billions while a corruption scandal worth about $100 million broke out in the energy sector. The question The previous piece stopped on 24 February 2022. Here we look at what Europe decided after the invasion, what it cost and what weight it gave Europe. The UN Charter prohibits aggression, recognises the right to self-defence and asks everyone, before anything else, to seek a peaceful settlement. The question is which of these paths Europe chose, and who reaps the benefits. The choices, one by one Choice What Who opted out Sanctions 22 packages; almost 4,600 individuals and entities listed nobody: every package requires unanimity Money for Kyiv EU loan of €90 billion for 2026-27, financed with joint debt Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic do not take part Rearmament NATO target of 5% of GDP by 2035; SAFE EU loans of €150 billion Spain stops at 2.1%; Germany does not use SAFE Refugees temporary protection for 4.43 million Ukrainians, extended to March 2028 nobody Ukraine's accession four of six negotiating clusters opened between June and October 2026 Hungary's new government wants a referendum Tariffs with the US 15% on European goods; zero tariffs on US industrial goods — Sources: Council of the EU, 12/10/2026 ; AP, 19/12/2025 ; Eunews, 23/6/2025 ; Grosswald, SAFE tracker ; Eurostat via Eunews, 10/9/2026 ; Euronews, 10/7/2026 ; European Council, conclusions of 16/10/2026 . The diplomacy that was missed In the first weeks of the war there were real negotiations. At the end of March 2022, in Istanbul, the Russian and Ukrainian delegations agreed a communiqué: Ukrainian neutrality, with no nuclear weapons or foreign bases, in exchange for security guarantees from the great powers. By May the talks had broken off. Why is still debated: the discovery of the killings of civilians in Bucha weighed, as did Western reluctance to give binding guarantees and Russian demands on Crimea and on Ukraine's armed forces. The claim that the talks were stopped by British prime minister Johnson, who visited Kyiv on 9 April, is made by some and disputed by others ( Foreign Affairs, 16/4/2024 ; The National Interest ). After 2022 the Union never opened a negotiating channel of its own with Moscow. Today the door is closed from the other side too: the Kremlin rejects a meeting between Putin and Zelensky outside Moscow ( House of Commons Library, 15/9/2026 ) and, according to a source close to the Kremlin quoted by Reuters, Putin will return to talks only after taking the rest of Donbas ( Meduza, 14/10/2026 ). Who pays In 2025 Washington cut its aid to Kyiv by up to 99%. Europe filled the gap: about €29 billion in weapons, two thirds more than the 2022-2024 average, and €39 billion in financial and humanitarian aid, almost all from EU institutions. The burden is not evenly shared: northern countries gave a third of Europe's military aid with 8% of the donors' GDP; southern countries, Italy included, gave 3% with 19% of GDP ( Kiel Institute via Euronews, 11/2/2026 ). Part of that money goes back to the United States. Through the NATO mechanism called PURL, European governments buy American weapons for Ukraine: more than 90% of what passes through this channel comes from US stocks ( Kiel Institute, 13/8/2026 ). On frozen Russian assets the Union split. About €210 billion is blocked in Europe, most of it at Euroclear in Brussels. The plan to use it for a "reparations loan" collapsed in December 2025 because of opposition from Belgium, which feared lawsuits and risks for Euroclear. In its place came the €90 billion loan backed by joint debt: European taxpayers pay for it, while the assets stay frozen (AP, cited above). Where the money goes On 22 July 2025 Ukraine's parliament passed, and Zelensky signed, a law stripping the two anti-corruption agencies, NABU and SAPO, of their independence. After days of street protests and European criticism, the law was reversed on 31 July ( Euromaidan Press, 31/7/2025 ). In November NABU made public Operation Midas: kickbacks of up to 15% on contracts at Energoatom, the state nuclear company, and about $100 million laundered. According to investigators, the scheme was run by Timur Mindich, a business partner of Zelensky, who fled before the charges. The justice and energy ministers were dismissed; on 28 November the head of the presidential office, Andriy Yermak, resigned on the day his home was searched ( Euromaidan Press, 28/11/2025 ). The scandal came out because those agencies, saved by the street, did their job. What it cost at home Prices. In October 2022 euro area inflation hit 10.6%, a record, driven by energy ( Eurostat ). Support against high energy prices. Between September 2021 and June 2023 EU governments allocated €540 billion, €158 billion from Germany alone, mostly through across-the-board cuts in excise duties and VAT ( Bruegel ). Sanctions and citizens. Economic sanctions also hit people who bear no blame: a report presented to the UN documents how banks and companies, afraid of making mistakes, also block permitted trade, including medicines and humanitarian goods ( UN, note by the Secretary-General ). Russia's war economy, meanwhile, has adapted: it grew by 4.9% in 2024 and by 1% in 2025 ( Trading Economics, 6/2/2026 ). Industry. In Germany, output of energy-intensive industries fell by 15.2% between February 2022 and March 2026 ( Destatis via Clean Energy Wire, 15/5/2026 ). The tariff deal In July 2025, in Scotland, the Union accepted a US tariff of 15% on most of its goods. In return it removed its tariffs on US industrial goods and promised energy purchases worth $750 billion over three years ( Reuters via BBC Bermuda, 28/7/2025 ). In February 2026 the US Supreme Court struck down the legal instrument Trump had used for the tariffs, and the European Parliament suspended its examination of the deal ( European Parliament, 23/2/2026 ). In June it approved it anyway, with 440 votes in favour, adding clauses to suspend it if Washington does not keep its side of the bargain ( Confectionery Production, 16/6/2026 ). At the peace table On 15 August 2025 Trump met Putin in Alaska, without Europeans. Three days later von der Leyen, Macron, Merz, Meloni, Stubb and Britain's Starmer flew to Washington to stand beside Zelensky ( Il Sole 24 Ore ). The pattern has stayed the same: the US envoys Witkoff and Kushner negotiate with Moscow and with Kyiv; at the Kyiv talks of 6 September 2026 the national security advisers of France, the United Kingdom and Germany took part in only one session ( House of Commons Library, 15/9/2026 ). On 9 October Trump announced a deal with Moscow for the sale of more than 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel; European governments criticised it. The same day Putin told him that an immediate resumption of negotiations was unlikely ( Al Jazeera, 10/10/2026 ). According to a Washington Post columnist, citing an anonymous US official and an anonymous European diplomat, the United States and the Europeans are preparing a joint plan: a truce along the front line, security guarantees for Kyiv, reconstruction funds and a large energy deal that would bring cheap Russian oil and gas back to Europe, with a timetable for lifting sanctions ( Meduza, 14/10/2026 ). No government has confirmed it. The European Council of 15 and 16 October reaffirmed that "the path to peace in Ukraine cannot be decided without Ukraine" and called on Russia to agree to an immediate and unconditional ceasefire. It "regretted" the temporary lifting by the United States of sanctions on Russian diesel and promised new sanctions. The conclusions contain no European negotiating initiative ( European Council, conclusions of 16/10/2026 ). Zelensky asked the Union for an extra €70 billion for 2027; leaders asked the Commission to set out options, and von der Leyen said Europe cannot cover it alone ( Euronews, 16/10/2026 ). What worked Ukraine has not fallen, and since 2025 it has held mainly thanks to European money. Sanctions have been adopted unanimously 22 times. More than four million refugees have received protection. And after the 2020 recovery fund, joint debt was used again, this time to support a country at war. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Condemning the invasion was a duty, and it remains one. But for us diplomacy comes first, always: it is the first duty the UN Charter imposes on anyone in a dispute. Europe put it last. It let the 2022 attempts drop, never opened a channel of its own with Moscow and handed the negotiation to Washington. Moscow, for its part, now refuses to negotiate until it has taken Donbas: the duty applies to it too. The conclusions of the 16 October summit confirm it: a ceasefire demanded of Russia, new sanctions, new money, and no European proposal for reaching a negotiation. Instead of diplomacy, the Union chose sanctions and aid. Economic sanctions also hit people who bear no blame: Russian citizens who did not decide the war, and European citizens who paid more for energy. Meanwhile Russia's war economy has adapted. The aid went to a government whose scandals came to light only thanks to bodies that the same government had tried to weaken. So Europe pays, but others decide. The plan being discussed in these weeks shows it clearly. If it were confirmed, Russian gas would return to Europe, but on terms negotiated in Washington: the same supplies that Europe gave up on principle would come back inside a deal it did not write. What to watch The Commission's options for covering the €70 billion Kyiv has requested for 2027. The three-way talks between the United States, Ukraine and Russia, and whether the plan reported by the Washington Post is confirmed. The opening of the two remaining clusters in Ukraine's accession negotiations. NABU's investigation into Operation Midas and the possible extradition of Mindich. Europe chose the electric car. Who builds it?
The EU set 2035 as the deadline without securing batteries and raw materials. Chinese cars now hold almost 12% of the market, coming in more and more through the hybrid door.

In brief In August 2026 Chinese brands held 11.7% of new car registrations in Europe, up from 7.1% a year earlier. Since 2024 the EU has imposed duties of up to 35.3% on Chinese electric cars, but not on hybrids : Chinese hybrid exports to the EU rose from about 3,800 cars a month (October 2024) to about 50,000 (July 2026). After the 9 October understanding with Beijing, the EU is preparing a cap of 350,000 Chinese hybrids a year , possibly from December. For Brussels it is half of what would have arrived; for Beijing it is 16% more than in 2025. On 15-16 October EU leaders took no decision on the cap, but asked for trade defence instruments to be strengthened “urgently”, without naming China . The ban on selling petrol and diesel cars from 2035 is under review. Northvolt, Europe's battery champion, went bankrupt in 2025; European car suppliers announced 104,000 job cuts in two years. The EU spends 2.2% of GDP on research, a share that has not moved in ten years; China has reached 2.8% . The question On 9 October Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič came back from Beijing with a “shared understanding”: China is to slow its exports of hybrid cars to Europe ( Eunews, 9/10/2026 ). Three days later the numbers came out: a cap of 350,000 Chinese hybrids a year, plug-ins included, rising by 6% a year for four years and possibly starting as early as December ( euperspectives, 13/10/2026 ). The same number can be read two ways. For the Commission, without a cap 800,000 Chinese hybrids would have arrived this year: exports are halved. For Beijing, 302,000 arrived in 2025: the cap leaves room for 16% growth (euperspectives, cited). On 16 October China's Commerce Ministry called the understanding “reciprocal and mutually beneficial”, reached under WTO rules and the principle of non-discrimination, and said the idea that “European pressure worked” was “groundless” ( Chinese Commerce Ministry via The Paper, 16/10/2026 ). EU leaders, meeting in Brussels on 15 and 16 October, took no decision on the cap, which the Commission can launch on its own. China is not named in the conclusions: they refer to “global macroeconomic imbalances” and call for the EU toolbox to be “urgently” strengthened with new instruments ( European Council, conclusions of 16/10/2026 ). According to officials quoted by Euronews, over lunch the leaders called for safeguards with quotas and tariffs for chemicals and machinery as well. “The competition must be fair,” said German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. “The toolbox will be bigger” ( Euronews, 16/10/2026 ). Hybrids thus become the test case for a tougher trade policy towards China. Meanwhile the numbers keep running: in August Chinese brands sold almost 98,000 cars in Europe, 11.7% of the market, against 7.1% a year earlier ( ChinaEVHome on Dataforce data, 24/9/2026 ). This is the second piece in the series on the choices of Europe's leaders. The choice: a date without a road In 2023 the Union decided by law that from 2035 new cars must emit no CO2: in practice, the end of the petrol and diesel engine ( Regulation (EU) 2023/851 ). Part of the industry wanted freedom of technology; under German pressure, only engines running on synthetic fuels were spared ( Euronews, 28/3/2023 ). The problem was not the direction but what was missing to get there. The heart of an electric car is the battery, and the supply chain for batteries and raw materials is largely Chinese. Sweden's Northvolt, Europe's most ambitious attempt, went bankrupt in March 2025 ( E&E News ). And in the 9 October understanding Beijing also promised to keep easing export licences for rare earths and magnets ( The Next Web, 12/10/2026 ): a sign of who depends on whom. In December 2025 the Commission proposed a change of course: a 90% cut in emissions instead of 100%, with hybrids and combustion engines still on sale after 2035 ( Automotive World ). Member states are divided; the European Parliament votes in November ( Council of the EU, 15/6/2026 ). The defence: duties on one door, the other left open Since October 2024 the Union has applied anti-subsidy duties to electric cars made in China, on top of the ordinary 10% duty: Manufacturer Extra duty on electric cars BYD 17% Geely 18.8% SAIC (MG) 35.3% Source: New Mobility, 22/6/2026 . Since January 2026 manufacturers can offer a minimum price and a volume cap instead ( Caixin, 13/1/2026 ). But the duties only hit fully electric cars, and Chinese manufacturers shifted to hybrids. Their hybrid exports to the EU rose from about 3,800 cars in October 2024 to about 50,000 in July 2026 ( EUobserver, 5/10/2026 ). In the first half of 2026 Chinese brands held 28.3% of the European plug-in hybrid market, according to Dataforce (New Mobility, cited). For Volkswagen's chief executive, Oliver Blume, the duties work, but “not with hybrids” ( The Next Web, 27/7/2026 ). This contradicts a common reading: the Chinese did not get in only thanks to the electric mandate. They also got in, more and more, through the hybrid door. What trade law says The 2024 duties are lawful: WTO rules allow duties against state subsidies, decided after an investigation (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2754). But that investigation did not cover hybrids, as Šefčovič himself acknowledged ( Diplomacy and Law, 9/10/2026 ). For hybrids there were two roads. The first was for Beijing to rein in its own exports: a “voluntary restraint”, the tool Japan used in the 1980s to limit its own cars, and which the WTO has banned since 1994 ( Agreement on Safeguards, Art. 11 ). Brussels chose the second: a “safeguard”, that is, a cap set by the EU itself. The rules allow it, on three conditions: proving serious injury to European industry, applying the cap to all countries of origin rather than one, and limiting it in time. Country quotas can be agreed with the main suppliers (Art. 5), and that appears to be the road taken with Beijing. Formally, then, the cap covers hybrids from every source, Japanese or Korean ones included, but the quotas for other suppliers have not yet been set. At first it would apply provisionally for 200 days; then member states would vote by qualified majority. Chinese-brand cars assembled inside the EU, for example in Hungary, stay out of the count (euperspectives, cited). The legal text is not yet public: it remains to be seen how the Commission will prove serious injury. The factories arrive, the technology stays in China Chinese manufacturers now also produce in Europe, partly to avoid the duties. Chery will start in Barcelona, in the former Nissan plant, between late 2026 and early 2027; Leapmotor will produce in Spain with Stellantis; SAIC is planning a plant in Galicia ( Reuters via MarketScreener, 2/6/2026 ). And cars assembled in Europe stay outside the cap. The factories create jobs, but design, software and batteries stay with those who developed them. Meanwhile the European supply chain is shrinking: car suppliers announced 54,000 job cuts in 2024 and 50,000 in 2025, against about 7,000 hires ( CLEPA via Just Auto, 19/1/2026 ). A lag that goes back further Duties defend a market, but they do not create an industry. And the gap with China opened well before 2023. In 2024 the Union spent 2.2% of GDP on research, almost the same share as ten years earlier and far from the 3% target ( Eurostat, 4/12/2025 ). In 2025 China reached 2.8%, above the average of the rich OECD countries ( South China Morning Post, 30/9/2026 ). There is another side too. Protecting oneself is not a European whim: for decades China forced foreign carmakers to produce only in joint ventures with a Chinese partner, and lifted the requirement only in 2022 ( Gasgoo, 2021 ). Protecting oneself is not a sign of weakness. It becomes one when it is the only thing one knows how to do. What worked The duties on electric cars curbed imports where they were applied, as European carmakers themselves admit. And electric cars now sell: in August 2026 they were 29.2% of European registrations (ChinaEVHome on ACEA data, cited). The market moved in the direction decided in 2023; what was missing were the tools to make sure Europeans gained from it. Our assessment Betting on electric was not a mistake: the world is going that way, and China understood it first. The mistake was setting the destination without building the road. Europe did not secure batteries, raw materials and software; it closed the electric door and left the hybrid door open for two years; and now it closes it with a cap that buys time, not competitiveness. That time is only useful if it is used. Yet for ten years Europe has not raised its research spending, and at the October summit the leaders “urgently” asked for new defensive instruments, while for cars they stopped at a package simplifying the rules. Without an industry able to invent, duties and caps become an admission of weakness, not a strategy. It is the same plot as energy: right goals, wrong dependencies. What to watch The legal text of the safeguard: how the Commission will prove serious injury, the quotas for Japan, Korea and other suppliers, the start date. Beijing's response: the Commerce Ministry warns the EU “not to underestimate” China's determination to defend its interests. The new trade defence instruments the leaders asked for, and whether they will be ready by the end of the year; the automotive package, which the leaders want concluded by December. The European Parliament's vote on 2035, in November, and the start of Chinese production in Spain. Europe stopped depending on Moscow. Who does it depend on now?
The EU cut Russian gas faster than expected, but households pay almost twice as much for gas and the new dependence lies across the Atlantic.

In brief In 2021 Russia supplied over 45% of the gas imported by the European Union; in 2025 about 13% . Today the largest supplier is Norway, with about 30% . The United States supplies 58% of liquefied gas , about a quarter of all the gas consumed in Europe. European households pay on average almost twice as much for gas as in early 2021: from 6.4 to 12.3 cents per kWh. In 2025 American liquefied gas was, on average, the most expensive of those bought by Europe. On 9 October Trump suspended sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027. The trial over the Nord Stream sabotage opens in Hamburg on 14 October . The question Europe is entering winter with its lowest gas reserves in almost twenty years: at the end of August storage was about 63% full ( Oilprice, 27/8/2026 , based on Gas Infrastructure Europe data). Qatari gas, blocked at Hormuz, has almost disappeared (see the Hormuz crisis ). Europe suffered this part of the crisis. But its fragility in the face of such a shock stems from a choice made four years ago. This is the first piece in a series on the major choices of Europe's leadership: for each one we ask what was decided, what alternatives existed, what it cost and what worked. The choice of 2022 After the invasion of Ukraine, the Union decided to exit Russian gas. The choice was not entirely free. In the summer of 2022 it was Moscow that cut Nord Stream flows to a fifth of capacity ( Bloomberg, 25/7/2022 ), and in September the pipeline was destroyed. The exit is now written into a regulation, 2026/261 ( EUR-Lex ). Short-term contracts are already banned: since 25 April 2026 for liquefied gas, since 17 June for pipeline gas. Long-term contracts end on 1 January 2027 for liquefied gas and on 30 September 2027 for pipeline gas. The question is how that gas was replaced. In 2021 Russia accounted for over 45% of European imports; in 2024, 19%; in 2025 about 13%, according to Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen ( ANSA via Il Nordest, 24/4/2025 ). Today the largest supplier is Norway, with about 30% ( European Commission, quarterly gas report, Q2 2025 ). The rest arrives mainly by ship, as liquefied gas, and 58% of that gas comes from the United States: about a quarter of all European demand ( ACER, 2026 ). The dependence on Moscow is over; the dependence on the sea, and on Washington, has begun. In July 2025, in the trade deal with Trump, the Union also pledged to buy 750 billion dollars of American energy over three years: a political, non-binding commitment that many analysts consider unachievable ( Oil & Gas 360, 28/7/2025 ). How much we pay Liquefied gas is more expensive by nature: it has to be cooled, shipped and regasified. But there is more to it. In the second quarter of 2025 gas in the United States cost 13.7 euros per megawatt-hour; once in Europe it cost 35.5 (European Commission, report cited above). That gap covers the costs, and the margins of those who sell. According to IEEFA, in 2025 American liquefied gas was on average the most expensive for European buyers, ahead of Qatari and Russian gas; from 2022 to 2025 the Union bought 131.5 billion euros' worth of it ( IEEFA, European LNG Tracker ). IEEFA is an American non-profit institute, funded by philanthropic foundations, which states that it supports the transition to clean energy. On the bill, the European average for households, taxes included, looks like this: First half of 2021 Second half of 2025 Average EU household gas price (cents per kWh) 6.4 12.28 Example: a home using 10,000 kWh a year about €640 about €1,230 Sources: Eurostat, 5/5/2026 for 2025; Eurostat figure for 2021 reported by Euronews, 26/2/2026 . The example is our own calculation on an indicative consumption level; differences between countries are very large. The price has almost doubled, and the late-2025 figures do not yet include the Gulf war: between February and April 2026 gas in European capitals rose by a further 6.8% ( Euronews, 14/5/2026 , HEPI index). It must be said, however, that wholesale prices had already started to soar in the second half of 2021, months before the invasion, with the post-pandemic recovery ( World Bank, monthly series ): the crisis does not stem from European choices alone. While Washington negotiates with Moscow Europe has set a date to give up Russian gas, and until then keeps buying it; its main ally is going in the opposite direction. On 9 October Trump announced a deal with Putin to receive Russian diesel: over 300,000 tonnes immediately, then growing quantities up to a few million. The US Treasury issued a licence suspending until April 2027 the sanctions on Russian diesel already loaded on ships ( OPB, 9/10/2026 ). Zelensky called it “a weak decision” by strong partners. On 8 October Reuters reported that envoy Jared Kushner and Kirill Dmitriev, an adviser to Putin, had discussed bringing an American investor into Nord Stream ( Reuters via WHBL, 8/10/2026 ). The White House says it has not been discussed recently; Berlin says a reopening is “not desired”. The pipelines are under European sanctions: under EU law a restart would remain illegal, whatever Washington decides. Who destroyed Nord Stream On 14 October the trial of Serhii Kuznietsov opens in Hamburg. A Ukrainian citizen extradited from Italy, he is accused of leading the group of seven people who planted the charges. According to German investigators, the order came from a Ukrainian state agency, to deprive Moscow of gas revenues. Kyiv denies it; Zelensky has said he knew nothing about it ( JusticeInfo ). A second suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov, was arrested in Croatia in August, after a Polish court had refused his extradition ( LIGA, 19/8/2026 ). The theories circulated in recent years blaming the United States or Russia itself have not been borne out by any judicial investigation. The charges, in any case, have yet to be proven in court. What worked In 2022 many predicted rationing and closed factories. It did not happen: Europe replaced most Russian gas in three years and stopped being open to blackmail by a supplier that used deliveries as a weapon. That is a real achievement. The price was a bill that has almost doubled and a new dependence, more expensive and more exposed to distant crises. Our assessment Leaving Russian gas was a defensible choice: no country should entrust the heating of its homes to a state that has just invaded a neighbour. The mistake was doing it without building real autonomy. Europe changed supplier, not condition. It tied a quarter of its gas to a single country, promised to buy even more, and now finds that this country is negotiating with Moscow on its own, on diesel and perhaps on Nord Stream, while European households pay the bill. A leadership able to choose, in a time of transition, should have asked not only whom to stop buying from, but whom never again to depend on so heavily. Update, 11 October 2026. According to the German organisation Urgewald , using data from the analytics firm Kpler, between January and September 2026 EU ports received 12.18 million tonnes of Russian liquefied gas from the Arctic Yamal project: 9.5% more than in the same period of 2025, a record. Of Yamal's deliveries, 85% end up in Europe; in September almost three quarters of those reaching the Union were unloaded in France, at Dunkirk and Montoir ( Euronews ). Urgewald estimates their value at about €7.9 billion, but warns that this is a calculation based on market prices, not the sum of actual payments or of Russian state revenue. In the third quarter deliveries fell by 13.6% year on year. The purchases are legal: short-term contracts have been banned since April, long-term ones will be from 1 January 2027. For this reason we have corrected the sentence that opened the section “While Washington negotiates with Moscow”, which said Europe “is giving up” Russian gas: it will, but for now it is still buying it. Update, 15 October 2026. The trial opened on 14 October before the Hamburg Higher Regional Court and is expected to run until early 2027. According to the prosecution, Kuznietsov and other Ukrainian servicemen acted on orders from Ukrainian state agencies; the defendant denies this and did not speak in court ( Courthouse News ). The defence argues that there is no evidence of his involvement and, at the same time, that the pipeline was a legitimate military target, “a weapon in the hands of the Russians”. The court will therefore have to decide whether this was an attack on civilian infrastructure, prohibited by the law of war, or a military operation. According to the BBC, in September 2022 Kuznietsov was on active duty in the Ukrainian armed forces ( LIGA, citing the BBC ). Ukraine's Prosecutor General says it has found no evidence of state involvement ( Kyiv Independent ). What to watch Gas storage levels on 1 November and the Hamburg trial, from 14 October. The Euro-Russian market that worried Washington: what the numbers say
Was a great market between Europe and Russia taking shape before the war? The data show that trade had already peaked in 2012. American interests against it, on the other hand, are documented.

In brief Trade between the European Union and Russia peaked in 2012 and then fell: by 2021, before the invasion, it was already almost a quarter lower. In 2021 Russia was the fifth market for European goods; 62% of what Europe bought from Moscow was energy. The United States openly opposed Nord Stream 2, with sanctions in 2019 and with Biden's promise of 7 February 2022 . Today the Union takes more than half of American liquefied gas, and 58% of the weapons imported by Europe's NATO members come from the United States. Over the same period Europe resumed selling weapons to Saudi Arabia and called Azerbaijan's gas "reliable". The question In public debate, in Italy and elsewhere, one idea keeps coming back: before the war a great market was taking shape between Europe and Russia, European industry joined with Russian raw materials. A prospect that would have weakened the United States, and that Washington would have had an interest in stopping. The idea has a true part and a part the numbers do not confirm. Here we separate them. This is the third piece in the series on the choices of Europe's leadership, after the one on energy . The dream "from Lisbon to Vladivostok" The project has a date. On 25 November 2010 Vladimir Putin, then prime minister, proposed in a German newspaper a great economic space "from Lisbon to Vladivostok", with a free-trade area ( Moscow Times, 25/11/2010 ). Berlin answered cautiously: Angela Merkel said she shared the idea, but that Russia was not moving in that direction ( AFP via bilaterals.org ). The project never went beyond statements. And the dollar? In 2019 Rosneft, Russia's largest oil company, switched all its export contracts from the dollar to the euro, to shield itself from American sanctions ( High North News, citing Reuters ). What the numbers say EU–Russia trade in goods (€ billion) 2002 2012 2021 2025 Imports from Russia 61 204 158 27 Exports to Russia 33 118 89 30 Sources: Eurostat, 7/3/2022 for 2012 and 2021; for 2002, Eurostat data reported by Chronicle.lu ; for 2025, Eurostat Comext data reported by The Trade Hub , consistent with the quarterly data from Eurostat . Trade grew until 2012, then fell with the Crimea crisis, the first sanctions and the drop in oil prices. In 2021 Russia accounted for 4.1% of European exports and 7.5% of imports, and 62% of what Europe bought from Moscow was energy (Eurostat, cited above). It was an important relationship but a simple one: Russian raw materials in exchange for European machinery. And before the war it was already shrinking. Russia's GDP, $1,830 billion, was about a tenth of the Union's, $17,300 billion ( World Bank via FRED ). Talk of an economic "empire" in the making finds no support in the data. Who had opposing interests American interests, on the other hand, are documented. On 20 December 2019 Trump signed a law sanctioning the companies laying Nord Stream 2. A few hours later the Swiss-Dutch company Allseas suspended work ( Reuters via PGJ ). The German government said it rejected "extraterritorial" sanctions ( EUobserver ). On 7 February 2022, next to Chancellor Scholz, Biden said that in case of an invasion Nord Stream 2 would be finished. Scholz avoided naming the pipeline ( CNBC, 7/2/2022 ). After 2022, who gained can be measured: Gas. In 2025, 54% of the liquefied gas exported by the United States went to the Union, 63% more than the year before ( Banchero Costa via Hellenic Shipping News ). The energy piece in this series showed at what price. Weapons. Between 2021 and 2025 the United States supplied 58% of the weapons imported by Europe's NATO members ( SIPRI via Defense News, 9/3/2026 ). On the dollar, by contrast, the war did not change the trend. In 1999 it made up 71% of central bank reserves; today it is at 56.7%, while the euro has risen to 20.6% ( IMF, 30/9/2026 ). An interest is not a cause Having an interest does not mean having caused an event. The full-scale war began on 24 February 2022, when Russian troops entered Ukraine. On 2 March the UN General Assembly demanded their withdrawal with 141 votes in favour ( UN, resolution ES-11/1 ). On 16 March the International Court of Justice ordered Russia to suspend its military operations ( ICJ, order ). How we got to that day, with everyone's responsibilities, is the subject of the next piece . The moral bill There is one point where the criticism of Europe fully holds. While giving up Russia in the name of principles, the Union built other relationships with fewer scruples: On 18 July 2022 Commission President von der Leyen signed an agreement in Baku to double gas from Azerbaijan by 2027, calling the country a reliable partner ( European Commission, IP/22/4550 ). A year later Azerbaijan took Nagorno-Karabakh with a military offensive, and more than a hundred thousand Armenians fled to Armenia ( UNHCR, via Reuters ). On 31 May 2023 Italy lifted the ban on selling bombs and missiles to Saudi Arabia, imposed over the war in Yemen ( Reuters via The New Arab ). In January 2024 Germany dropped its veto on Eurofighters for Riyadh, citing the Saudi attitude towards Israel after 7 October ( AP via PBS ). What worked Cutting trade took away the lever Moscow had used for years to influence European governments. Since the second quarter of 2025 the Union has had a trade surplus with Russia, for the first time in more than twenty years ( Euronews, 30/8/2025 ; Eurostat via Sofia Globe, 24/2/2026 ). A Europe that in 2021 bought 45% of its imported gas from a single country was exposed to blackmail; today it is much less so. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Those who argue that the United States had an interest in separating Europe from Russia are right: Washington said so and acted on it, with the Nord Stream sanctions and with Biden's promise. Those who argue that for this reason America "made the war break out" confuse an interest with a cause, and erase the choice of whoever sent in the tanks. The Euro-Russian market was not killed in 2022: it had stalled ten years earlier, when Moscow preferred Crimea to free trade. One fact weighs more than intentions. Whatever the cause of the war, its outcome left Europe with no alternative and made it more dependent on Washington, its main beneficiary. But the Russian alternative was itself a dependence. A sovereign Europe should have built its own autonomy, not chosen between two masters. And there is the double standard. The Union broke with Moscow in the name of principles, but at the same time resumed selling weapons to those who had bombed Yemen and called reliable a government that a year later would settle a conflict by force. Principles applied only to the enemy of the moment are not principles: they are convenience. What to watch Eurostat data on trade with Russia in 2026 and the 23rd sanctions package. From 1990 to 2022: how the war in Ukraine came about
Verbal promises never written down, treaties signed and then broken, ignored warnings, a trade dispute and eight years of war in Donbas: the facts that are uncomfortable for every side, in order.

In brief In 1990 Western leaders verbally assured Gorbachev that NATO would not expand eastwards. They never put it in writing. Russia has signed several times the right of every state to choose its own alliances , and in 1994 it guaranteed Ukraine's borders. The political clash begins around 2007-2008 . The rupture comes in 2013-2014 , when Europe and Russia compete for Ukraine's economy. Ukraine's far right existed and was armed, but it never won more than 5% at the polls. The war in Donbas killed about 14,300 people in eight years. According to the European Court of Human Rights, Russia controlled the separatist areas from May 2014 . The question The full-scale war begins on 24 February 2022, but the rupture between Europe and Russia goes back a long way. The previous piece distinguished between those who had an interest in that rupture and those who caused it. Here we set out thirty years in order, with one rule: for every fact that is uncomfortable for one side, we also look for those uncomfortable for the other, and we give the floor first to courts and international observers, then to governments. 1990: the verbal promise On 9 February 1990 US Secretary of State James Baker told Gorbachev, three times, that NATO would not move "one inch" eastwards. Bush, Kohl, Mitterrand and Thatcher said similar things. This is shown by the documents published in 2017 by the National Security Archive . But none of those statements ended up in a treaty. The treaty on German reunification only bans foreign NATO troops and nuclear weapons in the former East Germany. In 2014 Gorbachev himself said that eastward enlargement was not discussed in those years; he added, however, that the West had betrayed their spirit ( German Federal Academy for Security Policy ). What Moscow signed Helsinki 1975 and Istanbul 1999 : every state freely chooses its alliances. The Istanbul Charter adds that no one may strengthen its own security at the expense of others, the argument Moscow has always used, and that no one may consider any part of Europe its own "sphere of influence". Both are in the same paragraph. Budapest 1994 : Ukraine gives up the ex-Soviet nuclear weapons; Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom undertake to respect its borders. NATO–Russia Founding Act, 1997 : neither side has a veto over the other's decisions. And it was the Eastern countries that asked to join NATO: Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and the Baltic states remembered Soviet invasions and occupations. From cooperation to confrontation 1999. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic join NATO. In the same year NATO bombs Serbia over Kosovo without UN approval. Moscow will not forget it. 2002. It is still a time of cooperation: the NATO–Russia Council is born. In those months, standing next to Ukrainian President Kuchma, Putin says that relations between Ukraine and NATO are "a matter for those two partners" ( Kremlin ). 2007-2008. In Munich Putin openly attacks the US-led order. Warnings also come from the West: back in 1997 the American diplomat George Kennan had called enlargement the gravest error of American policy since the Cold War ( New York Times, 5/2/1997 ). In February 2008 the US ambassador in Moscow, William Burns, writes to Washington that Ukraine in NATO is the brightest red line for Russia's entire ruling class (cable published by WikiLeaks, Fair Observer ). In April, at the Bucharest summit, NATO announces that Ukraine and Georgia "will become members" ( NATO, 3/4/2008 ), but Germany and France block the concrete path to membership. The result: Moscow feels threatened, Kyiv is left without protection. In August war breaks out in Georgia; an inquiry commissioned by the European Union will conclude that Tbilisi fired first, but that Russia's response went beyond the limits of self-defence ( RTÉ, on the Tagliavini report ). Even then the road was not set: in 2010 the United States and Russia sign a new nuclear arms treaty, and in 2012 Russia joins the World Trade Organization, welcomed by Europe ( EUI ). 2013: two markets for one country The real rupture comes from an economic dispute. Moscow wants Ukraine in its customs union; Brussels offers it a free-trade agreement. It cannot have both. In August 2013 Russia blocks Ukrainian goods at the border for a week ( OSW ). An adviser to Putin calls signing with Europe "suicidal" ( Reuters via Moscow Times ). In November President Yanukovych gives up signing; on 17 December Moscow grants him $15 billion and a one-third discount on gas ( Moscow Times ). This is where the Maidan protests come from. 2014: Maidan, Crimea, Donbas Maidan. After three months of protests, Yanukovych flees in February. Between 18 and 20 February alone, in central Kyiv, 73 civilians and 11 police officers are killed ( Hromadske ). In early February a leaked phone call had already been released in which the American diplomat Victoria Nuland discussed with the ambassador who should join the government and swore at the European Union ( MPR, citing AP ): Washington wanted a say, and did not agree with Brussels. The far right. It existed and was armed. The Azov battalion was founded in 2014 and its first commander came from a neo-Nazi group; in 2018 the US Congress banned funding it ( The Hill, republished by Congressman Ro Khanna ). But at the polls it carried little weight: in 2019 the entire far right, running together, won 2.15% and stayed out of parliament ( Swedish Institute of International Affairs ). The same year Zelensky, from a Jewish family, won with 73%. Crimea and Donbas. In March Russia annexes Crimea; the UN General Assembly declares the referendum invalid, with 100 votes in favour, 11 against and 58 abstentions ( Library of Congress ). In April an armed group led by Igor Girkin, a former Russian intelligence officer, takes Sloviansk. Girkin will say he "pulled the trigger of the war", while admitting that by summer most fighters were local ( Moscow Times ). In 2025 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Russia controlled the separatist areas from 11 May 2014, and that it is responsible for shooting down flight MH17 ( ECHR, 9/7/2025 ). Odesa. On 2 May clashes between pro-Ukrainian and pro-Russian groups leave 48 dead; 42 die in the fire at the Trade Unions House, where the pro-Russian activists had barricaded themselves ( Kyiv Post ). In 2025 the European Court found against Ukraine for failing to prevent the violence, rescue the victims and investigate properly ( ECHR, 13/3/2025 ). The dead. From 2014 to 2021 the UN counts about 14,300 dead, at least 3,404 of them civilians, most in the first two years ( OHCHR ). Minsk: an agreement nobody kept The Minsk agreements (2014-2015) provided for a ceasefire, the withdrawal of weapons and foreign forces, and autonomy for Donbas. They were never implemented. In 2022 Merkel said Minsk had also served to give Ukraine time to grow stronger ( TASS, on Die Zeit ): for Moscow this is proof of Western bad faith. But Russia never withdrew its forces, as the agreement required. The last weeks In the days before the invasion OSCE monitors record a surge in shelling along the front: in Donetsk, between 18 and 20 February 2022, more than 2,100 ceasefire violations ( OSCE ). Each side blames the other. Moscow justifies the invasion with an alleged "genocide" of Russian speakers in Donbas. In March 2022 the International Court of Justice says it has no evidence of that genocide ( ICJ ). Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Explaining is not justifying. The West gave verbal assurances and then disregarded them, ignored its own diplomats and in Bucharest chose the worst path: announcing membership without granting it. Washington tried to shape the government born of Maidan. In Ukraine the armed far right was tolerated for too long, and in Odesa the state failed. These are facts, and an honest account must include them. But Russia had signed the right of every state to choose its alliances and had guaranteed Ukraine's borders. It used a trade blockade to stop Kyiv from making an economic choice, then took Crimea and Donbas. No Western mistake makes an invasion lawful: the UN Charter forbids the use of force to everyone, including those who feel threatened. It is the same yardstick we use for Washington, and it must be used for Moscow too. What to watch The next piece in the series: Europe's choices after 2022 and what they have cost. Libya: a deal to vote within two years, as militias shoot it out around the refinery

The Tripoli agreement promises elections within 24 months, but the High Council of State contests it, drones strike Zawiya and Washington negotiates a deal between families. At the end of October the UN decides its mission's mandate.

In brief On August 30, at the UN mission's headquarters in Tripoli, representatives of Libya's two camps signed an agreement: presidential and legislative elections within 24 months, under a single government. The House of Representatives in Benghazi has approved it; the heads of the High Council of State and of the Presidential Council in Tripoli contest it. In Zawiya, home to the country's main refinery, armed groups attached to ministries of the Tripoli government clashed in May (at least 13 dead) and in August. Between August 8 and 12, drones struck fuel tanks, a desalination plant and an electricity substation. Tripoli government sources, quoted by the Guardian, link the drone attacks to Saddam Haftar, Khalifa's son. There is no public evidence and no response from his camp has been reported. The UN mission's mandate expires on October 31: the Security Council must renew it this month. The background Since 2014 Libya has had two centres of power. In the west, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah's Government of National Unity, recognised by the UN, together with the High Council of State. In the east, the House of Representatives in Benghazi and General Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army, which controls most of the oil fields and terminals. The elections planned for December 2021 were postponed indefinitely and have never been rescheduled ( Security Council Report, October 2026 ). This year UN mediation has produced two results: in April the first unified budget in more than ten years, and in August an electoral agreement ( Al Jazeera, 8/7/2026 ). On the ground, however, the violence has not stopped. Who is who Institution or force Led by Position on the Tripoli agreement Tripoli · Government of National Unity, recognised by the UN Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, prime minister Signed through two of its delegates Tripoli · Presidential Council, collective head of state Mohamed al-Menfi Critical: questions the transparency of the talks and the role of foreigners Tripoli · High Council of State, second chamber Mohamed Takala Opposed: stayed away from the signing and on September 22 rejected the outcome together with other parties Benghazi · House of Representatives, the parliament elected in 2014 Aguila Saleh, speaker In favour: approved on September 14 Benghazi · Libyan National Army Khalifa Haftar, commander; his son Saddam, deputy commander Signed through two of its delegates Then there are the Zawiya militias , formally serving the Tripoli government: Mohamed Bahroun's Anti-Security Threats Agency (attached to the prime minister's office), Othman al-Lahab's 103rd Infantry Brigade (defence ministry), Muhannad al-Suwaisi's judicial security (justice ministry) and Mohamed Kashlaf's Petroleum Facilities Guard ( ACLED ; Libya Crimes Watch ). And the outside actors . The UN mediates through its mission, led by envoy Hanna Tetteh. The United States is working on a plan of its own through Massad Boulos and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Turkey, Tripoli's long-standing backer, has extended military cooperation to Saddam Haftar; Qatar and France have received or met Haftar ( Al Jazeera, 1/9/2026 ). Russia and the United Arab Emirates have been documented for years on Haftar's side. Italy hosted in Rome, in April, the first meeting of the small negotiating table that later wrote the agreement ( Security Council Report ). The facts The Tripoli agreement. On August 30 eight delegates, two for the Tripoli government, two for Haftar's command, two for the House of Representatives and two for the High Council of State, signed a seven-article text ( UNSMIL, text of the agreement ). The agreement reconstitutes the leadership of the electoral commission, revises the voting laws and sets presidential and legislative elections within 24 months, "under a single executive authority". The new rules allow military personnel to run for president, with neutrality safeguards, as well as dual nationals, provided they renounce their other citizenship before taking the oath. According to Al Jazeera, both Haftars are believed to hold US citizenship: the rule seems written with them in mind too. If the two chambers do not approve it within a month, the parties will seek the Security Council's endorsement. On September 8 the Council welcomed the agreement as "an important step" towards free elections ( Italpress, 9/9/2026 ). Who approves and who does not. On September 14 Aguila Saleh's House of Representatives approved it in Benghazi. Mohamed Takala, who leads the High Council of State, and Mohamed al-Menfi, who leads the Presidential Council, contest it: they argue that key institutions were left out of the talks, which were in practice conducted by Dbeibah's government and Haftar's command ( Libyan Express, 21/9/2026 ). On September 22 the High Council and some parties rejected the outcome of the talks, demanding that it not override the constitutional declaration or the powers of the institutions ( Xinhua, 22/9/2026 ). The rejection comes from the High Council even though two of the signatories are its members. Zawiya. Forty-seven kilometres from Tripoli stands Libya's largest operating refinery. In 2026 the monitoring group ACLED counted more than 30 armed clashes in the city, linked to territorial control and fuel smuggling ( ACLED, 12/8/2026 ). On May 8 fighting between rival groups killed at least 13 people, civilians included ( UNSMIL, briefing of 18/6/2026 ). On August 4 new clashes in Zawiya and Surman killed three civilians and injured four, including two children and a migrant. The groups involved, according to the NGO Libya Crimes Watch, formally report to the defence ministry, the justice ministry and the prime minister's office of the Tripoli government ( Libya Crimes Watch ). The drones. Between August 8 and 11 at least five drone attacks hit Zawiya: a naphtha tank, a desalination plant, a tank holding about 4.5 million litres of petrol, then two diesel tanks at the refinery. On August 12 an electricity substation was hit, causing a blackout south of the city. No one has claimed the attacks ( ACLED ; The New Arab, 7/9/2026 ). On September 6 Dbeibah's government announced the arrest of five people, Libyan and foreign, without identifying them or presenting evidence. On October 3 the Guardian reported that, according to sources in the same government, three of those arrested belong to a Libyan National Army brigade and were working for Saddam Haftar. The allegations have not been independently verified and no response from Haftar's camp has been reported ( The New Arab, 4/10/2026 ). The oil. On September 21 an armed group closed a valve on the pipeline that carries crude from the Sharara field to Zawiya, cutting production. On September 26 the UN mission warned that anyone who attacks or obstructs energy infrastructure may face Security Council measures under resolution 2213 of 2015 ( Libya Herald, 26/9/2026 ). The American plan. In parallel, Donald Trump's envoy for Africa, Massad Boulos, is working on a deal to unify the institutions. According to leaked and unconfirmed details, Saddam Haftar would become president and Dbeibah would remain prime minister. The United States would encourage its companies to invest in the oil fields ( Al Jazeera, 8/7/2026 ). On September 22 Boulos rejected the charge that he wants to hand the country to two families: "It's going to be an absolute partnership" ( Semafor, 22/9/2026 ). Russia and China, in the Council, insist instead on a Libyan-led process. Legal commentary The agreement. It is a political understanding between Libyan parties, not a treaty. Its strength depends on the approval of the two chambers, and that is where it has stalled. Article 5 provides, failing that, for recourse to the Security Council: an outside endorsement when the institutions at home cannot agree. Who answers for the clashes. In Zawiya it is not a government fighting its enemies, but armed groups wearing the insignia of ministries of the same government. Under the rules on State responsibility drawn up by the UN International Law Commission (article 4), the conduct of State organs is attributable to the State. The Tripoli government cannot present those clashes as the doings of militias foreign to it. International humanitarian law, including customary law, protects civilians and objects indispensable to their survival, such as a desalination plant. The UN mission has called for prompt and credible investigations into civilian casualties. The International Criminal Court. In May 2025 Libya accepted the Court's jurisdiction over crimes committed from 2011 to 2027. In July this year the Court confirmed 17 charges against Khaled El Hishri, a former official of Mitiga prison in Tripoli, for torture, rape and killings of detainees: it is the first Libyan case to go to trial. Eight suspects are still at large, in the east and the west ( Human Rights Watch, 16/7/2026 ). Among the wanted was Osama Almasri, arrested in Italy in January 2025 and sent back to Libya two days later. The 2011 arms embargo remains in force, violated by both sides, as we documented in July . Symmetry test Tripoli. The deaths in Zawiya were caused by groups formally serving the government recognised by the UN. The same government blames "external entities" without public evidence. Benghazi. The accusation against Saddam Haftar comes from his opponent's sources and is not proven. Haftar's camp controls most of the oil and would be among the beneficiaries of the American plan. The outsiders. Washington is negotiating a deal between families with an eye on the oil fields. Russia and China call for a Libyan-led process, but Chinese and Turkish weapons have been documented at Haftar's bases, alongside Russian and Emirati support (we reported on it in July). Italy sent a suspect wanted by the Court back home. What worked. April's unified budget, the first in more than ten years; the agreement on the electoral commission; the International Criminal Court's first trial over a Libyan prison. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. Libya today has two roads out of division, and they lead in different directions. The Tripoli agreement aims for the ballot box: imperfect, contested, but built on written rules and with a deadline. The American plan aims for a pact among those already in charge, with oil as the glue. The second may arrive sooner; the first is the only one that gives the choice back to Libyans. But neither road says what to do about the weapons. In Zawiya, groups paid by the State are fighting each other, and no one answers for the drones. As long as the guns stay with those who hold them, an election risks being just another negotiation between militias with a date on the calendar. The renewal of the UN mandate is the moment to say so: a political mission without a disarmament plan can accompany an agreement, not guarantee it. What to watch The renewal of the UN mission's mandate by October 31 and Hanna Tetteh's briefing to the Security Council. The High Council of State's formal approval or rejection, and any recourse to the Security Council. The investigation into the drone attacks and the evidence the Tripoli government has promised. The fate of the Boulos plan after the accusations against Saddam Haftar. The start date of El Hishri's trial. Are the world's wars "Muslim"? What the data say, and what the causes are

In 2025 the world counted 65 armed conflicts. How many involve Muslims, why there, and who pays the price: the data contradict both the "they are the problem" story and the "it's all the West's fault" story.

In brief In 2025 the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) counted 65 armed conflicts between states and organised groups, a record. In 23 the state is fighting jihadist groups; in 21 there is no Muslim party at all. Uppsala researchers have shown that conflicts with Islamist claims, absent in 1975, numbered 28 out of 50 in 2015. They last longer and flare up again more often: what explains this is the political programme of the armed groups, not the Muslim identity of the fighters. Muslims are 25.6% of humanity, and about 60% live in Asia and the Pacific: most of them in countries such as Indonesia, India, Bangladesh and Malaysia, which are not at war. In 2025, 62% of the world's battle deaths were in the war between Russia and Ukraine. The largest massacre of civilians, in Sudan, was committed by Muslims against Muslims. The causes lie on four levels: fragile ground (weak states, colonial legacy, oil), a spark (often abuses by the state), a banner (armed Islamism) and an external multiplier (a strategic position that draws in foreign powers). The question Anyone who follows news from the world's wars often has the same impression: Syria, Yemen, Afghanistan, the Sahel, Somalia, Gaza, Libya. It seems that almost everywhere there is fighting, Muslims are involved. The most common answer in the West is simple: the problem is Islam. The opposite answer is just as simple: it is all the fault of colonialism and of those who steal resources. Let us put both to the test of the numbers. What the data say The Uppsala Conflict Data Program, the Swedish university research centre that has been recording armed conflicts since 1989, counted 65 conflicts in 2025 in which a state fights another state or an armed group. It is the highest number since its records began ( Journal of Peace Research, 2026 ). We classified the full list according to who is fighting and what they are claiming: Group Conflicts Examples The state against jihadist groups 23 Islamic State in Iraq, Syria, Afghanistan, Nigeria, Mozambique, Congo; JNIM in Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, Benin, Togo; al-Shabaab in Somalia and Kenya; Pakistani Taliban Islamist movements or governments in wars over territory or power 8 Israel against Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis; Iran against Israel; the Afghan Taliban against opponents and Pakistan Muslim parties without religious claims 13 Turkey against the Kurdish PKK; Pakistan against Baloch separatists; India against Pakistan over Kashmir; Sudan; Syria against Kurdish forces No Muslim party 21 Russia against Ukraine; five conflicts in Myanmar; Congo against M23; Ethiopia; South Sudan; Colombia; Haiti The classification is ours and some cases are debatable: in Kashmir, for example, armed groups mix nationalist and jihadist claims. But the picture does not change. The initial impression has a real basis: in just under half of the conflicts there is an Islamist party. Yet one war in three involves no Muslims at all. The trend is recent. According to the Uppsala researchers themselves, in 1975 no conflict within a state was fought over Islamist claims; in 2015, 28 out of 50 were, as were 73% of the bloodiest civil wars ( SIPRI Yearbook 2017 ). A later study found that these wars are 29% less likely to end and 73% more likely to flare up again. The authors' explanation is not the fighters' religion: it is the Islamist programme, which brings with it transnational networks, foreign fighters and distant financiers. Muslim identity alone, they write, does not explain the effect ( Nilsson and Svensson, International Studies Quarterly, 2021 ). Two figures complete the picture. Muslims are 25.6% of the world's population, about two billion people, and about 60% live in Asia and the Pacific ( Pew Research Center, 2025 ). The exceptions at war are Pakistan and Afghanistan; but Indonesia, the country with the most Muslims in the world, Bangladesh, Malaysia and the roughly 200 million Muslims of India are not. If faith were enough to produce wars, the wars would be mostly there. And in 2025 the world's bloodiest war, with about 62% of battle deaths, was the one between Russia and Ukraine, two countries of Christian tradition. Why there If it is not faith, what is it? Research points to four levels that add up. The ground. Weak states, borders drawn by colonial powers, economies built to extract rather than to produce. Then oil, the only raw material that studies consistently link to the outbreak of civil wars. The effect, however, is conditional: countries with a great deal of it, such as Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Qatar and Kuwait, buy social peace with the rent. The risk rises where the state depends on oil but has little of it, or where producing regions are excluded from power ( European Political Science Review ). This ground, however, also exists where Islam plays no part: Congo, whose resources have been plundered from the colonial era to today, has been at war for thirty years without Islam being involved, apart from one militia in the east. The spark. In 2023 the UN Development Programme interviewed more than a thousand former fighters of extremist groups in eight African countries. The first reason for joining was finding a job (25%); religion came third (17%), and most knew little of the sacred texts. Almost half pointed to a specific event that had pushed them, and in 71% of cases it was an abuse they had suffered, often at the hands of the state's security forces: a relative killed or arrested ( UNDP, 2023 ). The banner. Armed Islamism has a recent and precise history. It took shape after the failure of secular Arab nationalism, with the defeat of 1967. It exploded in 1979, the year of the Iranian revolution and of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, against which the United States, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan funded the Islamist guerrillas from which the international jihadist networks were born. It fed on the petrodollars with which the Gulf states spread the Salafi current, the most rigid. It was reborn with the invasion of Iraq in 2003, from which the Islamic State emerged, and spread to the Sahel after the fall of Libya in 2011, which poured weapons across the region. The banner is not the first cause, but it is not neutral: it brings money, fighters and networks, and it makes wars last longer. In the Sahel the JNIM group finances itself with ransoms, stolen cattle, road tolls and gold taxed at artisanal mines ( African Security Network ). The external multiplier. Geography is a resource too. Yemen sits on the Bab el-Mandeb strait, through which about 12% of world maritime trade passes; Somalia on the Gulf of Aden. That is why their internal crises have become contests between powers: Saudi Arabia, the Emirates and Iran in Yemen, as we reported here ; Ethiopia, which is seeking access to the sea, and Israel, which in December 2025 recognised separatist Somaliland, around Somalia ( Al Jazeera, 3/10/2026 ). But a strategic position is not a sentence. Djibouti sits on the same strait as Yemen and rents its territory to bases of the United States, China, France, Japan and Italy: "our geography is our oil", a government official said ( Al Jazeera, 8/4/2026 ). Oman sits on Hormuz and is one of the most stable countries in the region. Geography does not explain why people fight; it explains why a local war becomes international, and why it then does not end. Who dies If Muslims often appear among those who fight, they appear even more often among those who die. The victims of terrorism. In 2025 terrorism killed 5,582 people. Seven of the ten worst-affected countries are Muslim-majority or have large Muslim communities: Pakistan, Burkina Faso, Niger, Nigeria, Mali, Syria, Somalia. The Sahel alone accounts for more than half of the deaths ( Global Terrorism Index 2026 ). Jihadists mostly kill other Muslims. But not only: in eastern Congo, the local Islamic State affiliate disproportionately targets Christians. Muslims against Muslims. In 2025 the world recorded the highest number of civilians deliberately killed since the Rwandan genocide, mainly because of the massacres in Sudan: at least 60,000 dead by mid-December according to Uppsala, mostly at the hands of the Rapid Support Forces. In Sudan perpetrators and victims are overwhelmingly Muslim. Muslims struck by others. The Rohingya in Myanmar, on whose case the International Court of Justice is due to rule on the charge of genocide. The Uyghurs in China, for whom the UN Human Rights Office in 2022 spoke of violations that may constitute crimes against humanity; Beijing rejects the accusations ( OHCHR ). The Palestinians of Gaza, for whom the UN commission of inquiry led by Navi Pillay concluded in 2025 that Israeli forces and leaders committed four of the five acts of genocide listed in the Convention; Israel rejects the conclusion, as we reconstructed here . Legal commentary International law already has an answer to the question "is a religion to blame?", and the answer is no, in two senses. On the one hand, it protects religious groups as potential victims . The 1948 Genocide Convention lists religious groups among those that may not be destroyed (art. II). The UN Covenant on Civil and Political Rights protects freedom of religion (art. 18) and obliges states to prohibit by law incitement to religious hatred (art. 20). On the other, it punishes people, never faiths . The principle was written at Nuremberg: crimes against international law are committed by men, not by abstract entities. Today it is in the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (art. 25). The Court has convicted Al Hassan, former head of the Islamic police imposed by jihadists in Timbuktu, to 10 years, and Ali Kushayb, commander of the Janjaweed militias in Darfur, to 20 years ( AllAfrica, 10/12/2025 ); its prosecutor has requested an arrest warrant for the head of Myanmar's junta. People are judged, not Islam or Buddhism. Any collective accusation against a religion overturns this principle. Symmetry test Armed religious extremism is not only Islamic. Buddhist nationalism in Myanmar accompanied the persecution of the Rohingya; in the Central African Republic both the Muslim Séléka militias and the Christian anti-balaka killed; in India Hindu nationalism fuels violence against Muslims; in the West Bank some settlers act in the name of a religious claim to the land. But today it weighs less in the numbers, and that must be said. None of these forms of violence today has the scale of the jihadist insurgencies in the Sahel, Somalia or Nigeria. Denying the role of armed Islamism would be the same shortcut, reversed, as accusing Islam. The West has also played a part , and not only as a colonial power: through support for the Afghan mujahideen in the 1980s, the invasion of Iraq and the intervention in Libya. The same goes for the Gulf states that funded the most rigid Islam, for Iran with its militias and for Russia in the Sahel. Our assessment This section expresses the site's position. It is separate from the facts set out above. The question "perpetrators or victims?" presupposes that "Muslims" are a subject that acts. They are not: they are two billion people, from Indonesia to Senegal, who mostly live in peace. Among those who fight, however, a real share do so under an Islamist banner, and that banner makes wars longer and crueller. Among those who die, Muslims are the majority in many of today's conflicts. The causes do not lie in the Quran, nor only in colonialism. They lie in states that do not protect their citizens and indeed strike them, in economies that live off a single rent, in geographical positions that attract foreign powers, and in an armed ideology that offers those who have nothing a job, revenge and an enemy. Removing just one of these elements is rarely enough; ignoring one, as both those who accuse Islam and those who absolve it wholesale do, leads to the wrong solutions. That is why the yardstick of law is the only one that holds: look at the facts, name those responsible, protect the victims, whatever their faith and that of those who kill them. What to watch UCDP's next annual report (June 2027), to see whether the share of jihadist conflicts rises or falls. The International Court of Justice's ruling on the Rohingya case. The evolution of JNIM in the Sahel and its expansion towards the coastal states of the Gulf of Guinea. The foreign military presence around Bab el-Mandeb and in Somaliland.
