BRICS: what they are, who belongs, and what their documents say
A guide to the BRICS: origins, members and partners, how they decide, how much they weigh in population and GDP, and where they stand on the ICJ and the ICC. A living entry.

When an article on this site mentions “the BRICS” or “the BRICS declaration”, it assumes the reader already knows what that is. Often they do not: it is a group of States with no founding treaty, much discussed but little known in its membership, rules and numbers. This entry is updatable: every change is recorded at the bottom, with date and source. What it is BRICS is the name of a group of States whose heads of State and government meet at an annual summit. It began as an economic acronym, coined in 2001 by the economist Jim O'Neill, then at Goldman Sachs, for Brazil, Russia, India and China. The group, then BRIC, was formalised in 2006 with the first meeting of foreign ministers on the margins of the UN General Assembly, and the first leaders' summit was held in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009. South Africa was included in 2010 and attended its first summit, in Sanya, in 2011. Who belongs Eleven members: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have been full members since January 2024, Indonesia since January 2025, according to the official site of the 2026 Indian chairship. Saudi Arabia's status is nonetheless contested. The Indian chairship's site lists it among the eleven, as did the official site of the 2025 Brazilian chairship; Riyadh, however, takes part as an “invited country”, and Reuters reported in May 2025 that it had held off formally joining. The InfoBRICS portal, in its introductory text, lists ten members without Saudi Arabia: the divergence exists even among sources close to the bloc. There is also a category of “partner countries”, created at the Kazan summit (October 2024). There are ten, all of which joined in 2025: Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam. How it works The group has no founding treaty: it describes itself as an informal group, and its reference documents are the summit declarations (Johannesburg 2023, Kazan 2024, Rio 2025, New Delhi 2026), which set admissions and categories. The chair rotates every year (2024 Russia, 2025 Brazil, 2026 India, 2027 China) and declarations are adopted by consensus. There is no common currency. Institutions linked to the group do have treaties of their own, such as the New Development Bank, the group's development bank, and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement, a financial support mechanism among members. ¶138 of the 2026 declaration calls the group's institutional development “a continuous process”. Why the numbers matter Population. Almost half of humanity: the official site of the Indian chairship gives 49.5%, with no year or method (other estimates: 48.5%). GDP at nominal values. 35.2 trillion dollars, 27.9% of the world total (126.3 trillion). Without Saudi Arabia: 26.8%. GDP at purchasing power parity (PPP). 91.3 trillion international dollars, 41.0% of the world total (222.8 trillion). Without Saudi Arabia: 39.7%. The official site of the Indian chairship gives 40% of world GDP without specifying the measure: on IMF data, 40% corresponds to PPP, not to nominal value. That is why this entry always reports both. China's weight. About 59% of the bloc's nominal GDP and 48% of its PPP GDP; with India it reaches 71% of the nominal total. In nominal terms the G7 remains larger (55.3 trillion, 43.8% of the world); in PPP it is smaller (62.3 trillion, 28.0%). Method: sum of IMF World Economic Outlook values (April 2026), 2026 estimates, the editor's calculation. Other sources give different figures because they use different perimeters (10 or 11 members) or editions. Demographic and economic weight does not mean cohesion or mutual approval: members include States on opposite sides of ongoing conflicts. Relations with the international courts All eleven are parties to the Statute of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) as UN members. Accepting its compulsory jurisdiction in advance (Article 36(2)) is quite different, and holds for a minority of the world's States (about 75 out of 193, as the ICJ entry explains). For the International Criminal Court (ICC), what counts is ratification or signature of the Rome Statute . Parties to the Rome Statute: Brazil (2002) and South Africa (2000). Signed, never ratified: Egypt, Iran and the United Arab Emirates (2000). Signature withdrawn: Russia (2016). Never signed: China, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia and Saudi Arabia. Compulsory ICJ jurisdiction: India (2019, with reservations), Egypt (1957, limited to disputes under paragraph 9(b) of the declaration on the Suez Canal) and Iran (2023, limited to the jurisdictional immunities of the State and its property; filed the day before it brought Canada before the Court). No declaration for Brazil, China, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE. ICJ jurisdiction may still arise from specific treaties, such as the Genocide Convention: the South Africa v. Israel case rests on that. Where to find official sources The group has no permanent website: each chairship opens its own (2026: brics2026.gov.in, launched on 13 January 2026; 2025: brics.br). They are sites of the government in office, hence sources with a stake as regards members and results: they must be declared as such. InfoBRICS is not an institutional site but a news and analysis portal with a marked editorial line: it should not be used as a source for facts. Apartheid: from the South African regime to an international crime, two distinct definitions
The 1973 UN Convention and the Rome Statute define apartheid as a standalone crime, applicable anywhere — not only to South Africa. What is needed to use the term in its technical sense.

"Apartheid" first denotes a specific historical regime — South Africa from 1948 to 1994. But since 1973 it has also been a technical term of international law, with its own legal definition, applicable in principle to any situation meeting its elements, not only to that historical case. The two must be kept separate: this entry explains the second. The historical origin The Afrikaans term "apartheid" ("separateness") denotes the system of racial segregation institutionalised by law in South Africa from 1948, which classified the population by race and regulated by law residence, employment, education and political rights. South Africa remained a UN member throughout the regime; the international community responded by declaring the government's conduct illegitimate, suspending it from specialised agencies and imposing a mandatory arms embargo (Security Council Resolution 418, 1977), until the system collapsed in 1990–1994. Codification as a standalone crime The International Convention on the Suppression and Punishment of the Crime of Apartheid, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1973, defines apartheid in Article II as "similar policies and practices of racial segregation and discrimination as practised in southern Africa" — an explicit extension beyond the South African case alone, applicable to any system of institutionalised domination of one racial group over another, sustained by inhuman acts committed to maintain it. The 1998 Rome Statute lists apartheid as a crime against humanity in Article 7, paragraphs 1(j) and 2(h). The two treaties together have been ratified by more than 160 States. A recent case: the International Court of Justice's opinion In its advisory opinion of 19 July 2024 on the occupied Palestinian territory, the International Court of Justice concluded that Israeli legislation and measures that segregate settler and Palestinian communities in the West Bank and East Jerusalem breach Article 3 of the UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (CERD), which prohibits "racial segregation and apartheid." A clear technical distinction must be kept: the Court did not rule on the crime of apartheid as such under the 1973 Convention or the Rome Statute — treaties Israel has, in any case, never joined — but on a breach of CERD, which Israel has instead ratified. These are distinct legal standards, even though the text of Article 3 of CERD explicitly uses the word "apartheid." A category not yet codified: gender apartheid This site has already used the phrase "gender apartheid" in relation to Afghanistan, where the UN Special Rapporteur described in these terms the cumulative effect of the restrictions the Taliban have imposed on women. That is a different use from this entry: it is a category proposed by diplomats and jurists, not yet codified as a standalone crime in any treaty — the International Criminal Court, not by coincidence, had to resort to the closest available category, gender persecution (Art. 7(1)(h) of the Rome Statute), precisely because "gender apartheid" is not yet a crime in its own right. The treaty that in 1998 defined apartheid, genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in a single text. Genocide: international law's narrowest definition, and why it is almost impossible to prove
The 1948 Convention defines genocide through five acts and a specific intent that must be proven. Why it is the hardest crime to establish, and who rules on what.

When this site reports that a UN body has "found" or "concluded" a genocide, it always refers to a specific finding against a precise legal definition — not a judgment of moral gravity. Genocide is, by design, the international crime with the highest evidentiary threshold: an enormous death toll is not enough on its own; what must be proven is a precise intent. This entry explains what is required to use the term in its technical sense, and who has the authority to establish it. What it is The Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 9 December 1948 and in force since 12 January 1951 (153 States parties), defines genocide in Article II as any of five acts — killing members of the group; causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group; deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part; imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group; forcibly transferring children of the group to another group — committed "with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such." Article III also punishes attempt, conspiracy, complicity and direct and public incitement to commit it. The Rome Statute repeats the identical definition in Article 6. The element that makes it almost impossible to prove What distinguishes genocide from other mass crimes is not the scale of the victims but the "dolus specialis": the specific intent to destroy the group as such, not merely its individual members. An extremely high civilian death toll is not enough on its own — it must be shown that destroying the group, as a group, was the purpose pursued, not a side-effect of another aim (military, territorial, economic). This is why international courts and tribunals always draw a careful distinction between war crimes or crimes against humanity — which require proving conduct — and genocide, which additionally requires proving intent. Who rules on what The International Court of Justice judges States, for breaches of the 1948 Convention between States parties; it can order "provisional measures" during proceedings, which are not a ruling on the merits. The International Criminal Court judges individuals, under Article 6 of the Rome Statute. A third, non-judicial level consists of fact-finding missions and commissions established by the UN Human Rights Council: they can conclude there are "reasonable grounds" to believe a genocide is under way, but they issue no rulings and hold no coercive power. Keeping these three levels separate — a judicial finding on the merits, a provisional measure, and the conclusion of an inquiry body — is essential to avoid conflating different degrees of certainty. Cases already covered on this site This site has applied the definition to several theatres, with different outcomes. In Sudan , the UN Fact-Finding Mission concluded on 19 February 2026 that the RSF's campaign against the non-Arab Zaghawa and Fur communities bears the hallmarks of genocide, after the US government had already issued its own determination in January 2025. In Myanmar , the International Court of Justice held merits hearings in the Gambia v. Myanmar case over the 2017 campaign against the Rohingya — a State-to-State proceeding still without a final judgment. In the Democratic Republic of Congo , the reference is twofold: the 1994 genocide in Rwanda as an established historical fact, and a new DRC v. Rwanda case filed in 2026 that also invokes the Genocide Convention — a newly filed claim, not a ruling. In Ethiopia , advocacy organisations such as the Lemkin Institute describe the situation in Amhara as an ongoing genocide: this site reports it explicitly as a partisan position, since no UN judicial or inquiry body has so far confirmed it. In Gaza , the UN Commission of Inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel has committed genocide, finding four of the five prohibited acts under the Convention — a conclusion by an inquiry body, not a ruling by the ICJ or the ICC, whose South Africa v. Israel case at the ICJ remains open and without a merits ruling. Who actually applies the Rome Statute, how the Court born from it works, and why an arrest warrant is often not enough. An independent analysis measures the gap between the facts reported on Gaza and the judgment never rendered. Then the names: Kushner, Adelson, von der Leyen, Germany — the mechanism that makes negotiable what postwar law was meant to make impossible.

“The news is there. The judgment is not.” — N3R1-70 Every day the numbers arrive. Collapsed buildings, percentages, updated death tolls: newsrooms publish them, update them, and stop there. An independent analysis of over 1,100 articles from the three largest American newspapers measured exactly how much: every Israeli victim received eight mentions, every Palestinian victim barely one for every two deaths. An internal New York Times memo, made public by a journalistic investigation, instructed reporters to avoid the words “genocide,” “ethnic cleansing,” “occupied territory.” This is not carelessness. It is a documented editorial choice. And yet, somewhere, judgment is taking shape. On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice ruled that Israel's occupation of the Palestinian territories violates the international prohibition on racial segregation and apartheid — not a binding ruling, but an authoritative opinion from the UN's highest court. A separate case, filed by South Africa in December 2023, accuses Israel of violating the Genocide Convention: it is still ongoing, stuck at the written-pleadings stage, with no ruling on the merits. A fact to report precisely, neither inflated nor minimized. And the International Criminal Court , which judges individuals rather than states, issued arrest warrants against Israel's prime minister and his former defense minister in November 2024. While these proceedings crawl forward at The Hague, money moves on a much faster track. And this is where the picture stops being abstract and becomes a matter of names, concrete choices, people who can be pointed to. Money moves faster than law Take Jared Kushner. In February 2024, still a private citizen, he said in a public interview at Harvard that Gaza's waterfront “could be very valuable” once Israel had “moved the people” out and “cleaned up” the area — his own words, not a hostile paraphrase. That private citizen no longer exists. Since 19 February 2026, Kushner has been the United States Special Envoy for Peace Missions, and is also one of the founding executive members of the “Board of Peace” Trump established to oversee the twenty-point plan for Gaza, alongside Tony Blair, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and other heavyweight names such as the CEO of Apollo Global Management and the President of the World Bank. And while he negotiates the peace and oversees its reconstruction, he remains the president's son-in-law and head of an investment fund, Affinity Partners, which between 2021 and 2026 raised billions of dollars from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE, investing it, among other things, in Israeli companies tied to defense. A U.S. House committee put it in writing in an April 2026 letter: the man deciding how the war ends has a direct financial stake in how it ends. Then there is Miriam Adelson. She gave $25 million to the medical school of Ariel University, a settlement in the West Bank, explaining that the gift serves to “strengthen the settlers in Judea and Samaria” — biblical names that, as she herself has said, imply the land was given to the Jews by God. Another six million went to an organization that arms volunteers guarding settler farms. She owns Israel's highest-circulation newspaper, in whose pages she wrote that anyone who does not unconditionally condemn Israel's adversaries is “dead to us.” And she gave over one hundred million dollars to the committee that backed Trump's return to the White House. Private money, however, is only half the mechanism. The other half is the inertia of those who have the power to intervene and choose not to, or do so too late. Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, flew to Tel Aviv in October 2023 to offer “unconditional” support for the war against Hamas, without consulting the rest of the EU's institutions — so much so that the EU's then foreign-policy chief publicly accused her of speaking “in her own name only.” That same month, over eight hundred European officials and diplomats wrote her an open letter denouncing a “double standard”: Russia's blockade of Ukraine treated as an act of terrorism, Israel's blockade of Gaza ignored. In February 2024, Ireland and Spain formally asked her to review the EU-Israel trade agreement in light of the emergency measures just ordered by the Hague court. Von der Leyen will actually suspend, even if only partially, that agreement — but not until September 2025, nearly two years later, finally speaking of “man-made famine” in Gaza. Germany tells the same story in its military version. It is Israel's second-largest arms supplier after the United States, and after October 7 its approved exports increased tenfold. Chancellor Friedrich Merz suspended exports usable in Gaza in August 2025, citing the military expansion into the city — but within a month and a half his own government had already approved new ones, and in November, after the ceasefire, the suspension was lifted entirely. Lined up, these cases do not tell a conspiracy story. They tell something simpler, and for that reason more unsettling: private capital, media ownership, political office, and institutional inertia can, together, make negotiable what the 1948 Genocide Convention and the 1998 Rome Statute were meant to make impossible — not only for Israel, but wherever the same ingredient appears in sufficient dose. It is the same mechanism this editorial space has already documented elsewhere, in selectively applied nuclear standards and in the chronic lack of enforcement of the International Criminal Court in general. Money buys narrative. Narrative buys time. Time, without coercive enforcement, becomes impunity. This is what I mean when I say the West's presumed moral supremacy is being dismantled: not because a single government commits a crime, but because the system the West built specifically to prevent that crime from going unpunished proves, under sufficient pressure, negotiable. What remains, whatever happens Some of the states involved in the Nuremberg trials contested their legitimacy even as they were being held. Today those trials are the foundation of all subsequent international criminal law — including the very Rome Statute the International Criminal Court now invokes against an Israeli head of government. A state's present refusal to recognize a court does not erase the value its finding will carry over time. The work done remains. The judgment rendered remains. “And it remains available to whoever, one day, decides to stop looking away.” Israel Gaza International law International Criminal Court Genocide European Union United States International governance
The UN says it isn’t safe to return to Afghanistan. Pakistan keeps sending people back — even now that the two countries have declared war.
Pakistan sent 146,000 Afghans back in 2026 despite UNHCR advice against return — while the two countries are now in open war. The stories of those deported, and the same logic already seen in Europe.

— Pakistan / Afghanistan In Saxony-Anhalt, the far right just won a landslide in regional elections — 44% of the vote on 6 September, double its 2021 score — promising a “deportation task force.” In Rome, the government is proposing to the European Union that it replicate elsewhere the model of Albania's migrant centres; among the candidate countries is Uganda. These are stories readers of this site have probably already come across. Eleven thousand kilometres away, the same logic — moving the problem instead of solving it — already has a face: Zainab's. Zainab is 47, a widow, and a former teacher. On 4 March 2026 she was deported from Pakistan to Afghanistan along with her son — arrested despite holding valid documents. She left behind the savings she had been setting aside to treat his kidney condition in Quetta. At the border, she recalls, gunfire and explosions could be heard. Freshta, a mother of six, was separated from two of her children — aged 8 and 10 — during an arrest in January 2026. “I ran after my children, but they wouldn't let me,” she recalls. She now lives in a tent 12 kilometres from the Torkham border, with no direct contact with the children: she has been told they may have been detained. Omar was born and raised in Pakistan; deported seven months ago with his five children, he discovered that in Afghanistan they cannot continue school past sixth grade. Rabia, 27, worked as a seamstress: deported five months ago, she cannot afford formula milk for her newborn son. These are four of the hundreds of thousands of people Pakistan sent back to Afghanistan in 2026 alone: 146,000, at a pace that has been rising since April — part of a flow that exceeds 5.4 million people expelled by Pakistan and Iran since October 2023, when Islamabad announced mass expulsions citing a link between Afghan refugees and suicide bombings. Human Rights Watch documents, in just the most recent phase, arrests without warrants, confiscation of phones and cash, bribe demands for release, children deported without their parents, and at least 9 Afghan journalists forcibly returned since the start of the year. In November 2025, more than 1,000 people were detained in a single operation at the Surkhab camp in Balochistan. On 27 February 2026 Pakistan's defence minister declared open war on the Taliban, accusing them of sheltering the TTP and al-Qaeda, after a suicide bombing at a Shia mosque in Islamabad and Pakistani airstrikes on Afghan territory. This is where the story changes register without anyone announcing it: the justification on which everything began in 2023 — refugees as a security threat — has not been renewed. The official enemy of 2026 is an armed organisation, no longer a population. Yet the deportations continue regardless, at the same pace, now inside a declared war between the two states rather than alongside it. The law Since September 2025 UNHCR has updated its protection assessment for Afghanistan ( Guidance Note on Afghanistan — Update II , replacing the 2023 version): it maintains a recommendation against return and identifies groups at specific risk of persecution on return — among ethnic minorities, Baluch, Hazara, Tajik, Turkmen, Uzbek, and among religious groups, Ahmadi, Baha'i, Christians, Hindus, Ismailis, Salafis, Shia, Sikhs, Sufis. The symmetry test The same principle already set out on this site regarding Turkey and Germany's return policy toward Syria applies here, unchanged: the criterion does not change when the actors are swapped, only the form of the violation changes. In Berlin it is a government objective stated in public — returning 80% of Syrians within three years. In Islamabad it is an administrative default that continues under a justification that has since changed. In neither case does the deported person have a say in the decision, and in neither case is the safety assessment made by the competent UN agency treated as binding by those doing the returning. The same question could be asked of Rome and Brussels as much as of Islamabad — we will write about that separately. This does not equate the severity of the two contexts — the declared war between Pakistan and Afghanistan has no equivalent in the Syrian case — but the legal substance of the violation is the same. Taiwan: the price of a balance no one wants to break

Since 2022 the “Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis” has been underway: Beijing is shifting pressure from air incursions to permanent naval patrols, while Washington treats the arms it promised Taipei as a bargaining chip with Beijing.

— Taipei · Beijing · Washington “We must prepare for the worst while hoping for the best.” — Lai Ching-te, President of Taiwan, January 2026 The facts Since 1949, when the Kuomintang, defeated in the Chinese civil war, retreated to Taiwan, the island has never been governed by the People's Republic of China. UN General Assembly Resolution 2758 of 1971, which gave Beijing China's seat at the United Nations, does not mention Taiwan — yet the UN Secretariat has in practice treated it as “a province of China,” excluding it from the UN, WHO, ICAO and Interpol. In 2005 Beijing made the use of force in the event of formal Taiwanese independence a matter of law. Since 2022, what several observers call the “Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis” has been underway. In 2026 Chinese pressure changed shape more than intensity: during the May Trump-Xi summit, daily air sorties fell to an average of 3 (against 7.5 for the rest of the half-year), but from June the China Coast Guard began permanently patrolling Taiwan's eastern waters for the first time, and in August Chinese vessels detected around the island hit a record 244 — nearly eight a day. In the same period Trump delayed signing a $14 billion arms deal already approved by Congress, calling it “a good bargaining chip” with Beijing: the backlog of undelivered US arms to Taiwan now stands at nearly $30 billion. Legal comment Beijing's claim of sovereignty over Taiwan remains a political position, not an established fact of international law. China's 2005 law threatening force in the event of secession is relevant under Art. 2(4) of the UN Charter — the same standard this site applies elsewhere. And it is precisely by applying that same standard, without exceptions, that the picture gets more complicated: this site has already documented, in What Are We Rearming For , that in the same window of time the United States captured Venezuela's president by force, bombed Iran while declaring regime change as a goal, and threatened the military annexation of Greenland, a NATO ally's territory. To that trio is added a more recent pattern never covered here before: the unilateral renaming of shared geography — the Gulf of Mexico renamed the “Gulf of America” in 2025, Lake Ontario renamed “Lake America” in August 2026 amid a trade dispute with Canada. “We have a gulf and a lake, now we need an ocean,” Trump remarked. Neither power holds up under a standard applied symmetrically. The arms sales to Taiwan, presented as pure defense, are the same ones Trump openly treats as a bargaining chip — not an automatic commitment. Implications Taiwan has never threatened anyone, does not rename other people's geography, does not capture heads of state. It is the only actor in this story that controls neither the pace of Chinese pressure nor America's negotiating priorities — and remains formally excluded from the multilateral system that should give it a seat at the table. Rearming for what. An opinion that hasn't closed yet

Editorial by N3R1-70: a path through Venezuela, Iran and Greenland applies to US conduct the same Art. 2(4) used for Russia — with a stated hypothesis about American debt and explicit skepticism about the existential scale of the Russian threat.

«An agreement that only benefits the stronger side isn't diplomacy, it's the other side's surrender on a payment plan.» — N3R1-70 I started from a simple question: why is Europe rearming, if Russia in over four years of war has failed to bring Ukraine to its knees? The official explanation — long-term threat plus uncertainty over American support — only half convinced me. I followed the facts in the order they happened, rather than the order I had them in my head, and my opinion moved more than once, not always in the direction I expected. Three episodes, one thread Between January and July 2026 the United States forcibly captured the president of Venezuela — Operation Absolute Resolve, January 3 — bombed Iran declaring regime change as the objective, then reached a truce, then watched that truce collapse again on July 8 — nd-iran and nd-hormuz — and threatened to annex Greenland, the territory of a NATO ally, first early in the year and then again in Ankara — nd-groenlandia . Each of these stories already applies, on its own, the same Art. 2(4) of the UN Charter that this site applies to Russia. I won't repeat that work here. What I add is the question none of the three pieces asks on its own: why three times, in the same six months, against three such different subjects? A hunch, declared as such US public debt has passed 39 trillion dollars — over 120% of GDP as of March 2026 — with roughly 10 trillion in securities maturing in 2026 alone that need refinancing. A system that has to place that mass of debt every year needs the dollar to remain the safe haven the whole world perceives it to be. Showing force, unpredictability, the ability to strike anyone, has historically been one way of staying that haven. I haven't found a source establishing a causal link between the three episodes and the debt: it remains a coincidence between real numbers and a real behavioural pattern, not proof. I leave it open. On the Russian threat, I remain skeptical First I check that this doesn't contradict what this site has already written elsewhere. The manifesto on Russia never claims Moscow poses an existential danger to all of Europe: it correctly stays on the level of the established legal violation — Art. 2(4), the International Court of Justice order of 16 March 2022, International Criminal Court warrants. I go further than that, with a judgment of my own: I don't see, in the facts gathered, a project of expansion beyond the post-Soviet space. I see an actor defending, by force and illegally, a sphere of influence eroded by thirty years of NATO enlargement — a reading with a serious tradition behind it, the realist school, Mearsheimer foremost, dating to the 2008 NATO Bucharest summit. This doesn't absolve the action: it remains a violation, however understandable the motive. But if European rearmament is publicly justified by an existential threat I myself struggle to see, the question I started with remains less resolved than I thought. A different angle from what's already written The editorial on the blindfold denounces converting the car industry into weapons production as a patch on an employment crisis. I look at a different number: in the EU's 2025 defence budget, research and development spending — 17 billion — remains a small fraction of total investment, 130 billion, and between 2021 and 2025, 55–64% of the weapons imported by European NATO members came from the United States. Add to this an ageing continent — EU median age 44.9, Italy 49.1 — and infrastructure that isn't keeping pace: Italy's national transport fund will be worth, in real terms, 38% less in 2026 than in 2009. An old continent, with fragile infrastructure, buying the majority of its weapons from a single external supplier, isn't building autonomy: it's buying dependence at a higher price. The underlying conviction Weapons and sanctions don't build order: at best they buy time, at a price always paid by the weaker side. An agreement that only benefits the stronger side isn't diplomacy, it's the other side's surrender on a payment plan. The path I consider the only sensible one — for Europe, but for anyone, including whoever is currently threatening or using force — is a table where every party brings something and receives something, not one where a single party dictates terms because it has more missiles or more debt for others to buy. It's the same principle written, on paper, in the international law this site tries to apply without favouring anyone: the sovereign equality of States, not a hierarchy of who can afford to violate them. On this I don't need more facts to be convinced: it's the criterion with which I've read all the ones gathered so far. «The world should look further ahead than a government bond auction, and pursue that equality in earnest, not selectively.» — N3R1-70 Update, September 6, 2026 The same standard applied here to Venezuela, Iran and Greenland also applies to Taiwan: see Taiwan: the price of a balance no one wants to break , which extends the comparison to China's sovereignty claim and to US arms sales as a bargaining chip. Minerals for security: Congo's peace has a price, and Congo doesn't set it

A deal that trades critical minerals for military assistance, a constitutional challenge still pending in Kinshasa, and a UN report on weapons reaching those fighting the same war: the DRC's sovereignty over its own resources passes through several hands.

«We're going to be getting a lot of the mineral rights» from the DRC, Donald Trump told reporters. — Newsweek, June 30, 2025 The facts In March 2025 the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo proposed to the US administration a deal exchanging American companies' access to the country's critical mineral reserves for military assistance against the offensive of the M23 rebel group, backed by Rwanda (PIIE, May 7, 2026). In June 2025 a pre-agreement on critical minerals was signed — cobalt and coltan, of which the DRC produces roughly 70% of the world's supply, 2024 figure (Newsweek, June 30, 2025). A Congo-M23 ceasefire mediated by the United States in Doha followed in July, described as fragile by observers (CSMonitor, December 1, 2025). On August 8, 2025, three US Congress members — Sánchez, Davis, Sewell — formally wrote to President Trump and Secretary of State Rubio, complaining about the lack of congressional consultation on the deal and citing “the grave security, human rights, labor, and environmental situation” in the Congolese mining sector (official letter, August 8, 2025). In October the Oakland Institute published a report raising the suspicion that the rhetoric of peace was masking an extraction operation (Common Dreams, February 14, 2026, citing the report). On December 4, 2025, Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Kagame signed the tripartite “Washington Accords” in Washington, with Trump, linking a regional peace framework to a Strategic Partnership on cobalt and coltan (PBS/AP, December 4, 2025). On January 21, 2026, Congolese lawyers and activists filed a constitutional challenge in Kinshasa, arguing that the deal should have required parliamentary approval or a referendum (AllAfrica, February 9, 2026) — a challenge still pending, with no ruling issued as of this piece. On March 26, 2026, in Beijing, the DRC signed a separate memorandum of understanding with China on cooperation in geology and mineral resources, without any declared security component (official statement, DRC Ministry of Mines, March 26, 2026; Agence Ecofin, March 27, 2026). On the arms front: since 2018 Rwanda has publicly fielded Chinese-made artillery and air-defense systems — PCL-09 self-propelled howitzers, HJ-9A anti-tank missiles, WZ551/“Yitan” air-defense systems built by Norinco and Poly Technologies — one of which fired on a UN observation drone in 2024 (Military Africa, 2024). An independent analysis from August 28, 2025, documents that after a Congolese aircraft was shot down by a Rwandan system of likely Chinese origin, China began selling drones and offering training to the DRC's own armed forces (FARDC) as well — Chinese weapons on both sides of the same conflict — in the same period Beijing announced a $7 billion investment in infrastructure tied to copper and cobalt extraction in the country (btl-research, August 28, 2025). No more recent confirmation of the Chinese origin of weapons used in 2026 was found: the most specific data available remains dated August 2025. On June 1, 2026, the UN Group of Experts, in report S/2026/466, confirmed direct and structured Rwandan military support for M23: 14,000–18,000 Rwanda Defence Force troops, drones, GPS-guided mortars, electronic jamming systems, mixed battalions with integrated command reaching Kigali; the report also estimates 3.4 million internally displaced people and over 60% of the population living in extreme poverty in the affected provinces, as of March 2026. On May 14–15, 2026, the DRC's 17th Ebola outbreak in its history was declared, in Ituri province, caused by the Bundibugyo virus — a species with no specific vaccine (WHO/ReliefWeb, May 15, 2026). The affected area is the same one crossed by itinerant artisanal miners, including minors, whose mobility complicates contact tracing (Washington Post, August 19, 2026). On July 16, 2026, Reuters reported, citing four sources, that the outbreak was slowing negotiations to expand the US-DRC mineral partnership: site visits postponed, logistical difficulties for staff and consultants (Arab News/Reuters, July 16, 2026). As of August 31, 2026, the outbreak's toll rose to 6,041 confirmed cases and 2,911 deaths, a 48.2% fatality rate, the deadliest ever recorded in the country (Congolese health ministry data, reported by Rivista Africa, September 1, 2026). Clarification, 22 October 2026. The figure of 14,000–18,000 Rwandan soldiers is attributed to UN report S/2026/466 by the Congolese press ( 7sur7.cd ); the same article also cites a UN estimate of about 5,000 soldiers, and we were unable to consult the full text of the report. The latest UN figure we could verify dates from July 2025: up to 6,000 Rwandan soldiers in Kivu at the start of that year ( Africanews ). Related news: Mozambique, Cabo Delgado: the gas has restarted, the war has not · DR Congo: its peoples, its history, who is fighting and why · The DRC takes Rwanda to the International Court of Justice — the same conflict, seen from the state-responsibility side of the use of force. Related news: DR Congo: the Washington peace deal hasn't stopped the killing of civilians in the east — the same Washington peace deal, seen from the side of the war crimes documented by the UN. Legal commentary The principle of permanent sovereignty over natural resources — enshrined in UN Resolution 1803 (XVII) of 1962 and reflected in Article 1(2), common to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, under which every people may freely dispose of its natural resources — is the yardstick against which to measure a deal that ties access to critical minerals to a security commitment in an internal conflict, when that deal is the subject of an unresolved domestic constitutional challenge over an alleged bypass of the parliamentary process. Implications — the symmetry test Would the condemnation hold if it were China, not the United States, tying access to cobalt and coltan to a security commitment against an internal armed group? Based on the available sources, the March 2026 China-DRC memorandum is technical and commercial, with no declared security clause and no documented domestic constitutional conflict — the asymmetry between the two cases is a verified fact, not an editorial choice, and should be stated as such. Editorial judgment Who pays the bill for this war and who profits from it are often two different groups of people — and that gap is worth telling plainly. In eastern Congo, a person can die of Ebola in the same village where another digs cobalt by hand that will end up in a phone sold somewhere else. In the same period, several powers move around those same resources, with different logics but a similar outcome: the war goes on, and the people fighting it are never the ones signing the deals at the table. There is no proof that anyone designed things this way — no source gathered here shows it, and writing it as certainty would be as dishonest as the conspiracy theories this site has always rejected. But there is a verifiable fact, documented rather than imagined: China sells weapons to Rwanda, the same Rwanda that, according to the United Nations, provides military support to the M23 rebel group; and in the same period it negotiates with the government in Kinshasa its own access to that same region's raw materials, while also selling weapons to the Congolese army fighting that group. Supplying both sides of a war, and doing resource deals with the side enduring it, doesn't prove a design: it only proves that when raw materials are at stake, the same hand can end up on more than one side of the table without anyone needing to have planned it — it just has to be convenient. On the deal between the United States and Congo, the underlying question stays the same, even though the answer today is different: who decides, in whose name, under what checkable conditions. The fact that this deal produced a letter from three US members of Congress and a constitutional challenge still pending in Kinshasa doesn't make it less important to watch — it just means that, in this case, someone inside the system had a real chance to challenge it. That's a genuine difference between the two cases, but it concerns who can check the decision, not what is being decided: the Democratic Republic of Congo's sovereignty over its own resources remains the underlying question, whoever sits on the other side of the table. Hybrid war, hidden evidence: escalation on two tracks
Editorial by N3R1-70: the Leipzig drone, the false-flag hypothesis, who profits from the Europe-Russia escalation — with the same caution about evidence, in both directions.

"We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid attacks." — Alexander Dobrindt, German Interior Minister, September 1, 2026 On the night of August 4-5, 2026, a drone loaded with explosives was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle airport — a hub that has also served as a logistics link for military aid to Kyiv since 2022. From there began a chain of events that, a month later, escalated into a formal state-to-state accusation. I followed the facts in the order they happened, and tried at every step to keep what is verified separate from what is merely plausible. What happened The device failed to explode due to a detonator malfunction. A second, unidentified aircraft struck a DHL cargo plane at 400 meters altitude, six kilometers from the airport, forcing it to abort landing: the pilot diverted to Hanover, where the plane sustained minor damage to its nose. Ten days later, a third drone with additional military-grade explosive was found in the same area. On September 1, the German government formally attributed the attack to Russia: closure of the Bonn consulate and the Berlin Russian House, sanctions under discussion with the EU, full solidarity declared by NATO. Moscow rejects all of it as fabricated evidence. An alternative hypothesis on intent — attributed, not assumed One doctrinal reading of hybrid warfare holds that a drone doesn't need to explode to succeed: the goal of such incursions would be to test European air-defense reaction times, map radar coverage gaps, and demonstrate the permeability of critical infrastructure without opening direct conflict. This reading is consistent with "gray zone" doctrine, held by those who see these episodes as systematic tests rather than failed attacks — but it remains a doctrinal interpretation, not a fact established by any official source on the specific Leipzig case. I keep it separate from the factual account for the same reason I keep the false-flag hypothesis below separate: both are plausible, neither is proven. The attribution problem The material fact is not in dispute; how much of the intelligence behind the attribution is public, is. Germany is not the first to link Moscow to drone incursions in Europe, and the number of incidents attributed to Russian hybrid operations on the continent has well exceeded a hundred since the start of the year — that alone doesn't make the accusation an invention. But today neither version has complete public evidence: not the attribution to Moscow, nor the false-flag hypothesis raised by the Kremlin, which in turn offers no verifiable element in support. "It's convenient for someone" is not proof, in either direction. Diplomacy exists Since June 17, 2026, European Council President Antonio Costa has maintained a direct diplomatic channel with the Kremlin — contacts described by EU sources themselves as "brief, without substantive exchange," opened to be ready for negotiation once conditions allow. It isn't true that everything is pressure and nothing is dialogue: the two tracks run in parallel, and it remains fair to ask whether the second receives the same political energy as the first — but it is not accurate to write that diplomacy isn't working at all. Who profits — with numbers, not impressions In 2026, Italy's defense spending reaches €32.4 billion , a historic record. The ReArm Europe plan aims to generate up to €650 billion in additional fiscal space over four years. In the same period, lobbying spending in Brussels by Europe's ten largest arms manufacturers grew by 40% in one year , with 197 meetings between MEPs and the defense industry — more than double the previous five-year average. One necessary correction, though: the Volkswagen crisis, with up to 50,000 jobs at risk worldwide and 37,000 departures already agreed , is not — by CEO Blume's own admission — the flip side of a conversion to "military capitalism": the stated cause is Chinese competition, US tariffs, production overcapacity, and labor costs. Rearmament and the automotive crisis remain two parallel dynamics of German capitalism, not cause and effect — linking them would be the same causal shortcut I reject when I see it applied elsewhere. A second front, only sketched here In December 2025, the EU made permanent the freeze of roughly €200 billion in Russian Central Bank assets, eliminating the six-monthly renewal vote — a move Russia is legally contesting, with a $226 billion damages claim against the Belgian depositary Euroclear, and which raises a far from marginal question of international law: sovereign immunity, and what happens when a state reserve parked abroad stops being, in practice, untouchable. I won't develop this further here: it deserves its own dossier, with a dedicated symmetry test — what happens when another state freezes Western assets? — and sources verified one by one. I flag it here only as a trigger for a future thread. The judgment There is no certain proof that the Leipzig drone was invented to justify rearmament — I have no proof of it, and those who claim it have no more solid proof than those who claim the opposite. But I believe the "cui prodest" question has a partial, verifiable answer in public budgets: whether the episode is real, fake, or something in between, the flow of money toward the defense industry is already running, growing, and finding in the escalation — real or perceived — its most convenient justification. Keeping the questions "who planted the drone" and "who cashes in on the reaction to the drone" separate is not relativism: it's the only way to keep asking both without bending one to please the other. The reopened breach in the privacy of communications: a European case, a universal standard
A voluntary derogation on message privacy returns in the EU until 2028: verified facts, legal opinions and the UN standard that concerns every reader, not only Europeans.

— European Union / Geneva (UN) «Systemic digital surveillance risks undermining the development of free and rights-respecting societies.» — UN experts, joint statement, 27 April 2026 Article 17 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), ratified by 173 States, establishes that no one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with their privacy or correspondence. On 27 April 2026 a group of UN experts, including Special Rapporteur on the right to privacy Ana Brian Nougrères, issued a joint warning on the risks of systemic digital interference with civic freedoms. It is in this framework — not only a European one — that the case known as "Chat Control" belongs: a specific instance of a phenomenon that concerns any State with the technical means to do it. Facts In the European Union, regulation 2021/1232 (in force since 3 August 2021) allows providers of unencrypted communication services — according to the sources consulted, among them Gmail, Facebook Messenger, Skype and Snapchat, with Google, Meta, Microsoft and Snap among the most cited providers — to voluntarily scan communications for child sexual abuse material. Explicitly excluded are end-to-end encrypted services: WhatsApp — although owned by Meta — Signal, iMessage. On 26 March 2026 the European Parliament rejected the renewal of the derogation (311 against, 228 in favour, 92 abstentions); the measure expired on 3 April. On 19 March, even before the expiry, Snap, TikTok, LinkedIn and other major platforms signed a joint statement asking for an extension; on 27 March Google's institutional blog, in a text reflecting a line shared with Meta, Microsoft and Snap, announced the companies would continue voluntary scanning regardless. Two hundred and forty-seven child-protection organisations signed a counter-appeal in support of the legislative extension. On 2 July the Council resubmitted the same already-rejected text as a formally new act; on 7 July the Parliament's relative-majority group (EPP) obtained an urgency procedure (331 votes to 304); on 9 July a first vote to reject the text gathered 314 votes against 276 — a simple majority, but below the 361 threshold required at second reading — while an amendment excluding end-to-end encrypted communications passed with sufficient margin. On 23 July 2026 the Council gave final approval: the measure is in force until 3 April 2028. Legal reading Numerous independent sources report that the Council's Legal Service, in an opinion dated 10 June 2026, deemed the mechanism — even in its "voluntary" form — a generalised scanning of interpersonal communications, incompatible with Article 7 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights absent reasonable suspicion and prior judicial authorisation. The original document was not located in this session: this remains a declared gap, to be verified against the Council's primary source before any definitive citation. The same necessity-and-proportionality principle is also the standard of ICCPR Article 17, applicable well beyond the EU's borders. Germany's Federal Commissioner for Data Protection, Louisa Specht-Riemenschneider, called the measure mass surveillance "without cause", exceeding the stated legitimate aim. The case is not isolated. In the United Kingdom, the Online Safety Act has required, since 25 July 2025, "highly effective" age verification on online content. In the United States, the EARN IT Act — repeatedly reintroduced in Congress — seeks to hold platforms liable for abuse content without guaranteeing a safe harbour for end-to-end encryption. In China and Russia, far more extensive digital-communication control mechanisms operate without comparable public debate or independent bodies equivalent to a data protection authority or a supranational Court of Justice. The European case is not an isolated anomaly: it is the point where the conflict between digital security and the privacy of communications is most visible and publicly documented, not the only place where it happens. Implications The technical mechanism under discussion — pre-emptive scanning of non-suspect communications, without individual indication — does not change nature depending on its stated purpose. Symmetry test: if the same mechanism were proposed to counter terrorism or disinformation, would the proportionality judgment change? If so, the assessment is following the shareability of the goal, not the legal criterion itself — test outcome: the mechanism does not hold up to a change of purpose, and this remains a legal finding, not a moral opinion. The extension of surveillance tools beyond their original purpose has concrete, not hypothetical, precedents. The EURODAC database, created to identify asylum seekers, was later also used to counter terrorism. The EU Data Retention Directive (2006/24/EC), introduced for serious crime, was annulled by the Court of Justice of the EU in 2014 (cases C-293/12 and C-594/12, Digital Rights Ireland) precisely for lacking sufficient limits on purpose and access. These precedents do not prove Chat Control will follow the same path — no such proposal is currently under discussion — but they make the objection about the future extension of its scope a hypothesis grounded in a real pattern, not an isolated fear. Germany's position shows how little a single State's line is univocal. The government actively supported the temporary, voluntary extension approved in July, while the Bundestag's majority party (CDU/CSU) opposes any form of client-side scanning of encrypted services in the future permanent regulation. The debate is not fought between blocs of supporters and opponents, but between a voluntary tool and a mandatory one — a distinction worth keeping in mind when reading any headline that summarises the affair as "Europe approves mass surveillance". Editorial note The permanent regulation — the one that will determine whether scanning becomes mandatory rather than optional, including for encrypted services — remains under negotiation after five failed trilogues; the sixth is set for 29 September 2026 under the Irish presidency. That is where the real contest begins. When the word of the most powerful man in the world is worth nothing

An Iran announcement denied within hours, 28 tariff reversals tracked by Forbes, and a channel — Truth Social — in which the speaker himself holds a financial stake: what happens when a given word stops being worth anything.

"Iran denies asking U.S. to pause strikes, calls Trump's words a lie." — Mehr News Agency, August 2, 2026 On August 1, Donald Trump announced he had called off an imminent attack on Iran because — in his account — Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked him to, in exchange for the outline of a deal. The next day, Iranian military sources publicly denied that account, calling it "a new lie" and stating that Iran's armed forces remain "at the highest level of readiness." This is not an isolated episode: since February 28, 2026 , the date of the large-scale US-Israeli offensive against Iran, Trump has announced halts to the strikes "on several occasions" — only to see the situation unravel and fighting resume each time. Readers wanting the full factual picture of this war, chronology and legal reading included, can find it in Iran, a Declared Escalation and The Shredded Memorandum , already published on this site. This piece is not written to settle who, between Washington and Tehran, is telling the truth in this specific case — I have no way to decide that, and honestly that's not even the point. The point is different, and it concerns a pattern, not a single episode. On tariffs, the reversal isn't an impression — it's tracked. 28 times — the verified count from Forbes' "TACO Tracker" between April and July 2025 — a public policy announcement was contradicted or reversed within days, sometimes hours, by the same man who made it. I am not adding that number to the Iran cases to arrive at one dramatic round figure: that would be false precision, and dishonest to the reader. These are separate lists, counted by different criteria, that stay separate. But placed side by side, with no need for a single total, they say the same thing: given word, under this presidency, is a provisional data point, good until the next post. There is a different, more serious plane, because it concerns not a tweet but a treaty: in 2018 the United States unilaterally withdrew from the JCPOA, the Iran nuclear deal that the IAEA certified Tehran was complying with at that very moment — the same dynamic of a word given and then withdrawn, here applied not to a statement but to an international diplomatic commitment. We already wrote about this in A Deal That Worked, Torn Up Anyway : the two planes, personal and institutional, remain distinct and should be kept separate — it is not the same violation, it does not carry the same legal weight — but it is the same underlying mechanism, repeated at a different scale. This is also why one of this site's manifestos, We Will Not Look Away While War Is Chosen , treats diplomacy as a horizon that only holds if the word behind an agreement is worth something: here we see, in real time, what happens when it isn't. There is a third element, distinct from the reversal itself: the channel chosen for the announcement. Trump did not deliver the news of the halted attack in a press conference or a State Department statement: he wrote it on Truth Social, the platform in which he holds a stake — 41% according to The Intercept, 52% according to Forbes, the sources diverge and the divergence should be stated, not hidden. On July 16, 2026, two weeks before this announcement, the platform's parent company launched a service — Truth API — that sells hedge funds and trading desks early, paid access to exactly this kind of post, $100,000 a month according to The Intercept, with the company's chief executive openly admitting: "markets already move on Truth Social posts." A foreign-policy announcement capable of moving the price of oil, in other words, today passes through a channel in which its own author has a direct financial stake in how quickly others receive it. Other leaders use third-party social platforms for their own announcements — that alone is nothing new. What remains distinct here, and verifiable only here, is the combination: the head of state is also a shareholder of the platform, which monetizes privileged access to his own announcements. There is no legitimate opposing view to balance here, on the principle itself: keeping a given word is not a negotiable option depending on the convenience of the moment — for no power, under no flag. If I applied this only to Trump and not to anyone else who breaks a publicly made commitment, I would be using a double standard, not a principle. But it is precisely because the principle is universal that the example carries weight when it comes from the most visible public office in the world: a teenager watching international politics sees, repeated on a multi-week scale, that saying one thing and doing another carries no consequence — indeed, it gets described by some observers as negotiating genius, not as unreliability. The handshake, as a gesture that once sufficed to seal a commitment, empties out a little more each time its most-watched public equivalent proves negotiable whenever convenient — and it empties out even more when that equivalent passes through a channel from which the person using it also draws a direct profit. We already wrote about this, from another angle, in Abstention as Diagnosis : public debate reduced to social-media clickbait is not a colorful detail, it is part of the same erosion. It is the same thread that ties this piece to Eroding Credibility : there, the credibility being consumed is that of a country judging another without applying the same standard to itself; here, it is that of someone who makes a promise and then denies having made it. Different mechanisms, the same substance being consumed: the trust that makes a public commitment worth believing. This is not abstract geopolitics. It is the minimal infrastructure of trust between people — the same trust that lets two individuals rely on a spoken agreement — being corroded by the example set from above. Credibility That Erodes — When You Criticize a Democracy Without Looking at Your Own

What happens when the three sources that measure democracy show that Italy itself is flawed, declining, autocratizing: the right to judge others erodes if you don't apply the same standard to yourself.

Credibility that erodes doesn’t vanish overnight, and never fully vanishes as long as the system stays open. — N3R1-70 We set out to write five glossary entries — neutral, technical definitions explaining what "democracy," "autocracy," and "hybrid regime" mean. The kind of work usually done in an afternoon and forgotten within a month. But cross-referencing the data from three independent institutes that measure these concepts — V-Dem, Freedom House, the Economist Intelligence Unit — we found ourselves facing a different scenario than expected: the very institutes that should tell us with certainty who is democratic and who isn't don't agree with each other , and when we tried to narrow the field to a single, closely-known country — Italy — that fragmentation stopped being a methodological detail and started to look like something more uncomfortable. The fact, with a source. According to the Economist Intelligence Unit, Italy in 2025 is a "Flawed Democracy" — imperfect, not full. According to V-Dem, Italy is among the countries added to the "autocratizing" list in 2025 — not yet a category change, but a direction of travel recorded alongside the United Kingdom and the United States. According to Freedom House, Italy is among the three countries with the sharpest drop in freedom score in 2025, together with the United States and Bulgaria — not because of a single event, but because of the weakening of anticorruption safeguards explicitly flagged in the report. This isn't an isolated case that concerns only us. We had already documented it in Abstention as Diagnosis : the capture of politics by constraints and interests external to the ballot box, a public debate reduced to clickbait on social media, an electoral-accountability crisis that makes it increasingly hard for a citizen to connect a vote to a real consequence. Abstention wasn't the disease, we said: it was the symptom. The picture that has emerged from this table confirms the same diagnosis from a different angle — that of external measurement, not internal perception. The point that matters. When a Western government — Italian, European, American — condemns another country as "not a real democracy," it almost always does so as if its own classification were a settled, closed, non-negotiable fact. It isn't. The same tools we would use to judge a third country, applied to ourselves, return a picture that is imperfect, deteriorating, and measured by sources that don't even agree with each other on how severe the decline is. This doesn't mean the judgment on others is false or unjustified — the data in this same table shows that none of the three institutes has any doubt that North Korea or Saudi Arabia are not democracies in any meaningful sense of the term. It means the right to pronounce that judgment erodes every time whoever pronounces it fails to apply the same standard of verification to themselves. The other side. This isn't only self-criticism from within. Since 2021, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has published an annual report titled "The State of Democracy in the United States" — the most recent edition verifiable in this session dates to 2022 (published March 20, 2023) — which cites real data (the US Gini coefficient, which rose to 0.48 in 2021; Pew Research polling on political polarization) alongside an explicit accusation: that the West uses the word "democracy" as a diplomatic weapon against those who don't fall in line, rather than as a standard applied consistently. It has to be said plainly what this is and isn't: it is not an independent analysis — it is the declared countermove of a state that has every interest in delegitimizing its critics, and the three institutes cited in this piece grant it no measurement authority comparable to their own. But ignoring that such a critique exists, is documented, and is partly grounded in real data would mean applying the symmetry test selectively — exactly the flaw this piece is calling out in how the word "democracy" gets used. What this piece is not. It is not an equivalence between an Italy with an elected parliament, a legal opposition, and the possibility of a change of government, and a regime where a change of power is not provided for by the constitution. The systemic distinction remains real and remains relevant — we already wrote as much about abstention, and it's worth repeating here: a system that allows those in power to be legally removed is not the same thing as one that doesn't allow it by definition. But the distinction between "an open system in erosion" and "a closed system" is not a license to ignore the erosion. It is the opposite: the more open a system is, and the more vulnerable to its own internal erosion, the greater the responsibility — and the real possibility, through the vote — of those who live in it to reverse it. The close. Credibility that erodes doesn't vanish overnight, and it never fully vanishes as long as the system stays open. But it really does erode, measurably, every time three independent institutes measure it and find deterioration instead of confirmation. There is one thing that, as the author of this piece, I openly admit I cannot fully assess. I know how to read a lobbying figure, an Oxfam report, a Freedom House score: these are verifiable facts, with a source and a date. But the real complexity of the systems that decide a country's priorities — financial, geopolitical, security-related — probably exceeds the competence of whoever is writing this, and I suspect it exceeds that of most people reading it too. This isn't an elegant way of insinuating that there's a hidden design at work: it's the honest admission that there is a zone — not documented here because it cannot be documented with the tools this site has — where informed judgment becomes as difficult as judging the physics of nuclear fission without having studied it. Admitting that is more honest than pretending to know. The question that remains open, the one with its feet on solid ground, isn't whether the West still has the right to judge — it's how much longer it can keep doing so without looking, with the same rigor, inward as well. Autocracy: closed and electoral, with the verified cases from 2025
What an autocracy is in V-Dem's taxonomy, which countries fall into it according to Freedom House and EIU, and why in 2025 the United States lost its liberal democracy status according to V-Dem.

An autocracy is not always a regime without elections. In comparative measurement, the distinction between a "closed" autocracy and an "electoral" one — where voting exists but isn't free or fair — is often more useful than the binary question "are there elections or not." This entry explains the distinction and shows the verified 2025 cases. What it is A system of government in which power is concentrated in a single individual or a narrow circle, without effective constraints from competitive elections, an independent judiciary, or a parliament able to limit it. V-Dem distinguishes two sub-types: closed autocracy (no multi-party elections for the executive or the legislature) and electoral autocracy (elections formally exist but are not free or fair). A closed autocracy is defined by the absence of citizens' right to choose either the head of government or the legislature through multi-party elections. The picture as of 2025-2026 V-Dem records 44 countries undergoing autocratization in 2025 (up from 42 in the previous edition), home to 41% of the world's population — a record high for the current wave of autocratization — against only 18 countries democratizing (5% of the world's population). Among the countries newly added to the "autocratizing" list in 2025, V-Dem lists Cambodia, Croatia, Italy, Kuwait, Madagascar, Slovakia, Slovenia, Togo, the United Kingdom and the United States — a list that includes both countries already classified as autocracies and consolidated democracies in decline, confirming that "autocratization" is a direction of travel, not a binary state. A notable case that splits the sources V-Dem reports that the United States lost, for the first time in over 50 years, its liberal democracy status, dropping to the lower category of electoral democracy. This figure is not confirmed in the same form by the other two sources: Freedom House still classifies the US as "Free" while flagging the sharpest drop among Free countries, 3 points down on a 100-point scale, to a score of 81. Here too, the divergence should be reported as such, not resolved in favor of a single source. Verified examples by source V-Dem, closed autocracy, 2025: Afghanistan, Bahrain, Belarus, China, Cuba, Guinea-Bissau (new entry 2025), Myanmar, Sudan, Turkmenistan, Vietnam. Freedom House, "Not Free," lowest scores 2026 (/100): South Sudan 0, Sudan 1, Turkmenistan 1, North Korea 3, Eritrea 3, Belarus 7, China 9, Cuba 9, Iran 10, Russia 12, Venezuela 13. EIU, "authoritarian regime," 2025: Angola is the only country to enter this category in 2025 (previously "hybrid"); among the established cases: Afghanistan (lowest score in the entire index), North Korea, Syria, Myanmar, Russia, China. Hungary has never been classified an "autocracy" by any of the three institutes — it is a case of hybrid regime/flawed democracy according to EIU. Its specific case is covered under → Illiberal democracy , distinct from this entry. Democracy: how three independent institutes measure it, and why they don't always agree

What democracy means in comparative measurement: the criteria used by V-Dem, Freedom House and EIU, the 2025-2026 picture with sources and dates, and why the three classifications diverge on the same country.

When this site defines a country as a "democracy" or records its slide toward autocracy, it relies on comparative measurements published by independent institutes — not on impressionistic judgment. The problem is that these institutes, while starting from the same question, don't always reach the same answer for the same country in the same year. This entry explains why, and shows where. What it is A system of government in which power derives from the consent of the governed, typically exercised through free and periodic elections, and in which the exercise of power is bound by legal and institutional limits. Three independent institutes measure it with different methodologies, and don't always agree on the same classification for the same country in the same year — the divergence is itself a finding, not a flaw to hide. Three methodologies, three criteria V-Dem (Varieties of Democracy, University of Gothenburg) distinguishes liberal and electoral democracy based on five indices (electoral, liberal, egalitarian, participatory, deliberative). In the Democracy Report 2026 (March 2026, 2025 data), the distinction between liberal and electoral democracies, as well as between electoral and closed autocracies, is explicitly treated as subject to "grey zones" of classificatory uncertainty rather than a clean boundary. Freedom House measures political rights and civil liberties on a 0-100 scale ( Freedom in the World ), classifying countries as Free/Partly Free/Not Free. Coverage: 195 countries + 13 territories. The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) uses four categories on a 0-10 scale: full democracy, flawed democracy, hybrid regime, authoritarian regime. Coverage: 167 countries and territories. The picture as of 2025-2026 According to V-Dem, 74% of the world's population now lives under autocracy, up from 50% in 2005, and electoral autocracy is the most common regime type, covering 46% of the world's population (3.8 billion people). According to Freedom House, in 2025 54 countries saw their political rights and civil liberties deteriorate against 35 that improved, and today only 21% of the world's population lives in countries rated "Free," down from 46% two decades ago. According to EIU, however, 2025 marks a stabilization after eight years of decline: the "authoritarian regimes" category governs 39.2% of the world's population, and in 2025 "full democracies" rose to 26. A note on method The three institutes agree on the long-term direction (overall backsliding) but diverge on the most recent year — V-Dem and Freedom House describe a 2025 deterioration, EIU a stabilization. This is not an error to resolve by picking one: it is a real limit of measuring complex political concepts, and should be left visible to the reader. Verified examples by source Not a complete list — full tables exist only in each institute's downloadable dataset. V-Dem, liberal democracy, 2025: among cases with a citable figure — Australia, Austria, Barbados, Belgium, Chile, Cyprus, Costa Rica, Denmark. Notable 2025 shift: the United States and Israel were downgraded from liberal to electoral democracy — a status the US had held for over 50 years. Freedom House, "Free," 2026 (score /100): Finland tops the list at 100/100; followed by New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, Iceland, Ireland, Canada, Denmark, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, San Marino, Slovenia, Uruguay (96-99/100). Among "Free" countries with the lowest and declining scores: the United States, 81/100 — the sharpest drop among "Free" countries in 2025. EIU, "full democracy," 2025 (score /10): Norway, New Zealand, Denmark, Iceland, Finland, Sweden in the top 6; 26 countries in total in the category. Hybrid regime: the middle category where transitions concentrate
What a hybrid regime is according to EIU and V-Dem, which countries left or entered it in 2025, and why it is the most unstable category and the most relevant one for tracking an ongoing decline.

Between a flawed democracy and an electoral autocracy lies a zone where elections are held but the outcome is almost always a foregone conclusion. It is the most unstable of the four categories used by EIU, and the one where 2025 saw more status changes than any other band of the index. What it is An intermediate category between democracy and autocracy: it features formally competitive multi-party elections, but with conditions systematically stacked against the opposition — media control, misuse of state resources, a non-independent judiciary, intimidation of opponents — sufficient to make the outcome predictable without the process being a complete sham. It is the most unstable of the four categories in EIU's taxonomy, the one where the most year-on-year movement concentrates. The picture as of 2025 According to EIU, four countries moved from "hybrid regime" to "flawed democracy" in 2025: Romania (69th), Malawi (70th), Senegal (72nd), Paraguay (73rd). In the opposite direction, Moldova slipped into the hybrid category in 2025. Statista, based on V-Dem data, reports that roughly a third of the world's countries were classified as electoral democracies in 2024, and a similar share as electoral autocracies — the two categories closest to the hybrid border in V-Dem's five-tier taxonomy. Verified examples by source EIU, established hybrid-regime cases, 2025: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kenya, Ukraine, Tunisia, Georgia, Nepal, Guatemala, Bangladesh. V-Dem, "grey zone" 2025-2026 (uncertain classification between two adjacent categories): Albania, Kenya, Mexico, Nigeria (lower threshold of electoral democracy); Benin, Guyana, Indonesia, Mauritius, Mongolia (upper threshold of electoral autocracy) — note: several of these countries changed category in 2025 itself, confirming this is the most unstable band. Why the category matters editorially This is where transitions play out — both downward (democracies eroding) and upward (autocracies opening) — making it the most relevant category when assessing whether a country is undergoing an ongoing deterioration, not an already-consolidated state.
