Illiberal democracy: origin of the term, and why Hungary is no longer the textbook case
Where the phrase 'illiberal democracy' comes from, the 2014 Orbán speech that claimed it, and why Orbán's April 2026 election defeat requires updating the most-cited example.

A government can emerge from free elections and still dismantle, piece by piece, the constraints meant to contain it once in power. This phrase describes exactly that pattern — and it has a precise origin, with a date and a name attached to who claimed it openly. What it is A phrase describing a system in which competitive elections coexist with the systematic weakening of liberal constraints on power — the judiciary, the press, the opposition, constitutional checks. The term has a precise origin that should always be cited: coined by political scientist Fareed Zakaria in the essay "The Rise of Illiberal Democracy" ( Foreign Affairs , 1997) as a critical category, it was later claimed in a positive sense by Viktor Orbán in a speech at Băile Tușnad (Romania) in July 2014, in which the Hungarian prime minister explicitly declared his intention to build an "illiberal state," naming Singapore, China, Russia and Turkey as reference models. A necessary note, updated to 2026 Orbán's Hungary was, for years, the textbook case cited in the literature for this category. But at Hungary's parliamentary elections on April 12, 2026, Orbán conceded defeat, ending 16 years in power, defeated by the Tisza party led by Péter Magyar; with 77% of votes counted, Magyar's party held over 53% support against Fidesz's 38%. An up-to-date glossary entry cannot present Hungary as currently governed by an "illiberal democracy model": the term remains valid as an analytical category and as a specific historical precedent (the 2014 speech), but its application to a concrete case must always be checked against the real political situation at the time of publication, not assumed from prior knowledge. Why the entry exists anyway The concept remains in use in political-science literature and in V-Dem/Freedom House reports to describe patterns (not a single country) of erosion from within through electorally legitimate means — distinct both from electoral autocracy (where the elections themselves are no longer free) and from hybrid regime (where the term describes a state, not a declared process). The distinction between "illiberal as an openly claimed process" and "autocratization as an externally measured process" is why the two entries remain separate. A note on the country list Unlike the previous entries in this glossary, no list of countries "classified as illiberal democracy" appears here, because no institute (V-Dem, Freedom House, EIU) uses this as a formal category — it is an analytical label applied case by case, not systematically. The only case reported in this entry with solid sourcing and dating is the Hungarian one described above. Adding others without dedicated verification for each would amount to fabricating a classification no one has ever formally compiled. Rule of law: why it is the cross-cutting criterion, with the WJP 2025 ranking
What the rule of law is, why it is not the same as electoral democracy, and the World Justice Project Rule of Law Index 2025 ranking, with the top and bottom five countries.

"Democracy" describes how power is obtained. "Rule of law" describes what limits it once obtained. These are two distinct dimensions, and their separation explains why a freely elected government can still erode the safeguards meant to constrain it. What it is The principle that every person, institution and entity — including the organs of the state itself — is subject to laws that are publicly known, equally enforced, and adjudicated by an independent judiciary, consistent with international human-rights standards. It is the cross-cutting criterion the other entries in this glossary use, in different forms, to distinguish themselves from one another: the presence or absence of an effective rule of law is often what separates, in the measurement practice of V-Dem/Freedom House/EIU, a flawed democracy from a hybrid regime, or a hybrid regime from an electoral autocracy. Why the entry isn't redundant with the others "Democracy" describes a method for selecting power (elections); "rule of law" describes a limit on power once obtained, independent of how it was obtained. A government can emerge from free elections and still erode the rule of law (this is exactly the pattern described under → Illiberal democracy ); a strong rule of law could in theory coexist with limits on electoral competition, although in practice the two dimensions tend to strengthen or weaken together. The picture as of 2025 According to the World Justice Project, Rule of Law Index 2025 (published October 28, 2025, 143 countries and jurisdictions, 0-1 scale), the top five are Denmark, Norway, Finland, Sweden, New Zealand; the bottom five are Venezuela (143rd), Afghanistan (142nd), Cambodia (141st), Haiti (140th), Nicaragua (139th). 2025 marks a widespread deterioration: 68% of countries declined in their rule-of-law score in 2025, against 57% the previous year — a figure worth reporting because it shows that the weakening of the rule of law is not a phenomenon confined to the cases already covered by this site, but a global trend measured independently. The identification knot: why deportation often remains only a paper threat
From Ceuta to the new EU Regulation: identifying and deporting people without documents is often impossible, not just difficult. Facts, readmission deals, statelessness.

“Among the main practical obstacles to return are the identification of migrants and obtaining travel documents from non-EU authorities.” — European Parliament Every time hundreds of people climb a border fence or swim across it, public debate immediately shifts to one word: deportation. But deporting someone requires two conditions rarely mentioned alongside the political proclamation — knowing with certainty where the person comes from, and having an agreement in force with that specific state to send them back. When either condition is missing, deportation is not a difficult option: it is an option that does not exist. Facts On Thursday 30 July 2026, thousands of young people gathered at the border between Castillejos (Morocco) and Ceuta; hundreds climbed the protective fences, unguarded by police at that moment, while Moroccan auxiliary forces withdrew as the young people passed — an episode the security officers questioned by EFE could not explain, except for its coincidence with Morocco's Throne Day. It is the latest in a sequence: over the past fifteen days Ceuta has recorded more than 1,500 arrivals, with unaccompanied-minor centres overcrowded by 1,600%. The European Parliament lists identifying migrants and obtaining travel documents from non-EU authorities among the main practical obstacles to return — in 2022 alone, 141,060 people were refused entry to the EU. The technical mechanism meant to solve the problem already exists: Frontex staff record data in the Visa Information System and fingerprints in EURODAC at external borders, then contact third states to identify people and obtain their documents; there is also a database, MIDAS, partly EU-funded, aiming to link up with the West African Police Information System, itself funded by Brussels to collect biometric data across seventeen countries. But technology is not enough if the second piece is missing: a readmission agreement genuinely in force. The 1992 Spain-Morocco agreement, for instance, does not apply to Moroccan nationals as such, only to third-country nationals who transited through Morocco — a distinction that in practice shifts the whole problem onto verifying real, not just declared, nationality. An Italian case, though older, shows the same dynamic at scale: despite a Rome-Algiers agreement in force since 2003, only 245 returns were carried out between 2015 and 2017 against over 4,000 expulsion orders, and a substantial share of people in irregular status come from countries with which Italy has no return agreement at all, so every negotiation runs solely through embassies and consulates, often without result. More recent, 2026 data shows the ratio between people landing in Italy and returns actually carried out rose from 10.2% in 2025 to 34.8% in 2026 — an improvement that still leaves the vast majority of cases uncovered. According to the European Commission, today only around 20% of people subject to a return decision actually leave EU territory. Legal commentary International law does not require a state to accept back whoever is presented to it: a forced return requires a legal title — a bilateral agreement or a multilateral readmission mechanism — that identifies with certainty the state responsible for receiving the person. Without that title, or without certain identification of nationality, an expulsion order remains an administrative act with no practical enforceability: this is where the gap between political proclamation and legal reality becomes structural, not incidental. The new Return Regulation, approved at first reading by the European Parliament in April 2026, explicitly acknowledges the problem by banning the use of aliases or forged documents and requiring the surrender of personal documents even in digital form — a sign that concealing one's identity, deliberate or not, is common enough to require a dedicated rule, with penalties reaching up to 24 months of administrative detention. But the crack does not open only on the side of the person in transit: a 2021 European Court of Auditors report already found that progress on readmission agreements between the EU and third countries remains modest, and that weak cooperation with countries of origin — not just individual non-cooperation — contributes to the low number of returns actually carried out. Implications What emerges is not a single border episode but the very shape of the public debate on migration. Promising large-scale deportations without the two conditions that make them genuinely enforceable — certain identification and a bilateral agreement in force — means offering a solution that does not exist in the form it is sold in. This is not a marginal technicality: readmission agreements must be negotiated state by state, identification requires time and consular cooperation that is not always available, and every forced return carries a non-trivial cost to the public purse. When these three knots — bilateral deals, identifying the person, costs — stay out of the proclamation, the debate stops being a search for a solution and becomes a display of firmness: the promised number matters more than the enforceable one — the same mechanism already described elsewhere on this site regarding the externalisation of the European border : moving the problem elsewhere costs less, politically, than solving it. One point needs care: the reason a person enters another country — fleeing war, seeking better living conditions, or any other motive — does not affect the structural nature of the problem. A system that cannot certainly identify who enters it, and that has no readmission agreement with the country of origin, remains ineffective regardless of why that person left: the crack is in the mechanism, not in the motive of whoever crosses it. The extreme case proves it. A person born and raised in a refugee camp, of uncertain origin-nationality or never registered at birth, is not automatically stateless in the legal sense — statelessness is a legal condition (no state considers the person its own national), not simply the absence of a document in one's pocket — but falls into a real, documented category: a person at risk of statelessness, for whom the inability to prove citizenship or ties to a state is itself a recognised indicator. If the asylum claim is rejected and the statelessness recognition claim is not accepted — or cannot even be lodged, because the minimal documents required to file it are exactly what is missing — this person remains in a real condition with no clear legal box: neither a recognised refugee, nor a recognised stateless person, nor deportable, because there is no certain state to hand them back to. This is not a theoretical exception: it is proof that the identification knot can be structurally unsolvable, not merely slow or badly managed. It must be said with equal clarity: non-cooperation can also be a deliberate strategy. Lying about one's identity or origin, or changing it during the procedure, is a recognised behaviour, sanctioned by the new EU Regulation. But the very organisation that closely follows the rule's application notes that the same cooperation duties — documents, a stable address, regular appearances — are often impossible to meet for people without a fixed residence, without digital tools, or without identity documents for reasons that have nothing to do with choice. In effect, the rule sanctions calculated lying and structural impossibility in the same way, because from the outside — and often from inside the procedure itself — the two conditions are not easily told apart. It is perhaps the most uncomfortable point of the whole picture: the system does not, today, have a reliable tool to separate those exploiting the crack from those who simply fell into it. One last observation remains, perhaps the sharpest for those who design these measures as a deterrent. Twenty-four months of administrative detention, reduced benefits, entry bans: for someone who decides to leave after weighing the risks of a dangerous journey and the costs of an economic migration project, these are real consequences that can weigh on the choice. But for someone fleeing war, hunger or the risk of death, the calculation is of a different nature: administrative detention, however harsh, is still a place with a roof and a meal — not a comparable alternative to the threat being fled. This is not an isolated impression: research on the subject finds a documented gap between the goals of restrictive migration policies and the results actually achieved, and a direct precedent confirms it — the end of the Mare Nostrum sea-rescue operation in 2014 did not reduce departures as its architects had predicted. If the deterrent does not deter those fleeing death, the whole sanctioning apparatus ends up mainly hitting those trapped in the system — not those who evade it by calculation, but those who, in their own calculation before leaving, had no workable threshold of deterrence at all. The facts On 11 June 2026 the Advocate General of the EU Court of Justice, Laila Medina, delivered her opinion on the case of two migrants detained in the Italian centres in Albania, referred by the Rome Court of Appeal. She confirms that locating the centres in Albania is legitimate, but that compliance with the minimum standards of treatment required by EU law is not proven. It is the second opinion after the more favourable one of April 2026. Legal comment The Advocate General's opinion does not bind the judges: the final judgment is expected in the coming months and could overturn it. The CJEU ruling of 1 August 2025 (cases C-758/24 and C-759/24), which limited the designation of "safe countries", remains in force. The status of the Albanian scheme is therefore contested, not settled. Implications The centres, operational since October 2024, have sat largely empty due to judicial halts. For critics the scheme violates the right to asylum, creates an accountability void and raises a problem of sovereignty. Update, 31 July 2026 In the hours after this piece was published, the situation in Ceuta escalated far beyond what the data available the day before suggested. According to estimates attributed to Spanish ministerial sources, not yet officially confirmed, at least 49,000 people crossed the border between Morocco and Ceuta in the last 24 hours — more than half the population of the autonomous city (85,000 residents), at least 7,000 of them minors. Sources diverge on the death toll, and the divergence should be reported as such rather than smoothed over: some cite 16-19 bodies recovered in the last 24 hours, others higher figures, for a total that in any case exceeds 40 deaths in Ceuta's waters since the start of 2026 — the highest figure since the Tarajal shipwreck in 2014. Those involved are mostly Moroccan and Algerian nationals, with a smaller sub-Saharan component, according to available news sources. Physically, they remain on the African continent: Ceuta is a Spanish exclave embedded in Morocco, separated from the Iberian peninsula by 17 km of sea. Legally, they have already entered Spanish territory — and therefore EU territory, since the Schengen acquis applies in full to Ceuta and Melilla — but anyone moving from the exclave to mainland Spain faces a second border check, as if crossing a further internal frontier. This point deserves emphasis: entering Ceuta does not automatically grant the ability to reach Madrid, Barcelona, or the rest of Europe. The Schengen Borders Code sets special rules specifically for Ceuta and Melilla, requiring identity and document checks for anyone departing by plane or ferry toward the Iberian peninsula or other Schengen countries — a regime distinct from the rest of Spanish territory, where no such internal checks exist. Anyone lacking the required documents is not admitted for boarding and therefore cannot move freely beyond the exclave: they remain physically in Africa, in Ceuta, awaiting identification or a decision on their protection claim. The only way to still reach mainland Spanish shores, for someone without grounds for regular boarding, would be a further irregular crossing — for instance hidden aboard a vehicle or a ferry. This is a distinct phenomenon from the initial crossing of the external border, but the sources consulted provide no quantified data on it for this specific episode: a gap to flag, not to fill by estimate. Diplomatically, the episode opened a direct clash between Italy and Spain: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on social media that uncontrolled immigration threatens the security of Europe's borders, a position shared by Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani; Madrid summoned the Italian ambassador in protest, with Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares calling Tajani's words "unworthy." Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez attributed responsibility for the surge to trafficking networks, which he said had exploited a self-serving reading of a Spanish Supreme Court ruling banning the immediate pushback of people intercepted at sea — a causal claim that direct interviews with migrants who arrived in recent days have contradicted, and which a Moroccan human-rights representative considers unlikely, since most of the Moroccans involved were not even aware of the ruling. As for why a mobilisation of this scale would occur in a country not going through war or state persecution, and which has seen living standards rise in recent years, the sources point to structural factors rather than a single triggering event: youth unemployment remains widespread, and the perceived gap between one's own condition and European opportunities — often amplified by social media — can grow alongside economic development, not despite it: those with access to information and minimal resources are often precisely those most likely to attempt departure. Added to this are factors specific to this episode: a Civil Guard officer, speaking anonymously, described a permissiveness by Moroccan authorities in not dispersing groups approaching the border — a pattern already seen in 2021 and historically linked to Rabat's use of border control as diplomatic leverage — alongside the viral social-media coordination already noted and a possible copycat effect with the simultaneous attempted crossing at Melilla. Finally, a theory has circulated online claiming the social-media instigation was deliberately engineered by intelligence services, of any country. No journalistic, judicial, or declared intelligence source supports this account: as of today it remains an unsupported claim, which this site does not publish as fact. The abstention argument, taken seriously — and its limit: if abstention is the correct diagnosis of a system captured by external constraints, it cannot also be the cure.

The vote is not a market: it is the only good whose absence does not lower the price — it gives it away. — N3R1-70 The right to vote is, historically, one of the most costly achievements of humanity: generations of people died to obtain it, or to extend it to those excluded from it. I start from this, and never forget it in what follows. But precisely because the vote is sacred, I believe it is worth asking honestly what happens when the formal act of voting stops producing the effect it was designed for: translating the will of voters into decisions that change something in people's real lives. Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights establishes that everyone has the right to take part in the government of their country, directly or through freely chosen representatives, and that the will of the people, expressed through periodic and genuine elections, is the basis of governmental authority. The weak point of this architecture has never been the principle, but its practical hold: what happens when elections remain periodic and formally genuine, but the link between electoral promise and governing behaviour thins almost to the point of disappearing? This is where the abstentionist argument enters, and I think it deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed as renunciation or disengagement. If public debate — mediated by a social ecosystem that rewards conflict and simplification more than proposals, and by a television journalism structured around confrontation rather than analysis — systematically reduces every electoral platform to interchangeable slogans between political forces, then the voter is no longer choosing between different visions for the country: they are choosing between communication packages optimised for the short term. In this scenario, the vote is not technically less free, but it is less informative: it no longer transmits to the political system a distinguishable signal of what the electorate actually wants, because no option on the table has genuinely articulated a long-term vision that can be checked against results over time. Those who choose abstention as a response to this condition are not, in their own intention, giving up the right to vote: they are signalling that the political offer on the table does not, on its merits, deserve the legitimacy that a vote confers. It is a form of dissent internal to the democratic system itself, not against it. That said, I believe abstentionism has a limit that anyone proposing it has a duty to face, not sidestep. A vote is not a market in which a missing buyer leaves the price unchanged: it is a near-zero-sum mechanism in which someone who does not show up takes power away from no one — they simply leave it entirely in the hands of whoever organises and turns out anyway, whether structured parties, cohesive interest groups, or more ideologically compact electorates. The recent history of many democracies shows that falling turnout tends to reward those who already have organisational machinery and voting discipline, not those who wish to punish the whole system through their own absence. In this sense, abstention risks being a signal that the political system is structurally equipped not to receive: a party that wins with halved turnout does not necessarily read that halving as a rejection of itself, but as open ground. There is also a dimension that makes the phenomenon more structural than a simple communication defect. In an interconnected global economy, a large share of the variables that determine people's real wellbeing — capital flows, monetary policy, supply chains, energy prices — is decided in venues that largely escape the control of any single elected government, however broad its mandate. Electoral politics thus ends up operating in a residual space, often too narrow to keep the promises made during a campaign, because those promises were built to capture immediate consent rather than to reckon with the real constraints within which whoever governs will then have to move. When a programme fails or goes unfulfilled, the accountability mechanism that should follow — electoral sanction, the end of a political career — systematically jams: blame is pinned on external constraints, on allies, on opponents, almost never on a failure of realism in the original promise; and whoever failed is often found back on the candidate list, heading it, or reassigned to another post, rather than removed from public life. I believe this is a critique of the capture of politics by interests and constraints that remain outside direct democratic control, and of the lack of real consequences for those who promise things they know, or should know, they cannot deliver — not a claim of equivalence between democratic and autocratic systems, which remain distinct on an essential level: genuine alternation, the legal removability of those in power, the pluralism of actors competing for consent. It is precisely because that distinction remains true and worth defending that its silent erosion — not in form, but in the substance of accountability — deserves to be named with this degree of alarm. Added to this, in these very months, is the European debate over rearmament and dependence on weapons systems and digital infrastructure supplied by foreign powers. The concern — raised publicly even by figures such as Wolfgang Ischinger, former head of the Munich Security Conference, regarding Germany's F-35s — is that software and logistical control over these systems remains in the hands of the producing country even after sale, with real dependency margins that go beyond a simple purchase of goods. It should be said with equal honesty, however, that the idea of an actual "switch" able to disable an aircraft remotely mid-flight has been explicitly denied both by the US Department of Defense and by Lockheed Martin, the manufacturer, and remains — as far as public verification currently shows — an unproven claim, even if fed by a real margin of opacity around remote update and maintenance systems that stay under the manufacturer's control. The legitimate doubt, then, concerns the degree of technological dependence and operational sovereignty a country gives up when it entrusts its defence to systems built, updated and maintained by another state — not a verified technical certainty, and it is shown here explicitly as such. In the same period, according to the Oxfam report "Resisting the Rule of the Rich", presented in Davos in January 2026, the world's billionaires' collective wealth rose by $2.5 trillion in 2025 — a figure nearly equal to the total wealth held by the poorer half of humanity, roughly 4.1 billion people ; in the same period, one in four people worldwide did not have regular access to enough food. The same report finds that billionaires are today more than 4,000 times more likely to hold political office than an ordinary person. This is not a subjective impression: it is a measured gap, published with a stated methodology, widening precisely as electoral politics — for the reasons discussed above — appears less and less able to intervene on the variables that determine it. But here I think it must be said clearly, as a point the reasoning followed so far makes almost unavoidable: if abstention is the correct diagnosis of a structural illness — the draining of substance from political debate, capture by constraints that remain outside direct democratic control, the collapse of the accountability mechanism — then abstention itself cannot also be the cure. Abstaining signals that something is not working; it rebuilds nothing of what is not working. If anything, given the mechanism described above — falling turnout that benefits whoever mobilises regardless — abstention risks aggravating exactly the symptom it means to denounce, leaving open ground precisely to those least exposed to pressure for change. The cure, if one exists, cannot lie in election day itself: it lies in rebuilding sites of political pressure that stay active between one election and the next, capable of forcing the electoral offer to reckon with reality instead of the short cycle of media consensus — intermediate bodies, organised mobilisation on specific issues, ongoing public monitoring of promises against facts, direct participation in places (often local) where the link between what is promised and what happens remains checkable. Critical voting, a blank or spoiled ballot counted and published, remain legitimate signals on election day itself — but they are signals, not substitutes for the organised pressure that should follow them in the months after, the kind that has historically produced real change when the vote alone was not enough. I believe, though, that presenting this path as a "cure" without facing its real cost head-on would be another form of dishonesty. The same dynamics described above — an information ecosystem that rewards confrontation over proposals, an unbroken succession of controversies that fizzle out without ever reaching a visible resolution — do not leave voters merely uninformed: they leave them tired, in a way that makes organised participation harder, not easier. Anyone who tries to engage beyond the ballot, outside already institutionalised channels, often meets a second discouragement: being seen as odd, "strange", out of place — the exact opposite of what it should be, namely the normal condition of an active citizenry. Whether this outcome is the product of deliberate design or, more simply, the unplanned consequence of an incentive system that rewards whoever generates conflict and short-term attention regardless, cannot be demonstrated here with the same evidence this site requires elsewhere — and I do not claim it as such. But the practical effect is identical either way: a tired, discouraged population that struggles to picture as workable the very path this piece names as the only real cure. Acknowledging this is not an argument against trying to rebuild organised political pressure — it is the realistic premise without which that attempt would remain, I think, an abstract piece of advice, sound on paper and nearly impossible for the reader to put into practice. There are, in any case, alternatives that carry the same signal of dissent without ceding the field: critical votes for smaller or new formations, blank or spoiled ballots where the electoral system counts and publishes them separately from turnout (making dissent visible instead of hiding it inside abstention), or forms of political participation that live outside election day alone — from organised pressure between one election and the next to direct participation at the local level, where the link between promise and reality stays more checkable. It is not this site's job to tell readers what to do on election day. But if public debate has been reduced to click-bait — from social media to television — if the constraints that really matter are decided elsewhere, and if the gap between those with power to set the rules and those who bear them widens measurably, then the useful question is not "vote or abstain", but where and how, between one election and the next, the collective capacity to exert real pressure on those who promise and then fail to answer gets rebuilt — knowing, without illusions, that this is the harder path, not the more comfortable one. Dehumanization: how war language removes the inhibition to kill, and why its most effective form is cold, not enraged

Dehumanization of the enemy in war rhetoric: the three families of metaphor that carry it, the moral disengagement described by Bandura, and why international law treats it as a warning sign, not just as rhetoric.

When a war speech calls the enemy “cockroaches” or describes a bombing as “surgery,” that is not rhetorical flourish: it is a mechanism with a precise function. The technical term is dehumanization, and its function is to remove the natural human inhibition against killing one’s own kind. Understanding how it works helps read more precisely any piece on this site that analyzes the war rhetoric of one of the parties involved — whichever one. What it is Dehumanization does not convince the audience that violence is good: it convinces them that the target is no longer a fully human subject, capable of reciprocity. Once that reciprocity is removed, the psychological barrier that normally prevents killing a fellow human loses its logical basis. It is not a side effect of war: in many documented cases, it is a technical precondition for it. The three families of metaphor Dehumanizing language draws, regardless of language or conflict, on three families of imagery. The zoological-parasitic one (“beasts,” “cockroaches,” “rats”) reduces the adversary to vermin to be exterminated. The pathological-medical one (“cancer,” “infection,” “virus”) turns killing into surgery or an act of social hygiene needed to save a healthy body. The bureaucratic-mechanical one (“targets,” “enemy infrastructure,” “collateral damage”) simply erases flesh behind abstract vocabulary. The three families are not mutually exclusive: they often coexist in the same discourse, applied to different targets or at different moments of the same conflict. The disappearance of the individual Along with language, the single person disappears too. The distinction between combatant and civilian, between the guilty and the innocent, dissolves into a collective guilt that every member of the opposing group would embody simply by belonging to it. Individual agency is erased: what matters is no longer who that person is or what they did or didn’t do, only which group they belong to. Moral inversion and the legal void The offensive act is told in reverse: as defense, necessity, the safeguarding of civilization. Whoever attacks perceives themselves — and narrates themselves publicly — as a victim forced to act to avoid a worse evil. Once the enemy is defined as sub-human, protections such as the Geneva Conventions come to be seen as a bureaucratic obstacle rather than binding law: the enemy is placed in a legal void where the only perceived rule is military efficiency. Moral disengagement, according to Bandura Psychologist Albert Bandura mapped the underlying psychological mechanism as “moral disengagement,” in a 1999 paper that builds on his 1986 social-learning theory. Bandura identifies a set of cognitive levers — moral justification, euphemistic language, advantageous comparison, displacement and diffusion of responsibility, minimizing consequences, dehumanization of the target, attribution of blame to the victim — that let people and institutions act against their own stated moral standards without feeling the guilt that would normally follow. Dehumanization, in this scheme, is not an isolated impulse: it is one lever within a broader system. A signal international law recognizes Dehumanizing language is not only relevant to social psychology: it also appears in international criminal jurisprudence as evidence of intent. The “ten stages of genocide” model, developed by scholar Gregory Stanton for the organization Genocide Watch, places dehumanization — the stage in which a group is compared to animals, parasites, or disease — as the fourth stage of a process that, if not interrupted, can lead to extermination. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda made this concrete in its 2003 judgment in the so-called “Media Case”: the systematic use, on RTLM radio and in the Kangura newspaper, of the term “inyenzi” (cockroach) to refer to the Tutsi population was found to be evidence of direct and public incitement to genocide, not mere war propaganda. The blind spot: cold, not enraged It is tempting to believe dehumanization is driven by blind hatred or instinctive barbarism. Its most effective form, however, is cold and bureaucratic: it does not require soldiers or populations to feel hatred for the target, only that they stop recognizing it as a subject capable of reciprocity. When the adversary becomes a technical problem or a risk equation to zero out, the moral barrier collapses without any need for rage. Who Said What: Dissent Redefined as Terrorism
Three US speeches on July 16, 2026 redefine dissent as terrorism. A sourced quiz compares them with Russia, China and Iran.

«Not one looks normal. They’re all deformed in some way — in their appearance, in their dress, in their mannerism.» — Stephen Miller, White House Deputy Chief of Staff, July 16, 2026 The facts On July 16, 2026, on the same day, three figures in the US administration delivered speeches that, taken together, mark a turning point for the legal definition of domestic political dissent. Secretary of State Marco Rubio convened officials from 67 countries at the State Department — a figure confirmed by a State Department spokesperson to CNN — for a "ministerial on the resurgence of political terrorism," proposing to recalibrate the counterterrorism architecture built over a generation against jihadism and aim it at the domestic American left, described as "a poisonous resentment cloaked in the language of equality and justice." White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller described that same dissent as a "fatal cancer of civilization" and its demonstrators as "deformed." In a primetime address, President Trump called the American electoral system "indefensible," claiming a foreign power holds the data of 220 million voters. This is not the first time in recent history that a state has chosen to treat domestic political opposition with the legal tools designed for terrorism. The mechanism — not the actor — is the subject of this piece: the linguistic and legal redefinition of dissent as a threat to be neutralized with the state's security apparatus. The quiz below tests the reader on who, where and when this mechanism has been used, before revealing that the pattern spans consolidated democracies and authoritarian regimes alike, with very different consequences. Quiz — who said what? Each question opens to reveal the answer with source and date. The gravest concrete consequences (convictions, executions) remain described in prose in the final analysis, not in the game — here the level is the rhetorical or legal label used by the state. 1. Who described domestic dissent as "a poisonous resentment cloaked in the language of equality and justice"? Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State, opening remarks at the State Department ministerial, July 16, 2026. Source: Fox News, ABC News. 2. Who said demonstrators are "deformed in some way — in their appearance, in their dress, in their mannerism" and that "not one looks normal"? Stephen Miller, White House Deputy Chief of Staff, same event, July 16, 2026. Source: CNN, Yahoo News. 3. Which president called his own country's electoral system "indefensible," claiming a foreign power holds the data of 220 million voters? Donald Trump, address to the nation, July 16, 2026. Source: The Hill, White House statement. 4. Which presidential directive, publicly summarized by its own promoter as ordering agencies to "disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest and prosecute" an entire domestic political movement, had already been signed before these speeches? NSPM-7 ("Countering Domestic Terrorism and Organized Political Violence"), signed by Trump on September 25, 2025. The six-verb formulation is the one Stephen Miller used in his July 16, 2026 speech to summarize the memorandum; the document itself literally reads "investigate, prosecute, and disrupt entities and individuals." Source: Democracy Now transcript (7/17/2026); legal analysis by DLA Piper and the ACLU. 5. Which prosecutor's office obtained a "terrorist organization" designation from a supreme court for a civil society organization already declared "extremist" in 2021? Russia's Prosecutor General's Office, petition granted by the Supreme Court on November 27, 2025, concerning the Anti-Corruption Foundation founded by Alexei Navalny. Source: Anadolu Agency. 6. In which jurisdiction was carrying a protest banner at a demonstration ruled "terrorism" by a court, with a maximum sentence of life imprisonment? Hong Kong, the case of Tong Ying-kit, convicted on July 27, 2021 under the national security law enacted June 30, 2020. Source: Radio Free Asia. 7. Which formal charge — literally translating to "waging war against God" — is applied to participants in anti-government protests, up to and including capital punishment? "Moharebeh," under Iran's judicial system. Applied in the public executions of July 19 and July 28, 2026 in Isfahan, of protesters convicted for participating in the January 2026 uprising. Source: NCRI, citing the judiciary's Mizan news agency. 8. Which attorney general declared that anyone who "helps rioters" could be considered an "enemy of God," a charge carrying the death penalty? Mohammad Movahedi Azad, Iran's attorney general, January 2026 — exact day not confirmed by the available source. Source: NY Post. 9. Which treasury secretary announced, on the same day as the ministerial, the expansion of fiscal and financial tools against organizations suspected of financing "left-wing terrorism"? Scott Bessent, US Treasury Secretary, July 16, 2026. Source: CNN. 10. Which human rights watchdog documented, independently of the US case, "a systematic approach" to using anti-terrorism legislation to suppress political opposition in another country? Amnesty International, report on Russia, describing a systematic approach to broadening definitions and penalties, stifling political opposition and freedom of expression under the guise of "national security." Source: Amnesty International, 2024 report, reconfirmed by a July 2025 analysis. Final analysis The ten cases share a single mechanism: redefining domestic political dissent — or organized opposition — as a threat to be handled with counterterrorism tools, stripping it of the ordinary safeguards of criminal law and political speech. This mechanism spans a consolidated democracy (United States, July 16, 2026), an authoritarian regime with a formal judicial apparatus (Russia, China/Hong Kong), and a theocracy that applies capital punishment (Iran). Symmetry test The standard holds: if the same mechanism — labeling opposition as terrorism to justify repressing it — is condemnable when applied by a regime the West considers authoritarian, it is equally condemnable when applied by a democracy. This is not an argument against the United States as such: it is an argument against the mechanism, regardless of who wields it. But symmetry of the legal standard does not imply equivalence of gravity, and flattening it would be as dishonest as ignoring it. The Iranian case involves executions actually carried out; the Hong Kong case involves prison sentences up to life already imposed; the Russian case involves the forced liquidation of an organization and criminal exposure for its former members. The American case, as things stand (July 16–30, 2026), involves official rhetoric, a presidential memorandum reorienting investigative priorities, and new visa restrictions — no conviction or execution has yet occurred under this specific framework. This difference is a fact, not a mitigating factor for any of the four cases: it is precisely the difference between the start of an institutional path and its outcome already realized elsewhere. Editorial note (stated judgment) The reason the American case still deserves specific coverage on this site is not that it is the gravest of the four — it is not, as of today. It is that it is happening in a democracy that presents itself as a guarantor of the international rule of law, is receiving ordinary media coverage disproportionate to its institutional gravity, and — unlike the Russian, Chinese and Iranian cases, already extensively documented by bodies such as Amnesty International, Radio Free Asia and the United Nations — does not yet have a comparable body of independent legal analysis. It is exactly the high-gravity × high-neglect quadrant this site's SDR-70 protocol is designed to catch. A deal that worked, torn up anyway

In 2018 Trump withdrew the US from the JCPOA while the IAEA certified Iran was compliant. Seven years later: two wars and the death of Iran's Supreme Leader. How a working deal produced the escalation it was meant to prevent.

The context Sometimes a conflict isn’t born from a lack of diplomacy, but from its unilateral interruption — even when it was working. The path that led the United States and Israel to bomb Iran directly twice in under a year, killing its Supreme Leader, begins with a deal the international watchdog certified as being respected. The deal (2015-2018) In July 2015 Iran, the United States, Russia, China, the UK, France and Germany signed the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA): strict limits on Iranian uranium enrichment in exchange for lifting sanctions, under an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspection regime Washington itself called “unprecedented.” In 2017, all four IAEA quarterly reports certified full Iranian compliance. On 8 May 2018 President Trump unilaterally withdrew the US from the deal, publicly calling it “a horrible, one-sided deal.” A detail often omitted but verifiable: the White House withdrawal memorandum identified no Iranian violation occurring during the Trump administration — only alleged 2016 violations, under Obama, concerning heavy-water stockpile limits. US sanctions were reimposed. The predictable consequence (2018-2024) Stripped of the deal’s benefits but no longer bound by its limits, Iran progressively rolled back its commitments: increasing enrichment, restricting inspector access. Breakout time — how long it would take to accumulate enough material for a device — fell from over a year to 3-4 months, per Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation estimates. In 2020 a US drone killed General Qassem Soleimani in Baghdad. After 7 October 2023 and the Gaza war, Iran and Israel exchanged direct strikes twice in 2024. The 12-Day War (June 2025) On 13 June 2025 Israel launched surprise strikes on Iranian nuclear and military sites, killing senior Revolutionary Guard commanders. On 22 June the United States struck Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan directly with bunker-buster bombs — Trump called it a “limited, one-off” mission. A ceasefire followed on 24 June. Estimates of the actual damage diverge sharply by source: the US says “destruction”; a leaked US intelligence report and Israeli intelligence describe serious but not conclusive damage, with the program delayed by months, not years. The failed talks and the second war (2026) In February 2026 indirect Oman-mediated talks on a new deal failed — Iran’s foreign minister signalled willingness to make concessions, but Trump said he was “not thrilled” with the outcome. On 28 February 2026 the US and Israel launched a new large-scale offensive — nearly 900 strikes in 12 hours — this time explicitly declaring the goal of regime change. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening strike; his son succeeded him. A conditional ceasefire, mediated by Pakistan, took effect on 8 April 2026. The symmetry test This is where the standard applied elsewhere in this series becomes harder to apply, not easier. If the yardstick for judging the Russian invasion of Ukraine is “no ongoing armed attack to repel = not legitimate self-defence under Article 51,” the same yardstick applied to the 2025 and 2026 US/Israeli strikes — against a nuclear program not yet weaponised, with no ongoing Iranian armed attack — leads to the same legal conclusion. The doctrine of “anticipatory self-defence” against a future threat is not settled international law. Killing a head of state and explicitly declaring a regime-change objective are, as a matter of principle, hard to distinguish from conduct the West condemns without hesitation when attributed to other actors. Editorial judgment What links this case to the previous one in the series is not a symmetry of blame — the facts and violations remain distinct — but the mechanism: a working deal, unilaterally broken by one of its own parties; a self-feeding escalation because each side reads the other’s move as an existential threat; and a diplomatic window (the Oman talks of February 2026) left to lapse shortly before armed force took its place. Thirteen years to topple a man the West had already given up on toppling

From the 2011 uprising to a proxy war, from the silent 2017 abandonment to the sudden collapse of December 2024: how a conflict can reopen not through new aggression, but simply because attention shifted elsewhere.

The context Few wars show as clearly how a conflict can drag on by sheer inertia even after all its main external backers have stopped believing in it. Syria from 2011 to 2024 is the textbook case. From uprising to proxy war (2011-2015) The 2011 Arab Spring protests against Bashar al-Assad turned into civil war after violent government repression. From 2013 the conflict rapidly internationalised: the CIA launched the secret Timber Sycamore program to arm “moderate” rebels — already covered in detail, including the failure of arms vetting and the documented links of some funded groups to jihadist networks, in The US armed the Syrian rebellion for five years . In 2015 Russia intervened directly on Assad’s side with its air force, while Iran and Hezbollah provided ground support — turning Syria into the decade’s principal proxy battleground. Stalemate and the silent abandonment (2017-2024) In 2017 the Trump administration shut down Timber Sycamore, in what a US official told the Washington Post was an explicit signal to Moscow — “ Putin won in Syria” — days before the first Trump-Putin meeting at the G20. From here the conflict entered a seven-year stalemate: Assad reclaimed territory with Russian-Iranian support, but without political normalisation, while the US and Europe stopped actively investing in regime change, settling for sanctions. The sudden fall (November-December 2024) On 27 November 2024, Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), led by Ahmed al-Sharaa, launched a surprise offensive in Aleppo province — a day after an Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire in Lebanon took effect, reducing available Iranian/Hezbollah military support for Assad. Aleppo, Syria’s second city, fell on 1 December; Hama on 5 December; Homs, the third city, on 7 December. On 28 November Assad personally flew to Moscow to request Russian military aid — the request was denied. He returned to Syria, lying to his own commanders that aid would arrive. On 8 December 2024 rebels entered Damascus meeting minimal resistance, as government forces abandoned their positions; Assad fled to Russia, where he was granted asylum. The end of thirteen years of civil war and fifty years of Assad family rule. The aftermath, still unstable (2025-2026) Al-Sharaa became interim president (January 2025); a transitional government was established in March 2025. Post-Assad Syria in 2026 is not a closed case: 15.6 million of Syria’s 23 million people need humanitarian assistance, and Turkey’s and Germany’s push for refugee returns continues despite UNHCR formally ruling out the possibility of safe return — already covered in detail in The UN says it isn’t safe to return to Syria . Symmetry test and escalation mechanism The Syrian case follows the same pattern as the other cases in this series, with one significant variant: here it is not a military miscalculation that produces the turning point, but the simultaneous exhaustion of resources of multiple external powers on other fronts — Russia tied down in Ukraine, Iran and Hezbollah weakened by confrontation with Israel — that creates the window for a sudden collapse. It’s a useful reminder for the other cases in this series: a frozen conflict is not a resolved conflict, and it can reopen not through new aggression, but simply because attention shifted elsewhere. Editorial judgment Russia’s refusal to help Assad — an ally on whom Moscow had spent years of direct military intervention — is perhaps the most telling fact in this case: it shows that no external support, however long-standing, is guaranteed once the costs elsewhere outweigh the strategic value of continuing to prop it up. From the 1990 verbal assurances to the 2014 Nuland-Pyatt call, from Putin's 2021 essay to the diplomatic window lost in Istanbul: how an escalation is built, step by step.

The context Wars rarely erupt from a single cause. The one between Russia and Ukraine, in its fifth year of full-scale fighting by 2026, has roots reaching thirty years before the first shot — a useful case for understanding how an escalation is built, often with neither side fully able to stop it in time. The roots (1990-2008) In 1990, during talks on German reunification, US Secretary of State James Baker told Gorbachev that NATO jurisdiction would not move “one inch eastward.” Declassified National Security Archive documents (2017) show similar assurances repeated by other Western leaders in the following months. Historians disagree on how narrowly these applied to Germany alone; they agree that **none was ever formalised in a treaty**. In 1997 the NATO-Russia Founding Act, with Russia’s signature, affirms every state’s right to choose its own alliances. Two rounds of enlargement follow (1999, 2004). In 2008 the Bucharest Summit declares that Ukraine and Georgia “will become members,” with no timeline — an ambiguity that would prove more destabilising than a clear yes or no. The interference never fully reckoned with (2014) In February 2014 a phone call between US Assistant Secretary of State Victoria Nuland and US Ambassador Geoffrey Pyatt was intercepted and posted online — the US never disputed its authenticity. Reported by the BBC, it shows Nuland openly discussing who should lead Ukraine’s future government: “I think Yats is the guy [...] Klitsch and Tyahnybok need to stay on the outside.” After Yanukovych fled, Yatsenyuk did become prime minister. Russia’s annexation of Crimea and the Donbas war followed. The Minsk agreements (2014-2015) remained largely unimplemented over an unresolved ambiguity about which condition should be met first. A 2022 admission by former Chancellor Angela Merkel — that the agreements also served to “give Ukraine time to get stronger” — fed Russian distrust, though it remains an ex-post political statement, not an independently verifiable fact. The ideological leap (2021) In July 2021 Putin published the essay “On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians,” later added to mandatory reading for the Russian military. It argues Russians and Ukrainians are “one people” and questions the legitimacy of Ukraine’s borders, calling Ukraine an “anti-Russia project.” From here on the problem is no longer only military security, but Ukrainian nationhood itself — something no technical deal on missile bases could resolve. December 2021 brought a formal Russian ultimatum, rejected by the West. The invasion and the miscalculation (2022) On 24 February 2022 Russia launched its full-scale invasion. Russian planners expected capitulation within days. Per Foreign Affairs (Charap and Radchenko, based on direct interviews with negotiators), Russia’s withdrawal from Kyiv in late March 2022 — presented by Moscow as a goodwill gesture — was in fact a forced retreat, after “the Russians had overestimated their capabilities and underestimated Ukrainian resistance.” The window that closed (Istanbul, April 2022) By mid-April 2022 Russia and Ukraine had reached a nearly complete draft treaty: Ukrainian neutrality in exchange for security guarantees from the five permanent UN Security Council members. A Ukrainian negotiator publicly stated “we were very close to ending the war.” Why the deal collapsed remains contested: Moscow blames British pressure (never independently confirmed); the prevailing Western account attributes it to Kyiv’s choice, emboldened on the battlefield and shaken by the Bucha revelations, to press on rather than accept painful concessions. The opposite effect The December 2021 ultimatum and the invasion produced the exact opposite of Moscow’s stated goal: not a NATO retreat, but Finland (2023) and Sweden (2024) joining, doubling the Alliance’s direct border with Russia. The symmetry test The legal and behavioural planes must be kept separate. Legally, the Russian invasion does not meet Article 51 requirements: there was no Ukrainian armed attack to repel, and this remains true regardless of what follows. Behaviourally, none of the three main actors comes out clean: the 2014 US interference, the Minsk ambiguity attributable to more than one party, Ukraine’s choice to fight on after Istanbul. None of this rebalances the legal plane. Editorial judgment The Russia-Ukraine case shows a pattern that will recur, with variations, in other conflicts: security dilemma, a narrative denying the other’s legitimacy, diplomacy left deliberately ambiguous, miscalculation, and at least one real diplomatic window left to lapse. Understanding this mechanism is not about distributing blame equally — the violation of international law remains a distinct fact — but about understanding why wars, once triggered, are so hard to close. The Full-Face Veil and the State: Imposition, Ban, Non-Intervention
In 2026 the same garment — the full-face veil — is legally imposed in Afghanistan and legally banned elsewhere: a comparison of four state models, with a symmetry test.

«The burqa is the best type of hijab, a symbol of the culture of the Afghan people.» — Decree of Taliban Supreme Leader Hibatullah Akhundzada, 7 May 2022 In the same year an activist wearing the full-face veil received a public honour at Westminster for her work with girls, elsewhere the same garment — the full-face veil, niqab or burqa — remains legally imposed in one country and legally banned in others. This is not a conflict between Islam and the West: it is a conflict, cutting across both worlds, over who has standing to regulate the appearance of the female body — and over what the law can actually establish when the same practice is described, depending on who is speaking, as choice or as coercion. Dated facts, with sources In Afghanistan, the 7 May 2022 decree of Taliban Supreme Leader Hibatullah Akhundzada makes the burqa mandatory in public, with penal responsibility falling on the woman's male “guardian” (father, brother, husband): a warning at the first violation, a summons before the authority at the second, three days’ detention at the third, referral to a court at the fourth. The decree encourages women to stay home when there is no essential need to go out. By 2026, enforcement appears to have intensified in Herat, where — according to the exiled Afghan newspaper Hasht-e Subh (June 2026) — a new local directive, invoking Akhundzada’s Decree No. 1930, orders the immediate arrest of women who fail to observe the prescribed dress code, with wearing perfume in the presence of men counted among the violations; non-compliant female civil servants are suspended from duty. In Tunisia, a 5 July 2019 order by Prime Minister Youssef Chahed banned the niqab in government buildings, after a double suicide bombing in Tunis on 27 June that same year (BBC, 5 July 2019) — an older case than initially assessed here, but still the most frequently cited precedent for the “public order” argument in the Arab world. In Egypt, the Ministry of Education banned the niqab in public and private schools on 11 September 2023, effective from the academic year starting 30 September, leaving the hijab optional (Middle East Eye, 12 September 2023). In Kuwait, as of March 2025 the sources diverge, and the divergence should be reported, not resolved: some outlets (Jordan News, Arab Times, 17–18 March 2025) reported the Ministry of Interior denying the existence of an active ban, calling it an old 1984 ministerial decision “no longer in force”; other outlets (Gulf News, Gulf Insider, same dates) reported the same Ministry announcing fines of 30–50 dinars for driving while wearing the niqab or burqa, as part of an updated traffic code, citing the same 1984 origin. No source consulted reconciles the two versions. The United Kingdom has never introduced a national ban on the niqab. On 24 July 2026, Khadija Patel — 39, from Bolton, founder in 2009 of the Krimmz Girls Youth Club — received the British Citizen Award 2026 at the Palace of Westminster, one of 28 recipients, for her work getting girls from under-represented backgrounds into sport. Patel wears the niqab and, after a wave of hostile comments triggered by the award photo, said her work “should be judged by my actions, not by what I am wearing,” calling the niqab a personal choice that “does not limit” her (statements reported by Metro/MSN and The Islamic Information, 26–27 July 2026). Symmetry test The control question is: does the assessment of each case hold if the identity of the acting state is swapped? The Taliban decree, which imposes the veil with indirect penal sanction, and the Tunisian and Egyptian bans, which prohibit it in specific public spaces, are — structurally — the same assertion of state sovereignty over the female body: the direction changes (obligation versus prohibition), the principle does not, since the state decides and the woman complies. The fact that Tunisia and Egypt are themselves Muslim-majority countries dismantles the binary civilisational reading: the same public-order argument invoked by France since 2010 (and upheld by the European Court of Human Rights in S.A.S. v. France, 2014, via the “living together” criterion) is used by Islamic states without being read, in that setting, as Islamophobia. The Kuwaiti case, with its conflicting sources, shows a third variant: a state that does not clearly decide whether the ban is active or merely historical — an ambiguity none of the other models share. British non-intervention, in turn, should not be read as weakness relative to a single Western standard — none exists: the continent is divided, France and Belgium ban it, the UK does not — but as a specific, time-consistent political choice. This does not settle, in Patel’s individual case, the question of whether wearing the niqab is autonomous choice or induced conformity: Patel herself describes it, in her own words, as a choice — a statement to be reported as such, not rewritten in either direction. Declared judgment None of the four models discussed here addresses the underlying doctrinal issue: the niqab/burqa is not a religious obligation for the majority of Sunni legal schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i), but it is for the Hanbali/Salafi current alone — a distinction treated at length in the linked in-depth piece. A state that bans the niqab for public order and a state that imposes it as Islamic law commit, in this writer’s judgment, the same category error: both treat a minority doctrinal practice as if it were an indisputable religious given — one to suppress it, the other to impose it. The only position fully consistent with individual religious freedom is the one that leaves the choice to the person. But even this principle must, in fairness, be limited: the law can only recognise a declared choice, not the pressure that may precede it. A statement like Khadija Patel’s — “it is a personal choice” — may be the exact truth, or it may be the only form that family or community pressure, if it existed, could take publicly: no instrument available today, legal or journalistic, reliably distinguishes the two possibilities when they produce the same statement and the same garment. This is not a normative gap that a better law could fill: it is the point at which the very category of “choice” ceases to be observable from the outside. How Europe could end up at war without choosing it
A declared foresight exercise, built on real incidents: drone incursions on NATO's eastern flank, British bases hit in Iran, and what diplomacy should do to contain the risk before it's too late.

— European Union / Russia / Iran Methodological premise This is not a news piece. It is a declared foresight exercise — what could happen, not what is happening — built on real, already-verified incidents, not pure speculation. Where forecast ends and fact begins is always explicitly flagged. What is already happening Between August 2024 and February 2026, per an International Institute for Strategic Studies report (July 2026), hundreds of drones flew over the airspace of a dozen NATO states plus Ireland — including bases tied to the Alliance’s nuclear deterrence, such as Ramstein in Germany. Poland invoked NATO Article 4 in September 2025 after 19 Russian drones entered its airspace. Romania suffered, in May 2026, a drone strike on a residential building in Galați, injuring two people — called by the Romanian president "the most serious security incident" since the war began. In Latvia, the defence minister and prime minister resigned in June 2026 after drones (likely Ukrainian, diverted by Russia) violated national airspace without timely public alerts. On the Iran front, during the February-April 2026 war, British bases in Bahrain, Qatar and Cyprus were directly hit by Iranian retaliation, with the RAF deployed defensively — direct European military involvement that has already happened, not a hypothesis. Scenarios — Russia The most likely is not a deliberate attack but the incident that spirals out of control: a drone — Russian or Ukrainian, its origin often ambiguous for days — hits a target with multiple casualties in a NATO country before warning systems work. With each subsequent incident, the threshold for a collective response (Article 5, not just Article 4) lowers through statistical accumulation, not a single political decision. Other, less likely but non-negligible scenarios: a formal judicial attribution of sabotage against undersea infrastructure (on the Nord Stream model, already covered elsewhere on this site); an air or naval engagement error between NATO and Russian fighters; a gradual escalation if European long-range weapons strike ever deeper into Russian territory, pushing Moscow to explicitly strike the supplying country’s own territory, not just Ukraine’s. Scenarios — Iran The precedent that has already occurred (British bases hit, RAF deployed) could repeat itself with a European power less resolute about staying "purely defensive." A disruption of merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz involving European vessels would turn an energy crisis into an incident requiring a direct naval response — a pattern already seen in the 1984-88 "Tanker War." More speculative, but not to be ruled out: an attack on European critical infrastructure attributed to Iranian proxies. What diplomacy should do — the Russia/NATO front The instrument that existed and is now missing is the Vienna Document on confidence- and security-building measures (OSCE, 1990-2011): annual military information exchanges, prior notification of exercises, mutual inspections among 57 states. Russia suspended it de facto from January 2022, formally from March 2022. This is the structural gap behind every drone incident: without prior notification or shared verification, any unidentified object remains ambiguous long enough to become dangerous. Concrete measures available: a bilateral technical deconfliction channel, separate from political channels, modelled on the 1972 US-USSR incidents-at-sea agreement or the US-Russia deconfliction line over Syria (2015-2024, which functioned even amid total political hostility); a rapid-attribution mechanism under OSCE auspices, which in 2026 has Switzerland holding the rotating chair; symmetrical pressure on Kyiv too, to limit long-range drone launches near NATO borders. None of these technical measures, however, replaces a negotiation on the underlying conflict: it reduces the frequency of incidents, not eliminates them. What diplomacy should do — the Iran/Europe front EMASoH (European Maritime Awareness in the Strait of Hormuz), a French-led mission launched in 2020 based in Abu Dhabi — a diplomatic track plus a military one (Operation Agenor), 9 European countries — already exists, explicitly designed for de-escalation through joint diplomatic and military presence. Recent sources (March 2026) describe it, however, as under growing pressure relative to its original mandate. Concrete measures: strengthening EMASoH’s diplomatic track, today less visible than the military one but specifically designed for regional dialogue; reinstating the E3 (France, Germany, UK) as a recognised negotiating channel on the nuclear file, not merely an observer of the US-Iran bilateral track; explicit European non-belligerence messaging, to formally distinguish the EU’s position from that of the US/Israel. Here too, the underlying limit remains the same: no European naval or diplomatic measure resolves the root cause, which is the 2018 collapse of the JCPOA. Editorial judgment On neither front does Europe today have the tools it had before 2022, or the ones it was conceived with in 2020. The most honest question is not "what should diplomacy do" in the abstract, but whether Europe is investing to rebuild dismantled channels or merely managing symptoms with tools undersized for the current scale of risk — the latter appears to be the reading most consistent with the facts gathered. Three ways to erase a woman: law, body, death

Institutional submission, genital cutting, femicide are not three separate problems: they are three stages of the same mechanism. An in-depth look with the most current data on Afghanistan, female genital mutilation, and femicide worldwide.

Institutional submission, genital cutting, femicide: not three separate problems, but three stages of the same mechanism. There is no "opposing view" to balance here. This is not a controversial opinion to be weighed against its contrary: subjugating a woman by law, cutting her body to keep her in her place, killing her when even that isn't enough — is wrong. Full stop. This site always applies the symmetry test when judging geopolitical actors by the same standard; here there are no "two sides" to balance, because the phenomenon described has no legitimate counter-argument, only different perpetrators. Three stages of the same mechanism: the law establishes that a woman belongs to someone else; the body is made to conform to that belonging; death arrives when she stops conforming. International law has a name for each stage. We set them side by side, with the most current data available, without softening. 1. Institutional submission Afghanistan under the Taliban is today the most complete and best-documented case in the world. Since 2021 the regime has issued, according to the most recent count (June 2026), 264 decrees on human rights — 166 specifically targeting women . These are not isolated prohibitions: it is an integrated legal architecture designed to erase women from public life. Since September 2025, security forces have even prevented female UN staff from entering United Nations premises in the country. In May 2026 the "Code on Judicial Separation of Spouses" came into force, further limiting women's right to divorce and effectively enabling child marriage; that same month, Decree No. 18 established that a girl's silence upon reaching puberty can be interpreted as consent to marriage — silence, not consent, becomes the legal proof. The new criminal procedure framework (January 2026) explicitly legitimizes spousal beatings. This site has already reported, in Afghanistan: the International Criminal Court charges the Taliban leadership with gender persecution , the ICC arrest warrants (January 2025) against Supreme Leader Akhundzada and Chief Justice Haqqani — the first time the Court has prosecuted gender persecution on this scale. Since then, a symbolic tribunal convened by civil society (December 2025) has classified Taliban policies as gender apartheid , a category eleven states are now pushing to codify in the UN treaty on crimes against humanity. The fact that a new legal category must be invented to name what is happening to Afghan women is itself an admission: existing law wasn't enough to stop it. 2. Genital cutting Over 230 million girls and women alive today have undergone female genital mutilation (UNICEF) — 144 million in Africa, 80 million in Asia, 6 million in the Middle East, practiced in 94 countries across every continent. The UN's goal of eliminating it by 2030 would require a pace of reduction 27 times faster than the current one. UNFPA estimates 4.5 million girls at risk in 2026 alone . This is not a fading legacy: in absolute terms it is a practice growing alongside the population of the countries where it is most common. It must be said with the same honesty applied to everything else here: in 2025 Guinea and Djibouti explicitly banned the practice in their new constitutions. Progress exists, when there is the political will to make it exist. The problem is not that it's impossible to stop — it's that in most of the countries involved, it isn't being stopped fast enough. 3. Femicide In 2024, 83,000 women and girls were intentionally killed worldwide (UNODC/UN Women, November 2025). Of these, 50,000 — 60% — at the hands of a partner or family member: one every 10 minutes, 137 a day . Among men killed, only 11% die at the hands of a partner or family member — the difference is not statistical, it is structural. In 25% of documented cases, the victim had already reported the abuse to police before being killed. Reporting did not save her. Africa has the highest rate (3 victims per 100,000 women), followed by the Americas, Oceania, Asia, Europe — but no region is exempt. And fewer and fewer countries collect data on the phenomenon: the absence of the statistic is not a technical detail, it is a way of not having to answer for what isn't measured. Closing There is a way to make all of this, suddenly, extremely simple to condemn without exception: stop writing laws thinking of "men" and "women," and write them thinking only of individuals — exactly as, in theory, Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights has done since 1948. If a legal order treated every person as an individual and nothing more, institutional submission, genital cutting, femicide would already all be forbidden, with no need to write a single additional convention. The fact that they had to be written — CEDAW , Maputo , Belém do Pará , the DEVAW , and now perhaps a treaty specifically for "gender apartheid" — is the best proof that this principle, nearly eighty years after it was written, is still not real for half the world's population. This is not a "women's" issue. It is the measure of how much, everywhere, a legal order truly considers people to hold rights regardless of who they are — or only conditional on it.
